articles.title: How old would you guess Stephen Curry is based on watching him now? Warriors coach Steve Kerr’s response says it all
articles.summary: Golden State Warriors superstar Stephen Curry continues to make his age look irrelevant. The 38-year-old guard has maintained a remarkable scoring pace, leaving head coach Steve Kerr searching for words to describe his longevity. Following Golden State’s overtime victory against the Orlando
articles._body: Golden State Warriors superstar Stephen Curry continues to make his age look irrelevant. The 38-year-old guard has maintained a remarkable scoring pace , leaving head coach Steve Kerr searching for words to describe his longevity. Following Golden State’s overtime victory against the Orlando Magic, a reporter asked Kerr to guess Curry’s age based solely on his performances. Kerr delivered a hilarious response when asked how old Curry looked on the court. “I don’t know. 30? 29? He’s something,” Kerr said, drawing laughter with his assessment of the veteran superstar. The exchange came after Curry scored 41 points in Golden State’s 126-119 overtime victory over Orlando. He also contributed six rebounds and six assists while shooting 13-of-19 from the field. Curry knocked down five three-pointers and converted all 10 of his free throws. His performance offered another reminder of his ability to dominate despite approaching his 39th birthday. The Head Coach also praised Curry’s late-game heroics, emphasizing his ability to deliver extraordinary shots under pressure. “He’s one of one… I don’t know if anyone else in the world can make that shot,” Kerr said. The two-time MVP has consistently challenged expectations about how long elite guards can maintain their production. His shooting range, conditioning, and movement continue to create problems for opposing defenses. Earlier this season, Curry also delivered a perfect shooting performance against the Denver Nuggets. He finished that contest with 24 points without missing a field goal or free throw. Kerr has witnessed Curry’s greatness throughout their championship partnership. However, the coach’s latest reaction suggests even he remains amazed by his star’s longevity. For Warriors fans, Curry’s continued excellence provides plenty of encouragement. Golden State still relies heavily on its franchise cornerstone, whose performances show little to no indication of slowing down. articles.summary: Bleak research warns not even a lifetime of savings would be enough to lift workers out of the middle class into the top 10%.
articles._body: The exact number of years of saving it would take for the average worker to claw out of the middle-class bracket has been revealed—and it’s nearly half a century. Sobering research released in October 2025 from the think tank Resolution Foundation shows that for aspirational Brits looking to move up the wealth ladder, the average worker would need to save their earnings for 52 years to raise £1.3 million ($1.7 million). That’s the amount needed to move from the middle and become as wealthy as the richest 10%. And it gets worse: That’s with zero bills being paid. “Wealth gaps in Britain are now so large that a typical full-time employee saving all their earnings across their entire working life would still not be able to reach the top of the wealth ladder,” wrote Molly Broome, formerly a senior economist at the Resolution Foundation and the lead author of the report. And for those who happen to be born in the working class, the odds are increasingly stacked against them.  “ Wealth mobility in Britain is low. People that start life wealthy tend to stay wealthy, and vice versa,” Broome added. As the saying goes, money makes money. The report revealed the key driver of widening inequality is the “passive” gains. Essentially, those who bought property and invested their money have seen their wealth balloon since 2010. Workers in the U.S. would need to save for 70 years to unlock the American Dream  As inflation squeezes workers in a cost-of-living vise, paired with a job crisis , and AI threatening to make it even worse , the salary it takes to be considered rich keeps climbing further out of reach. And the issue is transatlantic. Even in the U.S., workers say they’d need at least $2.3 million to feel rich. Meanwhile, separate research highlights they’d need a staggering $4.4 million to achieve the American Dream—the house in the suburbs, two children, an annual vacation, and a new car in the driveway. Achieving those milestones would cost over $1 million more than most Americans will make in their lifetime, according to an Investopedia calculation. With median weekly earnings of full-time workers averaging $1,232, according to the Bureau of Labor Statistics , it would take over 35 years of full-time work to feel rich with $2.3 million in the bank. That’s before a single bill is paid, and still $2.1 million short of affording the American Dream. It would take the average American worker nearly 70 years without a single expense being paid to reach that $4.4 million benchmark—far longer than most people will work in a lifetime. And that’s without even considering inflation, any unexpected financial shocks, or automation’s impact on the future of work. Warren Buffett says ‘accumulating great amounts of money’ doesn’t achieve greatness—He still lives in a $31,500 Nebraska home and clipped coupons
articles.summary: Berkshire Hathaway mogul Buffett, worth $163 billion, said kindness is more golden than big bank accounts. He still eats at McDonald’s, and said luxury purchases wouldn’t make him happier.
articles._body: Many entrepreneurs strive to one day add “millionaire ,” or even “billionaire ,” to their list of achievements: It’s a sign that they’ve finally made it in business. But billionaire investing mogul Warren Buffett hit back at the notion that eye-watering net worths equate to excellence. “Greatness does not come about through accumulating great amounts of money, great amounts of publicity or great power in government,” Buffett wrote in his final Berkshire Hathaway shareholder letter last November.  The 96-year-old “ Oracle of Ohama,” known as one of the most successful investors of all time, is the 10th richest person in the world, boasting a fortune of $163 billion. But that doesn’t mean he’s splurging on mansions and driving luxury cars off the lot. He’s been thrifty throughout his seven-decade professional career, despite adding billions to his name. Known for eating at McDonald’s, driving a beat-up old car, and living in his modest Nebraska home, it’s clear his bank account hasn’t changed his ways. Instead of feeling powerful by lavishing in the spoils of his riches, Buffett finds true value and greatness in non-material pursuits.  “When you help someone in any of thousands of ways, you help the world,” Buffett continued. “Kindness is costless but also priceless. Whether you are religious or not, it’s hard to beat The Golden Rule as a guide to behavior…Keep in mind that the cleaning lady is as much a human being as the Chairman.” Buffett’s thrifty lifestyle: clipping McDonald’s coupons and living in a $31,500 house Buffett’s golden rule is that everyone should be treated with kindness and respect, no matter if they’ve built a unicorn company, or are a junior-level worker. And he has treated the world’s most powerful business leaders the same way, unwilling to shell out on fancy meals to impress them.  The Berkshire Hathaway icon is known for stopping by McDonald’s for a cheap eat, choosing to order two sausage patties, an egg and cheese, or a bacon egg and cheese—all less than $4. He loves the fast-food chain so much he even took Bill Gates there for lunch years ago, instead of wining and dining him at a swanky restaurant. One time, the entrepreneurial pair were at a McDonald’s in Hong Kong, and Gates recalled laughing when Buffett offered to foot the measly bill, pulling coupons out of his pocket. But for the hedge-fund mogul, every penny counts. The same money philosophy applies to Buffett’s major life purchases. The former CEO still lives in the same five bedroom, two-and-a-half bathroom Omaha home he bought for $31,500 back in 1958. The house would be worth around $1.4 million today —far more affordable than the luxurious pads Buffett can afford— yet he said he “wouldn’t trade it for anything.” Buffett’s true fondness for the home lies in the memories of raising his three kids on the property, not its market value. Uber-rich people boasting net worths like Buffett may also be tempted to ball out on indulgences like expensive cars. But the investing magnate isn’t interested in getting behind the wheel of a Lamborghini or Aston Martin; he once drove a 20-year-old car because he felt it was safer than driving a speedy luxury alternative. And at one point, his license plate even read as “THRIFTY.”  Whether it be mansions or sports cars, Buffett steers clear of making major purchases that reflect his bank account. In fact, he feels giving in could be counterproductive to his happiness.  “I do not think that standard of living equates with cost of living beyond a certain point,” Buffett said at a Berkshire Hathaway shareholders meeting in 2014. “My life would not be happier…it’d be worse if I had six or eight houses or a whole bunch of different things I could have. It just doesn’t correlate.” A version of this story was published on Fortune.com on November 12, 2025. This story was originally featured on Fortune.com

articles.title: Jamie Dimon says the bigger your job gets, ‘the less you know—literally.’ The CEOs too insecure to admit it are the ones who get into trouble
articles.summary: The JPMorgan CEO says leaders get into trouble when their insecurity discourages employees from delivering bad news.
articles._body: Jamie Dimon , one of the banking industry’s longest-serving CEOs, has thoughts on why some CEOs rise to the occasion while others flounder—and it has little to do with how much they know about business. Dimon, who has served as CEO of JPMorgan Chase , the largest U.S. bank by market cap, for more than 20 years, said on the Master Investor Podcast earlier this year, that more than anything, insecurity is one of the biggest threats to a CEO’s career and their company’s success. As Dimon puts it, when executives climb the corporate ladder, they often go from being an expert overseeing one area of the business they know well to a generalist responsible for other areas of the company they know less well.  “The bigger job you get, the less you know—literally—about the job,” he told the podcast’s host, Wilfred Frost. Some CEOs handle that transition well, he said. They seek out people with expertise in areas they lack and don’t get embarrassed when they don’t know something. But for others, this change is a recipe for insecurity.  “It becomes PowerPoints, you know, make them look good, don’t tell them the bad news. And that is what causes the problem,” he said. Dimon said this type of insecurity, more than arrogance, speaks to a deeper weakness in leadership that causes other issues. A CEO needs to be able to absorb criticism and turn it into a plan for improvement, especially when it comes to customer complaints, he said.  “You’re not going to hurt my feelings by telling me we have a crappy product,” he said. “If you’re right, I’m gonna thank you for letting me know.”  In fact, Dimon said in an October interview with the Wall Street Journal executives should take a note from the leadership style of Ted Lasso, the relentlessly positive protagonist of the Apple TV series of the same name. Lasso, he said strikes a great balance between two leadership traits he said are needed in upper management, both a drive to win as well as empathy and humility. “I love Ted Lasso,” Dimon said. “He comes in and he doesn’t know anything about football, and he’s just gracious. He’s working with people—their insecurities, their bad behavior, their work ethic—and he’s getting them to function as a team.” Dimon’s record gives his leadership advice added weight. During his tenure, he has turned JPMorgan into a $894 billion banking giant. His “ fortress balance sheet ” strategy, which emphasizes high liquidity and conservative risk management, was key to helping the bank survive the 2008 recession. Dimon has also helped grow the bank over the past two decades by acquiring competitors in turmoil, such as Bear Stearns in 2008 and, more recently, First Republic Bank in 2023 .  His latest comments on insecurity are also consistent with his previous warnings that “bureaucracy, complacency, and arrogance,” can take down otherwise successful companies .  In April, Dimon said the best way to tackle these problems is to “get rid of the jerks,” or bureaucratic managers who care more about the process than the outcome. Holding back information, as might happen with an insecure CEO, breeds “ rope-a-dope politics ,” a reference to Muhammad Ali’s evasive defense strategy, which he has also said creates unnecessary debate and hinders results. Dimon’s philosophy aligns with that of other successful current and former CEOs. Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella previously told Fortune he encouraged his employees to maintain a growth mindset rather than be content and complacent. Nadella also tried to shift the company from a “know-it-all” culture to a “learn-it-all” culture where employees are encouraged to approach problems with curiosity. Ray Dalio, the founder and former CEO of Bridgwater Associates, also pushed for “ radical transparency ” during his tenure, encouraging employees to challenge one another openly and confront mistakes without defensiveness. The JPMorgan CEO, who also serves as chairman of the board, practices what he preaches. For the past 20 years, he has stepped out of every board meeting to give board members time to discuss without the pressure of his “ forceful ” personality, he said. He has previously said leaders like himself must earn the trust of their employees every day. Part of doing that, he argued, is being willing to admit mistakes without taking criticism personally. “I’m not trying to do the thing that I want to do, I want to do the right thing for the company,” he said Monday. A version of this story was published on Fortune.com on July 21, 2026. This story was originally featured on Fortune.com

Show HN: Nino – Fastest C# serializer, safe on untrusted input, also TS/Go/Rust
articles.summary: Nino is a source-generated binary serializer for C#, and as far as we know the fastest one. In the same BenchmarkDotNet run on GitHub runners against MemoryPack 1.21.4, it serializes classes and polymorphic types 3.5–7.2x faster and deserializes them 1.7–2.1x faster (arrays of unmanaged structs a
articles._body: Nino is a source-generated binary serializer for C#, and as far as we know the fastest one. In the same BenchmarkDotNet run on GitHub runners against MemoryPack 1.21.4, it serializes classes and polymorphic types 3.5–7.2x faster and deserializes them 1.7–2.1x faster (arrays of unmanaged structs are on par). Deserializing into existing objects allocates nothing. Reproduce: https://nino.xgamedev.net/en/docs/v4/benchmarks It is built to read bytes you do not trust: lengths are checked before allocating, depth is bounded, hash flooding is limited, and the read paths are fuzzed in CI. The bytes are a spec, not a memory dump, so CoreCLR, Mono, IL2CPP and 32-bit hosts write the same bytes, and runtimes for TypeScript, Go and Rust pass the same conformance corpus. Trade-offs: positional by default (VersionTolerant or Keyed for stored data), a 4-byte type id on polymorphic values, no System.Type, needs C# 9 and Roslyn 4.3+. articles.title: Saints using Shedeur Sanders’ smiling video as bulletin board material
articles.summary: Shedeur Sanders may have thought his smile was harmless. However, the New Orleans Saints are apparently taking it as extra motivation ahead of their Week 9 matchup against the Cleveland Browns. According to ESPN’s Jeremy Fowler, head coach Kellen Moore highlighted a viral clip of Sanders du
articles._body: Shedeur Sanders may have thought his smile was harmless. However, the New Orleans Saints are apparently taking it as extra motivation ahead of their Week 9 matchup against the Cleveland Browns. According to ESPN’s Jeremy Fowler, head coach Kellen Moore highlighted a viral clip of Sanders during a team meeting. That gave New Orleans’ defense some unexpected bulletin board material as it prepares to welcome Cleveland to the Caesars Superdome. The video showed Sanders being asked whether he had studied the Saints’ defense. Rather than offering a conventional scouting breakdown, the Browns quarterback responded with a knowing grin and an intriguing explanation. “Yeah I seen a lot, when I smile just know that means something,” Sanders said. “I’m maturing, you know what I’m saying, I’m maturing, I could have gave that a decent answer but now I’m just gonna smile when it’s some questions.” Sanders may simply have been having fun with reporters. The clip, though, reportedly generated plenty of discussion inside New Orleans’ facility. Veteran defenders such as Cameron Jordan and Carl Granderson will have an opportunity to respond on the field Sunday. The Saints enter Week 9 at 2-5. They are desperate to reverse a disappointing season. Their 2026 campaign has featured inconsistent offensive production, defensive struggles, and an alarming 0-3 record at home. Injuries, including the loss of running back Travis Etienne Jr., have further complicated Moore’s first season in charge. Coming off their Week 8 bye, New Orleans has also made coaching and personnel adjustments. Facing the Browns now present an opportunity to reset their season. Whether Sanders intended to motivate his opponents or not, his smile has certainly gotten their attention. The Saints will have their chance to make their response count on Sunday. articles._body: I saw a colleague log in to a website on my laptop by scanning a FIDO QR code. I wanted to do the same, but couldn't find a way to use the passkeys stored in Bitwarden on my phone to log in. So I asked Claude to build me an app. Claude found the task too daunting and only wanted to create a skeleton app. I was surprised by how complex the system actually is. Part of the process involves the phone sending an encrypted Bluetooth message as proof of presence, along with instructions on how to proceed. With the help of DeepSeek's free chat, I eventually managed to create a working implementation, after chasing quite a few hallucinations and dead ends... Claude then polished the app for me. The repository includes a full specification with test vectors, and the website has a nice, accessible explanation of how the process works. articles.title: Who will be Eagles QB Joe Milton’s backup vs. Giants as Tanner McKee battles cracked rib?
articles.summary: The Philadelphia Eagles have settled on Tanner McKee as Joe Milton’s backup quarterback for Sunday’s Week 9 matchup versus the New York Giants, despite the former starter dealing with a cracked rib, according to NFL Network insider Ian Rapoport. McKee is listed as questionable after s
articles._body: The Philadelphia Eagles have settled on Tanner McKee as Joe Milton’s backup quarterback for Sunday’s Week 9 matchup versus the New York Giants , despite the former starter dealing with a cracked rib , according to NFL Network insider Ian Rapoport. McKee is listed as questionable after sustaining the injury on the opening drive of Philadelphia’s 27-10 loss to the Washington Commanders last week. Although the 26-year-old managed to finish that contest, completing 23 of 34 passes for 212 yards with one interception and a lost fumble, his availability for Sunday’s game remained uncertain. He participated fully in Wednesday’s practice but was limited during Thursday and Friday’s sessions because of the injury. McKee’s move to the backup role comes after the Eagles decided to start Milton following three consecutive losses with the Stanford product under center. McKee went 0-3 after replacing quarterback Jalen Hurts, throwing for 638 yards and two touchdowns against two interceptions on 72-of-114 passing. Philadelphia managed just 45 points across those three defeats, contributing to a six-game losing streak that has dropped them to 2-6 and last place in the NFC East. Head coach Nick Sirianni initially backed McKee as the starter on Monday, but the decision changed two days later. Milton, whom Philadelphia acquired from the Dallas Cowboys’ practice squad on October 16, will now get the opportunity to lead the offense. The former sixth-round selection has recorded 424 passing yards, two touchdowns and two interceptions across five career appearances. He has not started an NFL game, but Sirianni pointed to his arm strength and athletic ability when explaining the change. Rookie Cole Payton, a fifth-round selection from North Dakota State, is the only other quarterback on the Eagles roster. McKee’s expected availability therefore gives Philadelphia another experienced option behind Milton. The Eagles will host the 4-2-1 Giants at Lincoln Financial Field, with kickoff scheduled for 1 p.m. ET on FOX. articles._body: The Seattle Seahawks could face another week without Sam Darnold as the quarterback continues dealing with multiple injuries. Seattle previously received concerning news about Darnold’s recovery, and his latest setback has created uncertainty ahead of Week 10. Darnold will miss Sunday’s matchup against the Arizona Cardinals because of a quadriceps injury. However, his absence could extend into Seattle’s upcoming game against the Las Vegas Raiders. According to ESPN’s Adam Schefter, Darnold is also in danger of missing Week 10. The veteran quarterback is dealing with an injured quadriceps and fractured ribs following Monday’s loss to the Chicago Bears. The combination of injuries complicates his recovery and raises questions about when Seattle can safely bring him back. Head coach Mike Macdonald previously described Darnold’s status as week-to-week. The Seahawks have not placed him on injured reserve, leaving open the possibility of a return. Seattle also has a Week 11 bye, which could influence its approach. Resting Darnold against Las Vegas would give him additional time to recover before the season’s final stretch. Meanwhile, Drew Lock will handle starting duties during Darnold’s absence. The backup quarterback has already gained experience leading Seattle’s offense this season. The Seahawks previously turned to Lock after Darnold suffered a hip injury during their season opener against New England. Seattle must now balance its immediate need for wins against Darnold’s long-term health. With multiple injuries affecting its starting quarterback, the team faces another difficult decision before Week 10. Seattle’s medical staff will continue evaluating his progress before determining whether he can resume full practice activities. articles._body: Atlanta Falcons linebacker James Pearce Jr. is eligible to play once again in Week 9 after serving out an eight-game suspension. However, his availability against the Cincinnati Bengals in the Madrid Game was in doubt due to a back injury. But as NFL insider Ian Rapoport pointed out on X, formerly Twitter, while quote tweeting the Falcons’ Week 9 inactives, Pearce is officially active against the Bengals despite dealing with back tightness. Pearce was the Falcons’ first-round pick last year. He played all 17 games in his rookie season, picking up 26 total tackles and 10.5 sacks. However, he was handed an eight-game suspension by the NFL after he was arrested on domestic violence charges in February. With Pearce absent, Za’Darius Smith has been the Falcons’ primary pass rusher this season. He leads the team with 4.5 sacks. Pearce’s return will give the Falcons another much-needed pass rusher against the Bengals’ prolific pass offense led by Joe Burrow. The Bengals are riding a three-game winning streak, with Burrow in unbelievable form. He’s completed well over 70% of his passes with at least four touchdowns passes in each of his last three games. He set new season-highs with 79% completion, 462 yards, five touchdowns, and three interceptions in last week’s 43-36 overtime win over the Tennessee Titans. As for the Falcons, they are looking to bounce back after losing three of their last four games. The Falcons defense didn’t give up a single completed pass but still lost 16-0 to the Tampa Bay Buccaneers after surrendering 324 yards on the ground amid poor weather conditions. articles.title: I told women to stop chasing balance. Now I’m telling them to ask for help
articles.summary: The mental load is measurably hurting women’s health.
articles._body: I welcomed my fourth baby on June 29, 2026, six days after writing this. These words capture the week before, when I was 38 weeks pregnant, and the question that kept me awake still feels urgent now. It was 11 p.m. I was 38 weeks pregnant with my fourth child, and instead of sleeping I was lying in the dark, silently running the list. Camp forms. The pediatrician follow-up. The board deck due to review. Who’s covering carpool the week I deliver? My body was begging me to rest, and my brain wouldn’t let it. By every external measure, I was doing it all. But lately, I could feel myself disappearing. Four years ago, I wrote an article urging women to stop asking about work-life balance. My advice? You can never be truly balanced. The goal is to live unbalanced, to teeter back and forth, but with conviction about which way you’re leaning. I was pregnant with my third child then, a hustling venture capitalist. Today, I am a mother of four, a growing portfolio behind me, and over three-quarters of a billion dollars raised to deploy into healthcare companies. Now I find myself reflecting on the advice I gave back then. The question I keep asking: did we perfect the art of teetering so well that we forgot to live? Four kids and a full career later, the list of to-dos is endless. Check one off, move on to the next. Whack-a-mole to the extreme. Focus on optimization. Prioritize. BE EFFICIENT. Get the to-do list done. Don’t worry if I’m the sacrifice. The mental load has changed from our parents’ generation. Gone are the days when kids ran free until dinner. Unencumbered freedom has been exchanged for meticulous planning. Our kids are overscheduled, and we bear the brunt. And it’s not just the kids. It’s our jobs. The expectation of how much to produce, how high to climb. “How does she do it all?” And the work never clocks out anymore. Hybrid and remote have blurred the line between the office and the kitchen table until there was no line at all. Now AI promises to make us faster, which somehow just means we’re expected to produce more, around the clock, forever. But is this having it all? Countless working moms tell me stories of their day, collapsing into bed with just barely enough energy to make it to the following day. We figured out how to live in the unbalance yet it appears we teetered too much, too quickly, and we started losing ourselves in the process. The trad wife movement has gained steam in part for this reason, a desire for simplicity. It’s not really about sourdough and aprons; it’s a referendum on a deal that stopped working. When “do it all” leaves you this depleted, opting out entirely starts to look like the only way to breathe. My work as an investor in healthcare companies serving women makes it impossible to ignore: the mental load is exhausting, and it’s measurably hurting women’s health. Without our health, we have nothing, and women are paying for it. Mothers carry 71% of the household’s mental load , the invisible work of remembering, planning, anticipating, despite the fact that fathers are more involved than at any point in modern history. They’ve nearly tripled their childcare hours since the 1960s, yet it still isn’t enough. And that load has a body count. There’s a name for what chronic stress does to a body: allostatic load, the cumulative wear and tear of a stress response that never fully switches off. It’s not a metaphor. It shows up as inflammation, hypertension, and disease, and it’s quietly accruing in women who are praised for how much they can carry. Women spend 25% more of their lives in poor health than men , roughly nine years each. Nearly half of working women say their job has damaged their mental health in just the past six months. This isn’t fatigue. It’s a deterioration we’ve normalized. The system that’s supposed to support us isn’t built to. Less than 9% of NIH research dollars over the last decade went to women’s health. Humans were supposed to be raised in tribes, in community, yet somehow today we are expected to accomplish more than we ever have, in isolation. Please your spouse, take care of your kids, crush it at work, don’t ask for help. In fact, don’t even tell anyone you have help. A friend of mine was on a panel and was asked how she had four kids. She replied honestly, “I have two nannies and lots of help.” Later she was scolded by the conference organizers, “shhh don’t tell the truth! We don’t want to scare people.” But isn’t asking for help one of the most important things we can do for ourselves and each other? Somehow, we have lost the ability to be honest and say “I can’t do this alone. I need you.” I felt that loss too. The optimization of my life was consuming me to the point I lost the greatest gift of all: time. So, I sought out help. First in small, confined ways, and later, more outwardly. It’s still incredibly difficult. I’m a high-performing woman with local family and resources to pay for help; shouldn’t I be able to do it all? In the pandemic, I found myself on a text chain with four other women. Half of us had never met in person. Six years later, we’ve texted every single day since, and I consider them some of my closest confidants. You want to know what we named our chat? The Womb of Silence. It’s where one of us admits she’s drowning before a board meeting. Where someone asks, with no shame, if anyone has a pediatrician they trust, a therapist taking new patients, a name for the thing they’re feeling or ailment they’re experiencing. Where “I can’t do this alone” is the price of entry, not a confession. Nothing you say there gets you exposed. Nothing gets you judged. You can always ask for help, and someone always answers. I’ve since replicated this feeling with other groups, my Core of Core and Bad Ass VC Mamas, to name a few. That chat taught me something the rest of my life kept trying to unteach me: asking isn’t the moment you fail. It’s the moment you actually start living and thriving. Little by little, I am tryi

articles.title: The gist of Lamar Jackson’s message to Ravens immediately after devastating hand injury
articles.summary: Lamar Jackson is not ready to let the Baltimore Ravens’ season slip away. That’s even if he cannot currently lead them on the field. After fracturing and dislocating his right thumb in Baltimore’s Week 8 loss to the Buffalo Bills, the two-time MVP delivered an encouraging messag
articles._body: Lamar Jackson is not ready to let the Baltimore Ravens’ season slip away. That’s even if he cannot currently lead them on the field. After fracturing and dislocating his right thumb in Baltimore’s Week 8 loss to the Buffalo Bills, the two-time MVP delivered an encouraging message to his teammates. “Just stay alive,” Jackson said. According to NFL Network’s Ian Rapoport, Jackson remains determined to return before the 2026 season ends. That should give a struggling locker room a reason to keep fighting. Jackson’s message reportedly energized teammates who feared the devastating injury could sideline their franchise quarterback for the remainder of the campaign. The thumb injury required surgery and landed him on Injured Reserve. There is an estimated recovery timeline of six to nine weeks. A late-season return remains possible. However, his availability will ultimately depend on his rehabilitation and medical clearance. The setback capped an agonizing stretch for Jackson. His 2026 campaign has been interrupted by consecutive injuries . He initially missed time after suffering a Grade 1 high ankle sprain in Baltimore’s Week 4 victory over Tennessee. His return against Buffalo was supposed to stabilize the offense. The thumb injury, though, quickly ended that comeback attempt. Jackson had helped the Ravens open the season 3-1 with several impressive performances. Those included a 324-yard passing display against Indianapolis. Now, Baltimore sits at 4-5 following its fourth consecutive loss. That included Thursday night’s 33-10 defeat to Jacksonville. Backup options have also been complicated by Tyler Huntley’s injury. That makes Jackson’s eventual return even more important. His message is simple but carries enormous weight. Baltimore must remain competitive long enough to give its leader a chance to return and potentially rescue its playoff hopes. articles.title: Is Deshaun Watson playing vs. Saints after clearing concussion protocol?
articles.summary: The Cleveland Browns were dealt a surprising quarterback injury this week. Deshaun Watson suddenly entered concussion protocol on Tuesday, which put his ability to play in Week 9 into question. Will he be able to convince the Browns that he is healthy enough to play on Sunday? Watson has already
articles._body: The Cleveland Browns were dealt a surprising quarterback injury this week. Deshaun Watson suddenly entered concussion protocol on Tuesday, which put his ability to play in Week 9 into question. Will he be able to convince the Browns that he is healthy enough to play on Sunday? Watson has already cleared concussion protocol but will not play in Week 9, per NFL insider Ian Rapoport. He only practiced one time and will instead cede starting reps to Shedeur Sanders . Cleveland will have Dillon Gabriel serve as the backup quarterback behind Sanders, per ESPN’s Jeremy Fowler. The Browns do expect Watson to resume starting duties in Week 10 against the Texans. Watson apparently suffered his concussion when taking a helmet-to-helmet hit in the first quarter in Week 8. He was pulled from the game, checked for a concussion and cleared to return. The Browns also had their medical staff check in with Watson on Monday, but he did not have symptoms then either. However, Watson told Cleveland’s medical team on Tuesday morning that he began experiencing concussion symptoms on Monday night. He was then immediately placed on concussion protocol. On one hand, it is great to hear that Watson has already cleared concussion protocol. That suggests his injury was not that severe considering he cleared the protocol in less than a week. That said, missing Watson for even one game could contribute to the Browns falling behind in the AFC North division race. Cleveland is 5-3 after getting smacked around by Pittsburgh in Week 8. They are still very much alive in the division race, but they need to start stacking wins again soon. There’s no better time to start than in Week 9, especially when going up against a young quarterback in Tyler Shough. Browns at Saints kicks off at 1 p.m. ET from Caesars Superdome in New Orleans. The latest status symbol of the 1% is a third kid. ‘It has become rarer for everyone else,’ says an economist
articles.summary: 49% of top-1% earners have three or more kids, vs. about 40% of the rest of the top 10%, economist Mike Konczal found in Federal Reserve data.
articles._body: For decades, the markers of extreme wealth were easy to spot: the second home, the fancy cars, the Ivy League education. New analysis of Federal Reserve data points to a subtler one: a third child. Mike Konczal, vice president of policy and research at the Economic Security Project and a former White House economist, studied households headed by 45- to 64-year-olds in his analysis of the Fed’s Survey of Consumer Finances , pooling five surveys from 2013 through 2025. He found that 49% of top-1% earners have three or more children, compared with about 40% of the rest of the top 10%. Families with four or more kids are about as common in both groups, so the gap comes down to the third child: 34% of the 1% stop at exactly three, versus 24% of the merely affluent. What changed isn’t the rich. Since the 1990s, families with three or more kids have become less common overall and among the rest of the top 10%, while the 1%’s share barely moved. “What’s new is that it has become rarer for everyone else,” Konczal writes. Big families thin out in the upper middle class. Rank families by wealth instead of income, and among those wealthier than about three-quarters of Americans their age, but well short of the top, only about a third have three or more kids. That’s well below families further down the wealth ladder. In the top 1%, half do. Many of these families earn too much for federal child care subsidies, which are capped at 85% of a state’s median income , but not enough to hire their way around the problem. Elaine Shi and her husband once thought they might have four kids. They stopped at three. Asked how much cost factored in, Shi, the CEO and co-founder of body-composition scanning company BodySpec, said simply: “None.” What settled it was their third child’s “firecracker personality,” along with her health during each pregnancy. Shi doesn’t see that divide among the people she knows. “Candidly, this has not been my experience,” she says. What stands out to her is timing: “Relatively few of my peers in our late 30s have chosen to have three children because they started having the first one relatively late in life.” Americans still say they want three Big families used to be ordinary. In 1976, about two-thirds of mothers in their early 40s had three or more kids; by 2016, 38% did, according to Pew Research Center . The U.S. fertility rate, close to two children per woman in 1995, hit a record low of 1.57 in 2025, by a Wall Street Journal calculation using federal data. Americans still say they want more: 42% called three or more kids ideal in Gallup’s July 2025 poll . But more than 7 in 10 say that raising kids is unaffordable for most people, according to BYU’s 2025 American Family Survey . Where the money goes Shi’s third child arrived at a hectic moment. Her older two, about two years apart, were starting school, and their needs were diverging. “It didn’t seem fair to drag an infant along to every gymnastics and swim class, nor did it seem fair to forego those kinds of activities to stick to a baby’s nap schedule,” she says. She was also mid-fundraise and needed to get back to work fast. “So we ended up investing in multiple caregivers to better meet everyone’s needs.” The biggest financial change from two kids to three, she says, was “definitely childcare.” Most families can’t hire their way out. Full-day care for a child cost $6,552 to $15,600 a year in 2022, or 8.9% to 16% of median family income, according to the Labor Department . And that’s for one child. By one LendingTree estimate, a two-child household needs to earn $400,000 a year for childcare to be affordable. A third kid often means a bigger house, too. The typical existing single-family home sold for $412,500 in 2024, about five times the median household income, according to Harvard’s Joint Center for Housing Studies . In the 1990s, it was closer to three times. Why it matters beyond the family budget The U.S. recorded just over half a million more births than deaths in 2025, and Census Bureau and Congressional Budget Office projections show that cushion ending in the next decade, the Wall Street Journal reported. After that, population growth would depend on immigration. Economists warn that fewer births mean a smaller future workforce, slower growth and more strain on Social Security. Konczal cautions that his numbers show a correlation, but it’s the one you’d expect if money solves the hard parts of raising kids. He argues that some of what money buys the rich, like stability and support, could be offered to families now, through policy aimed at the years when kids are young and budgets are tightest. Shi’s own fix is more about time than money. She and her husband run BodySpec together, and their favorite workday, she says, is Saturday. The office is empty, and one of the kids usually tags along, most often her son, the middle child. He gets to build a LEGO set without his sisters taking it apart, then has lunch alone with his mom. “Nobody told us this counted as work-life balance, but it’s the closest thing we’ve found,” Shi says. This story was originally featured on Fortune.com

articles._body: The Week 10 schedule was loaded with big-time games and season-altering results for the top teams, setting up big movement in ESPN’ FPI rankings. Unlike the polls which will follow on Sunday afternoon, this positions each team based on a set of computer numbers which track the best teams in college football. During the Week 10 slate, there were plenty results which impact how the numbers will shift, including an in-state rivalry showdown between BYU and Utah. Elsewhere, there were SEC showdowns between Missouri and Texas, Georgia and Ole Miss, Alabama and LSU, Kentucky and Tennessee, plus more. Then the headliner as Miami took on Notre Dame. [ $39.99 gets you a FULL year of On3 | Rivals national coverage ] With those and many more results now run through the computer, the Football Power Index spit out the updated Top 25 rankings. Here is an updated look at the biggest movers, the top teams and the new placements after Week 10. 1. Notre Dame (8-1): 27.3 Notre Dame picked up a huge win for their resume over the weekend, taking down Miami 31-24 at home. The win helps solidify a spot in the College Football Playoff picture over the final weeks of the regular season. Marcus Freeman and the Fighting Irish are set to face another ACC opponent next week when they host Boston College at home. The game is currently set for a 3:30 pm ET kickoff on Saturday afternoon. 2. The kickoff time for the matchup has not yet been set, but will take place on Saturday. 3. The game does not currently have a kickoff time listed, but will take place on Saturday. 8. Indiana (8-1): 21.4 Indiana got an opportunity to hit reset this week, using the bye week to prepare for the final stretch of the regular season and a potential postseason run. Firmly in the Big Ten picture, as well as the College Football Playoff conversation, they will return to the field hoping for improved offensive production. The contest is currently slated to begin at 3:30 pm ET on Saturday afternoon. 9. articles.title: D.C. is a New York town: The president, next speaker and Senate majority leader grew up within 11 miles of each other—what it means for the Big Apple
articles.summary: Gov. Kathy Hochul already wants ‘a few more billions’ for New York, starting with a tunnel Trump says Schumer spent 20 years chasing.
articles._body: On the eve of the midterm election, Gov. Kathy Hochul told a Brooklyn crowd how she planned to use New York’s new clout. “I cannot wait when I call up Hakeem Jeffries and say, ‘Mr. Speaker, I kind of need a few more billions of dollars for New York,’” she said at a rally in Williamsburg, according to THE CITY . “Then I call Chuck Schumer: ‘Mr. Majority Leader, I need a few more billions of dollars for New York State.’ Get used to it, America. Because we’re in charge.” Less than 24 hours later, Democrats won both chambers of Congress , and if Jeffries and Schumer win their leadership votes come January, two Brooklynites will lead Congress opposite a Queens-born president. For the first time in U.S. history, sons of New York are poised to run both chambers of Congress and the White House. Hochul, again, come Tuesday night: “Can you imagine New York state having both leaders of both bodies in Congress? Everybody’s going to want to move to New York because we’re the political club of the nation,” per Crain’s reporter Jack Grieve. “Imagine a world where I actually have a Congress, a House and a Senate, that are not fighting me, but working as partners to deliver even more for New York.” The three men grew up within about 11 miles of one another: President Donald Trump in Jamaica Estates, Queens, and Schumer and Jeffries just a few miles apart in Brooklyn, in Midwood and Crown Heights. The last time the House and Senate were led by people from the same state was when Texans Sam Rayburn and Lyndon Johnson held the top jobs, respectively, an overlap that ended in 1961. Jeffries would also be the first House speaker from New York state in nearly 160 years, in addition to being the first from New York City and the first Black speaker. New York came close once. In 2018, after Schumer became the Senate minority leader, Queens Democrat Joe Crowley was the House’s fourth-ranking Democrat and a likely successor to Nancy Pelosi. He also chaired what City & State called arguably the most powerful county committee in the state. Then Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez beat him in a primary and Jeffries succeeded Crowley as chair of the House Democratic Caucus, the post that set him on the path to the speakership today. New York’s reach in Washington extends beyond just Congress. Two of the nine Supreme Court justices were born in New York City: Sonia Sotomayor in the Bronx and Elena Kagan in Manhattan. Outside of Gotham, Chief Justice John Roberts was born in Buffalo and Federal Reserve Chair Kevin Warsh , who took over the central bank in May, was born in Albany. So the question now is what can the Big Apple and Empire State reap from the outer-borough love? Is it going to be like how Brooklyn’s own Biggie said in his 1994 instant bop “Juicy,” that the two chambers of Congress will get to “Spread love, it’s the Brooklyn way”? Or as the Queens-bred 50 Cent said, will the president tell them that he (and potential but improbable White House spox Nicki Minaj) is “from Queens where we are taught to handle beef on our own”? New York ‘will get its fair share’ Politics aside, it’s all about infrastructure for Gotham City. At the top of the list of wishes is Gateway, the $16 billion rail tunnel under the Hudson River. The idea dates to 2004 and survived New Jersey Gov. Chris Christie’s cancellation of an earlier version in 2010. Just last fall, during the government shutdown, Trump froze its funding. “It’s billions and billions of dollars that Schumer has worked 20 years to get—it’s terminated,” he wrote on Truth Social—and then he later suggested he’d restore the money if Penn Station and Dulles International Airport were renamed for him. This past July, a federal judge permanently blocked the freeze . There’s also Sunnyside Yard, a plan to build 12,000 homes over a Queens rail yard that the mayor’s office says would need more than $21 billion in federal grants. When Trump visited Gracie Mansion in September, the first visit by a sitting president in decades, he and fellow-Queens-rep Mayor Zohran Mamdani discussed the project . Trump said he’d been watching the site for 35 years. In the 1980s, he floated an arena there for his New Jersey Generals football team. “You’re going to need a lot of federal approvals and probably some federal money to do it,” he told Mamdani in front of reporters, before insinuating that he would be open to giving the city the funds to do it. New Yorkers also want money for the Second Avenue subway extension, plus relief for the more than 20,000 affected by changes to SNAP and the more than 400,000 facing Medicaid changes. Following Tuesday’s wave, Rep. Gregory Meeks of Queens predicted New York “will get its fair share,” per NY1 . Even Mamdani, who seems to have gain favor with the president, said following the midterms that having leaders “from our city and of our city” is “of incredible importance.” Far cry from ‘Drop Dead’ New York knows what it’s like to lose in Washington. During the city’s 1975 fiscal crisis, the New York Daily News summed up the federal response in a famous headline: “Ford to City: Drop Dead.” After Hurricane Sandy, the state’s congressional delegation sought about $60 billion in federal aid, and after a very public debate between Ted Cruz and Schumer, was offered just a little more than $27 billion. (Schumer, for his part, following the devastation of Hurricane Harvey in Texas, gave Cruz the funds he requested years later.) “It definitely would have been different if New Yorkers had been in charge,” Pete King, then a Republican congressman from Long Island, told the New York Times . “If you have to have Democrats in charge, as a New Yorker it’s better to have Schumer and Jeffries.” Who knows what happens next. articles.title: Republicans saw Indian Americans as ‘natural conservative voters.’ But Trump’s second term undid the gains as their support for Democrats shot up
articles.summary: Trump gained ground with Indian Americans in 2024, but his immigration politics and MAGA racism reversed that.
articles._body: In 2024, Donald Trump appeared to make inroads with Indian Americans, a traditionally Democratic voting bloc. He won the support of 30% of Indian Americans that year, up from 22% in 2020, according to a report published on Nov. 2 by the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace. Its charts show that up until January of this year, GOP support was increasing among Indian women and men aged 40 and older.  But two years into Trump’s second term, and those gains vanished ahead of the midterms. Just 19% of the 1,000 Indian American adults surveyed from Oct. 7 to Oct. 27 by Carnegie intended to vote for the Republican in their House district, compared to 62% intending to vote for the Democrat. In Senate races, Democrats held a similar advantage over Republicans at 63% to 21%. The reversal coincided with the Trump administration’s crackdown on legal immigration through H1-B visa restrictions , increasingly vocal anti-Indian rhetoric from some Republicans, and renewed concerns about the rising cost of living , contributing to the GOP’s declining appeal to even the Indian Americans it began winning over. Devesh Kapur, a professor of South Asia studies at Johns Hopkins University who co-authored the Carnegie report, told Fortune that economic concerns drew Indian Americans toward Trump in 2024, when voters were frustrated by inflation and the rising cost of living under Joe Biden. But those same anxieties, compounded by Trump’s immigration politics and a rise in anti-Indian racism, helped turn Indian American voters away again. “It’s a combination of these three factors,” he said.  A blatant example of what Kapur refers to as the “racist rhetoric in the MAGA crowd” came in September, when Bo French, the GOP candidate for Texas’s railroad commissioner, posted a photo on X of a crowd of South Asian students celebrating a University of Texas at Austin football victory.  “I heard UT graduation this year looked like this,” French wrote. “I didn’t believe it. The problem is now obviously far worse than anyone imagined.” While members of his party like Sen. John Cornyn condemned the post, its existence revived Indian Americans’ concern that Republicans don’t fully welcome the community. Amrita Bhasin, the CEO of AI-powered supply chain platform Sotira, told Fortune that more vocal anti-South Asian rhetoric by political figures pushed away Indian American voters more than changes to immigration policy alone. “I actually don’t think the racism is any worse than it was pre-Trump,” she said. “What’s different now is that politicians and people in power feel comfortable saying racist things out loud, specifically about South Asian people.” In her view, Trump proposing a $103,265 surcharge on companies hiring workers with an H1-B visa in August also played a role. H1-B visa holders generally can’t vote, but Indian Americans may have relatives, friends, or colleagues whose ability to work in the country depends on the program. Indians represent 71% of all H1-B visa approvals and have a strong presence in tech jobs and other highly skilled professions, so these restrictions send a message that they don’t belong, Bhasin said. “I think the H-1B is part of it, but really the H-1B is a symptom of a bigger issue,” she said. “When you see that this work is not being respected in the same way, it feels like the Republicans maybe are not on the side of Indians.” Religion as another wedge Republicans have long believed Indian Americans should be receptive to their platform. David Frum, a former speechwriter for George W. Bush, called Indian Americans “natural conservative voters ” because of their high incomes, educational backgrounds, and entrepreneurship. Indian journalist and now Council on Foreign Relations senior fellow Sadanand Dhume penned a 2012 essay for the conservative American Enterprise Institute saying that “interests, values, and history all suggest that the natural political home for Indian-Americans is the GOP.” But Kapur said the “growing grip” of evangelical Christianity in the GOP has limited its appeal to Indian American voters. The Carnegie report found nearly one in three Indian American Christians (31%) identified as Republicans, compared with 21% of Hindus, 10% of Muslims, and just 8% of those with no religious affiliation.  “Since the majority are not Christian, that alone becomes a singular sort of impediment,” Kapur said. “There’s no way to get around it.” The tension over religion surfaced notably in Texas politics. In 2023, Democratic state lawmaker James Talarico pointed to the potential alienation of Hindu students during a legislative hearing on a GOP bill requiring public schools to display the Ten Commandments. “How do you think it makes a Hindu student feel to have a poster in every classroom that says ‘thou shall not worship any God before me’?’ he asked . Three years later, Talarico beat GOP candidate Ken Paxton to become the first Democrat to win a U.S. Senate seat in Texas since 1988 . In Fort Bend County, which includes the Houston suburb of Sugar Land and its sizable Indian American community , Talarico won 63% of the vote compared with Paxton’s nearly 35%, according to county election returns . But Indian Americans voting against Republicans in the midterms doesn’t mean they did it out of stronger loyalty to Democrats. About 35% of Indian Americans who planned to vote Democrat in the midterms said they were motivated by opposition to Republicans, rather than support for Democrats, per the Carnegie report .  “Anger or feeling of antipathy towards the Republican Party was clearly an important factor over and above the support for the Democrat Party per se,” Kapur said. This story was originally featured on Fortune.com

appfuzz works with WASM and runs the .wasm th
articles._body: Hi HN, I'm Stephan. I'm an ex-CTO and many companies I look in today, want to get AI coded apps into production, but engineering code reviews are the new bottleneck - and engineers don't even love to do them. No more code reviews. Fuzz instead. appfuzz works with WASM and runs the .wasm thousands of times against a simulated backend and reports problems: crashes, n+1 queries, XSS, SQL injection, leaked secrets, blown IO/CPU/instruction budgets. Try it of your own - you don't need an app for the demo: https://appfuzz.dev Why: agents write code faster than anyone can review it, and in many companies people outside engineering (marketing, sales, support) want to ship apps too - pressure from the CEO is high. But then engineers get the pager alerts. One way to make them safer is to treat them like iPhone/iOS apps: sandbox, permissions, app review (what appfuzz does). It works with Wasm components in any language, Spin, wasmCloud, Fastly Compute, and Shopify Functions. MIT. Very early state. articles._body: My recipe app picked up users when a similar app shut down, and I kept noticing people scrambling to export their data, so I created this project to scratch my own itch. The 3 main purposes this serves are: 1. Give the public a way to find how to export their data or find a replacement if one of the apps they use shuts down. 2. Give app creators a way to get their apps in front of people who are actively looking for a replacement for a similar app. Sponsored spots are labeled and never change the dates or export steps. 3. Provide inspiration for app creators looking for ideas for what to build next. Just because apps shut down doesn't mean they were not good ideas; many times they shut down for other reasons, like poor execution, no marketing, over-spending, etc. Every date and export step links to the company's own notice. I'm always open to ideas to make it more useful. I read all the comments and constructive criticism and input are always welcomed. articles.title: Physicists listened to electrical noise to crack a superconductor mystery
articles.summary: Tuning in to electronic noise can tell us whether electrons have paired up or not.
articles._body: Superconductors carry electricity without resistance, but most only work a few degrees above absolute zero. In the late 1980s, copper-based materials called cuprates were found to superconduct at higher temperatures—reachable with affordable liquid nitrogen. Yet nearly 40 years later, physicists still don't agree on why. In a recent Science study, a team of physicists led by Milan Allan of Ludwig Maximilian University of Munich and Ingmar Swart of Utrecht University in the Netherlands has found some answers by listening to the faint electrical crackle of current flowing into a cuprate. The missing electrons Central to the mystery of cuprates’ high-temperature superconductivity is a strange state called the pseudogap. “The pseudogap is a phenomenon of missing electrons,” Allan said. Above the temperature at which cuprates become superconducting, some of their electrons seem to vanish—measurements find far fewer of them at the energies where they should be. “Everybody knows that from different probes, you see that there's these vanishing electrons, but nobody knows why,” Allan said. articles.title: Jason Witten opens up about whirlwind week as new Sooner offensive coordinator
articles.summary: Following Oklahoma’s offensive struggles, head coach Brent Venables made a significant coaching change by appointing Jason Witten as interim offensive coordinator. Despite his limited experience at the collegiate level, the former NFL tight end quickly embraced the unexpected responsibility
articles._body: Following Oklahoma’s offensive struggles, head coach Brent Venables made a significant coaching change by appointing Jason Witten as interim offensive coordinator. Despite his limited experience at the collegiate level, the former NFL tight end quickly embraced the unexpected responsibility and focused on uniting the Sooners during a challenging stretch of the season. Speaking with Colton Sulley of The Oklahoman, Witten addressed the team’s struggles and explained the message he delivered to his players during the transition. “Ultimately, we haven’t coached very well and haven’t gotten the results we wanted,” Witten said. “I told them what they could expect from me.” Asked #Sooners interim offensive coordinator Jason Witten about his whirlwind week. pic.twitter.com/LLlPO6UFSp — Colton Sulley (@colton_sulley) November 8, 2026 Witten also made it clear that he wanted players committed to the challenge. He understood that some might question the coaching change. However, he urged them to focus on moving forward as a team. This came after Oklahoma’s response following its loss to South Carolina . “Hey, listen, you don’t want to be here. I understand that. Go see coach Venables. But here’s what we’re (going to) do — we’re (going to) figure it out,” Witten told the players. The interim coordinator also stressed the importance of responding to adversity with the right mindset. He challenged the Sooners to approach the situation with purpose and take responsibility. Witten reminded them that fixing their struggles would require a united effort. “This wasn’t one person doing this. This is about the team,” Witten explained. His message seemed to connect with the locker room. Oklahoma’s players quickly rallied behind their new coordinator. After the game, they even doused Witten with Gatorade during the celebration. The moment highlighted the support he had earned in a short time. It also capped a demanding week for the former NFL tight end. articles.title: NFL Teams Turn to Bargain Backups With High-Priced QBs Sidelined
articles.summary: Kevin Jairaj-Imagn Images
articles._body: The NFL is going deeper into its pool of alternative starting quarterbacks this weekend. The Sunday of Week 9 of the season arrives with the Eagles’ Joe Milton III, the Cardinals’ Gardner Minshew II, and the Browns’ Shedeur Sanders slated to start for the first time this season. There’s also Drew Lock making another fill-in start for the Seahawks. Carson Wentz is penciled in to start Monday night for the Vikings. That’s after undrafted rookie Joe Fagnano became the Ravens’ third different starter of the season Thursday night to open Week 9. And starter No. 4 is on the way for Baltimore. The Ravens just completed a trade with the Cardinals to add Jacoby Brissett. He’ll try to hold things together for a team that’s reeling without its two-time MVP and $260 million quarterback, Lamar Jackson, and his veteran backup, Tyler Huntley. The 2026 starting debuts Sunday of Milton, Minshew, and Sanders will mean that the 32 NFL teams collectively will have used 47 different starters at quarterback this season. According to the Associated Press , that will be the league’s most through nine weeks of a season since there were 48 in 2019. The NFL’s leaders and rule-makers have always believed that high-scoring games and wide-open passing offenses are appealing to fans and integral to the league’s mammoth viewership figures. And nothing is more important to passing and scoring than keeping star quarterbacks healthy and on the field. Every time fans, viewers, and even analysts on broadcasts complain that quarterbacks are overly protected by officials throwing flags for roughing-the-passer penalties, they overlook just how important it is to the NFL’s overarching success for the most prominent quarterbacks to be in the lineup. According to the Front Office Sports ranking of the league’s heftiest contracts based on their average annual values , the NFL’s 13 highest-paid players are quarterbacks. Texans pass rusher Will Anderson is the highest-paid non-quarterback on the list, at No. 14 overall. The Cost of Injuries So it is an issue that Jackson, who’s in the fourth season of a five-year deal worth $52 million per year, is on the injured reserve list with a thumb injury that may have ended his season . It’s an issue that the Eagles are without Jalen Hurts, their $255 million quarterback, who is not expected to play again this season while being treated with blood thinners after blood clots were found in his lungs. Eagles coach Nick Sirianni, with his team on a six-game losing skid, made the switch from Tanner McKee to Milton for Sunday’s game against the Giants. The Eagles thus have gone from a quarterback with a contract worth $51 million per season and a former Super Bowl MVP, in Hurts, to a third-year pro who’s making his first NFL start and has a salary of $1.075 million for this season, the league minimum for a player of his experience level. “This is just what I felt we needed to do right at this particular moment to give ourselves the best chance to win this weekend,” Sirianni told reporters Friday of the switch from McKee to Milton. Jerome Miron-Imagn Images The Backup Carousel The Eagles will join the Giants, Ravens, and Bears as teams to use three different starters this season. The Giants are going with J.J. McCarthy after trading for the former first-round draft choice by the Vikings. He has followed Jaxson Dart, who is sidelined by a knee injury, and veteran backup Jameis Winston. The Bears have used Caleb Williams, Tyson Bagent, and Case Keenum. The Cardinals and Browns will join the Seahawks and Vikings among the seven teams that will each have used two different starters this season. Sanders gets the start for Cleveland after Deshaun Watson was in the NFL concussion protocol this week; he was cleared and reportedly was to travel with the Browns to New Orleans for their game Sunday against the Saints. Cardinals coach Mike LaFleur made the move to Minshew and temporarily dropped Brissett from first to third on the Cardinals’ depth chart, behind rookie Carson Beck, before he was traded to Baltimore. Lock makes another start for the Seahawks in place of Sam Darnold, who’s sidelined this time by a quadriceps injury. Wentz fills in again for Kyler Murray, who’s plagued by a hamstring injury, with the Vikings coming off their first loss of the season. The post NFL Teams Turn to Bargain Backups With High-Priced QBs Sidelined appeared first on Front Office Sports .

articles.title: Coffee giant Dutch Bros made all of its executives, including the CEO, do a two-week bootcamp where they learned how to pour drinks and run stores
articles.summary: Dutch Bros CEO Christine Barone and senior leaders have to complete six shifts of hands-on shop training, sharpening their hospitality skills and perfecting drinks.
articles._body: Dutch Bros CEO Christine Barone can do more than steer a $7.5 billion coffee chain—she can also hold her own behind the store counter. Like all other top leaders at the beverage giant, she embarked on a two-week bootcamp to learn the ropes of being a “broista.” And the chain’s workers weren’t afraid to call her out on mistakes.  “As I trained, people knew I was the CEO, and our teams would always point out when I was doing something wrong,” Barone tells Fortune. “That is one of the magical signs of a great culture that I need to make sure I build upon, because when my team cares so much about the customer that they’re going to tell the CEO that they were doing something wrong, I love that.” The executive’s beverage training is part of the company’s “growth from within” model. Dutch Bros staffers, from store owners to senior managers, have been put through the course for years to understand the hard work of the chain’s 25,000 broistas churning out drinks. During the training, leaders complete six shifts of hands-on shop training, sharpening their hospitality skills, perfecting drink orders, and learning how to deliver on the values of speed, quality and service. The chain says they witness first-hand how customer connections are made, and learn how to perfect drinks including the popular Golden Eagle coffee, so that everything tastes the same on Monday as it does on Wednesday. At the end, Dutch Bros leaders have to pass a “Flow” test, with questions ranging from drink recipes and company history to shop operations and culture. And the brand is serious about its standards; those who don’t pass have to retake the test. Barone says the broista bootcamp reflects the vision of Dutch Bros’ founders: brothers Travis Boersma and the late Dane Boersma, who named the company in honor of their grandparents who immigrated from the Netherlands. Aside from gaining technical and hospitality expertise, she says the training nurtures “compelling futures” at the company, and lights a path for employees to work themselves up the chain of command.  “As we rolled it out to the more broader team across HQ, we were very thoughtful about making sure our marketing teams went through the training, especially the folks who are helping to design and make beverages,” the CEO explains. “Just thinking through: What are all those decisions we’re making that touch where the customer interaction is? And how do we ensure that everyone who is designing programs for our teams, or designing marketing programs, or designing new beverages, really understands what the shop environment feels like?” How Dutch Bros has kept a strong culture as it grew into a $7.5 billion coffee giant After Starbucks and Dunkin’ Donuts, Dutch Bros is the third-largest coffee chain in the U.S. by sales and number of locations—and a huge hit among Gen Zers. But before ascending the caffeine mountaintop, the business was a humble roadside operation.  Their family dairy business was struggling, forcing the Boersma brothers to sell their cows and consider a new venture. Their coffee business started off with a pushcart and 100 pounds of coffee beans back in 1992, with the brothers slinging espresso by the railroad tracks of Grants Pass, Oregon. Friends, relatives, and loyal customers kept their dream alive as the business grew. In 1994, their pushcart was upgraded to a drive-thru stand; and just two years later, they had expanded to six locations. The first Dutch Bros franchise opened for business in 2000.  The brand is known for its high-energy service and sugary drinks, which have since made their way to high school classrooms and office cubicles across the country. By 2018, it was already at 300 locations and employed 9,000 staffers, then private equity TSG Consumer Partners acquired a minority stake in Dutch Bros to grow it even more.  The years following were marked by major milestones, including going public, surpassing $1 billion in revenue, and beefing up its store count. Dutch Bros reported record-breaking revenue of $1.64 billion in 2025, up 27.9% year over year. And now, the brand boasts 37,000 systemwide employees and 1,273 Dutch Bros locations across 27 U.S. states. It hopes to grow its store footprint to 2,029 in 2029. It can be difficult for businesses to preserve their home-grown culture as headcounts balloon, operations spread out, and outside investors get into the mix. One way to preserve it may be getting leaders to experience the business from the ground floor. The Dutch Bros CEO says that it has operators—a store or market leader responsible for running location operations—start off their career on the coffee line before moving up and into new markets. And as they advance into leadership and expand the number of locations they’re managing, they understand front-line issues and are skilled in building tight community connections.  “They’ll manage a region, so they’ll have their own set of shops that they’re managing. So why is that important?” Barone says. “Understanding this is the business that we’re in, and so when you have lived it yourself, your ability to understand where others on your team are starting from, you understand what that customer service feels like. That is important.”  Barone says that a “large number” of workers at HQ started off as broistas, enabling senior staffers to make decisions “through the right lenses.” That firsthand experience helps employees develop a sense of empathy that extends from the boardroom to the coffee counter—and serves them whether they stay at Dutch Bros, or choose to go elsewhere. “When we’re great at hospitality, the definition for me is almost the ability to think through how someone else will experience something, more so than ourselves,” Barone says. “It really is great to be able to be empathetic…I think it’s a great skill if folks come up with us, or if they go and choose to do something

articles.title: Brett McMurphy's college football AP Top 25 ballot after Week 10
articles.summary: Georgia is the new No. 1 team on my Associated Press Top 25 ballot this week. The Bulldogs replace Miami after the Hurricanes’ lost at Notre Dame. Undefeated Utah and UCLA move up to Nos. 2 and 3 behind Georgia. Notre Dame climbs to No. 4, followed by No. 5 Miami. New teams on my […]
articles._body: Georgia is the new No. 1 team on my Associated Press Top 25 ballot this week. The Bulldogs replace Miami after the Hurricanes’ lost at Notre Dame. Undefeated Utah and UCLA move up to Nos. 2 and 3 behind Georgia. Notre Dame climbs to No. 4, followed by No. 5 Miami. New teams on my ballot this week: Oregon, South Carolina, Duke and Oklahoma State. My AP Top 25 ballot after Week 10. 1. Georgia (8-1) The Bulldogs blasted Ole Miss 42-7, avenging last year’s College Football Playoff loss to the Rebels. RB Nate Frazier rushed for 106 yards. QB Gunner Stockton threw for 186 yards and four TDs. Since losing to Auburn , Georgia has defeated Florida and Ole Miss by a combined margin of 69-15. 2. Utah (9-0) QB Devon Dampier accounted for four touchdowns and the Utes’ defense picked off four passes in Utah’s 28-20 Holy War win vs. BYU . Dampier threw for 177 yards and two TDs and rushed for 89 yards and two scores. WR Braden Pegan finished with 86 receiving yards, including both of Dampier’s TD passes. The Utes have won 15 consecutive games, the nation’s current longest winning streak. 3. UCLA (9-0) UCLA QB Ty Dieffenbach threw for three touchdowns as the Bruins outlasted Minnesota 34-20. Dieffenbach threw for 303 yards on only eight completions, averaging 38 yards per completion. Aidan Mizell had two catches – both 75-yard touchdowns – for 150 yards and Semaj Morgan added a 54-yard reception. Wayne Knight had 109 yards rushing and a TD. 4. Notre Dame (8-1) The Fighting Irish made a huge statement, holding off No. 1 Miami 31-24. The victory all but locks up a playoff spot for Notre Dame as long as the Irish win their final three games. Against Miami, QB CJ Carr threw for 319 yards and three TDs. Micah Gilbert had nine catches for 98 yards and Jordon Faison had six for 77. 5. Miami (8-1) Playing their first game without injured WR Malachi Toney , the Hurricanes lost at Notre Dame 31-24. QB Darian Mensah shook off a slow first half to finish with 302 yards passing and three TDs. Cooper Barkate had 10 receptions for 118 yards and two TDs and Elija Lofton had seven for 113 and a score. RB Mark Fletcher rushed for 57 yards on 13 carries. 6. Indiana (8-1) The Hoosiers, who did not play last week, host USC on Saturday. Expect a close one. Of Indiana’s six Big Ten games, the Hoosiers have won four of five decided by one score. WRs Nick Marsh (17.61 yards per catch) and Charlie Becker (17.5) lead the Big Ten in yards per reception. 7. Alabama (7-2) The Crimson Tide rolled past LSU 31-13, despite LSU outgaining Alabama by nearly 200 yards. QB Keelon Russell threw for three TDs and 206 yards. Rico Scott had three receptions for 67 yards. Trailing 13-10 in the third quarter, Scott had a 57-yard reception that led to Alabama’s go-ahead touchdown. 8.
