articles.title: ‘Fast fires’ were just 2.7% of U.S. wildfires but destroyed 78% of the structures lost — and up to 449,000 could be lost by 2060
articles.summary: We found that roughly one-third of western neighborhoods facing the greatest future risk are low-income communities.
articles._body: As temperatures rise and development expands, the number of homes and other structures damaged or destroyed by wildfires across the U.S. is on pace to triple by mid-century , my colleagues and I found in a study just published. The 2026 wildfire season has been a sharp reminder of that risk and why making homes and properties less vulnerable to wildfires is increasingly crucial. Fortunately, strategies to lower the risk of losing a home to wildfire don’t have to be overly expensive . The 2026 western fire season The 2026 wildfire season began with historically low mountain snowpack , early snowmelt and exceptional warmth across much of the West. Even before the nation’s hottest summer on record intensified drought and dried vegetation, fires were breaking out. Colorado’s Aspen Acres Fire destroyed hundreds of structures in June. Four firefighters died from injuries suffered when the fast-moving Knowles Fire overtook them near the Colorado–Utah border in July. In August, wind-driven fires swept into neighborhoods in Spokane, Washington , damaging more than 800 homes and forcing tens of thousands of residents to evacuate. In Colorado, the summer monsoon season brought rainfall, helping firefighters gain ground. Across the Rocky Mountain region, lightning continued to start fires, but rain helped keep many fires small in many areas despite above-average temperatures. Despite this reprieve, Colorado fires had burned more than 318,000 acres by late October, nearly twice the annual average since 2000. Nationally, the total area burned was also well above average . The U.S. spent 48 consecutive days at Preparedness Level 5 – the highest level, indicating that firefighting resources were stretched nationally – compared with a 10-year average of 25 days annually. Reasons for rising fire risk Fire is a natural and often beneficial part of many ecosystems, shaping vegetation and supporting biodiversity. However, a century of fire suppression has allowed dry vegetation to accumulate in forests that historically had frequently burned. Rising temperatures caused by human activities such as burning fossil fuels have increased the rate at which the atmosphere pulls moisture from the land, drying soils and vegetation. Researchers estimate that this drying nearly doubled the area burned in western U.S. forests between 1984 and 2015 compared with what would have burned without human-caused climate change. More people also now live in and at the edges of wildland areas , raising the risk of fires reaching neighborhoods. Human activity has extended the fire season beyond summer, when most lightning-caused fires occur, too. Power lines, vehicles, machinery, burning of debris and campfires can spark fires year-round. These interacting factors have helped nearly quadruple the annual area burned in the western United States since 2000. They also contribute to the growing threat of fast-growing fires , which can overwhelm emergency response. In a 2024 study, my colleagues and I used satellite imagery to measure daily fire growth across the contiguous United States from 2001 to 2020. “Fast fires,” defined as those that burned more than 4,000 acres in a single day, represented just 2.7% of fires analyzed but accounted for 78% of documented structures destroyed and 61% of reported firefighting costs. A brief burst of growth, often fueled by strong winds or highly flammable materials, can matter enormously, even if a fire’s eventual size is relatively small. And in many ecosystems, fires are getting faster. More homes in harm’s way The number of people and buildings in harm’s way has also been increasing in the U.S., raising the risk of damage. Between 1945 and 2015, development in regions of the country with the highest wildfire risk expanded tenfold , increasing the amount of human exposure to wildfires while also introducing ignition sources and buildings that can burn. Once embers enter a neighborhood, fire can spread quickly from building to building. My team’s new research suggests that without further action to reduce wildfire risk, the annual number of structures damaged or destroyed nationwide could nearly triple by mid-century. That would mean up to 449,000 structures lost between 2026 and 2060. We used historical data about development patterns, wildfire area and the fires’ effects to reconstruct the past fire risk, then modeled future fire risk by incorporating weather, climate and housing-density expectations. We found that roughly one-third of western neighborhoods facing the greatest future risk are low-income communities . In these communities, people may struggle to afford measures to protect their homes, maintain insurance coverage and recover financially after a fire. How to lower your wildfire risk These projections are sobering, but actual losses will depend partly on the choices people make now. For example, homes can be made less likely to ignite with Class A fire-resistant roofs and ember-resistant vents that reduce the potential for burning particles to enter homes. Removing flammable debris , mulch, firewood and vegetation from around buildings also reduces the risk of fire spreading to the home. Community programs are available in many areas to help low-income homeowners reduce their home’s fire risk. Building homes to be wildfire-resilient can also cost less than people may expect. In a study of new home construction, my colleagues and I found that meeting the two protection levels established by the Colorado fire code increased minimum construction costs by approximately 0.6% and 4.2%. Access to lower-cost materials and homeowner education can help make wildfire resilience more affordable. Wildfire-resilient construction can lower the risk of losing a home, but it does not completely eliminate it. articles.title: Show HN: An online shop where your friends can hurry the courier
articles.summary:
I built an emulator of a flash-sale fashion outlet with no registration and fake checkout that never takes money. You can browse items that are on sale, watch in real time as they go out of stock one by one, and get notified when they are back on sale (possibly with different prices).

Every ord
articles._body: I built an emulator of a flash-sale fashion outlet with no registration and fake checkout that never takes money. You can browse items that are on sale, watch in real time as they go out of stock one by one, and get notified when they are back on sale (possibly with different prices). Every order placed on the website gets “tracking” which fails on the delivery day with one of 50 available reasons (for example, “a raccoon in the Newark depot has claimed your parcel; animal control reports that it seems happy there”). But you can also share the tracking with your friends, and they can hurry the courier; the more hurries, the more spectacularly it fails, until your parcel lands in the Svalbard seed vault, the North Pole, the International Space Station or some such place. The complete shop contents (campaigns, prices, item availability and stock levels) are computed from the current time with a fixed seed (FNV-1a for hashing, mulberry32 as the PRNG). I wrote the mechanism first in JS and then ported to PHP (for the website) and Flutter (for the mobile app); a test ran over several thousand random time points to verify they are identical. The Flutter app uses its own generator because it can work offline - no contact with the website is necessary. Item images are generated with OpenAI API, except models in swimsuits. OpenAI refused a lot of swimsuit image prompts, so I had to switch to Gemini for these as Gemini has no qualms about this kind of content. Does this kind of site feel like shopping to you? articles.title: The Bantu expansion changed Africa. Scientists are still tracing how.
articles.summary: Genes and archaeology are revealing how Bantu speakers spread across much of Africa.
articles._body: It’s not easy to extract iron from its ore. But the peoples of the ancient city of Great Zimbabwe—the capital of a thriving kingdom in southern Africa between 1000 to 1700 AD—were masters. At sites near the city’s stone ruins, clusters of iron-smelting furnaces survive today as mounds of rubble. At Mashava, a village 25 miles northwest, fragments bear fingermarks of those who long ago smoothed the structures’ clay interiors. Some of the furnaces were nearly an adult’s arm span in width, with walls thick and strong to contain the heat of more than 2,100° Fahrenheit needed to smelt iron. Unlike other furnaces that required workers to force air into them with bellows, these were designed to suck air in, then out through a chimney, no human labor required. This would have made it significantly easier to produce the iron, which was fashioned into hoes, axes, and arrowheads. Read full article Comments

articles.title: Wall Street banks brace for ‘political theater’ as Democrats return to power—but few expect major change anytime soon
articles.summary: “They can make life difficult, but they can't necessarily change the overall tenor of where the banks are projected to go,” a Citi analyst said.
articles._body: The giant blue wave that swept Congress this week has left Democrats in a celebratory mood. The vibe on Wall Street, however, is less upbeat as lawmakers like Sen. Elizabeth Warren (D-MA), who have expressed pointed hostility towards the financial industry, prepare to wield oversight power. This would seem to bode ill for behemoths like JPMorgan, Goldman Sachs and Morgan Stanley . But the banks can take comfort in the view of analysts and legal experts, who say that the fallout from the mid-term election is likely to amount to little more than “political theater” and public shaming—at least for now. For Wall Street, the first signs of the new political order are already appearing. Just days after the election, CNBC reported that Senate Democrats are gearing up to investigate JPMorgan for the bank’s relationship with late sex offender Jeffrey Epstein, citing a source familiar with the matter. JPMorgan declined Fortune ’s request for comment on the matter. Before that, on the same evening that polls closed, Sen. Ron Wyden, an Oregon Democrat who is expected to chair the Senate Finance Committee, posted a simple message on X : “Subpoenas.” It was a one-word preview of the scrutiny Wall Street could face when Democrats take control early next year. “I think there’s going to be a tremendous amount of political theater,” Joann Needleman, head of the financial services regulatory and compliance practice at law firm Clark Hill, told Fortune . That could mean subpoenas, investigations, hearings, and more strongly worded letters demanding answers from top executives. Among the lawmakers expected to lead that charge is Warren , who is widely expected to become the new chair of the powerful Senate Banking Committee. “Elizabeth Warren is going to bring all of these firms in and talk about all the billions that they’ve made and all the things that they have charged consumers,” Needleman said. “The bigger banks will just be called in and be put to shame by various committees that want to inquire about them.” Warren has already shown how aggressively she is willing to challenge the financial industry. She has previously called for criminal probes into banking execs, described the private-equity industry as legal “looting” and even written a bill that could make it easier to prosecute executives. Longtime Wall Street watchers, though, say any upcoming investigations or oversight hearings are par for the course. “The people who were elected have mandates, and you have to expect them to follow through on those mandates,” said Mike Mayo, Wells Fargo’s head of U.S. large-cap bank research. But that doesn’t mean all of this will result in significant disruption to how the big banks operate on a day-to-day level. “We could certainly see tougher language, more congressional hearings, and increased scrutiny of industries … but translating that rhetoric into meaningful legislation is an entirely different challenge,” Ken Mahoney, president and CEO of Mahoney Asset Management, said in a statement to Fortune . After all, President Donald Trump still has veto power. Plus, financial regulators such as the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation and the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency remain under Trump-appointed leadership. Those agencies still have the authority to enforce the rules for banks, so a change in the congressional majority would not reverse the administration’s agenda.  Wall Street has already benefited massively from Trump’s second term in the White House. The FDIC rolled back Biden-era merger policies, making it easier for big banks to facilitate megadeals. Regulators have also relaxed key capital constraints, giving banks greater flexibility to deploy their balance sheets.   “The legislative leaders, at a minimum, have a full pulpit to relay their messages,” Mayo, who started his career as a bank analyst at the Federal Reserve, told Fortune . “The degree that those messages translate to actual laws or regulations is a lot less. So I think it’s a matter of setting a tone, or the pace and degree of deregulation, as opposed to changing the direction.” Citi analyst Ben Gerlinger echoed that view. “They can subpoena companies. They can bring in management. But it really, frankly, can’t change their business models too much without a regulatory agency being that acting figure,” Gerlinger told Fortune . “They can make life difficult, but they can’t necessarily change the overall tenor of where the banks are projected to go.” “But at the end of the day, earnings drive banks,” he added. “I think earnings are still in a really good spot, in addition to capital levels.” If the blue wave outlasts Trump and brings new regulators to Washington, that’s a different story—but not one for today.  This story was originally featured on Fortune.com

‘Shock absorbers’: Korn Ferry says managers are carrying AI change that executives aren’t ready to lead
articles.summary: A Korn Ferry survey of more than 1,300 leaders finds managers absorbing AI uncertainty, while Gallup says just 25% of U.S. workers have heard a clear plan.
articles._body: Just 6% of talent and senior leaders believe their organizations’ top executives are fully prepared to lead AI-driven transformation, according to Korn Ferry’s Talent Trends 2027 report . Middle managers are expected to fill the gap. Two-thirds of respondents (66%) expect managers to spend more time helping their teams through change than overseeing their day-to-day work. The global organizational consulting firm published the findings on Oct. 22, based on a survey of more than 1,300 talent and senior leaders, from CHROs to CEOs and board members, in more than 75 countries. The concerns go beyond leadership readiness. More than three-quarters of respondents (77%) say capability gaps will pose a bigger challenge than talent shortages, and 78% believe too few people are prepared for how work will be done in the future. As companies bring AI into the workplace, middle managers are increasingly caught between executives’ ambitions and the realities of implementation. Fortune reported in October that the added responsibilities are straining managers and teams that already have little capacity to spare, and many of those managers now oversee larger teams after years of cuts to management layers . “Managers will become the shock absorbers of the organization,” Cathi Rittelmann, a senior client partner at Korn Ferry , said in the report. “Their job will be to help teams keep moving, even when they can’t tell them exactly where things are heading.” Managers are explaining decisions they didn’t make Susan De La Vega, senior vice president of global tech market and client experience at Korn Ferry, told Fortune that AI transformation requires redesigning the workforce, not simply rolling out new technology. The skills many roles require are changing, she said, which makes adaptability increasingly important. Asked whether companies expect managers to handle AI-driven uncertainty without adequate guidance from senior leadership, De La Vega replied, “Oftentimes, yes.” “Managers end up defending and communicating for AI mandates that they had no say in and little context,” she said. When leadership later changes course, employees are left redoing work. De La Vega warned that poor communication can erode trust, feed disengagement and drive away valuable employees. Clear AI plans track with higher engagement Korn Ferry isn’t the only firm highlighting the communication gap. As of May, just 25% of U.S. employees said their organizations had communicated a clear plan for integrating AI, even as 47% said their employers had begun integrating AI tools, Gallup found . That lack of clarity may carry a cost. A July Gallup analysis of employees at organizations that have adopted AI found that 43% of those whose employers had communicated a clear integration plan were engaged at work, compared with 28% of those whose employers had not or who were unaware of one. Managers made an even bigger difference. Employees who said their manager actively supports their team’s use of AI were engaged at 48%, versus 30% among those who did not. What getting it right looks like For De La Vega, the responsibility starts at the top. “Leaders go first. They learn the tools themselves, so they can speak credibly about what AI changes and what it doesn’t,” she said. She also stressed job-specific training: A finance analyst has different needs from a data scientist. Companies should give employees time to learn and room to experiment, even when their first attempts don’t work out. Managers also need to understand the decisions they’re expected to explain. De La Vega said they should be briefed on the reasoning behind leadership decisions before those decisions reach their teams, so they have enough context to answer employees’ questions. Instead of waiting for a flawless master plan, leaders need to share what they know, acknowledge what remains uncertain and lay out the broader roadmap. Companies may need middle managers to guide employees through the AI transition. But as De La Vega put it, “the ‘shock absorbers’ need a system behind them to operate.” This story was originally featured on Fortune.com

articles.title: Bullying rates reach 68% at some colleges, on par with emergency services — and students angling for better grades are the biggest source
articles.summary: Thirty percent of our survey respondents reported that students pressured them for a better grade.
articles._body: Faculty and university staff members report being bullied in two ways: by their colleagues and supervisors, and by their students over grades , according to an international study I conducted with colleagues Zahra Moradi and Deborah Circo . Researchers define workplace bullying as harmful acts of mistreatment between people that go beyond incivility and cross the line to intentionally cause harm. In other words, it’s behavior any reasonable person would know isn’t OK. Junior faculty and staff faced more workplace bullying from peers. Faculty members and staff who are Black, Indigenous or people of color were targeted more frequently. Senior faculty were more likely than younger educators to report being bullied by students over grades. Although bullying usually runs down the chain of power – for example, from a boss to an employee – grade bullying flips that. Researchers call it contrapower harassment – when someone with less formal power targets someone with more. More than 30% of adult workers in the U.S. and Canada experience bullying, harassment and sexual abuse in the workplace at any given time, harming both individuals and organizations . That rate is more than double in academia, where bullying rates are as high as 68% at some institutions, far exceeding those in general workplaces and aligning with high-stress fields like emergency services , according to our peer-reviewed findings published in the October 2026 Journal of Multidisciplinary Research and Practice. Why it matters Academic bullying undermines both the well-being of staff and faculty and the integrity of higher education institutions. Thirty percent of our survey respondents reported that students pressured them for a better grade. Students’ tactics included threatening grade appeals, malicious complaints, negative online reviews, emotional manipulation and intimidation. Women and minority faculty are particularly affected. Over time, the bullying creates a toxic environment that damages relationships between faculty and students and hurts the quality of education for everyone. Such pressure could result in mental health issues like anxiety and depression, decreased job satisfaction and reduced productivity. These dynamics not only affect individual faculty members but can also lead to long-term damage to the reputation of institutions and negatively impact students’ educational experiences. How we did our work We surveyed 189 faculty and staff at colleges and universities in Canada, the U.S. and U.K. Anonymous respondents reported how often they’d faced 22 common forms of mistreatment from colleagues and supervisors. A separate set of questions asked about pressure from students over grades. The most common issues related to colleagues weren’t shouting or threats. They were easier to dismiss: unmanageable workloads, withheld information and impossible deadlines. Pressure from students over grades was reported more frequently than bullying from colleagues. What still isn’t known Gaps remain in understanding the root causes of bullying of faculty. Studies that follow the same faculty over several years could show how grade bullying builds over time, and whether it pushes people to leave or lose trust in their institutions. One likely pattern is that grade bullying escalates when it works, wearing faculty down until they either give in or leave their jobs. Researchers need to test what actually works to stop bullying, and whether those fixes hold up at different kinds of colleges and universities. Bigger studies would help. So would sitting down with faculty and hearing their experiences in their own words to add context that a survey can’t capture. Future research could also explore interventions to mitigate bullying and measure their effectiveness across diverse educational contexts. Bullying at work is a form of violence. The harm is psychological rather than physical, but it’s real. Change starts with higher standards of conduct for everyone, from first-year students to senior administrators and leaders committed to enforcing respectful rules. The Research Brief is a short take on interesting academic work. Jason Walker , Associate Professor of Psychology, Health and Wellness, Adler University This article is republished from The Conversation under a Creative Commons license. Read the original article . This story was originally featured on Fortune.com

articles._body: Throughout this year I've been working on a game called Fermi Poker and have now published a guide on how to play and host a tournament. This guide includes a question set, a rule sheet to print out, and everything else you need to know. If you don't want to print out anything, you can also use fermi.org/play to see the questions on your device. Fermi Poker combines the betting mechanics of poker with Fermi estimation questions like "How many new smartphones were sold worldwide in 2024?" or "How many chickens were slaughtered for meat worldwide in 2024?" Once you've submitted a range estimate, there are four betting rounds, with two hints and the answer revealed between them. The aspiration was to create a game that teaches important rationality concepts (Fermi estimation, Bayesian updating, cognitive empathy, world-modeling, emotional regulation, etc.) If you want to host a tournament at your school or university, please consider reaching out as I can provide some funding to cover the cost of poker chips and small prizes. articles.title: This Archival Jordan Was Built Like a German Sports Car
articles.summary: Nike's Air Jordan 6 “White Infrared” returns in its original '91 design, bringing back the sneaker inspired by German sports cars and MJ’s winning streak.
articles._body: The Air Jordan 6 has never been short on personality. Between its slightly unconventional shape and a history that stretches well beyond the court, it's one of those sneakers that doesn't need much of an introduction. Still, every now and then, a release comes along that makes you stop scrolling for a second. Enter the Air Jordan 6 “White Infrared” in White and Light Crimson. It's a familiar combination, but that's kind of the point. Pristine white leather does the heavy lifting, while flashes of that punchy infrared shade give the sneaker its unmistakable flair. It's still a little sporty, a little nostalgic, but considerably more interesting than most other all-white sneakers. There's also something to be said for a shoe that has managed to stay relevant without constantly reinventing itself. The AJ6 has a shape that feels distinctive without being difficult to wear, and this particular version doesn't need an overly complicated fit to make complete sense. articles.title: Xero CEO: Why America’s entrepreneurship boom is only half the story
articles.summary: Right now, we’re flying blind on owner outcomes.
articles._body: One of the most consistent things I hear from founders is some version of: “The business is doing well, so why don’t I feel like I’m winning?” That question is critical. Because on every headline measure, they are winning. In 2025, the U.S. recorded approximately 5.7 million business applications, a new annual record. This rise was driven by AI, with 60% of new business owners saying they used it to help launch their business that year, double the rate from 12 months earlier. Small businesses generate trillions in economic activity. They create jobs. They power entire communities. And yet the owner, the person who took the real risk, is asking: Was it really worth it? We’ve seen this tension before, and speaking from experience, I have felt it. I think about my older sister Nicky, an optometrist who owned a practice in a shopping mall. She worked day and night to make her business succeed, but that stress never fully translated into her bank account. She had the company P&L, but not a framework for understanding whether she was thriving financially or personally. That gap is what’s hiding in plain sight in the American small business economy right now. The missing measurement We already measure revenue, job creation, and GDP contribution. These make up the scorecard. And by that scorecard, entrepreneurship looks healthy. But we don’t measure whether the owner is actually earning a living wage. Data from Xero’s payroll partner Gusto found that in 2025, the median small business owner paid themselves $4,800 per month, about $57,600 per year, in cash wages. The time investment is even starker. Most small business owners work at least 50 hours a week. Sixty percent work six or more days every week. And our research at Xero shows that owners spend nearly 22 hours a month on finance alone—just tracking and managing money. Success at the business level doesn’t tell you whether success is sustainable for the person living it. There’s a name for this gap. I call it the Ownership Gap . The hidden side of the small business economy that measures what owners actually get back from everything they put in. What success looks like Income matters, obviously. But so do things we don’t track, such as financial resilience, control over your time, access to capital when you need it, or peace of mind when you’ve had a tough month. The confidence that building this business is actually creating a better future for you as the owner, not just for the company’s P&L. Right now, we ask if the business is working. We rarely ask if business ownership is working for the owner . This extends to personal wellbeing too. There is a difference between “my business grew” and “my life improved.” A difference between a dream realized and a dream worth realizing. Business success should improve the owner’s life, not quietly consume it. Making owner experiences visible If business success should be measured by more than growth alone, we need to make the owner’s experience part of the conversation. That starts with listening to owners, understanding the realities they face and the changes they have made in how they run, measure and experience their businesses. Those stories can spark a broader conversation about whether business growth is creating greater opportunity for the people behind it. A healthier business should be measured by what it produces and what it gives back to the person who built it. Who needs to come along on the journey Owners cannot drive this change alone. Policymakers, economists, and investors must rethink how they make decisions. When all we measure is business output, we optimize for growth without asking whether that growth is sustainable for the people creating it. We celebrate record business formation without asking what kind of livelihoods those businesses actually create. We see higher small business revenue and assume owners are doing better—when in reality, they might be working harder for the same return or lesser return. This shapes lending decisions. It shapes the support programs we fund. It shapes how we think about entrepreneurship itself. The fix isn’t complicated. It’s not about replacing the metrics we already use. It’s about completing the picture. Adding owner health metrics alongside business health as a measure of entrepreneurial success. This starts by asking different questions. When business formation rises, ask what kinds of income those businesses are generating. When small business sales grow, ask whether owners have greater financial resilience. Create space for data that disaggregates by business type and owner circumstances. Build frameworks that let business owners connect what their business is earning to what they’re actually taking home. Then make that data visible with the wider business community. Right now, we’re flying blind on owner outcomes. We can see the business is thriving. We can’t see if the engine underneath is actually healthy. The path forward I’ve always believed that collective growth and individual reward go hand in hand. We need to help small business owners globally understand what ownership actually delivers. Not just in revenue, but in resilience, security, time, and wellbeing. This starts with changing what we measure. Owners should look beyond revenue and growth to what their businesses return to them personally as well. For policymakers, business leaders and economists, the ask is to broaden the definition of a healthy small-business economy beyond output and revenue. Put owners at the center of research, public debate and policy, and measure whether business success is improving their lives. In short, owners will help rewrite the scorecard. The wider ecosystem needs to start using it. We have a record number of people building businesses in different countries around the world. articles.title: ‘Like being hit between the eyes with a sledgehammer’: Meet the one town in America that defied election trends and voted in favor of data centers
articles.summary: Harwood, North Dakota residents voted against an initiative calling for a slowdown in industrial developments like AI data centers.
articles._body: In a midterm election punctuated by America’s overwhelming distaste for data centers, one small town in North Dakota has bucked the trend. Of the 45 ballot measures on data centers this past election, only one went the pro-data center way, according to data from Redbud Consulting. That initiative belonged to Harwood, a North Dakota town 10 miles from Fargo and home to about 940 people, which overwhelmingly voted against a ballot measure that would place limitations on large-scale industrial developments such as data centers. About 75% (325) of the 430 votes cast on Tuesday opposed the measure. Data centers were a major flashpoint of the midterm elections. With a new wave of moratoriums and restrictions, AI companies like OpenAI are scrambling to rebrand the buildout and market construction alongside promises of perks and community benefits to woo both local governments and residents. The Harwood initiative proposed an amendment to the town’s Home Rule Charter that would impose requirements limiting how the city evaluates, approves, and administers development or building projects, such as requiring independent reviews and holding public hearings for industrial projects. The measure was introduced following the ground-breaking of a 160-acre data center in Harwood, which Applied Digital Corp. was overseeing with Oracle as the end-user. The project was scheduled to be fully operational next year, and could possibly expand to 900 acres. Michael Swartz, a senior software developer who’s lived in Harwood for nearly 20 years, said the town’s relationship with data centers perhaps isn’t as cut-and-dry as the election results suggest.  “Long term, there’s some really serious implications that I don’t think have been fully fleshed-out, or vetted, or even are getting talked about, at the scale that I think they need to be addressed,” Swartz told Fortune . As the champion behind the ballot measure and the year-long fight against campus’s continued construction, Swartz believes the local data center expansion has the potential to harm the area, and that efforts to push the initiative were hampered by local authorities. Harwood’s data center battle Harwood residents only learned about the data center construction about three weeks before construction for the data center began in Sept. 2025, according to Swartz. At the time, the Fargo Forum reported that then-Fargo Mayor Tim Mahoney and Harwood Mayor Blake Hankey both signed nondisclosure agreements with Applied Digital Corp. in July. “When all of this came about, it was like being hit between the eyes with a sledgehammer,” Swartz’s wife Amanda told Fortune . “People deserve a say in projects of this scope.” Nick Phillips, the executive vice president of external affairs at Applied Digital Corp., told Fortune the developer chose Harwood for its cooler climate and access to energy, as well as its “pro-business landscape and the ability to have a positive impact on the community, from job creation to economic benefits.” “While our projects may seem fast to get going, they also involve an incredibly large amount of community conversations through both legally required as well as company-led events,” Phillips said in a statement. “We work very hard to provide a large amount of opportunities to learn about our potential projects before they are built including through town halls, one-on-one meetings, public forums, well above and beyond the public meeting requirements that exist.” Swartz had concerns about the project, in particular, the levels of noise pollution associated with data centers, given the location of an elementary school within a mile or so of the campus. After a city council meeting—in which Swartz claims he wasn’t allowed to speak—he got in touch with other residents, with whom he formed the grassroots advocacy group Voices of Harwood and by January, had drafted a Home Rule Charter amendment, what they saw as a stronger measure than an ordinance, which can be changed by city council members. In August this year, the petition to get the measure on the ballot received 91 signatures, more than twice the mandatory 40, in just three days, Swartz said. Then came the challenges. Swartz said in September, the Fargo Moorhead West Fargo Chamber of Commerce began disseminating anti-measure materials following Swartz’s distribution of a mailer that he paid for himself. Some of the materials, viewed by Fortune , claimed the passage of the measure would cost taxpayers an additional $300,000 to $544,000, and increase annual taxes due to lost projects by thousands of dollars. Cale Dunwoody, vice president for public policy for the Fargo Moorhead West Fargo Chamber of Commerce, told Fortune in a statement that the body “worked closely with Harwood residents and businesses to provide voters with accurate information about the proposed amendment to the city’s home rule charter.” Town officials, including Mayor Hankey, publicly opposed the measure , arguing the amendment would place an additional administrative burden on the town and set a precedent of requiring public votes for every town issue. Other officials like City Councilman Chris Higgins feared the measure would cause Applied Digital Corp. to de-annex the project, triggering a loss of tax benefits. Hankey said the data center would bring in $1.65 million in taxes by 2028. A North Dakota tax incentive would give Applied Digital Corp. a break from the state’s 5% sales tax on computers, cooling systems, and servers. Swartz was also troubled by the language of the measure which eventually made it to the ballot, which he said differed significantly from what Voices of Harwood presented to the election committee, making it harder for voters to understand what the initiative was about. “Had I not been involved with it, and had I not done my due diligence as a voter and read what Measure 2 was about, and I only was basing my decision on that summary, there’s no way I would have vot

articles.title: A new group of senators from both parties will vote on how to save Social Security. Here’s what they’ve said about it
articles.summary: From taxing higher earners to changing the retirement age, incoming lawmakers have offered different approaches to the funding gap.
articles._body: Democrats rode a blue wave of Senate pickups on Tuesday, flipping seven seats in red states and winning control of the chamber , while Republicans will also see some fresh faces. Together, the 17 newcomers from both parties will join the next Congress in taking on one of Washington’s most-dodged problems: how to keep Social Security paying full benefits.  The program’s trust fund is projected to run dry in late 2032 . After that, payroll tax revenue would cover only about 78% of scheduled benefits—forcing an automatic cut of roughly 22% unless Congress acts. Senators elected to full terms this week serve until January 2033, so the deadline falls on their watch. And because Social Security can’t be changed through budget reconciliation, a fix will likely need 60 votes and support from both parties. Nearly all the newcomers addressed Social Security during their campaigns. As Fortune previously reported , the issue isn’t quite the third rail it used to be, but “protecting” the program can mean very different things.  Here’s what each incoming senator has actually said they would do. Juliana Stratton, D-Illinois — Stratton said she would eliminate the cap on wages subject to the payroll tax, according to The Times Weekly . Social Security payroll taxes now apply only to the first $184,500 of a worker’s yearly earnings. Eliminating that cap starting in 2027, without increasing benefits for the additional earnings taxed, would close an estimated 58% of Social Security’s projected 75-year funding shortfall, according to the Social Security Administration’s actuaries . Josh Turek, D-Iowa — Turek said he would lift the $184,500 cap and opposes raising the age for full benefits. Adam Hamilton, D-Kansas — Hamilton would raise the earnings cap rather than eliminate it , arguing that someone earning $1 million shouldn’t pay the same Social Security tax as someone earning $184,500. He didn’t take a firm position on the retirement age.  Andy Barr, R-Kentucky — Barr opposed changes for people already retired and called for bipartisan reforms for younger generations. He didn’t name specific tax or benefit changes but said reforms should encourage more private and employer-sponsored retirement savings.  Troy Jackson, D-Maine — In a September Bangor Daily News op-ed , Jackson called for scrapping the payroll tax cap and increasing benefits, while ruling out privatization and raising the retirement age.  Abdul El-Sayed, D-Michigan — In his final debate, El-Sayed said the payroll tax cap should be removed and that Social Security benefits shouldn’t be taxed.  Eliminating taxes on benefits without replacing revenue would cost Social Security about $1 trillion over 10 years, plus an additional $700 billion for Medicare, according to a July analysis published by the Committee for a Responsible Federal Budget.   Peggy Flanagan, D-Minnesota — Flanagan backs Sen. Bernie Sanders’ Social Security Expansion Act, Bloomberg Government reported . The bill would apply payroll taxes to wages above $250,000, eventually eliminate the cap, and raise benefits. Her campaign site also supports eliminating taxes on benefits.  Kurt Alme, R-Montana — Alme says savings from cutting waste, fraud, and abuse elsewhere in government should go toward Social Security. In an October debate , he pointed to his experience as Montana’s budget director but didn’t propose changes to the cap or the benefit formula.  Chris Pappas, D-New Hampshire — Pappas opposes raising the retirement age, cutting benefits, and privatization. His campaign highlighted his cosponsorship of the Social Security Fairness Act, the 2025 law that boosted benefits for public workers with outside pensions.  Roy Cooper, D-North Carolina — Cooper made the 2032 deadline a staple of his stump speech. He opposes benefit cuts and says wealthy Americans should contribute more to the program but hasn’t specified how. Annie Andrews, D-South Carolina — Andrews supports eliminating taxes on Social Security benefits but hasn’t laid out a plan to close the funding gap yet.  James Talarico, D-Texas — Talarico wants to eliminate the payroll tax cap for people earning over $400,000, Texas Public Radio reported .  Barry Moore, R-Alabama — Moore’s Senate campaign website backed cutting taxes on Social Security benefits. He was also an original cosponsor of the Senior Citizens Tax Elimination Act , introduced in February 2025. The bill would remove Social Security benefits from federal taxable income and transfer general funds to replace the revenue the trust funds would lose. Harriet Hageman, R-Wyoming — Asked how to prevent Social Security cuts during an August 2026 primary debate , Hageman said growing the economy, creating jobs, and getting more people into the workforce would help shore up the program. Like Moore, Hageman was an original cosponsor of the 2025 bill to end federal income taxes on benefits. This story was originally featured on Fortune.com

articles.title: The lame-duck session gives Congress an opportunity to act on the national debt: $40 trillion is just the tip of the iceberg
articles.summary: Something has to change. But what can be done?
articles._body: Now that the midterm elections are over and we are entering a lame-duck session, Congress has an opportunity to get to work on restoring federal fiscal sanity and sustainability. In late August, the U.S. passed $40 trillion in total federal debt, a milestone that rightly generated serious attention. While this milestone drew headlines, nominal dollar numbers are the wrong metric to focus on in connection with fiscal matters. This $40 trillion number is only the tip of the financial iceberg that threatens to sink the United States. Based on the latest Social Security and Medicare Trustees Reports and the financial results for fiscal 2026, we estimate that total federal liabilities and unfunded social insurance obligations were at least $147 trillion as of Sept. 30, 2026. That is an increase of about $11 trillion in one year, and up from about $20 trillion in 2000. The primary reasons for the increases are the annual deficits, the growth in unfunded Social Security and Medicare obligations, and increased unfunded liabilities in federal civilian and military pensions and retiree health care. To better convey our past, present, and future financial condition, fiscal numbers need to be put in context. The easiest way to do that is to relate all data to the size of the economy (GDP). In short, how big is the slice of the pie? For example, $40 trillion in total federal debt represents about 124% of GDP, up from 56% in 2000, and $147 trillion in total federal liabilities represents about 452% of GDP, up from 199% in 2000. Looking ahead, the Congressional Budget Office’s (CBO) most recent projection estimated that total federal debt as a percentage of GDP will rise from 124% to 190% in the next 30 years. That must not happen. By looking at the interest burden linked to America’s current debt level, one can clearly grasp the problem associated with excessive government debt. In fiscal 2025, 36.5% of individual income taxes collected were used just to service the national debt. So, over a third of Americans’ tax dollars were siphoned away to service debt taken on in the past to finance government spending in years gone by. If that’s not bad enough, the CBO projects that by 2036 an estimated 50.6% of individual income tax dollars will be devoted solely to servicing the government’s debt. That would mean that over half of Americans’ tax dollars would not be used for the provision of government goods, services, and other payments. If Uncle Sam does not change course, America’s unsustainable fiscal mess will result in adverse economic, national security, foreign relations, and domestic tranquility consequences. Something has to change. But what can be done? Fiscal responsibility needs to be a priority in the lame-duck session, when the outgoing Congress meets after the election and before the new Congress takes office in January. Specifically, the current Congress should pass the bipartisan Fiscal Commission Act (H.R. 3289) before it adjourns. Doing so would help till the ground with the public and set the table in Congress for tough spending, revenue, and other choices in the future. Passing this bill would also be a great legacy accomplishment for Speaker Johnson, Chairman Arrington, lead Republican co-sponsor Huizenga, and others. But the Fiscal Commission Act remains in limbo. There are two possible avenues for the bill to be removed from limbo. One would be to add this bill to a new continuing resolution, if necessary. The other would be to add it to an increase in the debt ceiling, if applicable. Who said nothing significant can be accomplished in a lame-duck session? articles.title: Mark Zuckerberg’s fortune tops $200 billion. His 3 daughters won’t inherit most of it
articles.summary: The Meta CEO and Priscilla Chan pledged 99% of their shares in a 2015 letter to their newborn. Those shares were worth $45 billion then; his fortune now tops $200 billion.
articles._body: When Mark Zuckerberg and Priscilla Chan pledged to give away 99% of their Facebook shares in 2015, the stake was worth about $45 billion. Zuckerberg’s fortune now exceeds $200 billion, and their three daughters still aren’t slated to inherit most of it. That puts the Meta CEO and Chan, a pediatrician, in a cohort of ultra-wealthy households, including Bill Gates , Warren Buffett , and Michael Bloomberg , where the children won’t be inheriting the bulk of the balance sheet. The couple announced the decision in December 2015, after the birth of their first child, Maxima. In an open letter to their newborn, they introduced the Chan Zuckerberg Initiative (CZI) and committed to giving away 99% of their Facebook (now Meta) shares during their lifetimes. “Like all parents, we want you to grow up in a world better than ours today,” they wrote. “Our society has an obligation to invest now to improve the lives of all those coming into this world, not just those already here.” The pledge stands out against a larger backdrop: an estimated $124 trillion is expected to pass to younger generations as baby boomers hand down their portfolios. California’s billionaire tax looks set to miss his fortune Zuckerberg’s fortune also looks unlikely to be hit by California’s proposed “billionaire tax.” Proposition 40, a one-time 5% levy on the net worth of the state’s billionaires, was trailing 55% to 45% as of Nov. 6, with ballots still being counted. Proposition 42 , a billionaire-backed countermeasure that would nullify the tax and bar new wealth taxes in California, was leading with about 54% support. Zuckerberg had told Meta’s board he was weighing a move out of the state over the measure. The company responded by creating a new class of stock he could sell to cover a potential bill. Why CZI is an LLC, not a foundation The structure of the couple’s philanthropy is notable. CZI is a limited liability company rather than a conventional private foundation, which gives the couple flexibility over timing and cause areas and lets them invest in for-profit companies and fund policy advocacy. Gates took the foundation route. The Gates Foundation now plans to close in 2045 after spending down roughly $200 billion. Gates, for his part, cited Zuckerberg as a model of giving in a conversation with Fortune last year. “There are exemplars like Mark Zuckerberg, you know, through the Chan Zuckerberg Initiative, is committed to give over 90% of his wealth away and he’s off to a very good start,” Gates said. “He’s someone I talked to about a lot of things, including philanthropy, and they do education research; we partner on some of that.” From housing to AI-driven biomedical research CZI’s early years centered on broad social issues, including housing affordability in California and criminal justice reform. More recently, the organization has shifted its core funding toward technology-driven priorities, particularly AI-enabled biomedical research . In the letter, the couple tied the commitment directly to their daughter. “We will do our part to make this happen, not only because we love you, but also because we have a moral responsibility to all children in the next generation,” they wrote. What the pledge doesn’t require The pledge doesn’t require Zuckerberg to live like a monk. He still holds a roughly 13% stake in Meta that gives him majority voting control of the company. He has also assembled one of the most expansive real estate portfolios of any American billionaire, including a recent purchase in Miami . Near the end of the letter, the couple addressed their daughter by name. “Max, we love you and feel a great responsibility to leave the world a better place for you and all children,” they wrote. Their final line: “We can’t wait to see what you bring to this world.” This story was originally featured on Fortune.com

I built an automatic food-recall tracker that collects recalls from sources including the FDA, USDA, FSA, RASFF, and others. It currently covers the US, UK, Europe, Canada, and South Africa.

It uses ML to classify recalls by severity, cause, and category, and also tries to detect anomalies/outb
articles._body: I built an automatic food-recall tracker that collects recalls from sources including the FDA, USDA, FSA, RASFF, and others. It currently covers the US, UK, Europe, Canada, and South Africa. It uses ML to classify recalls by severity, cause, and category, and also tries to detect anomalies/outbreaks and identify similar recalls. You can sign up for daily email alerts based on your preferences, so you can be notified when a recall is relevant to you (The emails are best-effort and shouldn't be treated as an authoritative source of safety information). My goal is simply to make it easier to keep track of recalls that might otherwise be missed. I'd be particularly interested in feedback on the classification/anomaly detection, and other any other useful recall information could be added. articles.title: He went from washing lab equipment for $10 an hour to leading a $30 billion healthcare company. His advice to Gen Z: Raise your hand
articles.summary: Dexcom CEO Jake Leach says the secret to getting ahead isn't asking for a promotion—it's becoming the person willing to take on what others won't.
articles._body: The road to the corner office doesn’t always start with an Ivy League degree or prestigious internship. For Jake Leach, it started working as a lab dishwasher for just $10 an hour. Back in the 1990s, Leach was a teenager trying to save enough money to pay his way through community college in California. His high school sweetheart had just wrapped up a summer internship at MiniMed, an insulin pump company, and before heading back to school, she offered Leach the chance to take over her job. It wasn’t exactly glamorous work cleaning lab equipment like beakers and flasks, but it would mark the start of an entire career focused in diabetes management . Nearly three decades later, Leach is now the CEO of Dexcom , a roughly $30 billion company that develops non-invasive glucose-monitoring systems. And while he never had grand plans to be a healthcare executive, he told Fortune that his climb up the career ladder has come down to one simple recipe:  “It’s all about hard work,” Leach said. “There’s no shortcut.” How his grandfather and a childhood love of engineering shaped the career of Dexcom’s CEO Leach grew up in California’s San Fernando Valley, where his father worked in groundskeeping at a Catholic school and his mother was later a teacher’s aide. Money was tight, but he learned early that if he wanted something, he would have to find a way to earn it himself. In elementary school, for example, he desperately wanted a $350 bike—an expensive purchase for his family at the time. When he learned about layaway, he decided he could save up for it himself. “With the income of my family, I had no business having that kind of a bike, but I just wanted it so bad,” Leach said. He spent the summer washing cars for $2 apiece, slowly putting money aside until he could afford it. The experience taught him something that would follow him throughout his career. “Hard work gets you what you want, and you know you may not always succeed, but you can control it—you can control that outcome,” Leach said. He also developed an early fascination with how things worked, thanks in part to his maternal grandfather. A handyman who could tackle everything from plumbing to electrical work, he often brought Leach along to work on projects around the house. By the time he was 10, Leach was learning how light switches worked, how to wire them, and how electrical panels operated. Those afternoons helped spark an interest in electrical systems that eventually extended to experimenting with old VCRs and building homemade rockets. His grandfather would also become part of the reason Leach’s eventual career in diabetes technology carried a personal connection. After his grandfather’s gallbladder abruptly ruptured, the family learned the medical emergency was related to his diabetes. He would go on to take insulin for the rest of his life. Leach didn’t yet know it, but those experiences would help shape both his engineering interests and his eventual career. He eventually took classes at Glendale Community College before transferring to UCLA, where he studied electrical and biomedical engineering and became the first person in his family to earn a four-year college degree. That $10-an-hour job washing beakers and flasks at MiniMed eventually turned into a full-time position, too. Leach spent seven years at the company, which was acquired by Medtronic in 2001. But in 2004, he received an offer to join a startup of 30 people called Dexcom, which was looking to challenge the established diabetes technology industry.   The opportunity offered something different: a chance to help build a company from the ground up—and double his salary from $45,000 to $95,000. Dexcom’s CEO never asked for a promotion in his life—but tells Gen Z to get ‘outside your swim lane’ Now more than two decades after joining Dexcom, 48-year-old Leach has watched the company grow into a healthcare giant. The company went public in 2005 and, by 2025 , brought in $4.6 billion in annual revenue, had approximately 3.5 million users globally, and had around 11,000 full-time employees worldwide. The company has benefited from a shifting diabetes-treatment landscape, including the growing popularity of GLP-1 drugs , which are used to treat type 2 diabetes and have helped bring greater attention to glucose monitoring. In January, Leach reached the top of the organization as president and CEO. His compensation now includes an annual base salary of $1.15 million—a far cry from the $10 an hour when he first was exposed to the industry But his ascent wasn’t driven by an elaborate career plan. Leach, who became Dexcom’s chief technology officer in 2018 and chief operating officer in 2022, said he rarely thought about what position he wanted next. “It’s always been: keep doing a really good job, keep solving big problems, keep fostering leaders, teaching people, [and] learning from other people,” he said. Throughout his 22-year career at Dexcom, Leach said he never once asked for a promotion. Instead, he focused on proving himself in the roles he already held, allowing his work to speak for itself. Additionally, Leach made a habit of being the teammate willing to volunteer for the less glamorous assignments his colleagues weren’t particularly eager to take on. “A lot of times we tend to focus on our own work and what we’re trying to get done, and it’s really helpful sometimes to take a step back and say what’s right for the company, not necessarily what’s right for me or what’s right for the function I’m leading,” Leach said. For young workers hoping to distinguish themselves early in their careers, that willingness to look beyond their immediate responsibilities can be a major advantage, he added. “It’s like getting outside your swim lane,” Leach said. “Everyone kind of has their functional swim lane. Sanders is halfway through the sophomore campaign of his young NFL career. He started in some games as a rookie while Deshaun Watson rehabbed his Achilles throughou
articles._body: Shedeur Sanders looks to be a new and improved version of himself going into the Cleveland Browns’ Week 9 matchup this season. Sanders is halfway through the sophomore campaign of his young NFL career. He started in some games as a rookie while Deshaun Watson rehabbed his Achilles throughout 2025. With Watson back in the fold, Sanders has the backup quarterback duties. However, an opportunity has opened up for Sanders. Watson is dealing with an injury, paving the way for Sanders to handle starting duties for at least one game. NFL insider Judy Battista provided her thoughts on the young quarterback starting , believing his performance will be better than last year because of how much better the supporting cast will be. “That is largely because of the talent around him. It is better this season. KC Concepcion, one of the rookie wide receivers, you can get him the ball in space. It doesn’t require a perfect pass to get it to him. Denzel Boston is a really big boundary wide receiver, so another easy throw to him. They can make plays. Shedeur Sanders is not going to have to be the playmaker; he can just be the distributor,” Battista said on The Insiders show. “ I know Deshaun Watson’s job is not in jeopardy, according to Todd Monken, but they do wonder if Shedeur can play well enough to at least spark. spark a conversation about whether a change is made in Cleveland or whether one should be on the table. In Cleveland, we will see how he does. But certainly, this is an opportunity for Shedeur Sanders to show what he can do in Todd Monken’s system .” "Shedeur Sanders is not going to have to be the playmaker." @JudyBattista details how the Browns offensive pieces will benefit the QB pic.twitter.com/zxvUJyywoS — NFL Network (@nflnetwork) November 7, 2026 What lies ahead for Shedeur Sanders, Browns Shedeur Sanders looks to have a long career in the NFL. His ability to have solid drives while temporarily leading the Browns offense will be crucial to his hopes of achieving that objective. Cleveland has a 5-3 record this season, sitting at third place in the AFC North Division standings. They are above the Baltimore Ravens while trailing the Cincinnati Bengals and the Pittsburgh Steelers. In terms of the conference standings, they are eighth place. They lead over the Las Vegas Raiders and the Ravens while being under the New England Patriots and the Bengals. The Browns will conclude preparations for their upcoming matchup in Week 9. articles.title: A ‘geologic freak’ called the Smackover may end America’s lithium dependence on China, and Big Oil is already there
articles.summary: Standard Lithium, EnergyX, Exxon and Chevron are betting direct lithium extraction can turn the Smackover into a domestic supply hub and cut the U.S. reliance on China.
articles._body: Global lithium demand has jumped more than 400% just this decade, to over 1.5 million metric tons per year. By 2035, that demand could approach 4 million tons. Lithium-ion battery demand for electric vehicles, utility-scale and data center energy storage, and the emerging robotics industry are all driving the growth. The problem is the U.S. produces little more than 1% of the world’s lithium supplies, largely from Albemarle’s Silver Peak mine in Nevada. The world relies primarily on China for refining, as it does for many other  critical minerals and rare earths . That may be about to change. About 1,500 miles from Silver Peak lies the oddly named Smackover Formation in southern Arkansas and East Texas. Crude oil was discovered there a century ago. Now industry is fixated on its unusually large lithium concentrations in its massive underground aquifer. Early French settlers called the area “Sumac Couvert,” meaning “covered in sumac bushes,” and the name evolved into Smackover. “It’s a geologic freak with its very high lithium concentrations,” Standard Lithium CEO David Park told  Fortune . “We believe that our lands alone have the potential for over 150,000 tons per year of production.” The contenders Standard Lithium is, well, the standard bearer for the Smackover—the region with the most potential to turn the U.S. into a major lithium player. It is slated to authorize its South West Arkansas Project (SWA) late this year and start construction on the first 22,500-ton phase in the first quarter of 2027. Its brash challenger is Austin, Texas-based EnergyX (short for Energy Exploration Technologies), which is led by Elon Musk acolyte Teague Egan, 38. EnergyX could break ground on its 15,000-ton Project Lonestar commercial facility by the end of 2027. A 250-ton pilot plant came online earlier this year. Big Oil is following. ExxonMobil established its position three years ago and now holds more than 400,000 net acres, the largest in the formation. It plans to start building a pilot project there next year. Chevron also bought a lot of land, announcing a 125,000-acre position last year. The U.S. lacks the traditional resources of leading producers Australia, Chile, Argentina, and China. It has few open-pit, hard-rock deposits or economically viable evaporation ponds, such as Silver Lake. The reason Exxon and Chevron bought in is because the Smackover instead requires newer direct lithium extraction (DLE) technology. Operators drill wells much like oil and gas producers do, pump out the brine water, process and refine the lithium, and return more than 90% of the brine underground. No hydraulic fracturing, or fracking, is needed, limiting any seismicity concerns. Evaporation ponds can take two years to extract the lithium. DLE only requires about two days, though most of its costs come up front in the facility and well construction. “You extract the lithium, and then you reinject the remainder of the brine so that it leaves the ecosystem the same as it was before,” EnergyX’s Egan told  Fortune . “There are no huge pits or huge ponds. It takes basically one-hundredth of the land footprint.” Making the business case Max Yerrill, a critical minerals analyst at BMO Capital Markets, is both skeptical and optimistic. DLE remains unproven at a commercial scale and must compete in a global market vulnerable to Chinese price manipulation. The Trump administration also has eliminated EV tax credits, weakening the domestic market. Regardless, Yerrill said, “I think DLE is the only way. It’s more out of necessity. The geology is what the geology is in a particular region.” “In theory, there are huge amounts of lithium in the Smackover. It’s yet to be proven if it’s economic to do so,” he said. “But I think it makes sense. You’re not planning for one year out. These are 25-year projects. You have to look way down the road.” Even in a bad year, he added, lithium is still a market that’s growing at close to 20% or more a year. The nascent self-driving vehicle and robotaxi industry is being built up almost entirely on EVs. Tesla this week said it is discontinuing the costly Cybertruck to make way for the self-driving Cybercab, while Waymo, Avride, and Zoox are all betting on robotaxis. Egan sees them daily. “Living in Austin is seeing the future, and that is only going to spread.” Lithium is now about much more than just cars, medical devices, and electronics, including mobile phones, Egan emphasized. Utility-scale battery storage is the biggest growth area in the U.S. right now. “Batteries are the future, and lithium batteries have the most robust infrastructure, and that’s what we need for robotics,” Egan said. “That’s what we need for grid storage, for energy resiliency, for data center backup, and redundancy. It’s what we need for everything.” Standard Lithium The U.S. buildout Similar to rare earths, lithium isn’t actually rare. The challenge is economically extracting its nearly invisible ions from brine. Lithium doesn’t exist as a shiny metal in nature. It’s typically either in the salty brine aquifers or locked inside off-white or pinkish rock ore. China isn’t the top lithium miner, but it is the top refiner and battery manufacturer. The Smackover projects build refining on site, so the lithium doesn’t have to go to China for processing. U.S. battery manufacturing is also on the rise. “It’s critically important to bypass the Chinese bottleneck,” said Park, of Standard Lithium. “We’ve seen them weaponize other critical minerals. We’re strategically exposed. If they want to cut us off, they can.” The challenge is building up the necessary financing and customer contracts to start construction, Park said. In the past, China has used price dumping to prevent potential competitors from getting off the ground. articles.title: USC star Jazzy Davidson reveals her NBA, WNBA GOATS
articles.summary: Rapid fire segments used to be a great way to market athletes, but they have become rather cookie-cutter in this day and age. Similar answers tend to come up and underscore the ever-growing generational gap that exists in society. Jazzy Davidson added some welcome variety, however, and nicely sho
articles._body: Rapid fire segments used to be a great way to market athletes, but they have become rather cookie-cutter in this day and age. Similar answers tend to come up and underscore the ever-growing generational gap that exists in society. Jazzy Davidson added some welcome variety, however, and nicely showcased her personality in a short clip with the WSLAM X account. The USC women’s basketball star guard offered something for everyone. Davidson bared her old soul by naming Michael Jordan and Dennis Rodman as the greatest NBA player and greatest defensive player of all-time, respectively. She displayed the utmost school pride, naming Lindsay Gottlieb as the best coach ever, dubbing the 1983-84 championship Trojans as the best basketball team ever (also mentioned this year’s USC team) and labeling the Galen Center as the best court on which she has ever played. The two-way force also gave a shout out to teammate Rian Forestier for her apparently excellent playlist skills during pregame hype sessions. The loyalty did not stop there. When asked which team would win the 2027 NBA Finals, Davidson took a second to think before landing on the Milwaukee Bucks, the franchise that boyfriend and rookie forward Nate Ament calls home. Additionally, she crowned Maya Moore as the WNBA GOAT. The legendary forward made her Minnesota Lynx debut when Davidson was just 4 years old. The First-Team All-Big Ten selection respects the past and present, and most of all, she bleeds USC Cardinal and Gold. SLAM RAPID FIRE: JAZZY DAVIDSON pic.twitter.com/Rbev23wLvB — WSLAM (@wslam) November 6, 2026 Alongside fellow Trojans game-changers JuJu Watkins and Saniyah Hall, Jazzy Davidson is gracing the latest cover of SLAM Magazine, which she calls the greatest of all-time. USC women’s basketball is presently ranked No. 3 in the country and is eyeing a momentous season. No. 9 is fully aware of what this program is chasing. She hopes to join that storied 1983-84 group in championship excellence. Davidson knows her history. Now, she intends to make it. articles.title: Panthers looking for ‘potential solutions’ on offensive line vs. Broncos
articles.summary: The Carolina Panthers are considering potential adjustments to their offensive line ahead of Sunday’s Week 9 matchup against the Denver Broncos. After struggling to keep quarterback Bryce Young protected in recent weeks, the coaching staff is assessing different options in an effort to put
articles._body: The Carolina Panthers are considering potential adjustments to their offensive line ahead of Sunday’s Week 9 matchup against the Denver Broncos . After struggling to keep quarterback Bryce Young protected in recent weeks, the coaching staff is assessing different options in an effort to put together a more dependable unit. ESPN senior NFL reporter Jeremy Fowler discussed Carolina’s ongoing offensive line problems on NFL Network, saying that the team is exploring ‘potential solutions’ to address its protection issues. “Bryce Young has had 11 sacks in the last two weeks,” Fowler said. “He was under constant duress in that Thursday night game against Green Bay. So he was asked about it today. He would not tip his hand on that, but I know they have at least evaluated that situation. “Part of the problem is they’ve been pretty beat up with injuries. There’s only so much they can do. Their left guard, Damien Lewis, is already out for the second straight week. So they might have to stand pat, but they are looking at potential solutions.” Carolina’s offensive line has endured significant difficulties throughout the season, with a series of injuries forcing the coaching staff to experiment with different combinations. The Panthers are now focused on identifying a lineup that can provide better protection for Young while also improving the team’s ability to establish a consistent running game. Beyond their offensive struggles, Carolina has also encountered major problems on the defensive side of the ball. Those issues have contributed to significant coaching changes, including the dismissals of defensive coordinator Ejiro Evero and defensive passing game coordinator Jonathan Cooley . The challenge will be even greater against a Broncos team entering the matchup with a 6-2 record. Unless Carolina finds a way to shore up its protection, Young could be in for another difficult outing as the Panthers attempt to get their offense back on track. articles.title: Cardinals’ Mike LaFleur honors the late Pat Tillman on what would have been his 50th birthday with epic t-shirt
articles.summary: Arizona Cardinals head coach Mike LaFleur made a heartfelt gesture Friday, honoring franchise legend Pat Tillman on what would have been his 50th birthday. LaFleur, who recently made a major quarterback change involving Gardner Minshew, arrived at his media availability wearing a shirt featuring
articles._body: Arizona Cardinals head coach Mike LaFleur made a heartfelt gesture Friday, honoring franchise legend Pat Tillman on what would have been his 50th birthday. LaFleur, who recently made a major quarterback change involving Gardner Minshew, arrived at his media availability wearing a shirt featuring the late safety. The maroon shirt featured an image of Tillman wearing his No. 40 Cardinals jersey, offering a simple but meaningful tribute photo to one of the organization’s most respected figures. Cardinals reporter Mark Dalton shared a photo of LaFleur’s tribute, highlighting the coach’s decision to commemorate Tillman’s milestone birthday. Tillman, born November 6, 1976, played college football at Arizona State before joining the Cardinals in 1998. He spent four seasons with Arizona, establishing himself as a hard-hitting safety and earning widespread admiration for his dedication. Following the September 11 attacks, Tillman made the extraordinary decision to leave professional football and enlist in the United States Army alongside his brother Kevin. He served as an Army Ranger before passing away in Afghanistan on April 22, 2004, at just 27 years old. His legacy remains deeply connected to the Cardinals, who retired his No. 40 jersey and erected a statue outside State Farm Stadium in his honor. The tribute came as LaFleur prepared Arizona for its upcoming matchup against the Seattle Seahawks, with the Cardinals navigating significant roster changes after Jacoby Brissett’s departure to the Baltimore Ravens. Despite the demands of preparing for another divisional contest, LaFleur took time to recognize a figure whose influence extends well beyond football. His shirt served as another reminder that Tillman’s sacrifice and legacy continue to resonate throughout the Cardinals organization. The post Cardinals’ Mike LaFleur honors the late Pat Tillman on what would have been his 50th birthday with epic t-shirt appeared first on ClutchPoints .

articles._body: Silas Demary Jr. is enjoying life with UConn after putting up a strong performance in the No. 4 Huskies’ 85-77 win over the No. 16 Michigan Wolverines on Friday night. Demary has been playing college basketball since 2023, going through his second season with the Huskies. This marks his senior campaign, making it his last chance to shine on the national stage and grow his stock for the NBA level. Demary certainly came through with a big night against the reigning champions Michigan, who UConn lost to in the national championship game. In 36 minutes of action, he delivered a stat line of 21 points, seven rebounds, four assists, and two steals. He shot 7-of-17 from the field, including 2-of-4 from beyond the arc, and 5-of-7 from the free-throw line. Demary reflected on the win after the game on the TNT broadcast. Having his teammates surround him in celebration, the standout player made a clear declaration on his enjoyment being part of the winning program. “I’m having a lot of fun… more fun to come soon,” Demary said. The whole @UConnMBB squad pulled up behind Silas Demary Jr. for his postgame interview "I'm having a lot of fun… more fun to come soon." pic.twitter.com/XiHZGSVtVF — TNT Sports U.S. (@TNTSportsUS) November 7, 2026 How Silas Demary Jr., UConn played against Michigan Silas Demary Jr. looks forward to having his senior campaign be as great as it can be. Leading UConn to serious contention for the national championship would be a great feat for the senior star. Beating Michigan was a great step in the right direction for No. 4 UConn. They set the tone in the first half, outmatching the Wolverines 43-30 once halftime came around. Three players scored in double-digits for UConn in the win, including Demary. Braylon Mullins led the team with 23 points, four rebounds and one steal. He shot 5-of-12 overall, including 3-of-8 from downtown, and 11-of-12 from the charity stripe. Colben Landrew came next with 14 points and eight rebounds, while Jayden Ross provided nine points and four rebounds. The No. 4 Huskies will look forward to their next matchup, being at home. They host the Wagner Seahawks as tip-off commences on Nov. 9 at 7 p.m. ET. articles.title: TCU’s Hudson Hooper intercepts Arizona’s Noah Fifita for 93-yard pick-6
articles.summary: Arizona sits at No. 22 in the College Football Playoff rankings and has a murky path to the Big 12 championship, but if the Wildcats can upset No. 3 Utah at home next Saturday and get some help from Texas Tech, BYU and Houston, they can potentially force their way into the CFP picture late [̷
articles._body: Arizona sits at No. 22 in the College Football Playoff rankings and has a murky path to the Big 12 championship, but if the Wildcats can upset No. 3 Utah at home next Saturday and get some help from Texas Tech, BYU and Houston, they can potentially force their way into the CFP picture late in the year. Brent Brennan and company cannot look past TCU, however. Hudson Hooper made sure of it on Friday night. With a little more than four minutes remaining in the first half of this conference clash, the senior linebacker held his position and intercepted a Noah Fifita pass at the Horned Frogs’ 7-yard line. That alone would have been enough to swing momentum, but Hooper maximized the turnover and brought the ball all the way to the opposite end zone for a 93-yard touchdown . The visiting squad grabbed a 14-10 lead and let a stunned Tucson crowd know that this would not be a walkover. The game remains tight in the fourth quarter. Noah Fifita’s pick-6 gives TCU the lead pic.twitter.com/Xd9LNP8Cx5 — PHNX Wildcats (@PHNX_Wildcats) November 7, 2026 Hooper snags his first career interception, and boy was it a doozy. TCU overcame a 10-0 deficit and applied significant pressure on Arizona. Fifita is one of the feel-good stories in the sport, an undersized quarterback who has been a four-year starter at the same school during the NIL era. The Horned Frogs are not shedding a tear for him or the Wildcats, however. Their season is already in the mud amid a 4-4 start, but a road Big 12 win against a ranked team could give fans something to smile about, and it might cool Sonny Dykes’ hot seat a bit. Can one play be the difference between a new head coach in TCU and a strong finish to the Noah Fifita era in Arizona? Stay tuned.
