articles.title: Last-minute fantasy football streaming options for NFL Week 9: Quarterback
articles.summary: Finding a reliable quarterback streamer can be the difference between surviving a difficult fantasy football matchup and watching your team fall short. With injuries, inconsistent production, and changing offensive circumstances affecting several teams, Week 9 presents an opportunity to find valu
articles._body: Finding a reliable quarterback streamer can be the difference between surviving a difficult fantasy football matchup and watching your team fall short. With injuries, inconsistent production, and changing offensive circumstances affecting several teams, Week 9 presents an opportunity to find value outside the usual elite options. Whether you’re dealing with a quarterback injury or a difficult matchup, these four passers deserve consideration before kickoff. Jordan Love, GB (@ NE) Mandatory Credit: Jeff Hanisch-Imagn Images Jordan Love might be the most appealing streaming option of this group after delivering another productive performance in Week 8. Love completed 30 of 41 passes for 288 yards, three touchdowns, and one interception. He continued an impressive stretch of passing production . The interception did little to overshadow an otherwise efficient outing. The Panthers failed to record a sack, allowing Love to remain comfortable in the pocket and distribute the ball effectively throughout the contest. There are still some concerns about his decision-making. Love has thrown an interception in three consecutive games. However, he has offset those mistakes with six touchdown passes and an additional rushing score over that span. He has also averaged just under 280 passing yards per game during that stretch. That combination of passing volume and touchdown production makes Love an attractive option against New England. If he can limit the turnovers, he has the potential to deliver another strong performance. Managers looking for a streamer with legitimate QB1 upside should put him near the top of their list. Bo Nix, DEN (@ CAR) Bo Nix is another quarterback worth targeting. He completed 20 of 32 passes for 222 yards and two touchdowns in Denver’s victory over Kansas City in Week 8. Nix connected with Jaylen Waddle and Nate Adkins for touchdowns without throwing an interception. More importantly, he has now thrown four touchdown passes without a turnover across his last two games. His rushing production was limited against the Chiefs. Fantasy managers, though, should not overlook his ability to contribute outside the pocket. Even modest rushing numbers can provide a useful bonus. The Week 9 matchup against Carolina offers another opportunity to keep the momentum going. For managers seeking a quarterback with a favorable path to another productive outing, he deserves serious consideration. Matthew Stafford, LAR (@ WAS) Matthew Stafford is a more complicated streaming option. Still, his experience and passing ability make him difficult to ignore. He completed 17 of 25 passes for 157 yards, one touchdown, and one interception. The yardage total was underwhelming, particularly for fantasy football managers hoping for a more explosive performance. Stafford also faces an additional challenge with the Davante Adams hamstring injury. Losing a major receiving weapon could limit the Rams’ passing ceiling. There is, however, encouraging news regarding Stafford’s health. After reportedly dealing with elbow soreness, he participated fully in Thursday’s practice. The Commanders matchup offers some streaming appeal, but managers should temper expectations. He is best viewed as a deeper-league option or an alternative for managers dealing with quarterback injuries. Tyler Shough, NO (vs. CLE) Stephen Lew-Imagn Images Tyler Shough quietly put together a respectable performance against Pittsburgh back in Week 7. He completed 30 of 38 passes for 278 yards, one touchdown, and one interception. Shough’s accuracy was a positive takeaway. He completed nearly 79% of his attempts and consistently moved the ball through the air. Unfortunately, the Saints struggled to finish drives, preventing him from turning his passing volume into a bigger fantasy performance. The Saints emerge from theiur bye week and have an upcoming matchup against Cleveland. His 278 yards against Pittsburgh demonstrate that he can accumulate meaningful yardage. That said, fantasy managers will want to see more touchdown production before fully trusting him. Shough is an intriguing option in deeper leagues and two-quarterback formats. Final Takeaway Love and Nix are the strongest streaming candidates for Week 9. They combine recent touchdown production with favorable opportunities to keep rolling. Stafford offers experience but carries concerns surrounding his receiving options. Shough is a deeper-league alternative with promising passing volume. Evaluate your alternatives, monitor final injury updates, and prioritize quarterbacks showing consistent production rather than relying solely on name recognition. articles.summary: The Washington Commanders are losing players at a concerning rate. They already lost top receiver Terry McLaurin for the season, and just sent three players to injured reserve. Now, star quarterback Jaylen Daniels may have to make do without two more offensive weapons ahead of their Week 9 matchu
articles._body: The Washington Commanders are losing players at a concerning rate . They already lost top receiver Terry McLaurin for the season , and just sent three players to injured reserve. Now, star quarterback Jaylen Daniels may have to make do without two more offensive weapons ahead of their Week 9 matchup against the Los Angeles Rams. Per The Athletic’s Nicki Jhabvala, wide receiver Treylon Burks did not practice for the second consecutive day on Thursday due to a foot injury. Meanwhile, Dyami Brown has been added as a limited participant with a calf injury. Burks has been dealing with a foot issue for a few weeks now. However, he was still able to play against the Philadelphia Eagles and was a big difference maker. He picked up a season-high 81 yards on three catches, including a 53-yard bomb, in the Commanders’ 27-10 win. Through six games, Burks has 12 catches for 233 yards and two touchdowns, already surpassing his totals for all three categories last year in two fewer games. He has really stepped up in McLaurin’s absence. Through his last two games, he has caught seven balls for 147 yards. Meanwhile, Dyami Brown has nine catches for 94 yards in seven games this season. With McLaurin already out, losing Burks would be another blow to the Commanders’ receiving corps. That would leave veteran Stefon Diggs and rookie Antonio Williams as Daniels’ reliable wide receiving options, along with tight end Chig Okonkwo. The Commanders have been reportedly looking for wide receiver help at the trade deadline , although they are unlikely to go after Brandon Aiyuk. That need for another receiver could become even more pressing if Burks’ foot issues continue and he ends up missing time as well. articles.title: Stevie Nicks Predicted the Midterm Blue Wave in a Moving Poem: ‘The Light Creates a Circle of Angels’
articles.summary: The Fleetwood Mac singer said she wrote "Morning Symphony" three weeks before Tuesday's massive rebuke of the Trump agenda.
articles._body: While many Americans watched Tuesday’s midterm election results with either great anticipation or resigned dread, Stevie Nicks was not sweating the final tally at all because she already knew how the night would end. Related Queens of the Stone Age Crowned on ARIA Chart With 'Perfecth' ‘Dreams Do Come True’: Celebrities React as Democrats Sweep to Power In 2026 Midterm Election Lil Baby Brings 'Fresh' to Life: Stream It Now The Fleetwood Mac singer and solo star revealed in a post on X that she wrote a poem on Oct. 18 as a kind of wish into the universe. “It was sort of like a little prayer for the coming elections,” she said. “I really believed that what has happened was going to happen; it just had to. Good almost wins … I didn’t have time to get it out before the election — so here it is. That’s the dream …” The dream came true, as Nicks — who endorsed former Democratic Vice President Kamala Harris in the 2024 election — and the rest of the nation watched the electorate soundly rebuke the second Trump term agenda by giving Democrats a historic blue wave victory that has swept them into the majority in both the House and Senate, in addition to flipping five governorships and racking up massive wins on the local, state and national level. In the poem titled “Morning Symphony,” Nicks muses on the beauty of early mornings and her dog Lily, her sadness about what is going on in the country, ending with a final, flickering hope that the light will win out over darkness. Check it out below: I feel so much hope in the early morning symphony That I listen to — When I finally — Decide to sleep — Everything around me is so beautiful — My Lily, my lamps — My drapes — And I look forward — With anticipation — To the coming of the day — And then I remember — What I will see — Is that we are at war — People are starving — Right here — in the United States We are surrounded — in violence In chaos — in hate — I feel the tears — run down My cheeks — It’s been happening for weeks — I get up and walk to the window and I don’t sleep — No, I don’t sleep But I still believe It is still dark But the light creates A circle of angels Around this place Through those tall trees And I go to sleep That’s the dream — Back in August, Nicks, 78, made a surprise appearance at Olivia Rodrigo’s Daisy Chain Fields festival where they performed the Fleetwood Mac classic “Landslide.” The two women also contributed to the soundtrack of Practical Magic 2 , which featured “Landslide” and Rodrigo’s “The Cure.”

articles.title: Portugal’s manager breaks silence on Cristiano Ronaldo’s retirement amid their recent fallout
articles.summary: Just hours after Cristiano Ronaldo announced his retirement from international soccer, he received plenty of tributes from celebrities, athletes, and fans across the world. Retired at 41, Ronaldo is known for representing his team in six FIFA World Cups and leading them to the 2016 UEFA European
articles._body: Just hours after Cristiano Ronaldo announced his retirement from international soccer , he received plenty of tributes from celebrities, athletes, and fans across the world . Retired at 41, Ronaldo is known for representing his team in six FIFA World Cups and leading them to the 2016 UEFA European Championship. With 234 games and 146 goals for Portugal, Ronaldo announced his farewell from international soccer on social media. Shortly after, in an interview with Canal 11, Portugal’s manager Jorge Jesus broke his silence and shared that he tried to convince Ronaldo to continue representing his country. “We had the opportunity to talk about this matter before the first list. I asked him to continue with me,” Jorge Jesus shared, claiming that he intended to keep Ronaldo in the squad. However, following their conversation, Ronaldo decided to finish his international career after 23 years with the team. “He will always be in the hearts of the Portuguese. He is a global reference, an emblem for our youth and a fundamental piece of our national team’s history,” Jesus said while speaking to Canal 11. (Quotes via Heavy) The Al-Nassr forward’s international retirement comes just weeks after he left the national camp during Portugal’s ongoing UEFA Nations League matches after a press conference. Soon after, Ronaldo owned his mistake in doing so and accepted the punishment for it . Ronaldo was suspended from the national team and fined a small amount. While no official date for Ronaldo’s return was provided, Jesus had claimed that Ronaldo could return if he wanted to . Although not official, many fans have connected Ronaldo’s retirement with his recent fallout with Jorge Jesus. Current price of oil as of November 6, 2026
articles.summary: When oil prices change, it affects your energy costs—and even the price of everyday items. Here’s why.
articles._body: At 7:15 a.m. Eastern Time today, oil was priced at $102.05 per barrel with Brent serving as the benchmark (we’ll explain different benchmarks later in this article). That’s an increase of $2.53 compared with yesterday morning and around $38 higher than the price one year ago. Oil price per barrel % Change Price of oil yesterday $99.52 +2.54% Price of oil 1 month ago $103.38 -1.28% Price of oil 1 year ago $64.04 +59.35% Will oil prices go up? It’s impossible to forecast oil prices with detailed precision. Many different elements affect the market, but ultimately it boils down to supply and demand. When worries about economic recession, war, and other large-scale disruptions increase, oil’s path can shift fast. How oil prices translate to gas pump prices Gas prices at the pump don’t only track crude oil. They also include what it takes to refine and move that fuel, the taxes layered on top, and the extra markup your local station adds to stay in business. Since crude oil generally makes up a majority of the per-gallon cost, changes in its price have an outsized impact. When oil surges, gas prices typically rise in tandem. But when oil retreats, gas prices often lag on the way down, a trend sometimes described as “rockets and feathers.” The role of the U.S. Strategic Petroleum Reserve In case of emergency, the U.S. has a store of crude oil known as the Strategic Petroleum Reserve. Its primary purpose is energy security in case of disaster (think sanctions, severe storm damage, even war). But it can also go a long way toward softening crippling price hikes during supply shocks. It’s not a long-term answer and is more meant to provide temporary relief, assisting consumers and keeping critical parts of the economy running, like key industries, emergency services, public transportation, etc. How oil and natural gas prices are linked Both oil and natural gas are key sources of the energy we use every day. Because of this, a big change in oil prices can affect natural gas. For example, if oil prices increase, some industries may swap natural gas for some segments of their operations where possible, which increases demand for natural gas. Historical performance of oil To gauge oil’s performance, we often turn to two benchmarks: Brent crude oil , the main global oil benchmark. West Texas Intermediate (WTI) , the main benchmark of North America Between these two, Brent better represents global oil performance because it prices much of the world’s traded crude. And, it’s often the best way to track historical oil performance. In fact, even the U.S. Energy Information Administration now uses Brent as its primary reference in its Annual Energy Outlook. Looking at the Brent benchmark across several decades, oil has been anything but steady. It’s seen spikes due to factors such as wars and supply cuts, and it’s also seen crashes from global recessions and an oversupply (called a “glut”). For example: The early 1970s brought the first big oil shock when the Middle East cut exports and imposed an embargo on the U.S. and others during the Yom Kippur War. Prices dropped in the mid-1980s for reasons such as lower demand and more non-OPEC oil producers entering the industry. Prices spiked again in 2008 with increased global demand, but it soon plummeted alongside the global financial crisis. During the 2020 COVID lockdown, oil demand collapsed like never before—bringing prices below $20 per barrel. All to say, oil’s historical performance has been anything but smooth. Again, it’s hugely affected by wars, recessions, OPEC whims, evolving energy initiatives and policies, and much more. Energy coverage from  Fortune Looking to stay up-to-date regarding the latest energy developments? Check out our recent coverage: The Iran war has cost U.S. households nearly $2,000 each Cruise ship sold as a forever home left 203 residents in Cambodia as Iran war fuel costs hit up to $8,000 a cabin Startup Uranium Digital raises $16.5 million to modernize uranium trading Frequently asked questions How is the current price of oil per barrel actually determined? The current price of oil per barrel depends largely on supply and demand, including news about potential future supply and demand (geopolitics, decisions made by OPEC+, etc.). In the U.S., prices also move based on how friendly an administration is to drilling, as it can affect future supply. For example, 2025 saw the Trump administration move to reopen more than 1.5 million acres in the Coastal Plain of the Arctic National Wildlife Refuge for oil and gas leasing, reversing the Biden administration’s policy of limiting oil drilling in the Arctic. How often does the price of oil change during the day? The price of oil updates constantly when the “futures” markets are open. A futures market is effectively an auction where people agree to buy or sell oil in the future. As long as people and companies are trading contracts, the oil price is changing. How does U.S. shale oil production affect the current price of oil? In short, shale is rock that contains oil and natural gas. Think of shale as energy yet to be tapped. The more shale the U.S. accesses, the more energy we’ll have—and the more easily oil prices can keep from spiking as much thanks to a greater supply. How does the current price of oil impact inflation and the broader economy? When oil is expensive, it tends to make everyday items cost more. This can be related to energy (your heating, gas utilities, etc.), but it’s also due to the logistics involved with making those items accessible to you. Shipping, for example, can affect the price of things at the grocery store, as it’s more expensive to get those products from warehouses and farms onto the shelf. Schellman CEO: the giant loophole in the White House AI deal
articles.summary: Who audits the AI auditors?
articles._body: The White House recently brought together some of the world’s largest AI companies around an important commitment: independent oversight of the safeguards designed to keep their systems safe. The accord, released on Sept. 29 , calls on developers to monitor risks, establish internal controls and bring in outside auditors or evaluators to assess whether those controls work. It’s an encouraging development for an industry where companies have largely been responsible for evaluating their own technology. But the agreement leaves a critical gap. It calls for independent assessments without defining who qualifies to conduct them, what independence requires or how conflicts of interest should be handled. Without those standards, two developers could fulfill the same commitment through assessments with vastly different levels of rigor and objectivity, leaving businesses and regulators uncertain about how much confidence to place in the results. At Schellman, we provide accredited AI assurance, and we’ve seen firsthand why the credibility of that work depends on independence, clear scope and qualified professionals. The assurance profession has spent decades establishing standards for competency, independence and quality oversight across financial reporting, cybersecurity and privacy. Those standards exist because an independent opinion is only as credible as the people conducting the assessment and the evidence supporting their conclusions. Independence isn’t something you simply declare. It’s something you have to demonstrate. Independence has to hold up in practice Consider an AI developer hiring a firm to evaluate its safety controls. The evaluator agrees to a narrow scope, performs testing and issues a favorable report. If that same firm helped design the controls under review, its objectivity deserves scrutiny. If major risks fall outside the scope, customers might mistake limited findings for a broader endorsement of the system. For executives choosing AI vendors, these distinctions shape purchasing and deployment decisions. They need to know who performed the assessment, whether they had the right expertise, which safeguards they examined and what they excluded. The evaluator also needs access to sufficient evidence and the freedom to report unfavorable findings. A report is useful only when readers understand both its conclusions and its limits. Assessors should disclose relevant commercial relationships before work begins and document how they manage conflicts. They should use defined criteria, explain their methods and face independent quality review. Accreditation, where appropriate, adds another way to verify competence and impartiality. Independence matters most when problems emerge The real test of independent oversight comes when an assessment uncovers something a developer would rather not hear. The accord calls for internal teams to address identified risks, with an independent board committee overseeing findings and responses. But those safeguards depend on assessors having the independence to report concerns without pressure to soften their conclusions. Consider an evaluator who identifies a serious cybersecurity vulnerability in a frontier model. If the developer disputes the finding or pushes to narrow its scope, the evaluator must be able to stand behind the evidence and communicate the risk clearly. The developer then needs to determine whether additional testing, corrective action or release restrictions are warranted. Without an independent assessment that accurately captures the original risk, even a well-defined remediation process can fall short. Credible AI assurance also requires the right expertise. Technical evaluators understand model behavior, emerging capabilities and attack scenarios, while assurance professionals bring experience evaluating governance, internal controls and supporting evidence. Both perspectives are necessary, but neither automatically qualifies someone to assess every aspect of an AI system. As AI assurance evolves, the industry needs clearer expectations for the qualifications, methodologies and oversight required of those conducting assessments. We’re already seeing progress in how AI assurance is conducted. The AICPA and AIUC recently announced a joint offering pairing SOC 2 examinations with AIUC-1 certification, combining established assurance practices with technical testing of AI agents, including quarterly retesting as risks evolve. It’s a promising step toward more rigorous assessments, but stronger methodologies alone cannot guarantee credible results. The assessors applying them must also demonstrate the expertise, independence and accountability necessary to earn trust. Make oversight useful to the people relying on it The companies signing the accord have an opportunity to establish clearer expectations for independent AI assurance. That should include minimum qualifications for assessors, transparent assessment methodologies, conflict-of-interest disclosures and independent quality oversight. Reports should clearly communicate their scope, limitations and material findings so boards, regulators and customers can understand what was evaluated and how much confidence to place in the results. Standards also need to be practical for smaller developers. AI adoption extends beyond the largest technology companies, and an assurance process so expensive that smaller firms cannot participate would leave gaps across the market. Expectations should match the risks involved without compromising independence. The White House has taken an important step by putting independent oversight at the center of its AI safety commitments. But for that oversight to carry weight, the industry needs clear standards for who can conduct assessments, how their independence is verified and what accountability looks like when those standards aren’t met. JPMorgan’s M&A chief sees softer 2027–but a potential upside surprise in private equity exits
articles.summary: By the second half of 2027, some private equity firms may have to stop waiting for a better time to sell, JPMorgan’s global head of M&A says.
articles._body: Morgan Chittum here. Private equity firms have spent years waiting for a better time to sell. By the second half of 2027, some may have to stop waiting. That’s the view of Charlie Bouckaert, JPMorgan’s global head of M&A. He expects sponsors to start moving towards liquidity — not because he sees a dealmaking boom ahead, but because they’re running out of reasons to put it off. Their holdings are getting older, refinancing deadlines are approaching, and investors want their money back. “Ultimately, the private equity business model is reliant on exiting and returning capital to LPs,” Bouckaert told me . “And so that’s going to have to happen.” After all, backlogs are massive and growing. Private equity inventory of unsold investments hit 33,853 as of Sept. 30, 2026, up from 33,575 at the end of June, according to PitchBook figures reported by the Wall Street Journal. At the current pace of exits, PitchBook estimates it would take more than eight years to clear that inventory. This is, in part, a byproduct of private equity’s natural boom-and-bust cycle. A record-setting 2021 made way for sharp slowdown as aggressive interest rate hikes in 2022 ended the cheap-debt era. The recovery ever since then has been uneven. Although deal and exit values rebounded in 2025, the industry entered 2026 with roughly 32,000 unsold companies. Buyout holding periods have stretched to around seven years, compared with five to six years between 2010 and 2021, according to Bain. “You have a number of assets that have been held for a long period of time,” Bouckaert said. Some of those companies could also need to refinance in 2028 or 2029. As those deadlines get closer, private equity firms will have to decide whether to sell or keep holding—and how to finance those businesses if they do. “The more imminent nature of that is going to force a more definitive evaluation of what to do next,” he added.  Still, Bouckaert’s private equity forecast isn’t a call for a broader M&A surge. After what he described as a “very, very robust environment in 2026,” particularly during the first two-thirds of the year, dealmaking hit a lull. Activity remains relatively healthy, but Bouckaert expects 2027 to look more like the recent stretch than those earlier highs. “We expect the composition of [the market] to continue to skew towards larger deals the way that it has, but there to be slightly fewer of those,” he said, pointing to AI-related mergers and acquisitions. And for private equity firms, returning money to investors won’t always mean selling a company outright. “The exact format in which it happens may change,” Bouckaert said. “Maybe it’s a continuation fund. Maybe it’s the structure of a secondary deal.”  Continuation funds let sponsors move investments into a new vehicle they also manage, giving existing investors a chance to cash out. Investors can also sell their stakes to new buyers through the secondary market.  “But one way or another, we do expect to see greater deal flow materialize there,” he said. articles._body: After taking months to get confirmed, the status of Tyson Fury vs. Anthony Joshua, scheduled for late 2026 is again in danger. According to Frank Bruno, Fury may be nursing an injury ahead of the highly anticipated Heavyweight clash , and might also potentially withdraw from the fight. During a recent appearance on Fight Your Corner, in partnership with Midnite, Bruno and former cruiserweight Tony Bellew opened up about the Fury vs. Joshua fight. “I looked at him the other day, and I think someone was talking to me in the gym that he’s got some injury, which may stop him from going into the fight with Anthony Joshua? And having that on your head ain’t nice,” Bruno said. However, Bellew believes that Fury was playing up to the camera and is a master of mind games. “He plays up to the camera, Frank. I think he wants to, you know, he’s going to be saying certain things. I do think Tyson Fury is the master of the mind games. Yeah, he’s very, very good at it. Very, very good at the mind games,” Bellew said. As of now, there are no official confirmations regarding Fury’s injury or the fight being canceled . articles.title: How the Risk-Averse NFL Learned to Love Trades
articles.summary: Joe Nicholson-Imagn Images
articles._body: The NFL once was a virtual no-trades league. Not anymore. Not even close. As teams consider their options ahead of next Tuesday’s 4 p.m. ET trade deadline, there already has been a series of significant deals made this season. And those in and around the league say they expect more eye-catching trades to be completed in the coming days. “I do,” veteran NFL agent Leigh Steinberg told Front Office Sports this week, “because we’re starting to be at the halfway point in the season. And that’s enough time for evaluations. In other words, it’s enough time for the Kansas City Chiefs to say, ‘Gee, wouldn’t it be nice—isn’t it necessary for us to find wide receiving help?’ They’ve got enough proof.” This season’s major trades already have included defensive tackle Jeffery Simmons being dealt from the Titans to the Bears, quarterback J.J. McCarthy being sent from the Vikings to the Giants, cornerback Joey Porter Jr. going from the Steelers to the Cowboys, center Cam Jurgens heading from the Eagles to the Ravens, and wide receiver Marvin Harrison Jr. moving from the Cardinals to the Texans. The Colts have begun a potential fire sale in Carlie Irsay-Gordon’s second season as primary owner by trading guard Quenton Nelson to the Seahawks and defensive tackle DeForest Buckner to the 49ers. The Ravens, after losing quarterback Lamar Jackson to a thumb injury and top backup Tyler Huntley to a toe injury, officially completed a deal Friday with the Cardinals to get quarterback Jacoby Brissett. Some within the league still believe the Colts could part with a player or two from among running back Jonathan Taylor, wide receiver Josh Downs, and defensive tackle Grover Stewart. There has been trade speculation about Jaguars wide receiver Brian Thomas Jr., pass rushers Khalil Mack of the Chargers and Josh Sweat of the Cardinals, Arizona safety Budda Baker, and many other players. “Stay tuned,” a high-ranking official with one NFL team told FOS . “I’m guessing there’s much more to come.” Long gone are the days when the trade deadline would pass with a league-wide collective yawn and barely a notice. “We now have a situation much more like baseball … with teams identifying themselves as buyers, sellers, stand-pat,” Steinberg said. “And it’s much more like the wild, wild West. And it’s self-reinforcing. The very fact there are more trades means that there are [further] trades because it takes the stigma [away]. Obviously, general managers can be judged and focused on very easily with a draft pick. But they also can be evaluated very easily with a trade, for good or bad.” There have been eight in-season trades so far this year, including the just-announced Brissett deal. That’s after there were 22 in-season trades in the NFL last year between the roster cutdown and trade deadline. That was up from 18 such deals during the 2024 season and 15 in 2023. The average over the previous seven years has been 17.4 in-season trades annually. There have not been fewer than 13 in-season trades in any year over that span. That’s after there were only six in-season trades league-wide in 2016, nine in 2017, and eleven in 2018. The old-school NFL approach was that teams were built exclusively through the draft. That began to change in the 1990s with free agency and the salary cap. But even then, many GMs and coaches stuck with the notion that trades were mostly taboo, particularly during the season when a player would have to be incorporated into a new on-field scheme. Geoff Burke-Imagn Images “I’ve always thought that football was the most situational of any sport,” Steinberg said. “In other words, a player who … is an absolute bust in location A—because of the difference in systems and utilization and talent—can be a superstar in place B.” The mindset changed over time, however. “Why are teams trading more? The pressure to win now,” Steinberg said. “More aggressive front offices. Contract situations—teams approaching difficult contract decisions may trade a player rather than risk losing them in free agency. … Expanded playoff opportunities—more teams have reason to believe they can compete for [the] postseason.” The Rams famously valued adding prominent veteran players over the promise associated with retaining premium draft choices in their “Fuck Them Picks” roster-construction approach that led to their Super Bowl title in the 2021 season. Other teams surely took note. So while it’s still striking that the Bears sent a pair of first-round picks to the Titans last week as part of the Simmons trade package, it’s less shocking. The trade deadline being later in the season also has been a meaningful factor in the increased activity. The deadline is now the Tuesday after the Week 9 games after the NFL moved it a week later in 2024 (some teams had proposed moving it until after Week 10). Before 2012, it came after Week 6. Teams now have longer to decide whether they should be buyers with Super Bowl aspirations or sellers with an eye on rebuilding. Thus, there has been public conversation about whether the reeling Eagles might be trade-deadline sellers . They already traded Jurgens. They reportedly have told star running back Saquon Barkley that he won’t be traded. If not, that would eliminate the possibility of Barkley rejoining his original NFL team, the Giants, this season. Barkley recently told FOS that while he has “no hate in my heart for New York football, for the New York football Giants,” he was not focused on a prospective reunion. “I’m focused on where my feet is,” Barkley said. “And just right now obviously the season is not going the way we want [it] to go. But everything we want is still in front of us. I’ve got to get healthy and try to be the leader I can and try to turn this thing around.” The Giants, leading the NFC East in John Harbaugh’s first season as their coach, tried but failed to trade for Simmons, with Harbaugh even admitting he called Titans owner Amy Adams Strunk. articles.title: AI won’t pay off for the S&P 493 until CEOs rebuild the work
articles.summary: Stop counting layoffs as AI returns.
articles._body: Apollo Global Management chief economist Torsten Slok wrote on Oct. 24 that outside the technology sector, AI has delivered zero financial payoff . Revenue per worker and profit margins are rising at the Magnificent 7 and flat across the other 493 companies in the S&P 500. Outside tech, he writes, token spending is a cost center weighing on margins. The AI story “will be decided in the S&P 493, not the Mag 7.” Slok has the beneficiaries right. Thus far, the value has sat with the companies selling AI infrastructure, not the enterprises consuming the technology. The Oct. 28 earnings reports made the point: for the quarter ended Sept. 30, Azure revenue grew 48% and Google Cloud 103% , driven in large part by AI demand. The buyers of that capacity reported job cuts, not margin gains. The more interesting discussion is what is happening inside those companies that keeps their spend from converting to realized gains, what has to change, and when it will. The payoff is landing in people, not in companies Surveys this year from the St. Louis Fed and the Census Bureau put work use of generative AI at about 40% of workers and adoption at about a quarter of firms. Individuals are running ahead of their employers. Employees are saving real hours with AI. Some teams, and sometimes whole divisions, are seeing real benefit too. But those gains are not adding up across the enterprise, because the core operating model has not changed. The workflows, the processes and the decision approvals were built around people doing the work, and the reviews, handoffs and sign-offs are still there even after AI has taken over the task. In an AI-enabled operation, a process built for human pacing becomes the constraint, which is why the gains stay in pockets instead of reaching the whole company. What changing the operating model actually means Executives nod at “operating model.” Boards ask what it means in practice. Three things rise to the surface, and each is hard to enact in the companies Slok is describing. First, AI must be a CEO-owned initiative. That does not mean sponsorship. It means one accountable party for building a new operating system and making the difficult calls that come with it: declaring the outcome, setting the pace, redesigning the work, deciding how much trust to extend to a model, and choosing what gets measured. Nobody below the CEO carries the same authority to enforce those decisions in every function. The most common pattern I see in enterprises not realizing value is the opposite of ownership: the CEO has delegated AI to IT or a transformation office, approved a budget, and is waiting for a result that the organization has no mandate to produce. Second, picking the right problems and rebuilding the work around them. The filter is whether a workflow is material, not whether it is interesting: does it move revenue, margin, risk or cycle time, and will one business leader own the outcome. Pass that filter and the hard work begins: deconstructing workflows to eliminate dated processes, redefining roles so that work once performed, reviewed and approved by people alone is shared with AI without losing accountability, resetting approval authorities to the point where judgment is now applied, and establishing a governance model that operates at runtime, because AI produces output at a volume and speed that no manual review can keep pace with. That is where most of the time goes. Third, the AI itself. Slok is right that most companies do not need the latest model, and enterprises increasingly understand that. Less understood are the layers beneath that conversation. Start with whether an AI model is needed at all: significant improvements are available through deterministic automation that most organizations have never pursued, while many are using frontier models for routine tasks. Then comes infrastructure. Increasingly I am discussing the optimal mix of open and closed models, which revives the considerations of the cloud versus on-premises era with one difference: cloud took a decade to become multi-cloud, and model strategy is multi-vendor from the start. Finally, selecting a model is not a one-time event. That capability is very rare in most organizations today. None of this is a technology project. It touches every function and lives inside core processes. Boards then ask how long. Every executive team reaches the same realization: this is more expensive than we thought. Not because of token prices but because the build costs more than it returns until it is done. BCG’s Applied AI Index puts AI spending at 3.3% of revenue now, up from 1.7% in late 2025 . That is Slok’s cost center, seen from the inside. Why headcount will not shortcut it The temptation is to skip the build and cut staff. Barclays announced roughly 5,000 job cuts on Oct. 22 and cited AI, and markets read it as the payoff arriving. Barclays’ own chief executive called AI “the icing on the cake,” and the bank has not said how much of the number is attributable to AI at all. Measure the cost of the work The right number has two sides. On one, the quality of the outcome: did the work meet the KPI or service level the business set for it. On the other, the full cost of producing it: the model, the data, the orchestration, the validation, the human handling of exceptions, the rework and the governance, of which token spend is one line and rarely the largest. Enterprise AI will be measured this way, paying for outcomes accepted rather than intelligence consumed, and almost no company can produce that number today. Their dashboards show what is being used, by model, and nothing about what that spend returned. So the bill arrives before the value does, and the market reads layoffs instead. When Given the ownership, redesign and measurement work still ahead at most companies, I would not expect widespread acknowledgement of specific, measurable AI benefits before the end of 2027. articles.title: Cristiano Ronaldo receives touching tribute from FIFA President after retirement
articles.summary: Cristiano Ronaldo has retired from international soccer at the age of 41. After spending 23 years at the top of the industry, Ronaldo has finally decided to hang up his boots after 234 games and 146 goals for Portugal. A Portuguese soccer legend, Ronaldo was a part of the Portuguese national team
articles._body: Cristiano Ronaldo has retired from international soccer at the age of 41. After spending 23 years at the top of the industry, Ronaldo has finally decided to hang up his boots after 234 games and 146 goals for Portugal. A Portuguese soccer legend, Ronaldo was a part of the Portuguese national team for over two decades, where he represented the squad in 6 FIFA World Cups (2006, 2010, 2014, 2018, 2022, and 2026). Ronaldo’s step-down from the national team comes after a disappointing 2026 FIFA World Cup performance and a recent suspension and tussle with new manager Jorge Jesus . Recently, on social media, Ronaldo announced his retirement decision and even handed over his iconic number 7 jersey. Shortly after the decision became public, FIFA President Gianni Infantino also addressed Ronaldo’s retirement and shared a touching tribute to him on social media. “Few players have ever touched the heart of football fans around the world quite like [Cristiano Ronaldo],” he wrote. “A career defined by extraordinary talent, relentless determination and an unwavering desire to push the boundaries of what is possible. As the first player in history to score in six different editions of the FIFA World Cup and the all-time leading goalscorer in men’s international football, Cristiano has achieved milestones that may never be matched but his greatest legacy goes far beyond records, trophies and goals. “He has inspired generations, united millions of fans and carried the hopes and pride of Portugal onto the world’s greatest stages. Thank you, Cristiano, for the passion, the unforgettable moments and the immense contribution you have made to our beautiful game proudly wearing the “Seleção” shirt. Your international career will forever be part of football’s history,” Infantino finished. Ronaldo’s retirement caused a massive uproar on social media and soon became one of the most trending topics last night. As celebrities and athletes worldwide gathered to honour Ronaldo’s legacy, fans grew concerned about Lionel Messi’s silence on the former Real Madrid star’s decision, especially since Ronaldo had previously paid tribute to Messi upon his retirement. articles.title: Your customers are lying to you, and they’re lying to themselves too
articles.summary: Millennials were shaped by the pillars of their parents’ realities crumbling around them. That become the mood music for the next two decades.
articles._body: One little white lie at a time, some of the world’s biggest businesses are being undone by bad consumer data, and they don’t know it yet. Now that new tools like synthetic audiences are being thrown into the mix, the boardroom faces a novel problem. Let’s start at the beginning. It doesn’t take a genius to know that businesses need good data to understand their consumers. To market effectively, brands need to know what their audiences are thinking, feeling and doing. For almost 20 years, I’ve advised brands on how to and how not to connect with young audiences through “culture.” Working at VICE at the height of its influence, our job when we walked into the boardroom was essentially to scare the living daylights out of senior marketing execs, who had no idea about the attitudes, behaviors, tastes and desires that defined the young people they were trying to talk to. Working with us was the only way they would save themselves from certain death. Millennials were shaped by the pillars of their parents’ realities crumbling around them. That this would in fact become the mood music for the next two decades was at the time unknown. But the lack of accurate data available to decision-makers to educate themselves was itself what provided the opportunity for VICE to flourish. Fast forward 15 years and much remains the same. Big brands are drowning in lines of consumer data they have little use for, and their competitors are acting on the same generic narratives as them. Legacy polling companies have always told brands X percent of people think Y about their product. They ask direct, generic questions and they get direct, generic answers. These answers become polemic (for want of anything more interesting or, dare to say it, insightful) and the world keeps on spinning. It might seem like a small, or even interpersonal, problem. But brands regularly build multimillion-dollar projects on the backs of the lies people tell about themselves. Serious money is going to the wrong places: a study last year by the research organization Esomar estimated the “insights industry” was worth $150 billion, with $56 billion spent on market research alone. How many of the people holding these budgets would tell you that they are getting full value for their money (and have accurate data to back this up)? My co-founder, Alfred Malmros, is among those stung. He ran a startup called Anyone, an app that provided five-minute advice calls from anyone in the world. Like all responsible founders, he wanted to figure out whether people wanted what he was building and launched a product-market-fit survey. The results filled him with confidence that everyone wanted it. That prediction didn’t wash with the download statistics, which peaked at 25,000 and dwindled to 1,000 active users over time. The same people who claimed they would love an on-call advice service never downloaded the app. It was this painful lesson that taught us that the wrong questions generate the wrong answers. If my co-founder had known at the time why we lie and how lies fuel bad data, the crisis could have been averted. Why we lie Picture this. You’re at a dinner party with a half dozen people you don’t know that well. The conversation is about climate change and the scale of the challenge it presents to humankind. Everyone concurs: It’s a big one. A guest has just finished saying that climate change keeps her up at night, to thoughtful nods from the rest of the table, and then she turns to you and says: What do you think? In the moment most of us would agree. It would take a contrarian to take a different or contradictory position. Or even to admit that, honestly, what actually kept us up at night was our mortgage or the dreaded monthly 1:1 with our manager the next day. There are countless examples of this with brands: Ask people why they want an expensive watch, and they will say the craftsmanship; ask them why others want one, and they will say status. Whether conscious or not, we so often default to dishonesty. We lie to make sense of ourselves to others, to make sense of a world that is increasingly nonsensical. It’s not a moral failing, but it is a sticky conundrum for the businesses trying to understand us. So how can businesses ask better questions? The first solution is simple: Ask people what their friends think. Academics have shown that when people answer questions on behalf of their social circle instead of themselves, they effectively report on many people beyond themselves, which tells us a lot more about society than a direct question to one person. Second, stop asking people what they think only in that moment, and broaden it to what they’ve already experienced and what they expect to experience. Ask the same question about five years ago, today and three years from now and you’ll get back data on the direction of travel in beliefs and behavior, not just a snapshot. My business partner and I built our research consultancy on these parameters. Consumer data sets are so often made up of people’s projections and manifestations, the ways in which they’d like to be seen. To get to real truths, even better, hidden truths, researchers must solve for this. Even better, design for it. When enough intelligence (human or artificial, ideally a blend of both) goes into crafting a question, the question itself is enough to unlock new futures and opportunities, and for those who ask the question to see their worlds anew. Why should this be keeping C-suite leaders awake at night? Because bad data alone isn’t a new problem. It’s been compounded by the rise of synthetic audiences: AI-generated simulations of real consumers that businesses can interview and test ideas on before launching them. In theory it’s useful, but when these audiences are trained on flawed consumer data, the consequences are catastrophic. articles.title: Kickstarter’s CEO is championing human creativity in a flood of AI
articles.summary: Also: All the news and watercooler chat from Fortune.
articles._body: In today’s CEO Daily: AI is a catalyst and challenge in the creator space. The big leadership story: Tech stocks take a beating. The markets: A sea of red globally as U.S. stocks look set for a rebound. Plus: All the news and watercooler chat from Fortune . Good morning. Is Gen Z helping to create an economy of affection here in the U.S.? I first heard that term as a student at the University of Nairobi, when a classmate had to host a relative stranger in her apartment for two months because this person came from her village. As she explained to me, that’s just what you did. In a society without deep pockets, social programs, or job security, the bonds of community, kinship, religion, and tribe created a network of support. My son, 25, calls it the friendship economy: he’ll buy t-shirts and go to concerts for a friend in music, help with another friend’s startup or movie, or sometimes throw a little money into various projects through some peer-to-peer platform. As AI and an anemic job market spark anxiety about traditional career paths, entrepreneurial and creative pursuits—sometimes funded by one’s social network—become more attractive. Goldman Sachs projects the number of creators to grow from 67 million to 107 million by 2030 and the creator economy to generate half a trillion dollars by next year. I recently spoke with Kickstarter CEO Everette Taylor about how these trends are playing out on his crowdsourcing platform, which enabled more than 24 million backers to spend close to $9 billion in funding 277,302 projects as of April 2025, creating more than 1 million jobs. (Kickstarter launched in 2009 and became a public benefit corporation six years later.) Taylor says there’s one factor that’s both a catalyst and a challenge in the creator space: AI. “It leads them to being a creator or entrepreneur, which also leads more people to our platform,” said Taylor. But he’s unnerved by what the technology can create on its own, telling me that he asked ChatGPT to produce a script about a “Mosquito Man” from the Bronx and “it gave me a full film script. It was insane.” AI can write the script. What it can’t manufacture is the circle of people willing to back you, so Taylor is leaning into the human side of the equation. Kickstarter cohosted a special event with smart projector brand XGIMI yesterday in Times Square, showcasing technology launched on the platform, including XGIMI’s new AURA 3 laser TV that raised a record $10 million in two hours. The goal was not just to promote the product but to create a sense of community, reinforcing Kickstarter’s brand campaign that kicked off this summer with the tagline “ belief is human .” “You go around Times Square and what do you see? Nothing but AI, AI, AI ads,” said Taylor. But on his platform, backers seem to be voting the other way. One 2026 study tracked 63,000 Kickstarter campaigns and found projects with the “AI use” label raised about 40% less money and drew almost a quarter fewer backers. People want to know they’re supporting human-generated work and the human behind it. “We believe in the importance of human creativity no matter how much AI advances things,” said Taylor, who launched a $1 million Kickstarter Culture Fund to help independent creators make a living. “I don’t care if you have a million followers on social media. Those 25,000 people that you have on Kickstarter, those are your true supporters.” Contact CEO Daily via Diane Brady at diane.brady@fortune.com This story was originally featured on Fortune.com

articles.title: Can MLS Capitalize on Son-Mania?
articles.summary: William Navarro-Imagn Images
articles._body: As Son Heung-min’s last-minute strike kissed the post and bounced agonizingly away in LAFC’s 1–1 draw with New York City FC on October 17, the assembled crowd at Citi Field let out a collective groan. Although it was technically a home match for the New York-based club, the seats around the makeshift soccer field were filled with fans wearing South Korea and Tottenham Hotspur shirts. The crowd reached a fever pitch every time Son touched the ball, hoping South Korea’s all-time top scorer could work another moment of magic at the tail end of his illustrious career. “He makes me very proud to be Korean,” Paul Oh, a Seoul-born fan donning a South Korea kit who now lives in New York City, told Front Office Sports at Citi Field. “He’s just a great player; he has such a great personality, he loves his fans, and you can feel that from him.” MLS is, in many ways, built on the Son formula. David Beckham’s global stardom helped launch the league into the mainstream between 2007 and 2012, and Lionel Messi has made Inter Miami matches the hottest ticket in town since joining the club in 2023. Son’s arrival at LAFC—alongside former Tottenham teammate Hugo Lloris—has taken that experience to a new level, and one that has divided MLS fans. Tottenham supporters clubs are now organizing trips to see the man who starred for their club for a decade play for LAFC. In August, the Washington, D.C.-based Tottenham supporters group DC Spurs hosted an event titled “Captains in the Capital” in conjunction with LAFC’s visit to D.C. United. Named for Son and Lloris, both former Tottenham captains, the event featured a watchalong of a Tottenham match at a bar and a group march to Audi Field for the MLS match. Over 900 fans attended the match through the event after D.C. United provided DC Spurs a group ticket package, and the team and supporters club collaborated to donate a portion of the proceeds to local educational nonprofit DC Scores. Not everyone was pleased with the initiative. After DC Spurs posted on Instagram advertising the event, D.C. United fans filled the comment section with disapproval. “Supporters group completely unaffiliated with any of the teams participating in the match is marching against the team from their city,” one fan wrote. “Support your local,” two other fans chimed in. DC Spurs defended itself in the comment section, saying the outing was “not about supporting LAFC or rooting against D.C. United.” “We encourage everyone to celebrate our former Spurs players while also showing respect and support for our local club,” DC Spurs wrote. Eric Kmetz, a treasurer and board member of DC Spurs, told FOS he hoped attending the match would inspire Spurs fans to become more involved with their local club. She said it was a particularly special moment for her 6-year-old son, who looked up to Son as an idol and cried when he left Tottenham in 2025. “I think Sonny represents everything good in football in terms of his style and how generous of spirit he is,” Lynch said. “So he’s an easy player for people to fall in love with.” After the match, Son told FOS he still notices Tottenham shirts at away matches across the country. “Everywhere I go I see Spurs shirts [with] my name [on the] back,” Son said. “It makes me so so proud. I’m just so grateful to see those kind of fans.” Lynch said she thought most members of New York Spurs had little connection to NYCFC, and for those who did, their fandom didn’t have the same “passion and drive” as with Tottenham. “If it wasn’t for [Son and Lloris], would we have come to support our local team together?” Lynch pondered. “Maybe as like a big social activity, but it wouldn’t be something that we as a collective would repetitively do and come to support.” Walking the Tightrope MLS marketing and ticketing departments face the challenge of capitalizing on Son’s superstar status while converting previously apathetic first-time attendees into reliable supporters. United’s Faith and Family Night in September. “We see it as an intro into the club,” Lucas said. “Quite a few people that have come in, when they are experiencing that atmosphere, they start getting on an escalator where they’re coming out to one more match, then they’re coming to two or three more matches, then they’re becoming a partial season plan member, and then ultimately a season ticket member with us.” NYCFC took a similar approach to its home match against LAFC, which was initially scheduled for May but later moved to October. articles.title: Interscope Expands Into Brazil With Hip-Hop Artist BK, Supernova Entertainment Joint Venture
articles.summary: The new twin deals portend the label's significant expansion into the eighth-largest music market in the world, according to IFPI.
articles._body: Interscope Records is branching out into Brazil, the company announced Friday (Nov. 6), unveiling two new deals in the country: the signing of hip-hop star BK, and a new joint venture/distribution deal with leading urban label Supernova Entertainment. Related IFPI Global Report 2026 Takeaways: Vinyl Growth Outpaces Digital, China Surges & More Kenny MacPherson, Veteran Music Publisher and Big Deal Music Co-Founder, Dies at 71 Diddy Moved From New Jersey Prison to Similar Facility in Pennsylvania For BK, signing with Interscope coincides with the 10th anniversary of his debut album, Castelos & Ruinas ; his first release for Interscope will be a remix of that album with new production and new collaborations. The new JV with Supernova encompasses the Brazilian urban label’s catalog and a partnership for new signings. Jose Cedeno and BK. Pepe Rodrigues “We have shown through our successful track record over the past few years that wherever they come from, artists are attracted to the kind of global artist development platform we can provide at Interscope,” Interscope Capitol Miami executive vp/GM Jose Cedeño said in a statement. “Having BK as our first artist signing and Supernova as our first label deal, illustrate how serious our mission is to empower Brazilian artists to become global superstars.” The Brazilian market has been a particular focus of the majors in recent years — one that reflects both investment in the country itself and the subsequent growth in subscription streaming and consumption in general. In March, IFPI reported that the Brazilian music market had grown by 14.1% year over year, much higher than the 6.4% growth of the industry overall, jumping over Canada to become the eighth-largest market in the world. Pictured L-R: Laura Carter, Interscope; Nagalli, Supernova Ent. artist; Ramon Alvarez-Smikle, Interscope; Gustavo Pimentel, Founder and CEO, Supernova Ent. High Courtesy of Interscope “Brazilian music and culture are having an extraordinary impact around the world right now,” Interscope Capitol chairman/CEO John Janick said in a statement. “We see an opportunity to leverage our legacy and current success in urban music for important Brazilian artists like BK and labels like Supernova Entertainment. We are excited to expand the resources and opportunities for Brazilian artists to move culture on a global level.” Related How IFPI CEO Victoria Oakley Is Tackling AI & Streaming Fraud Head-On: ‘We’ve Got Work to Do’ Those opportunities were expanded upon by Victoria Oakley, IFPI’s CEO, in a new interview with Billboard this week. “I think we’re seeing the music economy emerge at the same time as we’re seeing the Brazilian economy emerge,” Oakley said. “It’s also a place of phenomenal talent, and their export story is much more successful so far, principally across their own region. But I think given that most of the music is in Portuguese and not in Spanish, so the obvious sellable market isn’t there in quite the same way, they’ve done a phenomenal job with their export story and they are on the increase. They too have a government that I think, from early on, places culture as an important part of the education system, and I think that is quite an important first step that we often don’t see the benefits of until much later.” “BK’s authenticity and distinctly Brazilian voice have made him one of the defining figures in Brazilian hip-hop,” Interscope’s urban music co-presidents Laura Carter and Ramon Alvarez-Smikle said in a statement. “His music reflects the depth, originality and cultural influence of hip-hop both in Brazil and globally. Our partnership with Supernova continues Interscope’s tradition of working with visionary labels that are deeply connected to their artists and culture, and we’re excited to deepen our commitment to hip-hop in Brazil together.”

Now, former UFC star Colby Covington also shared his thoughts on Dana White’s Zuffa Boxing salary. Once a part of the UFC roster and now far away from receiving another contract opportunity from White’s company, Covington has openly slammed White and the UFC’s salaries. During an interview with Ozoon Canada, Covington shared the following when asked about UFC fighters’ pay, “I don’t like it at all. It’s just tough. Ever since they got into the boxing space with Zuffa Boxing, it just was like a big slap in the face to us UFC fighters. “Why are you going to pay this bum Conor Benn $15 million? Who the f**k is Conor Benn? Like, no one knows who that is. He’s a nobody. And he quit in his fight, literally just went out there to collect a paycheck and just quit. “He didn’t even put on a good performance, he was out in like three or four rounds against Ryan Garcia, who’s nothing special. You know, that guy was beat up by Rolly Romero just a fight before. So, I don’t like it,” Covington added. Covington, 38, was part of the UFC roster from 2014 to 2026. articles.summary:
Hi HN,

I've been fascinated by aviation for some time now. Inspired by Fugleramme, I wanted a framed print of a cluster of aircraft over my house or a busy airport. So I built Overhead. (Photos in the README)

The hero photo shows planes departing and landing in Changi, Singapore.

How it wor
articles._body: Hi HN, I've been fascinated by aviation for some time now. Inspired by Fugleramme, I wanted a framed print of a cluster of aircraft over my house or a busy airport. So I built Overhead. (Photos in the README) The hero photo shows planes departing and landing in Changi, Singapore. How it works Flight data for a location is gathered from adsb.lol and adsb.fi as a fallback. (you can also point it to your own ADS-B receiver). The photo of the exact aircraft is gathered from planespotters.net and the photographer is credited on the page. The photo is then handed to an AI image gen service via fal.ai using your own key. It's then cut out and packed into a cluster on the page with packers adapted from Fugleramme. It costs about US$0.04 a painting but images are painted once and kept for the next time that aircraft is seen. You can also choose to only show photos. This widget is built on my open source, self-hosted e-ink platform, Tesserae. It's a one click install from the widget catalog. I'm looking for feedback and contributors. https://github.com/arnegiacomo/fugleramme https://github.com/dmellok/tesserae Comments URL: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50390605 Points: 1 # Comments: 0

Europeans are living and working for longer. Principal’s CEO says companies aren’t ready for the change
articles.summary: With average life expectancy across the EU now exceeding 81 years, Principal Financial chief executive Deanna Strable argues employers must rethink careers, training, and retirement.
articles._body: Europeans are living longer than ever. More than one-fifth of the European Union’s population is 65 or older, and the share aged 80 plus is set to more than double by the end of the century.   Deanna Strable, chief executive of Principal Financial Group, believes neither companies nor their staff are ready. “Employers and leaders are going to have to get used to people being in the workforce for a longer amount of time,” she says. “I don’t think we’re all prepared for that.”  Falling birth rates mean fewer young people are entering the workforce, while millions of baby boomers are reaching retirement age. As a result, older workers are make up a larger proportion of the labor market. In 2025, a record two-thirds of 55- to 64-year-olds in the EU were in employment, according to Eurostat .  As people stay in employment for longer, companies will have to adapt their working and hiring practices, job design, and provide training for people later in their careers.  Strable has led Principal since January 2025. The U.S.-based retirement and asset management company works with more than 200,000 American employers, and in Europe it manages money on behalf of pension providers.   Principal has five generations of workers on its payroll. Reskilling and flexible career paths are becoming increasingly important, Strable says. Over the past 18 months, Principal has trained all 19,000 of its employees in AI, offering the courses in different formats because, as she puts it, “some people want to do it very much on their own, other people want to do it with others sitting around the table.” It has also extended its rotation programs, once limited to actuaries, to IT, accounting, and finance, so staff can move into new roles as their careers grow longer rather than feeling the need to move companies.  Strable has spent her entire career at Principal, working her way up through 15 different roles, and thinks the company ‘lifer’ could make a comeback as workers look for employers that will help them adapt rather than gamble on starting again elsewhere. “You can have the equivalent of 10 different jobs with one company,” she says, “or you can start over at 10 different companies.”  Longevity’s gender problem Longer life expectancies will also mean people will have to save more for retirement, unless they stay economically active for longer.   This risks exacerbating the pension gender gap. A woman in the EU will spend about four fewer years in paid work than a man, yet she can expect to live five years longer. By the time she retires, she will typically receive a pension 24.5% smaller than a man’s—more than twice the size of the gender pay gap.  Strable says longer lives risks widening that gap unless employers and the pensions industry act. Women tend to earn less, work part-time more often and take career breaks to care for others, so they retire with less saved.   A woman born in the EU today can expect to live to 84, and the European Commission projects that will pass 90 by the end of the century, so that smaller pot will have to stretch across ever more years of retirement. “That is something we all should be paying attention to because it could actually make things much worse,” Strable says.  Across Europe, responsibility for retirement is shifting from governments and employers to individuals, and women are less confident than men that the state will provide. Only 29% of European women believe their government’s pension system will be enough to fund their retirement, compared with 39% of men, according to Principal Financial Group’s latest Global Financial Inclusion Index. In Germany, the figure for women falls to 17%.  The U.K. has automatically enrolled workers into workplace pensions since 2012, Ireland followed in January, and the Netherlands is replacing guaranteed pensions with personal savings pots. These strategies get more people saving, but they shift the job of funding retirement onto savers themselves.   “The workplace is still where most retirement saving happens, which gives employers influence over how much people put aside,” Strable adds. She recommends pairing auto-enrollment with auto-escalation, which is common in U.S. plans but rare in Europe, so contributions rise over time instead of staying at the minimum. “Let’s say you start at 5% but you ultimately want to get to a savings rate of 12%. That’s daunting to most individuals,” she says. Her answer is to tie each increase to the annual pay rise.  “Women’s savings tend to slip at predictable moments, such as starting a family, caring for a relative, or losing income,” Strable says. And “employers are often the first to know about those moments, through parental leave, carer’s leave, or sick pay, which puts them in a strong position to help staff take stock of their savings.”   Yet employer-provided financial guidance has fallen across advanced economies for two years running, according to Principal’s index. This, a time when women already feel less equipped to plan ahead: only 54% of European women say they can easily access the tools they need to plan a secure retirement, compared with 64% of men.  “Many women are left without professional financial advice—often at the moment they need it most,” Strable says. In many households the husband dealt with the advisor, so a widow may have no link to the person who knows the family’s finances. According to insurer Liverpool Victoria, 41% of U.K. women would not feel confident managing household finances if their partner died.  “We’re not all financial professionals that understand the complexity of income and longevity,” Strable says. “Having access to advice is important.” Principal now encourages its advisors to build relationships with both partners, so the advice continues if one of them dies.  For Strable, financial security is part of a bigger picture: helping pe

articles._body: I’m not the sort of person who typically pays for a house cleaner. I’m too frugal, and I kind of enjoy putting on a podcast and going to town on my tub with a Magic Eraser. But when I saw an X post about a new humanoid-robot cleaning service in San Francisco, I immediately signed up for the waitlist. I wanted my apartment to feel like The Jetsons , even if just for an hour. I was also motivated by journalistic interest. In order to ensure an authentic experience, I didn’t tell Tau Robotics, the startup behind the X post, that I was a journalist—though I did use my real name, so it’s possible someone looked me up. Tau’s long-term goal is to make autonomous cleaning robots a reality, but they’re not quite there yet: For now, the robots are piloted remotely by humans, who watch what’s going on via cameras mounted in the robots’ heads and wrists. As the robots clean, they collect data that Tau will use to train up their more independent descendants. Every counter successfully wiped and T-shirt successfully folded will help the models that power the robots learn to do better on the next go-round. Because this data is so valuable to Tau, the company charges less for cleaning than one might expect for such a cutting-edge product. At the time I booked, Tau was offering $30 for an hourlong cleaning with a single robot; now the charge is $60 per weekly cleaning with two robots, or $100 for a one-time visit. But even at the cheaper rate of $30 per hour, Tau’s robots aren’t a great bargain. They are thorough but slow, so if you, like me, are tempted to stand around watching them for their entire visit, it would probably be a better use of your time to just take care of the cleaning yourself.  But the robots are physically capable of cleaning, and they’re undeniably cute. Tau has armed each four-and-a-half-foot-tall robot with a 3D-printed “head” with antennae that allow it to communicate with Tau’s headquarters, as well as two 3D-printed claw “hands” (the more humanlike alternatives apparently aren’t durable enough, and claws do surprisingly well for most cleaning tasks). Mine was wearing a Tau Robotics shirt, and grippy socks so that it didn’t scratch hardwood floors. With all the human support they need, the robots are closer to radio-controlled cars than Waymos. Many tasks, such as making the bed and folding laundry, require what’s called kinematic guidance: The human pilot performs the necessary motions, and sensors transmit those movements to the robot, which copies them. These kinematically guided tasks produce especially valuable training data. Tau’s AI models might not have solved laundry folding yet, but learning from the examples of robots that have completed the task in the real world is how they’ll get there. But according to Tau cofounder Cornelia Weinzierl, to whom I came clean as a journalist a few weeks after the cleaning, the robot can already complete some other tasks—such as vacuuming and mopping—without any human help. If Tau succeeds in using all the data it is collecting to train truly autonomous cleaning robots, they could even become San Francisco’s newest tech tourist attraction as Waymos become more commonplace countrywide. The cleaning robot that came to my building last month was already a bit of a spectacle. It arrived in a blue minivan, out of which it was helped by Weinzierl and another Tau employee. That’s when the robot encountered its first obstacle: the eight stairs leading up to the building’s front door. I’d come down to greet Weinzierl and the robot, so I had a front-row seat to its struggles with my steps. It climbed as if it were drunk. Each successful step was as likely as not to be followed by a stumbling backward stagger that erased all its progress—though, impressively, it never entirely lost its footing. When I later discussed my experience with Weinzierl, she explained that the robot sometimes walks strangely because it is operated remotely from Tau’s headquarters, and the short signal transmission delay can affect its coordination. “The amount of work and time that we spend just optimizing, for example, timings and connectivity is crazy,” she said. Inside, the carpeted staircase leading up to my apartment defeated the robot entirely, and Weinzierl had to lug it up the last few steps. This, it turned out, was not typical. As the robot cleaned, it repeatedly stalled out, something Weinzierl attributed to it overheating in the unseasonably hot weather—until she heard from one of her colleagues that the heat had shut down not the robot but the equipment that its human controller was using to watch its progress through my apartment. Without remote assistance, the robot couldn’t clean, and so it, and Weinzierl, departed before my booked hour was up. (Back in September, Weinzierl or another Tau representative remained with the robot throughout its visit, but she says that’s no longer necessary.) You can’t fault Tau on customer service, though. Weinzierl quickly emailed me to apologize, comp the visit, and offer me another on the house (minus whatever price I assign to my data privacy)—and that was all before I told her I was a journalist. I scheduled the next cleaning for about a month later, after a couple of trips out of town, and it went much more smoothly—the robot got up my stairs without much assistance, though still with the drunken stagger. In the hour it was there, it did a creditable job of cleaning my kitchen (though it didn’t brave the stove) and even saved me my most dreaded cleaning task, the toilet. That was its most impressive performance: Three times the head fell off its toilet cleaning wand, and three times it managed to reattach it by poking around with the handle until it made contact at just the right angle. The robot is still rough around the edges, which is to be expected for a product in beta. It repeatedly left my taps dripping, it knocked over a (closed) bottle of olive oil, and it couldn’t manage to right an air purifier that i

articles.title: Painters Need Tough Ass Trail Shoes, Too
articles.summary: Hiking shoes for painters, please! Who knew art could be so rough and tumble? Phileo and KEEN, apparently.
articles._body: Art is often referred to as a soft science. In practice, and especially in handling it, it’s anything but. Anyone who’s ever done an install or de-install has the giant splinter scars from carrying crates to prove it. Art is actually a pretty rough-and-tumble job, and Philéo Landowski, designer of COMME des GARÇONS-approved footwear label Phileo, knows it. The people who build art deserve beautiful tools, and the Keens that Landowski is dropping today do the job while looking hard as hell. Phileo and Keen’s Fall/Winter 2026 collaboration comprises three shoes: the Evanston boot, Providence clog, and hairy suede Targher shoe. Landowski’s design approach is inside-out, meaning workwear components typically concealed, like the Evanston’s toe cap and heel counter, become design details all on their own. The Evanston’s shaft even folds down to reveal a botanical illustration on the inside which, like, art. Who better to illustrate — pun intended — the art-multipurpose of Keen than Matt Dillon, iconic actor with a classic Hollywood face who is also a painter, something most people probably don’t know. He debuted his first solo exhibition, Porto Novo to Abomey , at The Journal Gallery in April, presenting paintings developed while filming Claire Denis’ The Fence and traveling through Benin. I bring this up to say: Dillon lives the rugged art life that these Keens communicate. Photographer Ari Marcopoulous captured Dillon in his studio for this campaign, and the Phileo Keens look as natural in a painter’s sink as they might on a rugged trail. The fact that we don’t talk about Dillon’s painting career is a little like how we don’t consider trail shoes performance footwear outside the trail. Phileo and Keen say: fuck that. I agree. Painting a large-scale canvas means standing for hours, moving around, and occasionally making a mess. These Keens, and perhaps all Keens, aren’t for any one thing, just whatever labor constitutes a hard day’s work. The painter-in-Keens thing might sound like working-class fetishism, but it’s actually practical. And all three would look incredible paint-splattered. Art is rough-and-tumble. Might as well dress accordingly. Highsnobiety has affiliate marketing partnerships, which means we may receive a commission from your purchase. Want to shop the products our editors actually love?
