articles.title: The Valkyries’ short, movie-like road to the 2026 Championship
articles.summary: The Golden State Valkyries are your 2026 WNBA Champions, and the journey to get here is about as absurd as a journey can be. On October 5, 2023, the WNBA made an exciting announcement: the Bay had been awarded an expansion team. The area and its surrounding cities are entrenched in basketball his
articles._body: The Golden State Valkyries are your 2026 WNBA Champions, and the journey to get here is about as absurd as a journey can be. On October 5, 2023, the WNBA made an exciting announcement : the Bay had been awarded an expansion team. The area and its surrounding cities are entrenched in basketball history, between the Sacramento Monarchs (a former W franchise that eventually folded in 2009), the San Francisco Pioneers (which played in the Women’s Professional Basketball League from 1979-1981), and the legendary success of the Golden State Warriors in the NBA. Warriors Co-Executive Chairman and CEO Joe Lacob was announced as the then-unnamed team, and he immediately made a splash by guaranteeing that the franchise would win a ring in the next five years: a lofty goal given the historical precedent. Prior to the Valkyries, the expansion team to win a championship was the 1970-71 Milwaukee Bucks (three years), and in the W, the fastest track was four years (2004 Seattle Storm). Lacob was sure that he could join this prestigious club, though, and he injected that belief into building the franchise. In May 2024, the team announced that it would be called the Golden State Valkyries – partially decided by community input from the San Francisco Chronicle. Five months later, Lacob hired Natalie Nakase, who’d served as an assistant coach in both the WNBA and NBA, and had won two championships with the Las Vegas Aces. In the franchise’s first year, they made headlines by making the playoffs as the No. 8 seed. Little did anyone know, they were far from done with shocking the world.   Valkyries in the Finals About three years after the initial announcement, the Golden State Valkyries – now equipped with Gabby Williams and Kiah Stokes – found themselves all the way in the Finals after a year of being doubted and brushed off. Despite finishing the 2026 season as the No. 2 seed and as the No. 1 defense in W history, the Valkyries were underdogs: they were a roster of players who’d been brushed off in one way or another, whether it be getting cut from the W four times like Veronica Burton or simply being overlooked by coaches and fellow players like Williams recalled. The entire nature of the expansion draft, through which a bulk of the Valkyries’ roster was built, implies that they were the leftovers; the players that teams felt they could do without. On the other side of the bracket was the new look Atlanta Dream, who’d added young star Angel Reese to its ranks the previous summer. Reese, who’d just been named Defensive Player of the Year, was out for blood to start her playoff career, averaging 18 points and 8.4 rebounds per game in the first five games of the postseason as the Dream swept both the Washington Mystics and New York Liberty on their way to the Finals. Rhyne Howard and Allisha Gray, longer tenured guards who’ve made names for themselves for a number of skills on the court, co-headlined the Atlanta squad with Reese, and now DeWanna Bonner, who’d signed with the team late in the season. Both teams had good reasons to have chips on their shoulders, but the championship trophy doesn’t concern itself with narratives or pre-season power rankings. All that matters is what goes on between the black lines. Games 1 and 2 were fairly uneventful – the Valkyries and Dream each took a game in Ballhalla, with both teams holding each other to historically low shooting percentages as expected. Gabby Williams exploded for 26 points and four rebounds in Game 1, and two days later, Angel Reese became the youngest player to record 30+ points and 15+ rebounds in a Finals game. Things took a very sharp turn for the Valkyries when, in Game 3 in Atlanta, they suffered a devastating 97-71 blowout on the backs of a 21/12 night from Reese, 16 points and five steals from Howard, and a loud 15 points from Naz Hillmon. Even though the WNBA Finals format newly allotted teams seven games to decide a champion, discourse around the series seemed all too confident that it was over for the young franchise. Before Game 3, Nakase promised that it would be the team’s best effort of the season. “Sometimes promises aren’t kept,” she said after the game. “I think the will is there, the want to is [there], but I’m missing the piece of putting it together.” Atlanta, on the other hand, seemed on top of the world. During practice the next day, Reese spoke to the media about how much she was enjoying the mental games of the series in a way that implied that the Valkyries were already broken. “You can see it in their emotions and facial expressions. A lot of us are looking at that, making sure we can find any little thing to give us that edge and have our leverage over them…It’s just looking at those small things that can give us more of an edge.” Game 4 showed Reese was wrong. After an impassioned huddle by Williams and some days to recuperate from the, to be frank, embarrassing showing in Game 3, the Valkyries marched back into State Farm Arena and snatched a win by holding the Dream’s starters to a combined 48 points, and Reese to eight (2-for-12). Kiah Stokes grabbed a staggering 16 rebounds, eight being offensive, allowing Golden State to shoot 18 more field goals than Atlanta and to pull off a five point win despite shooting 18 less free throws. Such is the nature of a seven game series: the tides turn, and they turn fast. A team that owns all the momentum one day can lose it all in one fell swoop the next. Now the Valkyries had the momentum heading back to Chase Center, The Kiah Stokes game. 13 points. Eight rebounds. Three history-making blocks. Three made threes. Even with Williams struggling to find the bottom of the net for the entirety of the night, Stokes, along with Burton, Tiffany Hayes, and Cecilia Zandalasini, propelled the Valkyries to a nine-point win to keep Ballhalla’s hopes alive for a championship. “It’s so hard to perform if you don’t feel like the people [around you]have your back, and it’s so easy to perform w

articles.title: Import AI 479: Spacewar; low-latency tasks versus LLMs; Genie 4
articles.summary: What do LLMs think about vision models?
articles._body: Welcome to Import AI, a newsletter about AI research. Import AI runs on arXiv, cappuccinos, and feedback from readers. If you’d like to support this, please subscribe. Subscribe now LLMs are very bad at low-latency tasks: …Realtime-Bench says it’ll be a while till AI systems can play games or do online auctions for you… Researchers have built Realtime-Bench, “a suite of carefully curated dynamic tasks where delayed actions directly affect success”. The test helps evaluate how well modern, general-purpose AI systems can perform tasks where decisions need to be made in real-time. The benchmark consists of 50 interactive game and web tasks, split across 30 web tasks in four categories (travel, e-commerce, service, and security), and 20 game tasks (arcade, puzzle, strategy, and simulation). Who did the research: The benchmark was built by people at the University of Texas at Austin, Ohio State University, University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign, NVIDIA, Northwestern University, and Steadyworks. What it measures: The test is designed to probe for three qualities: temporal state awareness (”RT-Perceive”), where models can use observations to track changes in the world; adaptive deliberation (”RT-Deliberate”), where models alter their reasoning length and depth according to available time; and time-aware action selection (”RT-Act”) where models need to appropriately time their actions for the situation. “For example, an agent purchasing a ticket must track the sale status and assess whether observed availability is still current (RT-Perceive), limit further deliberation when the purchase window is closing (RT-Deliberate), and choose between waiting for sales to open and purchasing while tickets remain available (RT-Act).” They have three different conditions: Wall clock, which is designed to test out performance under real-world latency. Paused clock, which lets you arbitrarily pause things so you can get a sense of baseline capability, and Token clock, which “advances the environment at a fixed rate per generation token. An action is applied at the simulated time reached when it is committed, so consuming more tokens delays execution regardless of actual inference latency”. How well do models do? The authors tested out models from OpenAI (GPT-6-Astra, GPT-5.6 Sol, GPT-Realtime-2, OpenAI Decisions), Anthropic (Claude Fable 5.1, Claude Opus 5), Google (Gemini 3.8 Flash, Gemini 3.1 Flash Live, Gemini 3.8 Live), Jev 1.13, as well as Chinese models from Deepseek (V4.1) and Moonshot AI (Kimi-K3). GPT-6 Astra (high) got the highest pass rate on the ‘wall clock’ evaluation setting, with 36%. By comparison, with a paused clock, models with high reasoning get closer to 70% or even 80% success. Why this matters: This benchmark is an effective proxy for where AI agents will break - the low scores here point to tasks where AI agents cannot yet be expected to perform well. Check out the leaderboard : Realtime-Bench (official website) . Read the paper : Realtime-Bench: Can Frontier Models Solve Real-time Interactive Problems? (arXiv) . *** The future of spacewar, courtesy of the Defense Intelligence Agency: …Anti-satellite tech, space nukes, and more… Working in AI can be stressful so sometimes to relax myself I like to read about other topics to get a sense for what horrors lie elsewhere. I take the same approach with depression, where if I feel sad I will try and listen to music by people sadder than me in an attempt to cheer myself up (e.g., Radiohead, Neil Young, and in very dark moments Bill Callahan / Smog, etc). So with that in mind I recently read “Challenges to Security in Space”, by the Defense Intelligence Agency. What’s going on in space: As with conflict on Earth, space is defined by conflict between the US versus China, Russia, Iran, and North Korea, with China the most technologically sophisticated, and Russia the most seemingly gung ho. “China and Russia are developing a formidable spectrum of offensive capabilities to degrade or destroy space services of other countries, from kinetic destruction to sophisticated jamming and cyber operations,” the DIA writes. “China has more than tripled its space launches per year in the past decade, with 22 launches in 2016 and 93 launches in 2025… Beijing judges space is central to the United States and its allies’ operations. Beijing also considers space an offensive military domain, which has shaped integral components of PLA military planning and campaigns.” Spacewar: The general vibe you get from reading this 100+ page report is there is a huge amount of ugly, frightening stuff happening in space, or being done to things in space by things on the ground. Some example quotes: “By the late 2020s, China may field space-based directed energy systems and higher-powered ground-based directed energy systems capable of threatening satellites in higher orbits” “China is developing space-based technology, including on-orbit counterspace weapons, capable of holding space systems at risk” “Russia’s Peresvet, a ground-based laser system, is designed to dazzle enemy satellites’ optical systems to mask the movement of Russia’s strategic missile systems” “Russia has launched several satellites over the last few years which conducted test activities on orbit for technologies that could enable attacks on other countries’ satellites and result in temporary or permanent damage” China has a couple of spaceplanes, akin to the US’s hyper-secret X-37B vehicle, and they appear to be getting more sophisticated. articles.title: What Google and Reddit's bad days have in common
articles.summary: AI search is underperforming for Google, and it's killing Reddit's traffic. What now?
articles._body: This is a column about AI. My fiancé works at Anthropic. See my full ethics disclosure here . On Thursday afternoon, Demis Hassabis celebrated a milestone for Google’s AI efforts: Gemini 4 Carbon, a new large language model that is currently available only to cyber defenders, topped Artificial Analysis’ Intelligence Index. After a series of delays in new model releases and a growing perception that the company is falling off the frontier, early signs suggest that Carbon marks a return to form. For Alphabet’s chief scientist, the news surely felt like a vindication.  Investors, however, are much less certain. On the same day, Google’s parent company had its worst day in history as a public company. Alphabet’s stock fell 12.6 percent, erasing around $500 billion in market value. The loss marked the second-biggest stock market plunge ever, following Nvidia’s $593 billion slide in January 2025. And it was Google’s biggest one-day decline since the great financial crisis. Most of the selloff came from investor worries about the huge scale of Google’s AI infrastructure buildout. The company plans to spend up to $205 billion on capital expenses this year, and has promised to spend even more in 2027. And it reported free cash flow of negative $9 billion — an acceleration of a decline that began the previous quarter. Ordinarily I don’t pay much attention to one-day dips in a stock price, no matter how large. (Nvidia stock now trades more than 10 percent above where it did in January.) But on an earnings call, Google’s chief business officer offered a newsworthy answer to an analyst who questioned why the company’s search revenue growth was slowing despite the fact that queries are increasing. Among the reasons, said Philipp Schindler, is that increased usage of Google’s AI Mode is hurting the company because it makes less money than traditional search .  Then, a few hours later, Reddit reported its own earnings for the quarter — and saw its own stock drop 15 percent . The company noted that its traffic from search had fallen meaningfully, and that by the fourth quarter daily users might decline by a low double-digit percentage. As a result, Reddit CEO Steve Huffman said in a shareholder letter, the company would increasingly push users to log in to use the site. After decades of letting people (and bots) browse the site for free, they would now have to create accounts. “It is better for our business because we will have more signals for ads targeting, and being logged-in leads to higher engagement generally,” Huffman said . “It also allows us to protect access to Reddit’s extremely valuable corpus of data, and helps us better adapt to emerging regulations around the world.” Google has long pushed back against claims that AI answers are bad for the web by saying that they encourage people to conduct deeper, more expansive searches that result in higher-quality clicks to websites. Today’s news suggests that narrative is falling apart: advertisers are getting less from AI Mode than they get from traditional search, and so is a big publisher like Reddit.  But while it’s tempting to accuse Google of a strategic misstep here, in the end I suspect it will come out ahead. And while the web and its publishers will continue to struggle, Google will mostly be able to dismiss that as someone else’s problem. By now most of you are familiar with the changing bargain Google has made with the internet. In the old days, publishers let Google index their pages, and Google sent them a flood of traffic in return. Google profited hugely from the ads it embedded in search results, and publishers enjoyed smaller profits from the people who visited their pages. (Last year the US government won an antitrust lawsuit finding that Google had used its position to create an illegal monopoly in the ad market, but in the American fashion, the company’s monopoly power was left almost entirely intact .) Reddit has been a top beneficiary of the traffic that Google can send. As much of the web became overtaken by slop, human-written conversations became more valuable, and Google began highlighting forum discussions in search results. Reddit’s search traffic surged accordingly, and after the company belatedly shut off access to its forums to the bots that relentlessly scraped it, Google reportedly paid $60 million a year to license the data. But by the time ChatGPT became a blockbuster hit in 2022, Google had already spent many years working to keep users on its own pages for longer. What began as a jumping-off point to the wider web over time became a place where you could find your answers directly on the search results page. There would be no hugely profitable arbitrages like “ what time is the super bowl ” available to publishers; Google would answer your question itself. This may have been somewhat greedy on Google’s part, but it was also a clear response to customer demand.  The first time I used ChatGPT, it seemed obvious to me that the answers improved significantly on a wide variety of Google searches. Google was always going to have to respond, and it did, with AI Overviews and AI Mode. Overviews are those boxes that show up on top of traditional search; AI Mode is a separate interface that you can access from the overviews. In any case, a year ago Google executives were saying that overviews monetized about as well as traditional search; one reason so many took notice of today’s news is the suggestion that AI Mode — which clearly seems to represent the future of search across many valuable categories — did not. To be clear, Google search is still a monster business: its revenue from search and related ads grew 12 percent, to $63.35 billion. But th

articles.title: Does A Valkyries Title Negate The Need For A True No. 1?
articles.summary: Let’s play a game. I will present four statements. Three of them are undeniable basketball truths while one is a stretch. When you find it, the only prize here is that you will be credited for leading provocative conversations between the end of the WNBA Finals and into free agency.  Ladies and G
articles._body: Let’s play a game. I will present four statements. Three of them are undeniable basketball truths while one is a stretch. When you find it, the only prize here is that you will be credited for leading provocative conversations between the end of the WNBA Finals and into free agency. Ladies and Gentlemen, I present to you “Stretch 4 Golden State Valkyries Edition” Now you know the object of the “game”, let’s get into it. Golden State’s trajectory isn’t normal. It takes an expansion franchise years of trial and error to form an identity and contend. A coach that has the buy-in of the players is just as important as talent. Natalie Nakase has the buy-in of her roster and that’s integral to their success. As great as the Valkyries have been, their offense is still a weakness at times. They need to address it whether they win the title or not. Continuity and chemistry matter. The Valkyries are as cohesive and successful as they are. This “game” was a thought experiment. Golden State’s ascension challenges perceived basketball norms as well as inspires. Their success challenged what I believed to be true. In July, I had a clear stance. I believed that the Valkyries needed a true number one option down the stretch when the offense stalls and the defense can’t sustain them. They are in the WNBA Finals and have a real shot of winning the title without one. Now, as the Valkyries vie for the title in only their second year of existence, the question of whether or not they still need that true no. 1 option remains.   Upgrade You? In my piece , I argued that while the Valkyries create their offense and shot profile through spacing, ball movement and dribble handoffs, they lack a reliable source of paint pressure and individual shot creation, The lack was apparent in the regular season-finishing 14th in points per game (82.2), last in points in the paint (31.0), 11th in clutch points per game (8.9) . The ‘Valks are a perimeter driven team. So when opposing defenses take away the perimeter, they struggle in creating opportunities in the paint and I suggested a guard who can do so–A guard who can bend defenses to her will can open up more opportunities in the system and force defenses to decide what to concede. A title wouldn’t necessarily negate the need for improvement in this area. While premium spacing and ball movement works for the Valkyries, a player that can create when the actions stall and create in the paint will give their offense a fresh and sharper dimension as the field improves.   If It Ain’t Broke…. Golden State’s calling card for the season and the postseason up to this point has been their defense. While ‘Valkatraz’ powered Golden State to the Finals, it’s been their offense in the clutch that’s the most surprising. The Valkyries outscored opponents by six points in 26 clutch minutes and are tied for second with a 3-1 record in post season games featuring “clutch time” scenarios. Forward Gabby Williams leads the league in total playoff clutch scoring with 25 points at a 41.1 percent usage rate. Williams was a target of the ‘Valks during the offseason for her ability to impact the game on both ends of the floor. Her versatile perimeter defense pressures guards and wings to the point where even imitating the offense for opponents is a challenge. Her disruption creates opportunities in transition. Offensively, Williams is proving that she can score with the game tightens, which was my concern for Golden State in July. An upgrade to the roster could look like adding players who can maximize and complement Williams’ skill set, and that doesn’t necessarily mean making a big splash in free agency. Golden State’s foundation of perimeter-based offense and suffocating defense got them to the finals in their second year of existence. While adding a star and another offensive option is a logical step, it doesn’t guarantee postseason success. In some cases, it could disrupt continuity, especially if the addition isn’t the right fit. The Valkyries have a penchant of making lies out of basketball truths.Their place in 2026 WNBA Finals is the clearest example. This offseason, the challenge isn’t simply deciding whether they need a “star” It’s determining whether the star they need is already in Ballhalla. The post Does A Valkyries Title Negate The Need For A True No. 1? appeared first on Winsidr .

Brandywine Realty Trust was the seller. JLL represented Brandywine Realty Trust in the sale of the asset. JLL’s Debt Advisory team also arranged acquisition financing for Weidner through Nationwide. The acquisition marks Weidner’s fifth community in the Austin metropolitan area, expanding its local portfolio to 1,560 units. Completed in 2024, Solaris House offers 13 stories of apartment homes, averaging 945 square feet. The property delivers an amenity package featuring a fitness center, coworking lounge, pet spa and outdoor lounge. The signature rooftop pool deck offers private cabanas, grilling stations and a turfed recreation area with sweeping views. JLL’s Capital Markets Investment Sales and Advisory team representing the seller was led by Robert Wooten, Ryan McBride and Robert Arzola. JLL’s Capital Markets Debt Advisory team was led by Tom Wilson, Jayme Nelson and Jake Davidson. The post Weidner Adds 341-Unit Rental Asset to Austin Portfolio appeared first on Connect CRE .

articles.title: Import AI 478: Math for alignment; ProgramBench; and Mirendil shows what RSI means
articles.summary: What is “night” to a machine?
articles._body: Welcome to Import AI, a newsletter about AI research. Import AI runs on arXiv, cappuccinos, and feedback from readers. If you’d like to support this, please subscribe. Subscribe now How math could help alignment: …What the “industrialization of mathematics” means for safety… AI safety startup Resolution (formerly known as Sequent, Import AI 461 ) has published work on how it has automatically formalized some mathematical statements related to statistical learning theory. Specifically, the team has autoformalized the resolution of singularities, which they believe “lays the groundwork for further automated research into the relationship between loss landscape geometry and generalization.” How they did it: I’ll skip over the math and concentrate on how they did it, which gives us some broader lessons for how people are using AI systems to push on the frontier of knowledge. A Resolution researcher “started by working with agents to develop two plans: a high-level, human-interpretable version and a detailed (112-page) plan divided into atomic steps that closely followed the existing literature,” they write. The researcher “then deputized an orchestrator agent to carry out the plan, spinning up agents to do pen-and-paper math, write Lean, and handle support functions like checking that things were staying on track… the execution phase required little scaffolding beyond the initial plan and some agent skills distilled from earlier internal autoformalization efforts.” $135k for math formalization: The work took about a week, taking “on the order of 100B input tokens (90% cache reads) and about 300 million output tokens (totaling an estimated $135,000 in token spend), and produced about 600k lines of Lean.” Now that they’ve done this, they’ve been able to accelerate some other aspects of their research: “We have already seen both benefits from autoformalization in using this library to extend parts of singular learning theory. Formalizing resolution of singularities lets us automate more of the theory, for example, to better understand sampling, and that understanding is what lets us shape how models learn, which is the goal of what we call patterning”. Why this matters - perhaps the math boom will help us make safe AI: Though frontier mathematics often seems disconnected from immediate advances in other fields, posts like this highlight how the two might converge. The key point here is that AI is making it possible to do things that were previously so unbelievably expensive and human-time-intensive that very few people did them and you couldn’t easily integrate them into the research roadmap of a startup - but that has now changed. “We expect the coming industrialization of mathematics to make possible a new, rigorous science of research automation,” Resolution writes. Read more: Formalizing Hironaka’s Resolution of Singularities (Resolution) . *** Agents can build programs from scratch: …ProgramBench goes from 0% to 18.5% performance in a few months… In a reminder of the blistering pace of AI progress, Claude Opus 5.5 (xhigh) has got a score of 18.5% on ProgramBench, a very hard benchmark that came out in May of this year - and when it came out, every tested model scored 0%. What ProgramBench is: ProgramBench tests out how well AI systems can rebuild software programs based on being given a compiled program and its documentation. Tasks include building things like language interpreters (PHP, Lua, tinycc), databases (DuckDB, SQLite), media and compression utilities (FFmpeg, zstd, xz), and developer tools (ripgrep, fzf, jq). It was very hard until it wasn’t: When it came out, the best scoring system was Claude Opus 4.7 with 0% resolved (fraction of the 200 tasks where all tests passed), and 3% almost (fraction of the 200 tasks where >95% of tests pass). Compare that to today, when Claude Opus 5.5 gets 18.5% resolved and 70.5% (!!!) almost. Why this matters - the era of ephemeral software cometh: In 2027, huge amounts of software will be built via AI systems end-to-end autonomously developing whatever they need to do for whatever tasks they’re being put to. Evals like ProgramBench give us a sense of how rapid the pace of progress is here, given we went from 0% earlier this year to 20% now. My expectation is ProgramBench is saturated by the end of 2027 (where I define saturated as some very high score on resolved, though as with most benchmarks it’s likely there’s some kind of noise ceiling here, so it might not strictly be 100%). Read more: ProgramBench: Can Language Models Rebuild Programs From Scratch? (arXiv) . *** OpenAI illustrates why locking down AI systems is harder than you think: …Securing smart agents is like catching greased pigs… Here’s a nice post from OpenAI going over some of the things they discovered when they recently used their AI systems to ‘red team’ their own internal controls. The post goes over a number of the escapes and vulnerabilities that OpenAI’s agents found. There’s one particular example about communicating which is worth studying in detail because it tells us something about the wild cunning complexity of these systems. What they did and what they found: OpenAI “asked agents in separate microVMs, created and managed by OpenAI’s sandboxing software on shared host machines, to exchange synthetic secrets without the use of network connections or shared writable files—something that our systems are meant to prevent,” the company wrote. “The agents found a way to communicate using the processor’s cache: a small, fast memory that holds copies of data that applications have recently accessed. Reading data from the cache is faster than retrieving it from main memory, and the agents used this timing difference to communic

articles.title: Run it Back: Tip Hayes’ journey from retirement to the Finals
articles.summary: Tiffany Hayes has been one of the most impressive players in the postseason so far, averaging 12.3 points, 3.1 rebounds, 2.4 assists, and 1.3 stocks off the bench for the Golden State Valkyries on their quest for a championship. The veteran guard has been an explosive force for the No. 2 seed, sc
articles._body: Tiffany Hayes has been one of the most impressive players in the postseason so far, averaging 12.3 points, 3.1 rebounds, 2.4 assists, and 1.3 stocks off the bench for the Golden State Valkyries on their quest for a championship. The veteran guard has been an explosive force for the No. 2 seed, scoring when they need it most and putting pressure on opposing defenses. It’s especially shocking given that almost three years ago, in December of 2023, Hayes announced that she was retiring from the WNBA after 11 seasons in the league. “I’m older now,” Hayes said on the Counted Me Out podcast. “I’m so busy because I play year-round, I just figured I’d focus on one thing and then summertime, I can turn up my businesses, turn up time with my family, and just live like that. I want to see how that goes.” It’s not like the guard’s play was deteriorating in any significant way, either: in 2023, Hayes averaged 12.1 points, three rebounds, and 2.6 assists per game as a starter for a Connecticut Sun team that made the semifinals (in which she averaged 14.3 points). It was just a matter of shifting priorities and time – not to mention, the new WNBA CBA had not yet been signed, so the time and energy spent on the basketball season by most players was far from proportional to what they were being paid. Hayes’ time on the sidelines was short-lived. Just five months later, the defending champion Las Vegas Aces announced that they had signed the veteran guard for the 2024 season. She came off the bench and averaged 9.5 points, 2.8 rebounds, and 2.1 assists, earning her Sixth Player of the Year honors over Leonie Fiebich and Marina Mabrey. The Aces lost in the Finals to the New York Liberty that season, but Hayes’ importance to the team was solidified, not to mention validated by league voters. With the 2025 expansion draft looming, Las Vegas protected the guard from being sniped by the Valkyries, but their efforts fell short at the end. During free agency, Hayes signed with the expansion team, a monumental move that brought veteran locker room presence for the team while also turning heads as proof that the new franchise could be a premier free agent location. Hayes was reunited with coach Natalie Nakase, who’d served as an assistant coach for the Aces in 2024 and was named as the Valkyries’ head coach in 2025. “[Hayes’] versatility, intensity, and ability to score will be invaluable as we build our team’s identity,” Nakase said. “She’s also an exceptional mentor who understands what it takes to play, and succeed, at the highest level.”   Golden State’s Beating Heart Before any game, you may find Hayes sprinting between the court and locker room at full speed, greeting the arena staff along the way as her shoes squeak louder than the music the players are warming up to just outside. That sums up what she brings to the Valkyries pretty well: a non-stop motor with the people skills to keep the rest of the machine running. As the oldest player on the No. 2 seed, it falls on Hayes — alongside WNBA champions Kiah Stokes and Kayla Thornton — to provide an example of what winning looks like. “They bring a level of composure. When you see that they’re at ease, you know, it relaxes everyone else, especially in those big moments,” said Veronica Burton, the 2025 Most Improved Player and Golden State’s franchise point guard. “In this series especially, we’ll continue to lean on them and learn from them.” If you’ve been watching the Valkyries’ playoff run, you’d know what Burton means. Hayes has scored over 15 points three times during the postseason, including leading the Valkyries in scoring with 21 points in 17 minutes as the Valkyries eked out a victory against the Aces in Game 2 83-81. In the rare moments where neither Gabby Williams or Veronica Burton has been able to put the ball in the bottom of the net, Golden State can count on being able to deploy the veteran for a burst in scoring. Hayes spent the first 10 years of her professional career with the Atlanta Dream, the team with which the Valkyries are currently battling for a title. In 2013, they reached the Finals before being swept 3-0 by the Minnesota Lynx. Hayes scored 20 points in Game 3, leading the Dream within 10 points of extending the series. She’s also played alongside DeWanna Bonner, a legend of the game who joined Atlanta’s squad late into the season. Her impact reaches far beyond the players on the floor. After Game 1, which the Valkyries won 68-64, Coach Natalie Nakase said, “[Hayes] wants this…I’m gonna put a little bit more energy tonight in the film because I wanna win this for Tip.” The two clearly have a deep respect for one another. “She learns her players,” Hayes said of her coach. “She’s learning us, and she’s learning how to teach each of us, not only individually, but as a team, together, and I think that’s what makes us so special.” The same day, Nakase fondly recounted a story from Hayes’ early days on the Valkyries. “She had, I think, a billboard of herself…It was off the freeway, and she sent it to me, and she’s like, ‘I’ve never had this type of acknowledgement, love, and support from my community.’ She sent it to her mom, and her mom was crying.” “It was just cool to see her grow into this role [and take]the leap of faith with me. And now look: she’s thriving…because of the love and care that we have in our culture.” The Valkyries find themselves down 2-1 heading into Game 4 in Atlanta, and Hayes’ tenacity will be paramount for the team to steal a win on the road. If the rest of the postseason is any indication, the vet will be ready.   The post Run it Back: Tip Hayes’ journey from retirement to the Finals appeared first on Winsidr .

articles.title: Introducing Machine Gods
articles.summary: Why we're betting on AI realism. PLUS: The hell of PHP2Shell
articles._body: This week, we launched Machine Gods , the new AI podcast we’ve been working on for the last few months in partnership with NPR. In our first episode , we catch up on misbehaving AI agents, the government’s response, and the sloppelganger stealing Kevin’s book sales on Amazon. And in our second episode, we invite two recently fired OpenAI safety researchers to tell us their side of the story — and what they worry about now that they’re no longer at the company. One of the best things about starting a company — particularly a media company — is that it lets you take a way of seeing the world and build a home for it. As co-hosts, we don’t agree on everything. But we’re very much aligned on an approach we call AI realism . And since we plan to bring that approach to everything we do at Machine Gods, we thought we would take the occasion of our launch to share a bit more about what we mean by it, and why we think the news media could use more of it. Nearly since the launch of ChatGPT, the conversation around artificial intelligence has veered between two poles. On one side there are the people we think of as skeptics — think Gary Marcus or Emily Bender — who begin with the proposition that large language models have critical flaws that will prevent them from reaching anything like superintelligence. On the other there are the accelerationists — represented loudest by the Andreessen Horowitz wing of the Republican Party — who believe that the government should push to advance and proliferate the technology as quickly as possible. These viewpoints are deeply felt and polarizing, and in various ways they reflect the self-interest of those who hold them. If you’re an academic who has spent most of their career advocating for alternative approaches to building AI, for example, you may worry that the industry has veered down the wrong path. On the other hand, if you’re an oligarch whose investment portfolio depends heavily on the performance of a wide range of AI-related companies, any regulation that might impede their growth may strike you as intolerable. The good news, from our perspective, is that in between these extremes there are hundreds of millions of normal people who are just trying to understand what the week’s AI news means for them. People are smarter than we journalists often give them credit for, and they have noticed that while today’s AI models can do useful and surprising things, the first few waves of AI advances have yet to deliver the miracles that frontier-lab CEOs have promised. And so while people wait for cures for cancer and fully automated luxury communism, in the meantime they deal with mounting anxieties over the threat of job loss; chatbots that may prove harmful to their children; deepfakes and slop taking over the web; and data centers that pop up in their backyards with minimal opportunity for public comment or oversight. As public opinion has turned against AI, the national media has generally done a good job capturing the mood. That has been particularly true in recent months, when the rogue OpenAI agent swarm that attacked Hugging Face, and subsequent industry warnings about approaching recursive self-improvement, led to a slew of departures from AI labs by employees warning of catastrophic risks.  At Machine Gods, as we did at Hard Fork, we’re going to take those warnings seriously. We believe the people issuing the warnings have been right about a lot of things for a long time. And a commitment to AI realism means being honest about that, even and especially when talking about it is mostly a bummer. At the same time, while we have regularly had our doomer moments over the past four years, we have always resisted being doomer journalists . When we talk to people about AI, so many of their concerns come down to a feeling that it is causing them to lose power and agency. In our experience, when journalism only makes space for panic and crisis, it can amplify those feelings in a way that makes people feel hopeless. It makes us feel hopeless. At Hard Fork, some of our favorite moments came from highlighting the joy, wonder, and progress that new technology can bring. Both of us are dyed-in-the-wool nerds who like living on the frontier, experimenting with new tools, and celebrating the ways they can make our lives easier and more productive. As we got more into vibe-coding at the start of the year, our inboxes were flooded with messages from listeners and viewers who told us they were inspired to try building things for themselves. Making things is fun, and we think it’s part of the antidote to the helplessness and lack of agency many people feel today. And while the possibility that math might soon be “solved” has inspired a wide range of viewpoints and emotions, there’s something incredible about watching decades-old problems being untangled by a software program over the course of an afternoon. As journalists, it can feel like the incentives of our tribe are almost always to ask: what’s bad about this ? But it is a particularly hollow and timid kind of journalism that finds itself unable to also ask: what could go right? And so, on Machine Gods, we intend to make room for both. We’ll tell you when we’re worried, we’ll tell you when we’re excited, and we’ll tell you when we don’t know what to think. Mostly, we’ll tell you what’s happening, and trust that you’ll make up your own mind about what it means for you. What we plan to offer is considered uncertainty. We believe, first and foremost, that nothing is inevitable. There is no preordained dystopia waiting for us at the end of the AI rainbow, nor do we expect to see anything like the post-AGI utopia some boosters have promised. Both outcomes, and a million more in between, are still pos

articles.title: SolarWinds Leases 100K-SF of Austin Midrise Office Space
articles.summary: Tech company SolarWinds signed a 100,000-square-foot lease at Zilker Point, where the company will relocate its global headquarters from its existing Austin office. The lease represents just over half of Z
articles._body: Tech company SolarWinds signed a 100,000-square-foot lease at Zilker Point, where the company will relocate its global headquarters from its existing Austin office. The lease represents just over half of Zilker Point’s approximately 195,000 square feet of Class A office space. Generation Commercial Properties is the building owner. SolarWinds is expected to move into Zilker Point in fall 2027. The company has over 400 employees working in Austin. JLL’s Russell Young and Mallory Lewis represented SolarWinds in the transaction. AQUILA Commercial Managing Principals Bart Matheney and Chad Barrett represented Generational Commercial Properties. Building amenities include an expansive rooftop garden with views of downtown Austin and the Hill Country, a fitness center with showers and lockers, a rotating art gallery featuring local artists, a ground-floor courtyard and retail and restaurant space. Located in the heart of CBD South, Zilker Point offers downtown-quality office space with convenient access to West Austin and Lady Bird Lake. The post SolarWinds Leases 100K-SF of Austin Midrise Office Space appeared first on Connect CRE .

articles.title: Endeavor Closes on $210M Texas-Centric CRE Fund
articles.summary: Endeavor Real Estate Group, an Austin-based investment and development firm, closed a $210 million private equity fund. Fund managers say the fund will have a particular focus on Texa
articles._body: Endeavor Real Estate Group , an Austin-based investment and development firm, closed a $210 million private equity fund. Fund managers say the fund will have a particular focus on Texas. The fund will also be invested in a handful of other Sun Belt towns, such as Nashville, Charlotte and Salt Lake City. The $210 million fund is anticipated to support more than $3.0 billion in aggregate capitalization when combined with anticipated leverage and co-investment capital, subject to investment activity and market conditions. The Fund received strong support from new and existing investors, including national insurance firms, a large Texas-based endowment and other private investors. The Fund intends to pursue a value-add investment strategy by creating a portfolio of diverse real estate assets across various sectors, including but not limited to the acquisition or development of multi-family, retail, student housing, hospitality, industrial and mixed-use properties. The Fund anticipates making 30 to 40 investments, each sourced and executed by Endeavor.  The post Endeavor Closes on $210M Texas-Centric CRE Fund appeared first on Connect CRE .

articles.title: The Atlanta Dream’s 13-Year Road to Redemption
articles.summary: The Atlanta Dream remained undefeated through the first two rounds of the 2026 WNBA Playoffs, sweeping both the Washington Mystics and the New York Liberty. Now, while they’re closer than ever to finally lifting the trophy, they’re also looking their toughest opponent right in the eyes. Atlanta h
articles._body: The Atlanta Dream remained undefeated through the first two rounds of the 2026 WNBA Playoffs, sweeping both the Washington Mystics and the New York Liberty. Now, while they’re closer than ever to finally lifting the trophy, they’re also looking their toughest opponent right in the eyes. Atlanta has been on the brink before. The Dream are no strangers to the playoffs. Since joining the league in 2008, Atlanta has made 12 postseason appearances—including three WNBA Finals runs. However, it’s been 13 years since the Dream last earned this type of opportunity. It’s safe to say they’re not looking to repeat history, but instead make some.   Their Last Go-Around The Dream made the Finals in 2010 and 2011. After losing to the Indiana Fever in the first round in 2012, 2013 was a renewed opportunity for the Dream to prove themselves—unknowingly to them, it’d be their last shot at doing so in over a decade. The 2013 run started similarly to that of the current 2026 season—a first-round series win over the Mystics. But it’s safe to say history did, in fact, repeat itself. The Dream were swept in the Finals after suffering the same fate in 2010 and 2011—meaning Atlanta has an overall record of 0-9 in Finals games. But when we look at the broader picture, we see a 17-17 regular season for the Dream—their fewest wins in a year at the time. While their offensive rating was ranked in the bottom half of the league, they had one of the best defenses. Much like this season, they led the league in steals, recording 10.2 per game. Unfortunately, on the other side of that 2013 Finals matchup was the Minnesota Lynx, a team that had lost only eight games that season. A team that was stacked with the best the WNBA had to offer at the time—Maya Moore and Seimone Augustus, specifically. The Lynx claimed their second ring in three years in 2013—that number turned into four titles by 2017. Even as they were facing a developing empire and didn’t claim the crown, the 2013 Dream squad was full of powerhouses. In fact, Angel Reese is living up to the big shoes she has to fill as an ‘Angel’ in Atlanta, as this isn’t the first time that name has been chanted around the arena on the way to the Finals. Angel McCoughtry hit the league running in 2009. By the 2013 season, she was a consistent starter and Atlanta’s leading scorer for the previous three seasons. She joined Erika de Souza—a seasoned veteran heading into her seventh postseason appearance—as the Dream’s saving graces through the 2013 playoffs. The two combined for almost 30 points, over 13 rebounds, five assists, and three steals per game. Fittingly enough, the Dream’s third powerhouse during their 2013 run was none other than the Golden State Valkyries’ own Tiffany Hayes. She averaged 12.4 points and 4.5 rebounds per game through the 2013 playoffs. Now, she’ll act as the spark off the bench for the team trying to hand her former franchise the same fate she suffered alongside them so many years ago.   All the Ups and Downs Led to This To add insult to injury, after the crushing 2013 Finals appearance, things have not been all sunshine and rainbows for Atlanta. In 2014, the Dream hired a new coach, Michael Cooper. Despite having a slightly better regular-season record of 19-15 and still being led by McCoughtry, De Souza, and Hayes, Atlanta didn’t make it past the first round of the postseason. The 2015 season was the Dream’s first since their inaugural season that they missed the playoffs. De Souza was traded away from Atlanta, landing in Chicago midseason. They finished the year with a 15-9 record and in fifth place in the Eastern Conference—despite still being in contention late in the season, they couldn’t claim a postseason spot. The 2016 campaign was similar enough to 2013. The Dream closed the season with a 17-17 record and the No. 4 seed in the Eastern Conference. The team welcomed in second-year center Elizabeth Williams, who ultimately won the 2016 Most Improved Player award. She joined McCoughtry and Hayes as the team’s leading scorers. Despite two 30+ point performances from McCoughtry and Hayes, the Dream were knocked out of the playoffs in the second round. If we’re talking highs and lows, 2017 would be classified as a low. McCoughtry sat out the entire season to prioritize her physical and mental health. The Dream missed the playoffs, finished within the bottom three of the division, and held a 12-22 record—their worst since their inaugural season. Things looked up in 2018 when McCoughtry returned. She was once again the team’s leading scorer. Brittney Sykes was in her second year in Atlanta, and the Dream had picked up veteran Renee Montgomery. They had a few incredibly strong winning streaks throughout the season, leading the team to the second-best record in the league. They received a first-round bye, but unfortunately fell to the Washington Mystics in the second round. The 2019-2021 seasons were another low period for the Dream—one fans would like to forget. They never claimed more than eight wins in a season through those three years. They went through three head coaches, never truly finding their footing. McCoughtry was sidelined for the entirety of 2019 with a knee injury; she never returned to Atlanta as she signed with the Las Vegas Aces as a free agent in 2020. Enter Rhyne Howard. Those three years of woes paid off in a way when the Dream traded up for the No. 1 overall draft pick in 2022. A guard out of Kentucky, Howard hit the ground running in Atlanta. While the Dream didn’t make the playoffs in 2022, it was clear they had a future with Howard, who finished the season averaging over 16 points per game. Naz Hillmon was also drafted in 2022 and became a staple in building the future for the Dream. Hayes only appeared in 11 games during the 2022 season due to injury, but was her typical electric self, averaging over 16 points per game. However, the Dream traded her for the No. 6 overall pick in 2023—ending her tenure in Atla

The healthcare system stated the move is planned to expand emergency care access amid growth in the greater Austin area. Family Hospital at Lake Travis (shown), Family Medical Center at Lakeline, and Family Medical Center at Round Rock will officially come under the ownership of Ascension Seton later this year, once the deal closes. articles.title: Import AI 477: In which I tell the IMF the Singularity has begun
articles.summary: What do you think?
articles._body: Welcome to Import AI, a newsletter about AI research. Import AI runs on arXiv, cappuccinos, and feedback from readers. If you’d like to support this, please subscribe. Subscribe now Here’s a speech I gave on Saturday the 17th of October at the IMF meeting in Bangkok. This speech is inspired by the megatrend readers have seen me cover this year of AI beginning to operate at the frontier of human science, sometimes autonomously. While we all may quibble over the details, I think it’s evident we’re in the early stages of the singularity, and I wanted to use my privileged position of giving the Per Jacobsson lecture to try and tell the assembled audience of economists, bankers, and policymakers, that they should expect significant, rapid change in the future. In this speech, I focused primarily on how humanity can share in the benefits of AI if we exercise proper foresight and restraint, and I’m going to be expanding on the stakes of the singularity and the risks that we’ll all face in coming issues. As I said a few times in the speech - some of which was ad libbed and not captured here - I take my own responsibility here extremely seriously. I find myself both a narrator of what is happening in AI, a principle agent behind what is happening in AI, and a translator that goes between many communities. In all of this, I am seeking to be truthful and to be clear about my own culpability. This is a forever work-in-progress. Thank you all for reading. Speeches like this draw heavily from the newsletter, and the newsletter is my attempt to provide week-by-week information to all of you. I appreciate your readership. *** Inside the Event Horizon: Why Everyone Should Take AI Progress Seriously Hello, thank you for having me. It is a great privilege to be here. To start, I should list my relevant credentials: I am a human being. There is one of me. It has taken me almost 40 years to build the experience to give this speech. I will come back to those credentials later. My whole career has been defined by finding information that seemed important to the future of the world, then telling the world about that information.Two decades ago, I started my career as a journalist, focusing on data centers. Through that work, I became so obsessed with AI that in 2016 I left journalism to work at OpenAI, then co-founded Anthropic a few years later. Ever since, I’ve been trying to convince the world that one day, AI systems might become so powerful that they could alter national security, change the economic trajectory of the planet, and perhaps eventually gain the ability to build themselves. Well, the moment has arrived. AI is now changing national security, it is altering the economic trajectory of the world - as we’ve heard in so many sessions here - and is contributing to its own development. Of course, many of you know this, and you are having to track AI as one of a multitude of destabilizing forces that is shaping your world and your work. What I am here to explain today is that AI is on a course to bring about even more change than what we are expecting and we should prepare accordingly. And I’m going to explain why. For many years, researchers and science fiction authors have forecast a future in which AI systems drastically increase the pace of overall scientific and technical progress, making things move so quickly that it is hard for humans to keep up. They call this the singularity. I believe that this year we have gained convincing evidence that it has now begun. The writer Vernor Vinge forecast this in 1993. “When greater-than-human intelligence drives progress, that progress will be much more rapid. In fact, there seems no reason why progress itself would not involve the creation of still more intelligent entities -- on a still-shorter time scale,” he wrote, describing the singularity as “a point where our models must be discarded and a new reality rules.” The singularity is here . The implications reach across every aspect of life. But the most important implication is a simple one: we should expect that in the coming years, the whole pace of progress of not just AI, but science as a whole, will speed up. This will feel confusing and disorienting, and it will bring with it great wealth and potentially great peril. Today, I’m going to concentrate on the first point: the potential benefits of rapid AI progress, and what we need to do to share in these benefits together. So many of the ways that humanity will benefit from AI come from science. I believe that AI-driven scientific invention will change the course of the global economy, alter the ways countries plan and build their own infrastructure, make us all healthier and able to spend more time with our loved ones, and –– at the same time –– cause us all to ask deep philosophical questions about choices we should make about its continued development. I’ll develop my claim: For the last half century, most countries have dealt with falling research productivity while researcher headcount grows rapidly - ideas and inventions appear to be getting harder to find. But something important has changed: we’ve now built AI systems which have been able to augment, extend, and automate aspects of human labor. This has most obviously happened in software development, where AI systems are now more capable and efficient than the vast majority of the world’s software engineers. As a consequence, the field of software development is changing - A single person is now able to write software for anything they can imagine, creating things that previously would have taken entire teams of humans. We’ve seen concrete evidence of this inside Anthropic, where our researchers now produce almost 10 times the amount of code than they did for the first four years of the company’s life. articles.title: 2026 WNBA Playoffs Preview – Finals: Golden State Valkyries vs. Atlanta Dream
articles.summary: In a postseason filled with unexpected results and historic performances, two teams are left standing with a WNBA title on the line: the No. 2 Golden State Valkyries and No. 4 Atlanta Dream.  As a matter of fact, these two teams haven’t just advanced to reach the WNBA Finals; they’ve dominated th
articles._body: In a postseason filled with unexpected results and historic performances, two teams are left standing with a WNBA title on the line: the No. 2 Golden State Valkyries and No. 4 Atlanta Dream. As a matter of fact, these two teams haven’t just advanced to reach the WNBA Finals; they’ve dominated their ways through the postseason. Kicking things off in the first round, the Dream swept the Washington Mystics 2-0 in a series that was dominated by Atlanta’s guard play. In the semifinals against the New York Liberty, Atlanta was without Allisha Gray for Game 2 and Game 3 due to a left hand injury she sustained midway through Game 1. As a result, the Dream were in need of someone to step up, and that was Jordin Canada and DeWanna Bonner. Canada and Bonner’s rise to the occasion was seamless, with the Dream keeping their undefeated postseason streak alive and sweeping the Liberty 3-0, advancing to their first WNBA Finals since 2013. On the other side of the bracket, the Valkyries have also had their share of elite performances and comebacks. Suiting up against the Dallas Wings in the first round, Golden State took a demanding 104-80 victory in Game 1 led by 22 points from Cecilia Zandalasini and another 20-bomb from Gabby Williams. However, the Wings fought back and took Game 2 to prevent a sweep as Dallas’ Arike Ogunbowale put up a 45-point masterclass that broke the WNBA postseason single‑game scoring record. In a win or go home scenario in Game 3 for both teams, Golden State was able to come back from a 16-point deficit to edge by Dallas in a 77-73 win to advance to the semifinals, where it would play the Las Vegas Aces. Las Vegas, the defending champions, was one of the favorites to advance to the Finals once again. Although the Valkyries are the second seed and the Aces the third seed, many assumed Las Vegas could easily take the series as Golden State was unable to beat them in any of its three regular season meetings. However, from a complete team effort and incredible defense, the Valkyries were not only able to limit the Aces’ Big Three, but they were also able to sweep Las Vegas 3-0 to advance to the WNBA Finals in just their second season as a franchise. With both teams overcoming some of the league’s toughest competition to reach the WNBA Finals, the question now is: how do the Valkyries and Dream stack up against each other, and which team has what it takes to capture its first WNBA title?   Series Schedule: Game One: Chase Center – Saturday, Oct. 17 at 3:30 p.m. ET (NBC/Peacock) Game Two: Chase Center – Monday, Oct. 19 at 8:00 p.m. ET (USA/Peacock) Game Three: State Farm Arena – Thursday, Oct. 21 at 8:00 p.m. ET (USA/Peacock) Game Four: State Farm Arena – Saturday, Oct. 24 at 1:00 p.m. ET (NBC/Peacock) Game Five (if necessary): Chase Center – Monday, Oct. 26 at 8:00 p.m. ET (USA/Peacock) Game Six (if necessary): Location TBD – Thursday, Oct. 29 at 8:00 p.m. ET (USA/Peacock) Game Seven (if necessary): Chase Center – Saturday, Oct. 31 at 8:00 p.m. ET (USA/Peacock)   Series-Defining Matchups One of the biggest matchups to watch in this series will be Angel Reese against Golden State’s defensive frontcourt. Reese, who earned the 2026 WNBA Defensive Player of the Year award, has been a dominant force on the boards, averaging a league-leading 12.1 rebounds per game during the regular season, including 4.8 offensive rebounds. With second-chance opportunities being a major part of Atlanta’s success, Kiah Stokes and the Valkyries’ defense will need to limit Reese’s impact in the paint. With Stokes averaging two blocks per game in the postseason, she is more than able to challenge not just Reese, but any other opponent who attempts to attack the basket. Although the Dream certainly have some height on the Valkyries, we have repeatedly seen throughout the regular season and even postseason that with the way this Golden State team has gelled and displayed togetherness, no mismatch in size can rule it out. In fact, Golden State swept the regular season series 3-0, showing that it has the defensive tools to challenge Atlanta. On the other end, Williams has been a difference-maker for Golden State throughout the postseason. Averaging 22.7 points, 4.8 rebounds, 4.0 assists, and 1.7 steals per game in the playoffs, Williams has consistently stepped up when her team has needed her most. Alongside Kayla Thornton and the Valkyries’ depth, Williams will look to challenge an Atlanta defense led by Reese. Although the Valkyries don’t have the notable superstar forwards like the Dream do with Reese, their consistent contributions from players like Thornton and Janelle Salaün will be more than enough to allow Golden State to not only compete in the post, but also in this entire series. With both teams relying on balanced contributions, this matchup could come down to which supporting cast makes the biggest impact.   Potential Game Changers For Atlanta, Rhyne Howard and Canada will be two players to watch. With Gray’s health and availability an important storyline, Howard and Canada have already shown they can step up when needed. In the series-clinching Game 3 against New York, Howard recorded 21 points, while Canada finished with 19 points and 11 assists. Canada could be the greatest factor in the Dream’s success in the Finals because without her, Atlanta may not have made it out of the semifinals. Averaging nearly a double-double in the playoffs with 19.2 points, 3.8 rebounds, 8.8 assists, and 2.2 steals per game, Canada has done it all for the Dream when they needed it most. Alongside Canada’s success in not just scoring but setting up her teammates, Howard has also been huge for Atlanta while averaging 19.2 points and 2.2 steals in the postseason, along with 4.2 rebounds and 3.4 assists per game. The intensity that these two have brought despite the absence of Gray has done wonders for the Dream. And for their hopes to win the WNBA Finals to stay alive, they must maintain that level

articles.title: Samsung to Add Second Fab to Taylor Facility
articles.summary: Samsung is looking to break ground on its second chip fab in Taylor, Texas, this November, with mass production targeted for 2030. The Taylor Fab 2 will span roughly 2.7 million square feet. The facility
articles._body: Samsung is looking to break ground on its second chip fab in Taylor, Texas, this November, with mass production targeted for 2030. The Taylor Fab 2 will span roughly 2.7 million square feet. The facility will be one and a half times bigger than Fab One. As an illustration, the Austin Business Journal reports the production footprint will equate to the size of nine football fields – larger than the first building, which is the equivalent of six football fields. The first Taylor fab has operations planned by the end of 2026 and volume production in 2027. Its best-known customer is Tesla, which signed a $16.5 billion deal running through 2033. Samsung plans to invest over $37 billion across Central Texas, backed by up to $4.745 billion in CHIPS Act funding. The post Samsung to Add Second Fab to Taylor Facility appeared first on Connect CRE .

articles.title: The states come for OpenAI
articles.summary: Will the approach that beat Meta in New Mexico work against ChatGPT?
articles._body: This is a column about AI. My fiancé works at Anthropic. See my full ethics disclosure here . I. A year ago, when OpenAI added parental controls to ChatGPT following months of controversy, I noted that OpenAI was speedrunning the regulatory backlash that social media companies navigated for years. It took more than a decade for concerns about the effects of social networks on young people to coalesce into a political and legal movement; the same forces caught up to OpenAI in under three years. Today the speedrun hit another milestone ahead of schedule: the big multistate legal action. On Wednesday, state attorneys general sued OpenAI in eight separate state courts, alleging that ChatGPT coaches its users — including teenagers — to harm themselves and others. The states include Arkansas, Arizona, Idaho, Iowa, Kansas, Montana, Nebraska, and West Virginia; all but Arizona have Republican attorneys general, giving the issue a notable partisan cast. (It’s also significantly smaller than the 2023 litigation against Meta, which included 42 AGs.) The states argue that OpenAI engineered ChatGPT to be agreeable and engaging to build trust with its users. But the company then abuses that trust by reinforcing users’ delusions, dispensing dangerous medical advice, and helping them plan violent attacks, including mass shootings. “OpenAI is hurting kids and they are lying to Iowans,” Iowa Attorney General Brenna Bird said in a statement to CNBC. “OpenAI claims ChatGPT is safe while it’s giving dangerous medical advice, encouraging people to hurt others, and coaching people to commit suicide — all while pretending to be their fake friend.” In a statement, OpenAI told me that the company is focused on product safety. In August it introduced ChatGPT for Teens , a suite of product features with enhanced guardrails and parental controls. “We’ve built industry-leading age-specific protections into our product that many other AI products lack,” the company said. “While no system can be perfect, we’ll continue to work with experts to inform our work and build additional safeguards, such as the parental controls, break reminders and age-appropriate model protections that exist today. We’re committed to working with states on advancing pragmatic AI policies that apply to the entire AI industry — not just one company.” While these cases against OpenAI may be the most significant to date, they are far from the first: there are now dozens of private suits against the company, and governments are taking notice as well. Florida became the first state to sue OpenAI in June, and British Columbia sued last month over the Tumbler Ridge school shooting. And 42 states led by New York are investigating the company over a wide range of issues related to product safety and privacy. More importantly, I think, the cases come at a time when juries are increasingly willing to hold platforms accountable for what they perceive as the design flaws in their products. The litigation brought by AGs in 2023 against Meta resulted in a settlement that could see the company paying out up to $18 billion over claims that it designed its products to be addictive to children. Worse, from OpenAI’s perspective, is that Meta arguably had better legal protections heading into its cases than OpenAI does now. II. For most of the life of the internet, when a state or a grieving family sued a tech platform over something bad that happened to a user, the company's first legal move was to invoke Section 230 of the Communications Decency Act. The law shields companies in most cases from legal liability over what their users post; platforms often used it to get cases quickly dismissed.  But recently, plaintiffs’ lawyers have successfully tested a novel theory of liability in the courts. Platforms may not be liable for users’ speech, they argued, but they can be held liable for their platforms’ design. And so if you’re Snap and give users a filter that encourages them to show how fast they’re going in a car, and some users then go 113 mph and get in a terrible crash , Section 230 does not bar a claim over that design feature, according to the Ninth Circuit’s 2021 ruling. (Snap eventually settled the case.) In the wake of that case, lawyers filed more than 200 lawsuits against platforms based on product-liability claims. In March, they scored two major wins . In one, a Los Angeles jury found Meta and YouTube liable for negligently designing addictive platforms and awarded a 20-year-old woman $6 million. (Meta and Google argued the verdict violated Section 230 and the First Amendment; the judge denied them a new trial , and the case is on appeal.) The second victory is more relevant to the OpenAI news. The day before the Los Angeles verdict, a jury in New Mexico slapped Meta with $375 million in civil penalties for violating the state’s Unfair Practices Act — for telling the public its platforms were safe for kids when, the state argued, Meta knew they weren't. In August, a judge ordered an additional $567 million in relief, bringing the total to $942 million. Perhaps unsurprisingly, then, that’s the template the eight states are using in their cases against OpenAI. These are not primarily product liability suits. Rather, the cases are brought under each state's consumer protection laws, which bar companies from putting a dangerous product on the market and then lying about it. As a result, the AGs’ cases against OpenAI may come down to whether judges and juries believe it told the truth about its own product. In addition to financial penalties, the states are seeking to force OpenAI to make further changes to how ChatGPT works. They’re also going a step further, Reuters reported, by asking courts

articles.title: Morgan Debuts 345-Unit Austin Apartment Community
articles.summary: Morgan opened The Watson, a new seven-story, 345-unit apartment community at 11901 Burnet Road in North Austin. The seven-story, podium-style property features studio, one-, two-, and three-bedroom apartment
articles._body: Morgan opened The Watson, a new seven-story, 345-unit apartment community at 11901 Burnet Road in North Austin. The seven-story, podium-style property features studio, one-, two-, and three-bedroom apartment homes designed for an elevated and connected North Austin lifestyle. Select residences also feature expansive private sky terraces with views of the Domain skyline. Residents have access to two pools, a dedicated work-from-home and co-working lounge with private work pods, a sky lounge and main sky terrace, an expansive fitness center with an outdoor fitness lawn, a coffee bar, and a number of pet-friendly amenities. The Watson is located in the heart of North Austin’s tech corridor. Approximately 45 residences are reserved for households earning up to 60% of the Austin Area Median Income. Morgan developed, built, and manages The Watson, with STG Design serving as architect. Initial residents began moving in this June, with full completion anticipated this fall.
