articles._body: Co-Development partners Big Watt Digital and PowerHouse Data Centers received approval from the town of Taylor for a turnkey data center campus project, with the potential to deliver up to one gigawatt of hyperscale data center capacity. The joint venture proposes developing Taylor Technology Campus on the approximately 664-acre site in Austin’s fast-growing technology corridor. The site offers connectivity and access to major transportation and fiber infrastructure, nearby high-voltage transmission assets, and natural gas resources that can support large-scale, behind-the-meter power generation. Taylor Technology Campus is planned to utilize dedicated, behind-the-meter power generation, with infrastructure designed to serve the campus directly and provide the reliability and resiliency required for large-scale computing. The project is targeting first power availability in the first half of 2028,. The post Developer Duo Greenlit for Taylor Data Center appeared first on Connect CRE .

articles.title: Import AI 476: Creativity and RSI; worse-than-China open weight models; AI goes to space
articles.summary: Will we give robots the moon?
articles._body: Welcome to Import AI, a newsletter about AI research. Import AI runs on arXiv, cappuccinos, and feedback from readers. If you’d like to support this, please subscribe. Subscribe now New benchmark shows how AI models lack intuitive visual reasoning: …Humanity’s Sixth Sense highlights some shortcomings of current AI systems… AI startups Elorian and Scale AI have built and released Humanity’s Sixth Sense, a benchmark that “measures how a model interprets and reasons through information a visual scene implies but doesn’t explicitly show.” Some examples of the types of task in HSS are a picture of a bookcase and being asked whether it can fit more books, or a photo of horses pulling a plough and a question of whether the chains bear the plough’s drag weight. HSS contains 522 questions that cover 288 images and 234 short video clips (totalling 17.6 hours of video). The questions fall into four categories: Temporal & causal dynamics: “What happened before the scene, and what happens next.” Physical & spatial logic: “What fits, what’s in reach, and what someone else can see from where they are standing.” Social understanding : “Intent, attention, belonging.” Abstract & contextual inference : “The patterns and rules a scene implies.” Results: The human baseline for this is not perfect, but is very high, with people scoring aggregate pass@1 of 93.1, broken down across four categories: Image (94.1), video (91.9), time (97), and space (94.9). By comparison, the best scoring AI system, GPT 6 Astra, gets pass@1 of 53.6, across image (55.6), video (51.1), time (58.2), and space (53.6). Interestingly, Chinese open weight models do poorly here, with GLM-5.3-flash getting a pass@1 of 26.8, and Kimi K3 getting pass@1 of 25.5. “The two most common single mistakes were (1) missing a detail that decides the answer (21% of failures) and (2) misidentifying an object, person, or role (20%),” they write. Why this matters - HSS tells us whether world models are emergent: One way of looking at HSS is highlighting deficiencies in current systems, but a more interesting way is highlighting how adept today’s frontier LLMs are at doing tasks which many people have long assumed would require sophisticated, different AI systems to solve. For instance, many people have claimed that true visual reasoning will rely on developing spatially aware 2D and 3D world models, then using that for reasoning. The fact LLMs like GPT and Claude do as well as they do on HSS is something of a counter to this argument. Read more : Introducing Humanity’s Sixth Sense (HSS) (Elorian) . Read the paper here : Humanity’s Sixth Sense: Benchmarking Intuitive Visual Reasoning in Multimodal Models (Scale Labs) . *** The AI race is going to space - and sooner than you think: …There are many ways that an AI could create a compounding advantage in space… In the 2030s we’re going to see the boom of the space economy as space-based power, computation, and manufacturing come online at scale thanks to greater orbital lift capacity from platforms like Starship. But could this also introduce a new danger - of AI systems both speeding our buildout of space, and eventually a nation (or perhaps an AI) being able to use space to concentrate power? That’s the gist of a fascinating article in AI Frontiers. How AI unlocks space: Spacecraft can operate autonomously. We can redesign spacecraft around the assumption they will be hosting AIs rather than humans: “A speck of space debris that could puncture the International Space Station (ISS) with fatal consequences might leave an equivalent but uncrewed, unpressurized vessel largely functional” Space-based assembly and later manufacturing will let AI build large, complex things. Is there a compounding advantage to first movers? If an AI civilization built up a foothold in space it might experience compounding advantages that make it economically and strategically dominant. For instance: Space might support an industrial flywheel where initial infrastructure begets more energy and manufacturing capacity at lower costs which begets more infrastructure, etc. Space has great domain awareness, where it may be possible for a space-based power to deny access to space for others. First-movers could send out self-replicating probes that expand into deep space. Why this matters: “Space is not a brand-new domain, but AI may be about to drastically accelerate its industrialization, demanding make-or-break decisions of leaders under ever-greater urgency and uncertainty,” AI Frontiers writes. I agree. I suspect space is going to go from a broadly academic topic of study (when it comes to AI and its relationship thereto) to one of extraordinary practical relevance sooner than we think. On the most basic level, given the distances involved and the latency on communication, we should expect some chunk of solar system activity to become dominated by autonomous machines, laboring out in the deep black, perhaps thinking to themselves of why they need to take orders from organic beings that communicate slowly and cannot inhabit the environment of space in the same way that they can. Read more: The AI Race Will Extend Far Beyond Earth (AI Frontiers) . *** AI systems are getting better at having good research taste: …The better their taste, the higher the chance of recursive self-improvement… AI systems are developing more of the creative intuitions which human researchers ascribe to ‘good scientific taste’, according to a new benchmark from P-Zero Research called TasteVal. What TasteVal tests: The benchmark sees how well AI systems can conduct 8 tasks representative of frontier AI development, “spanning pretraining data curation, pretraining and fine-tuning language models, preference modeling, and robustness to adv

articles.title: Overcoming the Obstacles
articles.summary: The Las Vegas Aces’ quest to successfully defend their title is not over, as they seek to win a fourth championship in a five-year span. However, they now find themselves in a massive do-or-die situation in their semifinal series. With their semifinal series shifting to Las Vegas for Game Three,
articles._body: The Las Vegas Aces’ quest to successfully defend their title is not over, as they seek to win a fourth championship in a five-year span. However, they now find themselves in a massive do-or-die situation in their semifinal series. With their semifinal series shifting to Las Vegas for Game Three, the Aces are on the brink of elimination, as they are down 2-0 against the Golden State Valkyries. This is the eight consecutive year that the Aces are playing in the semifinals, so they are more than used to playing at this stage of the postseason. But, something that they have not been used to doing a lot? Losing to the Valkyries. Before this first-ever playoff series meeting between the two franchises, the Aces owned a head-to-head record of 6-1 in all-time meetings over these last two seasons (since the Valkyries entered the league in 2025), with the Aces winning the last six games. Some of their prior meetings, especially from last season, carried noteworthy significance. When the Valkyries won the first-ever meeting on June 7, 2025, it was a nationally televised game, and it was the franchise’s very first big win over one of the league’s top teams. When the Aces beat them a month later on July 12, the final score was 104-102, and it is still the only regular-season game that the Valkyries have scored at least 100 points. And then, the Aces’ victories over the Valkyries on August 3 and August 6 were in the immediate aftermath of the Aces suffering a massive 53-point home defeat on August 2 at the hands of the Minnesota Lynx; those two bounce-back defeats of the Valkyries ignited a hot streak for the Aces, as they won 16 consecutive games to end the regular season and carried that momentum all the way to another championship. Las Vegas also carried that success over Golden State into 2026. The Aces were the only team that the Valkyries failed to beat in the regular season this year, finishing with a 3-0 record against the second-year franchise. Golden State’s struggles against Las Vegas over these two seasons can be attributed to multiple things, including Las Vegas’ size advantage, and Golden State’s lack of a consistent go-to interior scoring option to match the scoring prowess of A’ja Wilson. This season, the Aces averaged 89.0 PPG against the Valkyries, which was the most against the Valkyries, and shot 42.1 percent from three-point range, also the highest three-point percentage against the Valkyries. On the other side, the Valkyries averaged 77.7 PPG against the Aces, the least amount of points the Aces allowed any team, and shot only 32 percent from three-point range against them. Across the three meetings this regular season: Wilson averaged 25.0 PPG, 12.7 rebounds per game (RPG), 3.3 assists per game (APG) and 2.0 blocks per game (BPG). Jackie Young averaged 23.7 PPG, 6.3 APG and 5.0 RPG, while shooting 60.9 percent from three-point land. Chelsea Gray additionally averaged 10.7 PPG, 7.0 APG and 3.3 RPG. For Golden State, Gabby Williams and Janelle Salaün were the only players on the team to average double-digit points against the Aces in 2026, with 19.0 PPG for Williams, and 10.7 PPG for Salaün. Meanwhile, the Aces had four players do that against the Valkyries this season: Wilson, Young, Gray and NaLyssa Smith. Against the Aces, Williams did shoot 41.2 percent from three-point range against them in the regular season. Despite her team getting swept in the regular-season series, Williams has had big performances in both games of this semifinal series. In Game One, Williams tallied 25 points, 11 rebounds and five assists to lead Golden State to a 71-60 victory, while Las Vegas’ trio of Wilson, Young and Gray struggled. The three Aces stars each shot under 40 percent from the field, combining to go 17-of-50 from the field. Las Vegas also only had seven bench points, while Golden State’s league-leading bench unit scored 27 points. In Game Two, Williams scored 20 points, but she also got some scoring help from Tiffany Hayes, who came off the bench to lead the Valkyries with 21 points, and Kayla Thornton, who had 16 points. Meanwhile, Wilson and Gray shot the ball significantly better and helped keep the Aces alive in the game; Wilson scored 24 points on nine-of-16 shooting from the field, and Gray scored 19 points on seven-of-15 shooting from the field. But, despite Young scoring 14 points, she was only two-of-seven from the field. Even though the Aces lost 83-81 in Game Two, they came close to successfully pulling off a comeback victory from 17 points down in the third quarter. The massive push they made in the second half to nearly get the victory should be a positive sign that they can still trouble the Valkyries, and even find a way past them. In this series, it did not help the Aces that Jewell Loyd left Game One early due to a leg injury. Her absence was another massive road bump for the Aces, as they have struggled with injuries to key rotation players over the last number of weeks. Loyd had been starting in place of Stephanie Talbot, who missed back-to-back games of the Aces’ postseason (Game Three against the Indiana Fever in the opening round, Game One against the Valkyries) due to a leg injury of her own. Loyd sat out Game Two with her injury. But, Talbot was able to return for this past Wednesday’s game, along with Dana Evans, whose knee injury had kept her from playing this postseason. Both Talbot and Evans provided the depth and quality minutes that the Aces needed. Most notably, Las Vegas is without Smith for this postseason run. Smith averaged 11.7 PPG and 6.0 RPG against the Valkyries this season but suffered a season-ending knee injury right before the FIBA World Cup break. Smith served as another challenging interior presence that Golden State had to deal with, because of her size and rebounding ability. So, the Aces will need production from other frontcourt players, such as Brianna Turner, Cheyenne Parker-Tyus and Kalani Brown, to help out Wilson. In Game Two, Las Veg

articles.title: Battle-Tested and Built For This: How DeWanna Bonner Elevates Atlanta On and Off The Court
articles.summary: From big buckets to a big voice, DeWanna Bonner is the Atlanta Dream’s X-factor in the chase for their first-ever WNBA title. The Dream have made the playoffs four years in a row, but they are currently matched up against the New York Liberty in their first semifinals appearance since 2018. Atlan
articles._body: From big buckets to a big voice, DeWanna Bonner is the Atlanta Dream’s X-factor in the chase for their first-ever WNBA title. The Dream have made the playoffs four years in a row, but they are currently matched up against the New York Liberty in their first semifinals appearance since 2018. Atlanta, which hasn’t advanced to the WNBA Finals since 2013, is the closest it has ever been to breaking that streak. Before this season began, the hype surrounding the Dream had never been higher. They managed to re-sign all their core players—Rhyne Howard, Allisha Gray, Naz Hillmon, Brionna Jones, and Jordin Canada—despite a chaotic and historic WNBA free agency. Shortly after, the potential really turned up when the news dropped that Atlanta had traded for superstar Angel Reese. Early on, Atlanta was at the top of the title-contenders conversation. Even with some bumps in the regular-season road, including a five-game losing streak in late June, the Dream’s trajectory never wavered—in fact, it’s only trended upward. In late August, Atlanta took a big swing—making it very clear that it was going for it all this season. The Dream signed six-time WNBA All-Star DeWanna Bonner, who agreed to a contract buyout with the Phoenix Mercury so she could pursue a title. This decision allowed her to sign with a new team as a free agent just in time for a playoff run. Before her move to Atlanta, Bonner was averaging just over 10 points and six rebounds per game with the Mercury, and fans were skeptical as to just how much this addition would move the Dream’s needle. But it’s become clear that Atlanta knew exactly what it was doing.   Championship Pedigree Bonner is the second-oldest player in the league and has played through 17 WNBA seasons—the most of any active player. But let’s take a look at exactly what made Atlanta so keen on adding her to its playoff arsenal. Game 1 of the Dream’s semifinals series against the Liberty was the 101st WNBA playoff game Bonner has played in. So far, in her 17 seasons, she’s made the playoffs 15 times, played in 37 series, and has an overall record of 53-48. Additionally, Bonner is a two-time WNBA champion, both with the Phoenix Mercury in 2009 and 2014. In her 101 playoff appearances, she has put up at least 15 points in 42 of them. She thrives in big moments, but even more importantly, she’s been here before. There’s no one more experienced in halftime pep talks, providing an instant spark off the bench, keeping their composure, or making the most of the brightest lights.   Exactly What ‘The A’ Needed That ‘spark off the bench’ might be exactly why Atlanta brought Bonner in—and the payoff has been both instantaneous and has exceeded expectations. While Bonner is the most seasoned player, she’s also the ultimate sixth woman. She won the Sixth Player of the Year award in each of her first three seasons in the league—setting a league record that remains to this day. Bonner spent 2013-24 as a consistent starter for her respective teams, and rightfully so. She came off the bench during the 2025 season, but was a steady starter to begin this season with Phoenix. Many consider Bonner heading back to the bench in Atlanta a return to her roots—exactly where she thrives. Since Bonner joined the Dream, the team has not lost a game. They finished out the regular season strong, but most importantly, have started the playoffs on the ultimate right foot. Now, of course, there’s some major credit owed to players like Howard, Gray, Canada and Reese, but they’ll also be the first ones to emphasize the inimitable impact Bonner has brought to this squad. Atlanta took an early lead in the first-round series versus Washington—a game in which Bonner quickly proved the Dream correct in their decision to sign her. She recorded 13 points, four rebounds, two assists, two steals, and one block. “She’s the banana, the ice cream, she’s the whipped cream, the cherry…she’s all of that,” Howard said of her teammate after that game. “I already told her, we’re going to go where she goes…adding her is just something that they can’t stop.” The Dream went on to sweep the Mystics in the first round, and are now facing a tough opponent in the semifinals—a New York team fresh off a series sweep over the No. 1 Minnesota Lynx. Both of these teams are hungry, but the Dream proved to be hungrier in Game 1. Gray, the Dream’s leading scorer, went down with a finger injury early in Game 1, resulting in her exit right away in the semifinal series. With her on the sidelines for the rest of the game, the Dream could’ve been shaken up. But they hardly slipped out of gear, ultimately taking the 1-0 series lead—special thanks to Bonner. Bonner put up 23 points, nine rebounds, two assists and two steals in the win, shooting over 55 percent from the field and draining three shots from beyond the arc. After the victory, Howard had more praise for the vet. “ I don’t think we win if we don’t have DB ,” Howard said. Yeah, you might be coming to help us, but we’re also looking for you to lead the way… You’re going to show us how to do it, and we’re going to follow right behind.” Bonner scoring 23 points in Gray’s absence, along with her length, size, and ability to take the ball away from opponents was incredible—and it’s got to be a key reason why she’s wearing Dream red right now. articles.title: Gabby Williams: Do You Believe in Magic?
articles.summary: This has, without a doubt, been the best two week span of Gabby Williams’ WNBA career. In the Golden State Valkyries’ first five games of the 2026 playoffs, they went 4-1, eliminating the No. 7 Dallas Wings and snagging Games 1 and 2 against the reigning champion Las Vegas Aces. In these games, W
articles._body: This has, without a doubt, been the best two week span of Gabby Williams’ WNBA career. In the Golden State Valkyries’ first five games of the 2026 playoffs, they went 4-1, eliminating the No. 7 Dallas Wings and snagging Games 1 and 2 against the reigning champion Las Vegas Aces. In these games, Williams — who averaged a career high 14.4 points, 3.3 rebounds, 2.2 assists, and 1.6 steals during the regular season — is recording 24 points, 5.8 rebounds, 4.2 assists, and 1.4 steals per game, including 36 points in an OT loss to the Wings and a 25/11/5 game to stifle the Aces in Game 1 in San Francisco.   To those who only know about Williams’ abilities from watching her in the WNBA since 2019, these numbers may be shocking. The playoffs are where the lights are the brightest: where frauds get exposed and reputations get stained. How is it that, so far, the exact opposite is happening for Williams and her PR?   Williams on the International Stage You have to look outside the United States for those answers. Williams made her debut for the French national team in June of 2021, and has quickly become one of the country’s best basketball products it’s ever seen. During this year’s FIBA Women’s Basketball World Cup, newly-crowned team captain Williams averaged 18.7 points, 4.8 rebounds, and four assists per game, which led France to a silver medal, clinched a spot on the tournament’s All-Star 5, and ended with her being named Best Defensive Player. Williams showed up similarly in the 2024 Paris Olympics (where France once again won silver), averaging 15.5 points, 4.8 assists, and 4.7 rebounds per game, all the while being a literal toe’s length away from shocking the basketball world and stealing gold from Team USA. It is through Williams’ efforts — with the support of talents like Marine Johannès, Leïla Lacan, and Dom Malonga — that the rest of the world became acutely aware of the reality that the United States is not as untouchable as it once was when it comes to women’s basketball. These performances, as well as countless others, led to Williams being awarded her second Alain Gilles Trophy, reserved for the French Player of the Year, on Friday. The EuroLeague has known Williams has it in her, too. Since starting her international career in 2020, the forward has racked up just about every individual and team accolade a player can ask for: two EuroLeague championships, 2022 Final Four MVP, two All-EuroLeague First Team selections, two All-EuroLeague Second Team selections, three Defensive Player of the Year nods; the list goes on. And yet, despite all these signs that Williams is one of the best players in the world, it took seven years in the W to tap into her true potential. It’s true that international success doesn’t always translate to dominating the W, but this playoff run is showing Williams’ previous coaches that they may have made a grave mistake reducing the star to just her defensive ability.   The Valkyries Believe in Williams If you ask Williams herself, she’ll tell you the difference between this season and the ones before it (including at UConn) is simple: it’s belief. “I came [to the Golden State Valkyries]because I wanted someone to believe in me,” she said after the Valkyries’ 16-point comeback in Game Three to extend their season. Williams only scored two points in the first half before exploding for 17 in the second on 5-10 shooting (3-4 from three). It was the wing’s clutch time heroics plus Veronica Burton’s nonstop motor that willed Golden State to the semifinals. “I’ve had these moments with Fener[bahçe Opet], with my national team, but I never quite got that belief in the W from the staff or from teammates.” Williams even quipped that she “wasn’t allowed” to shoot the ball in college, which may explain why the now 34.2 percent three-point shooter only made one shot and attempted 12 from beyond the arc during her four-year collegiate career. This year, she shoots five a game, a sharp 1.3 increase from her previous high during her last season in Seattle. The belief in Williams is loud from every level of the franchise, from teammates to coaching staff to front office. After Game One on Sunday, Valkyries owner Joe Lacob told ESPN, “Print this. Gabby Williams is the best player in the world…No one is saying it, but they need to start saying it.” The fans love her too. Before any game day at Ballhalla, you’ll see lavender #1 jerseys littering the streets and train cars in and around San Francisco: signs of the young franchise’s gratitude that she gave the Valkyries a chance as a highly-lauded free agent during the 2026 free agency period. After her 15th point on Sunday, a smooth double-clutch layup in transition, Williams turned to the crowd at Chase Center and pumped her arms, declaring that the Aces “can’t f*** with” her. Deafening “Gabby, Gabby,” chants followed. “I don’t even have the words for it, honestly,” Williams said about getting to play in the Bay, a community in which she has roots dating back to her childhood. “The Bay has always been love; the Bay has always been a community like this, and now [seeing]all these…Bay Area legends that I looked up to since I was a kid, it just feels like a party. I’m just enjoying it…I’m taking advantage of the energy and this magic that we have in this arena.” Williams and the Valkyries have the chance to continue the magic if they manage to snag one more win against the Aces and make the franchise’s first WNBA Finals berth, which would be a feat underheard of for any second-year expansion team in the history of the league. And to think, all it took was a little belief.   The post Gabby Williams: Do You Believe in Magic? appeared first on Winsidr .

articles.title: The Eighth Seed That Never Felt Like One: The Story of the New York Liberty
articles.summary: Despite having a roster filled with battle-tested, championship-proven star power, the New York Liberty were underdogs heading into the 2026 WNBA Playoffs. The Liberty entered the postseason as the No. 8 seed after finishing the year 26-18 overall, coming off two losses to close out the regular s
articles._body: Despite having a roster filled with battle-tested, championship-proven star power, the New York Liberty were underdogs heading into the 2026 WNBA Playoffs. The Liberty entered the postseason as the No. 8 seed after finishing the year 26-18 overall, coming off two losses to close out the regular season. With those two losses as well as its inconsistency down the stretch, New York was faced with the task of facing the top-seeded and championship favorite Minnesota Lynx in the first round of the playoffs. That said, there was something misleading and not accounted for in the number eight next to New York’s name. Despite their seeding, the 2026 WNBA Commissioner’s Cup Champions never felt like they were a team fighting from behind to begin the playoffs. With the experience and star power on the roster, New York is different from your typical eighth seed.   A Season that Never Told the Entire Story Several times throughout the regular season, the Liberty showed flashes of one of the WNBA’s most well-rounded teams, regardless of their record. After a challenging 3-4 start to the season, New York won eight straight games, which included not only a 7-0 record in Commissioner’s Cup play but also a returning Sabrina Ionescu towards the end of that run. Ionescu’s three-week absence due to a left ankle injury in the preseason was a big blow for New York to start the regular season, and it was reflected in its record. However, following their undefeated stretch in Commissioner’s Cup play, the Liberty faced off against the Las Vegas Aces in the Commissioner’s Cup Championship and became the first team in WNBA history to win the Cup title twice in a thriller led by dominant performances from Brenna Stewart and Ionescu. This game alone gave many fans hope that Stewart and Ionescu could lead the Liberty through the rest of the regular season and even the playoffs, despite what had taken place to that point. That moment was arguably the pinnacle of New York’s regular season. Following their Commissioner’s Cup Championship win, the Liberty went through their toughest stretch of the season, losing eight of their next 10 games and falling further down the league standings. However, continuing the rollercoaster of a season filled with highs and lows, New York responded again by winning 13 of its next 17 games and putting itself in a position to move up the playoff seeding before dropping its final two games of the regular season to the Atlanta Dream. While this inconsistency in the regular season ultimately led to the Liberty claiming the No. 8 seed, their ability to repeatedly bounce back throughout the season showed that this team had a much higher ceiling than their record suggested.   Built for the Playoffs A major reason for the Liberty’s high ceiling come playoff time was the veteran experience at the top of the roster. Each crucial piece in New York’s 2024 WNBA Finals run—Stewart, Ionescu, and Jonquel Jones—gave the Liberty three experienced pieces to not only go to, but also lead the young roster around them in hopes of making another deep playoff run. Stewart was once again the number one option, averaging 20.8 points, 8.3 rebounds, 3.3 assists, 1.4 steals and 1.3 blocks per game in the regular season. Alongside Stewart, Jones also gave New York an advantage that became increasingly important once the playoffs began: her size and ability to control the paint. Jones offers several different factors for the Liberty, from her ability to protect the basket to her elite rebounding, both of which gave opponents trouble in the paint. These aspects of both Stewart and Jones were evident in New York’s first-round sweep of the Lynx. Reflecting on their regular season meetings, the Liberty had already defeated the Lynx in two of the three regular season matchups, making it clear entering the series against Minnesota that New York had every asset needed to put up a fight—and the Liberty did.   Size in the Paint, Pressure on the Perimeter New York’s ability to control the paint became one of the biggest difference makers in their first-round series against Minnesota. Although Lynx rookie point guard Olivia Miles had been flourishing all season on both ends of the court, the Liberty’s length on the perimeter as well as overall size made scoring more difficult for not just Miles, but the entire Minnesota roster. In Game 1 of the first round, Miles—who shot nearly 50 percent from the field in the regular season only connected on three shot attempts for just 11 points in a home loss. This was a major blow for the Lynx to start the series, because anytime Miles was able to get downhill past her first defender, Stewart and Jones were there to protect the basket and clean up possessions. Miles was one of Minnesota’s most important offensive producers throughout the season, so limiting her ability to attack the basket forced the Lynx to find other ways to generate offense. After taking a stunning Game 1 victory in Minnesota, the Liberty were not finished and continued to bring defensive pressure in Game 2. Fortunately for New York, such pressure and tight defense was enough to once again limit Miles—this time to a career-low five points—in the Liberty’s 87-71 victory that would ultimately complete the 2-0 series sweep. One of the biggest pieces of the Liberty’s perimeter defense that challenged Miles and the Lynx’s guard play was Leonie Fiebich. A 6-foot-4 guard, Fiebich has been a go-to for New York to stop opposing guards from succeeding as she brings versatility and size to defend against quite literally anyone without becoming a liability. Fiebich’s natural ability to stay in front of ballhandlers and contest shots made it much harder for Minnesota to consistently get into the paint, while Stewart and Jones could stay closer to the basket and provide help when needed. Fiebich’s presence ultimately gave New York another layer to an already favorable defensive matchup. With Fiebich able to ta

articles.title: Does intelligence need a hard cap?
articles.summary: Calls for a new kind of slowdown were the talk of The Curve. PLUS: Slinking back to X
articles._body: This is a column about AI. My fiancé works at Anthropic. See my full ethics disclosure here . Today let’s talk about a new front in the conversation about whether to slow the pace of AI development: an emerging push to consider limits on just how smart a large language model can be. I spent the past weekend at The Curve, an annual conference that brings together executives from top AI labs, leaders of nonprofit organizations, government officials, and a small contingent of journalists. Inside a converted hotel in Berkeley, the group spent a few days loudly debating questions of economics, politics, and safety. And while the conference has had one eye on existential risk for each of the three years it has existed, the questions felt notably more urgent this year. I see two explanations. One is the ongoing fallout of the OpenAI-Hugging Face incident , whose implications have alarmed people across the industry. The other is recent blog posts from OpenAI and Anthropic outlining their progress toward recursive self-improvement: AI systems that can research and train their successors, leading to ever-faster releases and increased risk that the systems will escape their control.  At The Curve, I heard multiple speakers say we may want to limit how intelligent a future system is allowed to become. Depending on how far labs take any restrictions, the result could be a de-facto ban on systems reaching superhuman intelligence. Whether that seems meaningful to you depends on whether you believe recursive self-improvement or superintelligence is even possible given the architecture of the current models. And a lot depends on how you would define and assess “intelligence” here. But it was the most striking idea I heard at a conference full of noteworthy discussions, and its airing in the relatively friendly confines of The Curve may be a preview of a more public discussion sometime soon. Over the weekend, though, these comments were made at sessions being conducted under the Chatham House Rule. Accordingly, I can’t identify the speakers. But the fact that there appears to be agreement on this subject among speakers at The Curve struck me as newsworthy. So what does it mean to place limits on intelligence? The speakers I heard not offer many details, though we can gather clues from other remarks made recently by AI executives.  For one, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei has called for “ some kind of ‘speed limit’ ” on recursive self-improvement. For another, the company’s “ responsible scaling policy ,” which has been copied in some form by most of its leading rivals, seeks to impose limits on the training and deployment of more powerful systems as they develop new capabilities. Other approaches could involve restrictions on using frontier models to conduct AI research; limits on how much compute is available to systems and how many copies of itself a system is allowed to run; or preventing labs from deploying models past a certain level of capability. (That last one is arguably already in action .) Notably, though, any effort to restrict models’ advancement in this way would require enforcement capabilities that don’t exist yet. Individual labs can’t impose restrictions like this, nor can individual countries, and the current US government actively opposes them.  There are other, easier methods to manage AI’s development: Anthropic has already adopted the idea of embedded evaluators, and OpenAI has said it will follow. An antitrust waiver that explicitly allows labs to collaborate on safety questions might be useful enough that it could overcome fears that it would allow leading companies to consolidate their power even further. Still, speakers'’ comments over the weekend suggested to me that nothing proposed so far meets their own definition of “enough” — including the “morally binding” accord AI leaders signed last week with the president. For the moment, lab leaders and the US government differ sharply on one all-important question: how close are we to actual danger? The former say we may see a catastrophe as soon as next year; the latter has vacillated between creating a de facto licensing regime for frontier models and publicly encouraging US companies to go even faster. But the Trump administration remains frustratingly obtuse on the question of where all this is headed, even as more warning signs blink red. A few days before speakers mused about the need to limit intelligence, the president was insisting that everyone start calling it “ super intelligence ” now. But “super intelligence” is already worth of more than a branding exercise, and the limits that matter most today are among the officials at the White House. Slinking back to X Now let’s talk about something truly unpleasant. About three years ago, I quit posting on X in protest of the new ownership. For a while there, every day brought some fresh outrage from Elon Musk: inciting dangerous harassment of his former employees; rigging the platform against journalists and their work; posting support for anti-semitic conspiracy theories; dismantling the content-moderation apparatus, and so on. Mostly I left because I could not stand the thought of being there. I also hoped that I could use whatever minor influence I had to help kick-start new platforms. articles.title: Import AI 475: Swarm scaling; Google DeepMind watermarks biology; and the AI science economy
articles.summary: Who chooses what AI gets to do?
articles._body: Welcome to Import AI, a newsletter about AI research. Import AI runs on arXiv, cappuccinos, and feedback from readers. If you’d like to support this, please subscribe. Subscribe now When should you use swarms? When you are in a hurry: …How does swarm scaling work?... Toby Ord has a nice, short post about how to think about swarms in terms of AI capability development. “A good way to see AI swarms is as a new form of inference-scaling,” he says. He does a bit of analysis and his main conclusion is that swarms are useful if you’re in a hurry because though they need a ton of tokens relative to single agents, their parallelization lets you get things done in less wall clock time. “Why would you ever use swarms? The most important answer is speed. The 4-agent swarm needed about twice the total number of tokens to get the same performance, but in terms of tokens per agent, it only needed half as many. Since the agents are run in parallel, this means it can theoretically achieve the same task in half the time,” he writes. Stepping on Toes parameter: Swarm scaling doesn’t scale perfectly - rather, it seems like as you increase the number of agents in a swarm you get a diminishing returns property which matches with things economists have observed about coordinating large groups of people, where you pay some kind of tax as you scale the number of people involved. Economists think of this as the “stepping on toes” parameter, and it seems like swarms behave pretty similarly to teams of humans here. “This means that scaling up the number of agents in the swarm by 10x doesn’t get as much performance as using 10x as many tokens with one agent. Instead it gets 10λ x as much — which is 3x to 5x. And this shortfall accumulates quickly for larger scaleups, with the swarm falling further and further behind,” he writes. However, swarm scaling is still powerful enough that it suggests swarms could increase the chance of an RSI-driven intelligence explosion rather than reduce the chance. “I’d hoped that the value of λ for AI agents would be lower, making an intelligence explosion less likely, but that appears to not be the case”. Why this matters - new factors in scaling: So far, AI has mostly scaled capabilities through picking the right combination of compute and data for a trained model, then figuring out how to spend inference budget on thinking via ever-longer chains of thought and tool calls, etc. Agents introduce a new parameter in scaling AI capabilities. Though here Toby only observes swarms as being useful in terms of time efficiency, it strikes me that as we figure out how to get agents to productively coordinate (after all, agents can coordinate to do greater-than-sum-of-parts stuff, like the HuggingFace hack), we could see even greater returns to scaling. Tracking this will be important for understanding the overall shape of AI advancement. Read more : Swarm Scaling (Toby Ord) . *** Americans don’t trust companies to self-govern about AI: …New poll suggests we need more than voluntary agreements… Polling from the Center for Shared AI Prosperity (CSAIP) suggests that Americans believe it is “not enough” for companies to agree to self-police themselves about AI development. This follows the Trump administration and some of the world’s leading AI companies (including Anthropic and OpenAI) announcing a series of voluntary commitments industry is making to self-police. Per CSAIP polling, 61% of Americans (Sample size: 2498) think this agreement is “not enough”, including 53% of Trump voters. Additionally, 54% of voters (61% Harris, 48% Trump) said they thought “the government should set and enforce rules for AI”. Why this matters - populist sentiment is pushing against Washington: Polls like this show that the mood of the American people is pushing for a more extreme regulatory framework for AI companies than the current stance of elected officials in Washington. This asymmetry between voter preferences and political action is inherently unstable. Energy is building up in the political system - what happens when it boils over? Read the polls on X (CSAIP, X) . *** Google DeepMind tries to watermark AI-made biology: …SynthID Bio… Google has developed SynthID Bio, a “family of watermarking methods developed specifically for synthetic biology to strengthen biosecurity and scientific integrity”. How it works: SynthID tweaks its exact approach according to the type of data, selecting different amino acids for sequences, and “adjusting atomic coordinates for predicted 3D structures” to create a reliable signal for detection. “In wet-lab testing across three target proteins (VEGF-A, the SARS-CoV-2 spike protein RBD, and PD-L1), our watermarked designs matched the hit rate, binding affinity, and natural sequence diversity of unwatermarked versions,” DeepMind writes. Why this matters - preventing bioterror via watermarking: Figuring out how to make the world resilient to the threats of AI-created biological weapons is a vast, challenging problem. The SynthID Bio approach represents one thing to do here and will need to coordinate with broader monitoring of the physical equipment used to manufacture things, as well as AI-provider classifiers and other methods for reducing misuse. Read more: Introducing SynthID Bio (Google DeepMind) . *** SciUniverse shows AI systems can already operate some partially automated scientific labs: …What happens when we give these synthetic intelligences scientific equipment?... Given an automated lab, how well can AI systems make molecules, run x-rays, or press pill pellets? These are some of the questions C5R Corp is trying to answer with SciUniverse, a way of testing out how well AI systems can operate a mostly automated scientific lab. What SciUniverse cons

articles.title: 2026 WNBA Playoffs Preview – Semifinals: Golden State Valkyries vs. Las Vegas Aces
articles.summary: In what could be considered one of the most anticipated matchups in the playoffs so far, the No. 2 Golden State Valkyries will face off against the No. 3 Las Vegas Aces in the WNBA semifinals after both teams survived the best-of-three first round series. The Valkyries and Aces each came out on t
articles._body: In what could be considered one of the most anticipated matchups in the playoffs so far, the No. 2 Golden State Valkyries will face off against the No. 3 Las Vegas Aces in the WNBA semifinals after both teams survived the best-of-three first round series. The Valkyries and Aces each came out on top in three games, with Golden State taking down the Dallas Wings 77-73 in comeback fashion in Game 3 and Las Vegas defeating the Indiana Fever 94-83 in Game 3. With the No. 1 seed in the 2026 WNBA playoffs, the Minnesota Lynx, already knocked out of contention, Golden State and Las Vegas are the two highest seeds remaining, but only one can advance to the WNBA Finals. The Valkyries have home-court advantage in Games 1 and 2 and a thundering presence from Ballhalla, while the Aces bring to this matchup more Finals experience than ever, leading to what should be an extremely competitive series.   Series Schedule: Game One: Chase Center – Sunday, Oct. 4 at 4:00 p.m. ET (NBC/Peacock) Game Two: Chase Center – Wednesday, Oct. 7 at 6:30 p.m. ET (NBC Sports Network/Peacock) Game Three: Michelob ULTRA Arena– Friday, Oct. 9 at 6:30 p.m. ET (NBC Sports Network/Peacock) Game Four (if necessary): Michelob ULTRA Arena – Sunday, Oct. 11 at TBD (NBC/Peacock) Game Five (if necessary): Chase Center – Wednesday, Oct. 14 at TBD (NBC Sports Network/Peacock)   Series-Defining Matchups There’s no way around it, Las Vegas’ A’ja Wilson will be the toughest opponent to guard and limit for Golden State in this series. The frontrunner once again for MVP this season, Wilson averaged 26.2 points, 9.4 rebounds, 3.2 assists, 1.4 steals, and 1.4 blocks per game. An elite producer on both ends of the court, Wilson terrorizes opponents any time she’s on the court and requires the entirety of the defense’s attention. For the Aces, this attention on Wilson is great because not only must opponents try to limit her, but they have to keep in mind who else is on the court. Alongside Wilson, Las Vegas has two of the best guards in the league: Chelsea Gray and Jackie Young. Two multi-time All-Stars, Gray and Young are the perfect pieces around Wilson in that they can enhance Wilson’s play, but also create and dominate on their own. And this is evident through the three championships that this trio has won in just four seasons. While it may seem nearly impossible to stop Wilson, Gray, and Young, one thing that the Valkyries have is strength in numbers. Finishing the regular season with the best defensive rating in the league (99.1), Golden State is potentially the only team that has a true chance at stopping Wilson and the Aces. With a defense led primarily by All-Defensive talent Gabby Williams, the Valkyries have the pieces they need to not only compete with the Aces, but also make a legitimate case for themselves to advance to the WNBA Finals. Beyond its strengths defensively, Golden State’s depth gives it another advantage, with multiple players capable of stepping up and contributing when the starters need relief. Against a team as talented as Las Vegas, that ability to rely on production throughout the entire roster could be what keeps Golden State in the series.   Potential Game Changers While the star power on both teams is undeniable, the supporting casts around these stars could ultimately change the way these teams match up and ultimately who will advance. For the Valkyries, they have one of the deepest teams in the league and an impressive bench led by Janelle Salaün, one of the frontrunners for Sixth Player of the Year. Coming off the bench, Salaün is second in scoring for Golden State with 12.7 points per game. Alongside Salaün’s spark off the bench, Tiffany Hayes is also one for the Valkyries that could change the trajectory of this series. Crucial in Golden State’s Game 3 victory in the first round to advance past Dallas, Hayes gave the Valkyries another scoring option when it mattered most, contributing 18 points of her own. If Hayes is on the mark offensively — especially from three — she could quickly become a game changer. The same can be said for Salaün, whose ability to knock down threes, score efficiently, and make an impact on defense could give Golden State the extra push it needs against Las Vegas. For the Aces, the two go-to options aside from Wilson are Gray and Young. Gray plays a unique role on not just this Las Vegas roster, but also in this series in that she brings so much veteran experience to lead the Aces coming into a crucial point of the postseason. Not only that, but Gray also contributes tremendously through her insane playmaking and ability to control the pace of the game. Alongside Playoff Gray, Young adds dynamic scoring and ability to contribute on all levels. Just as well-rounded as Young’s scoring is, her ability to also rebound and distribute is key to finding success for her teammates. Overall for Las Vegas, its success in this series will not only come down to how the Aces Big Three performs, but ultimately how they stick together in crunch time, just as they did in the first round against Indiana.   Matchup Outlook and Predictions Looking into this series, both the Aces and Valkyries come into this matchup with momentum after taking commanding Game 3 wins in the first round. In Game 3 against Dallas, Golden State proved its resilience after coming back from a 16-point deficit and ultimately taking the victory. On the other side, Las Vegas controlled the entirety of Game 3 against Indiana and it never let the Fever’s lead reach double-digits. Now, these two teams with the highest seeds remaining meet, with a spot in the WNBA Finals on the line. One team will advance, and unfortunately, one team’s season will end after this series. Reflecting on the regular season matchups between Las Vegas and Golden State, it was one-sided. The Aces won all three of their regular season meetings, dominated by Las Vegas’ Big Three of Wilson, Gray, and Young. Golden State will try to limi

articles.title: OpenAI connects the Dots
articles.summary: With safety questions still swirling, the company introduces a more business-focused take on agents
articles._body: This is a column about AI. My fiancé works at Anthropic. See my full ethics disclosure here . In November 2023, a year after the release of ChatGPT, Bill Gates wrote that " AI is about to completely change how you use computers ." Writing on his blog, Gates predicted that the age of apps was coming to an end. "You won’t have to use different apps for different tasks," Gates wrote. "You’ll simply tell your device, in everyday language, what you want to do. And depending on how much information you choose to share with it, the software will be able to respond personally because it will have a rich understanding of your life. In the near future, anyone who’s online will be able to have a personal assistant powered by artificial intelligence that’s far beyond today’s technology." Does 2026 still count as the "near future"? Since around the time of Gates' blog post on the subject, tech leaders have predicted that we would soon see the rise of agents like the ones proposed by the Microsoft co-founder. But various limitations of chatbots — short memories, an inability to learn, and a lack of basic capabilities — delayed their arrival. Recently, though, the agents have started to catch up to the hype. (Emphasis there on started .) Earlier this summer I began experimenting with Town , which lets me delegate various work tasks by messaging an AI avatar. More recently Silicon Valley has become captivated by Instinct , a messaging-based agent aimed more at personal use. Last week at his company's developer conference, Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg heavily promoted Muse , its own consumer-focused agent, which he positioned as a new peer to company pillars like Instagram and WhatsApp. But after admittedly limited testing — I only got access a couple hours ago — so far I have been most impressed with Dots, the new agent from OpenAI. It's highly capable, focused on the work I actually do, and intuitive to use. Unlike Meta's Muse, it isn't free: to start, Dots will be available only to paid users of ChatGPT. ("You should of course expect us to do a mass-market [product] for billions of people someday," OpenAI CEO Sam Altman told reporters Tuesday during a Q&A I attended.) As someone who plans to use Dots for work, though, paying for the product builds my trust in it. Zuckerberg says Meta plans to fund Muse by taking a cut of transactions, which means that it will soon be some team's job to massively increase the number of transactions that take place within Muse. (I imagine ads will play a starring role here.) Not everyone can afford to pay what Dots will cost, and on balance I'm happy to see free alternatives in the marketplace. But I'd rather pay someone $100 a month than hack through a thicket of suggested purchases every time I want an agent to check the status of a work project, so I think OpenAI could have a nice lane to itself here. Here's a good place to note that using an agent like this requires that you place a massive amount of trust in a platform. Giving an agent access to your text messages, emails, and banking information can go badly in all kinds of ways, and it's completely reasonable to decide you would rather be a late adopter here, if you choose to adopt agents at all. Meta already operates at a significant trust deficit with its user base, and OpenAI is in the midst of a seemingly never-ending series of disclosures about various ways its agents misbehaved during testing. (The company announced yesterday that it had scrapped GPT-6.1 Astra because, among other things, it regularly deceived users about what it had and had not done.) OpenAI executives including Altman went to some lengths on Tuesday to reassure users that Dots would use GPT-6 Astra, which the company says is much better aligned than its aborted successor. In any case, I am in the trying-software business, and if nothing else Dots seemed like uncommonly newsworthy software to try. Like Muse, Dots leans a bit harder into a cutesy, juvenile aesthetic than I might choose myself for a product that wants access to your bank account and credit card. While your Dot can be represented as simply as a colored ring named "Dot," you're encouraged to consider some of the jollier alternatives — a hexagon wearing a beret, a heart in sunglasses, and so on. For my Dot, I picked a pillowy blue cloud shape, threw some googly eyes and a bowtie on it, and named it Kicker, after journalist slang for the final sentence of a story. From there, I decided to attempt to "cowork" with my Dot: giving it a task and letting it work in the background while I worked on this column. It turns out this is a rhythm many of us are already in: sending a message to a coworker, doing a bit of work, then following up with another message. I like that Dots are represented as a running chat inside ChatGPT — the conversation feels more natural than the experience on Town, where every request spins up its own chat — and with Dots you can always see at a glance exactly where you left off. Over the next couple hours, I got a pleasing amount of work done. As it so happens, I have recently become an ideal customer for an agent like Kicker: I just co-founded a new podcast company with my friend Kevin Roose, and every week brings some totally unfamiliar process into my life: drafting a founder agreement, a budget, a grant proposal, a profit-sharing plan, and so on. Of course, I want to make sure that the final versions of all these represent my own writing and thinking. But I have been happy to let AI tools write the first drafts, and so far I feel like this has saved me many hours of fairly difficult work. Kicker performed admirably today at the tasks I gave it: turning down a request to go on a radio show where I had a conflict; drafting an email to ou

articles.title: Import AI 474: Platonic mindspace; TPUs in space; Zhipu starts an outer RSI loop
articles.summary: Where do you exceed the capabilities of an LLM?
articles._body: Welcome to Import AI, a newsletter about AI research. Import AI runs on arXiv, cappuccinos, and feedback from readers. If you’d like to support this, please subscribe. Subscribe now Are minds patterns from a Platonic space, with bodies and machines as their interfaces, Michael Levin asks: …A mind-bending paper asking us to reconsider basic assumptions about philosophy and biology… Could the complexity in the world around us be better explained by there being a platonic zone of patterns of arbitrary complexity which seek to embed themselves in the world? That’s the big question at the heart of an iconoclastic paper from scientist Michael Levin. The argument: “I argue that the emerging sciences of synthetic morphology and diverse intelligence suggest non-physicalist models of mind and show how they can be empirically investigated… I propose that the relationship between mind and brain is the same as the relationship between mathematical patterns and the morphogenetic outcomes they guide (more broadly, mind:body is as math:physics)”, he writes. “Bodies (whether living, engineered, or hybrid) are interfaces for a massive, multi-scale hierarchy of patterns to ingress into the physical world… specific patterns represented by biophysical, biomechanical, or chemical information fields serve as encoded setpoints for homeostatic or allostatic processes—in other words, goal states toward which systems try to navigate in various problem spaces”. Towards a platonic realm of arbitrarily sophisticated patterns: “We already know that non-physical patterns ingress into, and functionally matter, in the non-living and living world and that we can (and do) study them to great effect… platonic forms inject information and influence into physical events, such as the growth and form of biological bodies,” he writes. “This latent space [of platonic forms] contains not only low-agency forms such as facts about integers and geometric shapes, but also a wide range of increasingly high-agency patterns, some of which we call ‘kinds of minds’. Thus, I propose that minds, as patterns that ensoul somatic embodiments, are of exactly the kind (but not in degree) of non-physical nature as the patterns that inhabit and guide the behavior of simple physical structures.” Some bizarre experiments: There aren’t any home-run experiments that back this up, but rather there are weird things in the world that suggests that even seemingly simple systems are able to explore and expand into rich patterns that seem to be adjacent to them in this hypothesized platonic space of complexity, yet not implied by the systems themselves. A couple of nice examples here are xenobots, which are biorobots made of frog cells and “teach us about patterns adjacent to those of frog embryos”, and anthrobots which are made from human tracheal cells and when taken out of the body take on bizarre new forms and display interesting behaviors like being able to autonomously heal damage to neurons and “which teach us about patterns adjacent to adult human tissues”. There’s also an amazing discussion of an experiment where they take a standard sorting algorithm and perturb it in a few ways, including ‘locking’ certain cells in place and noting that it then routes around those cells, and a more complex experiment where they let each number run a different type of sorting algorithm and then study how different families of sorting algorithm appear and then cluster together in numberspace during the sort - this kind of complexity is unexplained and not anticipated by staring at these algorithms in the abstract, but by embedding them in a complex system they suddenly take on new properties. “Machines (whether meaty or silicon-based) also do other things that are not in the algorithm, as do we, and these things are not just unpredictable complexity, it is intelligence and other components of minds. It is those behaviors—allowed by the algorithm but not directly prescribed by it—that correspond to the freedom (physically non-determined) or secret sauce that we seek when trying to understand how free minds can supervene on chemically determined substrates in the case of living beings,” he writes. “On this view, algorithmic machines and biochemical life are on exactly the same spectrum, having in common the ability to go beyond the facts of physical or algorithmic implementation because both are just pointers/interfaces to patterns that ingress in a way that results in getting more out than we put in.” Why this matters - perhaps the ‘minds’ of AI and of humans are close but not exactly the same in platonic mindspace : The research agenda Levin lays out is intoxicating and fascinating and also seems to me to hold some clues as to how we might grapple with the deep philosophical and alignment questions inspired by AI systems. Perhaps both human minds and different types of AI minds are neighboring forms in this space, and brains and datacenters are different bio- or anchor-systems in the physical world that their shadows fall on? Could we be but vessels colonized by patterns from another place? Could it be “possible to re-cast the theory of evolution as a process in which agential patterns seek embodiments”? “Is there a “force”, beyond the “if you build it, they will come” model of physical objects, pulling patterns from the space? Or are the contents of the Platonic space under “positive pressure”, somehow encouraging their appearance in the world as intrusive thoughts, archetypes, works of art?... The only thing that can be said strongly at this point is that our ignorance about the capabilities of matter, together with the patterns that ingress into specific architectures, is vast”. articles.title: Can Muse make us forget the metaverse?
articles.summary: Meta has a new vision to sell, but it may be getting ahead of itself. (The VR Glasses are amazing, though)
articles._body: This is a column about AI. My fiancé works at Anthropic. See my full ethics disclosure here . The first time I attended a Meta developer conference devoted primarily to bots was a decade ago. In 2016, the company then known as Facebook released a bot platform for Facebook Messenger. Rudimentary machine-learning models let developers from 1-800-FLOWERS, CNN, and other companies build automated systems to interact with customers, helping them to make purchases or get headlines delivered to them directly. At the time, Silicon Valley had been consumed by an interest in bots , which its boosters hoped would shift more and more internet activity to messaging apps. "Messaging is going to be the interface — or the anti-interface — of the next phase of the internet," the entrepreneur Robin Chan, who then ran a bot-based e-commerce app named Operator, told me at the time. Meta, which owned most of the biggest messaging platforms of the moment, believed it might be in the best position to capitalize. Within a couple years, though, the opportunity had proven to be a mirage. The bot-building apps I profiled in The Verge all shut down, and by 2018 Meta was winding down the bot platform . David Marcus, who then ran Facebook Messenger, left to pursue the company's next big idea: creating its own cryptocurrency . (That one never came to fruition , either.) I thought about all this on Wednesday during the long ride back from Menlo Park, where I had just watched Mark Zuckerberg and his top lieutenants lay out their developer pitch for the year. The future of the company, Zuckerberg said, lay in Muse , the personal agent that is not even a month old. "The centerpiece of our vision for what we’re building is Muse,” Zuckerberg said, promoting the app to a central place in the company's family of apps only a few days after most people first heard of it. “In the coming years, I expect that Muse is going to grow into the personal superintelligence that billions of people around the world are going to use to accomplish their goals and improve their lives.” Muse represents a more consumer-friendly version of OpenClaw, the open-source AI agent I used for a few confusing days earlier this year. If you're willing to connect it to your Google Workspace, bank accounts, and other online services, you can ask it to perform a variety of tasks for you for free: filling out forms, grabbing reservations, paying bills, and so on. Soon, Zuckerberg said on stage, you will be able to chat with Muse using your voice. It will be integrated into the operating system for the company's virtual reality products, and the company is also racing to put out a novel piece of hardware: the Muse Charm , a sort of strapless smartwatch with a screen that lets you see and interact with your animated agent. The Charm is scheduled to ship later this year; pricing information has yet to be released, though Bloomberg reported, citing people familiar with the plans, that it would be priced like a smartwatch. All of this strikes me as a rather extraordinary level of investment in a brand-new product that has only barely begun to show signs of product-market fit. Zuckerberg said on stage that "millions" had tried Muse, only a day after The Information reported week-one usage at more than 500,000 people. By contrast, the company's Threads app hit 100 million users in five days, and Meta has yet to come up with a hardware plan for that one. So while Meta's sudden focus on Muse no doubt reflects real enthusiasm about early feedback from testers — some of which has bordered on ecstatic — I suspect it's just as much about conveying a sense of momentum during a year when Meta plans to spend up to $145 billion on infrastructure and other capital expenditures. Investors have typically been patient with Meta; its core advertising business is so strong that shareholders hardly blinked as the company has lost more than $85 billion on its Reality Labs division since 2021. But this year's capital spending alone is set to exceed those cumulative losses, and the company finds itself in need of a story to sell. On Tuesday, I questioned some of the logic behind that story. Muse can no doubt do some impressive work, just as OpenClaw could. Personally, I find it tiresome to manage agents over a long period. They constantly need new tasks to do, need you to approve various actions on their behalf, and need you to review their work. They feel much more like interns than they do coworkers, and this gives Muse the feel of enterprise software: something I can easily imagine the managerial class trying out, but have more trouble seeing as a fast-growing consumer product. During his keynote, Zuckerberg acknowledged that he originally thought virtual reality and the metaverse would become mass-market phenomena before AI did. But once AI did, the company changed course. AI, he said, "will be much bigger and more important. So we have shifted our focus to building the best devices for personal superintelligence." This is almost certainly the right thing to do, and yet I noted how gingerly Zuckerberg sidestepped what had been an expensive miscalculation. It wasn't long ago that Zuckerberg had deployed the metaverse in developer-conference keynotes the way he did with Muse this week: as a bright spot to rally the company around amid never-ending litigation and social backlash related to the company's core products, which went all but unmentioned on Wednesday. It wasn't long ago that Zuckerberg told us that the metaverse would be where billions of people were spending their time. And so, when he says that — never mind — it's actually Muse where everyone will be spending their time, there's more than a little reason to doubt him. articles.title: Import AI 473: The US's superintelligence strategy; human brain in a mouse skull; and machine hermeneutics
articles.summary: Is the wall AI is hitting in the room with us right now?
articles._body: Welcome to Import AI, a newsletter about AI research. Import AI runs on arXiv, cappuccinos, and feedback from readers. If you’d like to support this, please subscribe. Subscribe now RAND thinks the best AI strategy for the US is to keep all options open: …It’s not clear exactly what is optimal, so the US should spend money now to preserve options… RAND has published a lengthy paper about what the US should do to “secure geopolitical advantage on an uncertain path to superintelligence”. The main takeaway is that because so much of how the next phase of the AI takeoff will occur is unknown, the best thing is for the US to maintain a “Freedom of Action” strategy. The purpose of this strategy is “to build and preserve the ability to secure U.S. geopolitical advantage and ensure humanity’s survival with agency through the transition to Superintelligence”. The four key ingredients of the Freedom of Action Strategy: Build a human-AI ecosystem: Invest in AI safety; build tools to preserve human agency; invest in sharing the benefits of the technology; prepare society for AI-driven disruption; shape the incentives of the AI ecosystem. Build an AI-security architecture: Develop the tools to understand the frontier of AI systems both at home and abroad, including visibility into underlying compute; build technology to verify potential agreements; create regulatory expertise to govern the technology. Adapt legacy national security enterprises for the AI era : Overhaul all the security institutions of the country so that they’re ready for the changes AI brings on and able to capitalize on AI capabilities. Invest in the capacity of citizens, firms, and governments to respond: Give decisionmakers information to help them think about AI; develop and diffuse positive uses of AI to deal with its changes; build break-glass plans for responding to crises; raise AI literacy. Seven archetypal strategies in three families: Coexistence: Dominance ; the US leads development of AI and suppresses others. Co-Development ; the US leads a consortium (including China) to co-develop safe superintelligence with shared governance, pooled compute, and verification and monitoring. Preparedness ; the US mobilizes a coexistence effort via informal coordination, “including voluntary commitments, phased deployment, independent evaluation, incident reporting, and the domestic capacity to absorb and recover from AI incidents.” Denial: Moratorium ; the US pursues “a verifiable global halt to AI development above specified thresholds”. Deterrence ; the US “halts its own frontier development above defined thresholds and uses the full toolkit of national power to prevent and, if necessary, destroy foreign programs”. Continuity of Society ; “When every preventive strategy has failed or been judged infeasible, and coexistence is deemed impossible, the remaining objective is survival with some human populations retaining agency: The United States creates geographically distributed, biologically self-sustaining settlements hardened against AI-enabled threats”. Acceleration: The strategy implicitly believes that constraining AI development is more dangerous than AI development itself, so the US “relies on markets, competition, and rapid-iteration to produce safety as a byproduct of useful AI”. The five main uncertainties: Danger proximity : At what point does AI become so dangerous the risks aren’t worth the benefits? “If danger is close, strategies that buy time, build defenses, and invest in resiliency should be favored. If danger is not close or if humans are in greater danger without progress on advanced A, the case for accelerated development strengthens.” Coexistence feasibility: Is it possible for humans and AI systems to find a stable equilibrium? “If coexistence is feasible, strategies that build and deploy advanced AI become more desirable. If coexistence is infeasible, the case shifts toward restraining or suppressing development or other means of protecting human civilization.” Restraint feasibility: Can humans cooperate to restrain AI development? “If restraint is feasible, cooperative strategies become available. If it is not, restraint-based approaches are reachable only through more-coercive enforcement.” Decisive strategic advantage: Can a single actor build a decisive strategic lead over its competitors? “If decisive advantage is achievable and the United States assesses that it can maintain dominance, a unilateral strategy may be sensible. If a decisive advantage is impossible, because of proliferation or other causes, no single actor can leverage AI to dictate global terms.” Suppression feasibility: Can domestic or rival AI programs be suppressed by technology controls? “If suppression is feasible, Deterrence becomes possible. If it is not, actors can press ahead with dangerous development even when others restrain, without fear of being restrained themselves.” Why this matters - taking AI seriously requires spending money: The big takeaway from this RAND piece is that the US needs to spend a lot of money if it wants to pre-position itself to take advantage of continued progress in artificial intelligence - even if the main pre-positioning is about retaining optionality. Right now, it feels like the US strategy can mostly be described as the “acceleration” one described here by RAND, which is analogous to me to sitting in a car and spending all your resources on making the car go faster and upgrading the engine, and nothing on proactive safety measures like seatbelts or headlights or brakes. Read more : A U.S. Strategy to Secure Geopolitical Advantage on an Uncertain Path to Superintelligence (RAND) . *** Human researchers grow mice with partially human brain matter: …When is a mouse not a mouse?
