articles.title: VideoPrism: A foundational visual encoder for video understanding
articles.summary: Posted by Long Zhao, Senior Research Scientist, and Ting Liu, Senior Staff Software Engineer, Google Research
articles._body: Posted by Long Zhao, Senior Research Scientist, and Ting Liu, Senior Staff Software Engineer, Google Research An astounding number of videos are available on the Web, covering a variety of content from everyday moments people share to historical moments to scientific observations, each of which contains a unique record of the world. The right tools could help researchers analyze these videos, transforming how we understand the world around us. Videos offer dynamic visual content far more rich than static images, capturing movement, changes, and dynamic relationships between entities. Analyzing this complexity, along with the immense diversity of publicly available video data, demands models that go beyond traditional image understanding. Consequently, many of the approaches that best perform on video understanding still rely on specialized models tailor-made for particular tasks. Recently, there has been exciting progress in this area using video foundation models (ViFMs), such as VideoCLIP , InternVideo , VideoCoCa , and UMT . However, building a ViFM that handles the sheer diversity of video data remains a challenge. With the goal of building a single model for general-purpose video understanding, we introduce “ VideoPrism: A Foundational Visual Encoder for Video Understanding ”. VideoPrism is a ViFM designed to handle a wide spectrum of video understanding tasks, including classification, localization, retrieval, captioning, and question answering (QA). We propose innovations in both the pre-training data as well as the modeling strategy. We pre-train VideoPrism on a massive and diverse dataset: 36 million high-quality video-text pairs and 582 million video clips with noisy or machine-generated parallel text. Our pre-training approach is designed for this hybrid data, to learn both from video-text pairs and the videos themselves. VideoPrism is incredibly easy to adapt to new video understanding challenges, and achieves state-of-the-art performance using a single frozen model. VideoPrism is a general-purpose video encoder that enables state-of-the-art results over a wide spectrum of video understanding tasks, including classification, localization, retrieval, captioning, and question answering, by producing video representations from a single frozen model. Pre-training data A powerful ViFM needs a very large collection of videos on which to train — similar to other foundation models (FMs), such as those for large language models (LLMs). Ideally, we would want the pre-training data to be a representative sample of all the videos in the world. While naturally most of these videos do not have perfect captions or descriptions, even imperfect text can provide useful information about the semantic content of the video. To give our model the best possible starting point, we put together a massive pre-training corpus consisting of several public and private datasets, including YT-Temporal-180M , InternVid , VideoCC , WTS-70M , etc. This includes 36 million carefully selected videos with high-quality captions, along with an additional 582 million clips with varying levels of noisy text (like auto-generated transcripts). To our knowledge, this is the largest and most diverse video training corpus of its kind. Statistics on the video-text pre-training data. The large variations of the  CLIP similarity scores  (the higher, the better) demonstrate the diverse caption quality of our pre-training data, which is a byproduct of the various ways used to harvest the text. Two-stage training The VideoPrism model architecture stems from the standard vision transformer (ViT) with a factorized design that sequentially encodes spatial and temporal information following ViViT . Our training approach leverages both the high-quality video-text data and the video data with noisy text mentioned above. To start, we use contrastive learning (an approach that minimizes the distance between positive video-text pairs while maximizing the distance between negative video-text pairs) to teach our model to match videos with their own text descriptions, including imperfect ones. This builds a foundation for matching semantic language content to visual content. After video-text contrastive training, we leverage the collection of videos without text descriptions. Here, we build on the masked video modeling framework to predict masked patches in a video, with a few improvements. We train the model to predict both the video-level global embedding and token-wise embeddings from the first-stage model to effectively leverage the knowledge acquired in that stage. We then randomly shuffle the predicted tokens to prevent the model from learning shortcuts. What is unique about VideoPrism’s setup is that we use two complementary pre-training signals: text descriptions and the visual content within a video. Text descriptions often focus on what things look like, while the video content provides information about movement and visual dynamics. This enables VideoPrism to excel in tasks that demand an understanding of both appearance and motion. Results We conduct extensive evaluation on VideoPrism across four broad categories of video understanding tasks, including video classification and localization, video-text retrieval, video captioning, question answering, and scientific video understanding. VideoPrism achieves state-of-the-art performance on 30 out of 33 video understanding benchmarks — all with minimal adaptation of a single, frozen model. VideoPrism compared to the previous best-performing FMs. Classification and localization We evaluate VideoPrism on an existing large-scale video understanding benchmark ( VideoGLUE ) covering classification and localization tasks. We find that (1) VideoPrism outperforms all of the other state-of-the-art FMs, and (2) no other single model consistently came in second place. This tells us that VideoPrism has learned to effectively pack a variety of video signals into one encoder — from sem

articles.title: Advances in private training for production on-device language models
articles.summary: Posted by Zheng Xu, Research Scientist, and Yanxiang Zhang, Software Engineer, Google
articles._body: Posted by Zheng Xu, Research Scientist, and Yanxiang Zhang, Software Engineer, Google Language models (LMs) trained to predict the next word given input text are the key technology for many applications [ 1 , 2 ]. In Gboard , LMs are used to improve users’ typing experience by supporting features like next word prediction (NWP), Smart Compose , smart completion and suggestion , slide to type , and proofread . Deploying models on users’ devices rather than enterprise servers has advantages like lower latency and better privacy for model usage. While training on-device models directly from user data effectively improves the utility performance for applications such as NWP and smart text selection , protecting the privacy of user data for model training is important. Gboard features powered by on-device language models. In this blog we discuss how years of research advances now power the private training of Gboard LMs, since the proof-of-concept development of federated learning (FL) in 2017 and formal differential privacy (DP) guarantees in 2022. FL enables mobile phones to collaboratively learn a model while keeping all the training data on device, and DP provides a quantifiable measure of data anonymization. Formally, DP is often characterized by ( ε , δ ) with smaller values representing stronger guarantees. Machine learning (ML) models are considered to have reasonable DP guarantees for ε=10 and strong DP guarantees for ε=1 when δ is small. As of today, all NWP neural network LMs in Gboard are trained with FL with formal DP guarantees, and all future launches of Gboard LMs trained on user data require DP. These 30+ Gboard on-device LMs are launched in 7+ languages and 15+ countries, and satisfy ( ɛ , δ )-DP guarantees of small δ of 10 -10 and ɛ between 0.994 and 13.69. To the best of our knowledge, this is the largest known deployment of user-level DP in production at Google or anywhere, and the first time a strong DP guarantee of ɛ < 1 is announced for models trained directly on user data. Privacy principles and practices in Gboard In “ Private Federated Learning in Gboard ”, we discussed how different privacy principles are currently reflected in production models, including: Transparency and user control : We provide disclosure of what data is used, what purpose it is used for, how it is processed in various channels, and how Gboard users can easily configure the data usage in learning models. Data minimization : FL immediately aggregates only focused updates that improve a specific model. Secure aggregation (SecAgg) is an encryption method to further guarantee that only aggregated results of the ephemeral updates can be accessed. Data anonymization : DP is applied by the server to prevent models from memorizing the unique information in individual user’s training data. Auditability and verifiability : We have made public the key algorithmic approaches and privacy accounting in open-sourced code ( TFF aggregator , TFP DPQuery , DP accounting , and FL system ). A brief history In recent years, FL has become the default method for training Gboard on-device LMs from user data. In 2020, a DP mechanism that clips and adds noise to model updates was used to prevent memorization for training the Spanish LM in Spain, which satisfies finite DP guarantees ( Tier 3 described in “ How to DP-fy ML“ guide). In 2022, with the help of the DP-Follow-The-Regularized-Leader (DP-FTRL) algorithm , the Spanish LM became the first production neural network trained directly on user data announced with a formal DP guarantee of (ε=8.9, δ=10 -10 )-DP (equivalent to the reported ρ=0.81 zero-Concentrated-Differential-Privacy ), and therefore satisfies reasonable privacy guarantees ( Tier 2 ). Differential privacy by default in federated learning In “ Federated Learning of Gboard Language Models with Differential Privacy ”, we announced that all the NWP neural network LMs in Gboard have DP guarantees, and all future launches of Gboard LMs trained on user data require DP guarantees. DP is enabled in FL by applying the following practices: Pre-train the model with the multilingual C4 dataset. Via simulation experiments on public datasets, find a large DP-noise-to-signal ratio that allows for high utility. Increasing the number of clients contributing to one round of model update improves privacy while keeping the noise ratio fixed for good utility, up to the point the DP target is met, or the maximum allowed by the system and the size of the population. Configure the parameter to restrict the frequency each client can contribute (e.g., once every few days) based on computation budget and estimated population in the FL system . Run DP-FTRL training with limits on the magnitude of per-device updates chosen either via adaptive clipping , or fixed based on experience. SecAgg can be additionally applied by adopting the advances in improving computation and communication for scales and sensitivity . Federated learning with differential privacy and (SecAgg). Reporting DP guarantees The DP guarantees of launched Gboard NWP LMs are visualized in the barplot below. The x -axis shows LMs labeled by language-locale and trained on corresponding populations; the y -axis shows the ε value when δ is fixed to a small value of 10 -10 for (ε, δ)-DP (lower is better). The utility of these models are either significantly better than previous non-neural models in production, or comparable with previous LMs without DP, measured based on user-interactions metrics during A/B testing. For example, by applying the best practices, the DP guarantee of the Spanish model in Spain is improved from ε=8.9 to ε =5.37. SecAgg is additionally used for training the Spanish model in Spain and English model in the US. More details of the DP guarantees are reported in the appendix following the guidelines outlined in “ How to DP-fy ML ”. Towards stronger DP guarantees The ε ~10 DP guarantees of many launched LMs are already considered reasonable for M

articles.title: Learning the importance of training data under concept drift
articles.summary: Posted by Nishant Jain, Pre-doctoral Researcher, and Pradeep Shenoy, Research Scientist, Google Research
articles._body: Posted by Nishant Jain, Pre-doctoral Researcher, and Pradeep Shenoy, Research Scientist, Google Research The constantly changing nature of the world around us poses a significant challenge for the development of AI models. Often, models are trained on longitudinal data with the hope that the training data used will accurately represent inputs the model may receive in the future. More generally, the default assumption that all training data are equally relevant often breaks in practice. For example, the figure below shows images from the CLEAR nonstationary learning benchmark, and it illustrates how visual features of objects evolve significantly over a 10 year span (a phenomenon we refer to as slow concept drift ), posing a challenge for object categorization models. Sample images from the CLEAR benchmark. (Adapted from Lin et al . ) Alternative approaches, such as online and continual learning , repeatedly update a model with small amounts of recent data in order to keep it current. This implicitly prioritizes recent data, as the learnings from past data are gradually erased by subsequent updates. However in the real world, different kinds of information lose relevance at different rates, so there are two key issues: 1) By design they focus exclusively on the most recent data and lose any signal from older data that is erased. 2) Contributions from data instances decay uniformly over time irrespective of the contents of the data. In our recent work, “ Instance-Conditional Timescales of Decay for Non-Stationary Learning ”, we propose to assign each instance an importance score during training in order to maximize model performance on future data. To accomplish this, we employ an auxiliary model that produces these scores using the training instance as well as its age. This model is jointly learned with the primary model. We address both the above challenges and achieve significant gains over other robust learning methods on a range of benchmark datasets for nonstationary learning. For instance, on a recent large-scale benchmark for nonstationary learning (~39M photos over a 10 year period), we show up to 15% relative accuracy gains through learned reweighting of training data. The challenge of concept drift for supervised learning To gain quantitative insight into slow concept drift, we built classifiers on a recent photo categorization task , comprising roughly 39M photographs sourced from social media websites over a 10 year period. We compared offline training, which iterated over all the training data multiple times in random order, and continual training, which iterated multiple times over each month of data in sequential (temporal) order. We measured model accuracy both during the training period and during a subsequent period where both models were frozen, i.e., not updated further on new data (shown below). At the end of the training period (left panel, x-axis = 0), both approaches have seen the same amount of data, but show a large performance gap. This is due to catastrophic forgetting , a problem in continual learning where a model’s knowledge of data from early on in the training sequence is diminished in an uncontrolled manner. On the other hand, forgetting has its advantages — over the test period (shown on the right), the continual trained model degrades much less rapidly than the offline model because it is less dependent on older data. The decay of both models’ accuracy in the test period is confirmation that the data is indeed evolving over time, and both models become increasingly less relevant. Comparing offline and continually trained models on the photo classification task. Time-sensitive reweighting of training data We design a method combining the benefits of offline learning (the flexibility of effectively reusing all available data) and continual learning (the ability to downplay older data) to address slow concept drift. We build upon offline learning, then add careful control over the influence of past data and an optimization objective, both designed to reduce model decay in the future. Suppose we wish to train a model, M , given some training data collected over time. We propose to also train a helper model that assigns a weight to each point based on its contents and age. This weight scales the contribution from that data point in the training objective for M . The objective of the weights is to improve the performance of M on future data. In our work , we describe how the helper model can be meta-learned, i.e., learned alongside M in a manner that helps the learning of the model M itself. A key design choice of the helper model is that we separated out instance- and age-related contributions in a factored manner. Specifically, we set the weight by combining contributions from multiple different fixed timescales of decay, and learn an approximate “assignment” of a given instance to its most suited timescales. We find in our experiments that this form of the helper model outperforms many other alternatives we considered, ranging from unconstrained joint functions to a single timescale of decay (exponential or linear), due to its combination of simplicity and expressivity. Full details may be found in the paper . Instance weight scoring The top figure below shows that our learned helper model indeed up-weights more modern-looking objects in the CLEAR object recognition challenge ; older-looking objects are correspondingly down-weighted. On closer examination (bottom figure below, gradient-based feature importance assessment), we see that the helper model focuses on the primary object within the image, as opposed to, e.g., background features that may spuriously be correlated with instance age. Sample images from the CLEAR benchmark (camera & computer categories) assigned the highest and lowest weights respectively by our helper model. Feature importance analysis of our helper model on sample images from the CLEAR benchmark. Results Gains on large-scale da

articles.title: DP-Auditorium: A flexible library for auditing differential privacy
articles.summary: Posted by Mónica Ribero Díaz, Research Scientist, Google Research
articles._body: Posted by Mónica Ribero Díaz, Research Scientist, Google Research Differential privacy (DP) is a property of randomized mechanisms that limit the influence of any individual user’s information while processing and analyzing data. DP offers a robust solution to address growing concerns about data protection, enabling technologies across industries and government applications (e.g., the US census ) without compromising individual user identities. As its adoption increases, it’s important to identify the potential risks of developing mechanisms with faulty implementations. Researchers have recently found errors in the mathematical proofs of private mechanisms, and their implementations. For example, researchers compared six sparse vector technique (SVT) variations and found that only two of the six actually met the asserted privacy guarantee. Even when mathematical proofs are correct, the code implementing the mechanism is vulnerable to human error. However, practical and efficient DP auditing is challenging primarily due to the inherent randomness of the mechanisms and the probabilistic nature of the tested guarantees. In addition, a range of guarantee types exist, (e.g., pure DP , approximate DP , Rényi DP , and concentrated DP ), and this diversity contributes to the complexity of formulating the auditing problem. Further, debugging mathematical proofs and code bases is an intractable task given the volume of proposed mechanisms. While ad hoc testing techniques exist under specific assumptions of mechanisms, few efforts have been made to develop an extensible tool for testing DP mechanisms. To that end, in “ DP-Auditorium: A Large Scale Library for Auditing Differential Privacy ”, we introduce an open source library for auditing DP guarantees with only black-box access to a mechanism (i.e., without any knowledge of the mechanism’s internal properties). DP-Auditorium is implemented in Python and provides a flexible interface that allows contributions to continuously improve its testing capabilities. We also introduce new testing algorithms that perform divergence optimization over function spaces for Rényi DP, pure DP, and approximate DP. We demonstrate that DP-Auditorium can efficiently identify DP guarantee violations, and suggest which tests are most suitable for detecting particular bugs under various privacy guarantees. DP guarantees The output of a DP mechanism is a sample drawn from a probability distribution ( M ( D )) that satisfies a mathematical property ensuring the privacy of user data. A DP guarantee is thus tightly related to properties between pairs of probability distributions. A mechanism is differentially private if the probability distributions determined by M on dataset D and a neighboring dataset D’ , which differ by only one record, are indistinguishable under a given divergence metric. For example, the classical approximate DP definition states that a mechanism is approximately DP with parameters ( ε , δ ) if the hockey-stick divergence of order e ε , between M ( D) and M ( D’ ), is at most δ . Pure DP is a special instance of approximate DP where δ = 0 . Finally, a mechanism is considered Rényi DP with parameters ( 𝛼 , ε) if the Rényi divergence of order 𝛼 , is at most ε (where ε is a small positive value). In these three definitions, ε is not interchangeable but intuitively conveys the same concept; larger values of ε imply larger divergences between the two distributions or less privacy, since the two distributions are easier to distinguish. DP-Auditorium DP-Auditorium comprises two main components: property testers and dataset finders. Property testers take samples from a mechanism evaluated on specific datasets as input and aim to identify privacy guarantee violations in the provided datasets. Dataset finders suggest datasets where the privacy guarantee may fail. By combining both components, DP-Auditorium enables (1) automated testing of diverse mechanisms and privacy definitions and, (2) detection of bugs in privacy-preserving mechanisms. We implement various private and non-private mechanisms, including simple mechanisms that compute the mean of records and more complex mechanisms, such as different SVT and gradient descent mechanism variants. Property testers determine if evidence exists to reject the hypothesis that a given divergence between two probability distributions, P and Q , is bounded by a prespecified budget determined by the DP guarantee being tested. They compute a lower bound from samples from P and Q, rejecting the property if the lower bound value exceeds the expected divergence. No guarantees are provided if the result is indeed bounded. To test for a range of privacy guarantees, DP-Auditorium introduces three novel testers: (1) HockeyStickPropertyTester, (2) RényiPropertyTester, and (3) MMDPropertyTester. Unlike other approaches, these testers don’t depend on explicit histogram approximations of the tested distributions. They rely on variational representations of the hockey-stick divergence, Rényi divergence, and maximum mean discrepancy (MMD) that enable the estimation of divergences through optimization over function spaces. As a baseline, we implement HistogramPropertyTester , a commonly used approximate DP tester. While our three testers follow a similar approach, for brevity, we focus on the HockeyStickPropertyTester in this post. Given two neighboring datasets, D and D’ , the HockeyStickPropertyTester finds a lower bound, ^ δ  for the hockey-stick divergence between M ( D) and M ( D’ ) that holds with high probability. Hockey-stick divergence enforces that the two distributions M ( D) and M ( D’ ) are close under an approximate DP guarantee. Therefore, if a privacy guarantee claims that the hockey-stick divergence is at most δ , and ^ δ   > δ , then with high probability the divergence is higher than what was promised on D and D’ and the mechanism cannot satisfy the given approximate DP guarantee. The lower bound ^ δ &

articles.title: Graph neural networks in TensorFlow
articles.summary: Posted by Dustin Zelle, Software Engineer, Google Research, and Arno Eigenwillig, Software Engineer, CoreML
articles._body: Posted by Dustin Zelle, Software Engineer, Google Research, and Arno Eigenwillig, Software Engineer, CoreML Objects and their relationships are ubiquitous in the world around us, and relationships can be as important to understanding an object as its own attributes viewed in isolation — take for example transportation networks, production networks, knowledge graphs, or social networks. Discrete mathematics and computer science have a long history of formalizing such networks as graphs , consisting of nodes connected by edges in various irregular ways. Yet most machine learning (ML) algorithms allow only for regular and uniform relations between input objects, such as a grid of pixels, a sequence of words, or no relation at all. Graph neural networks , or GNNs for short, have emerged as a powerful technique to leverage both the graph’s connectivity (as in the older algorithms DeepWalk and Node2Vec ) and the input features on the various nodes and edges. GNNs can make predictions for graphs as a whole (Does this molecule react in a certain way?), for individual nodes (What’s the topic of this document, given its citations?) or for potential edges (Is this product likely to be purchased together with that product?). Apart from making predictions about graphs, GNNs are a powerful tool used to bridge the chasm to more typical neural network use cases. They encode a graph's discrete , relational information in a continuous way so that it can be included naturally in another deep learning system. We are excited to announce the release of TensorFlow GNN 1.0 (TF-GNN), a production-tested library for building GNNs at large scales. It supports both modeling and training in TensorFlow as well as the extraction of input graphs from huge data stores. TF-GNN is built from the ground up for heterogeneous graphs, where types of objects and relations are represented by distinct sets of nodes and edges. Real-world objects and their relations occur in distinct types, and TF-GNN's heterogeneous focus makes it natural to represent them. Inside TensorFlow, such graphs are represented by objects of type tfgnn.GraphTensor . This is a composite tensor type (a collection of tensors in one Python class) accepted as a first-class citizen in tf.data.Dataset , tf.function , etc. It stores both the graph structure and its features attached to nodes, edges and the graph as a whole. Trainable transformations of GraphTensors can be defined as Layers objects in the high-level Keras API , or directly using the tfgnn.GraphTensor primitive. GNNs: Making predictions for an object in context For illustration, let’s look at one typical application of TF-GNN: predicting a property of a certain type of node in a graph defined by cross-referencing tables of a huge database. For example, a citation database of Computer Science (CS) arXiv papers with one-to-many cites and many-to-one cited relationships where we would like to predict the subject area of each paper. Like most neural networks, a GNN is trained on a dataset of many labeled examples (~millions), but each training step consists only of a much smaller batch of training examples (say, hundreds). To scale to millions, the GNN gets trained on a stream of reasonably small subgraphs from the underlying graph. Each subgraph contains enough of the original data to compute the GNN result for the labeled node at its center and train the model. This process — typically referred to as subgraph sampling — is extremely consequential for GNN training. Most existing tooling accomplishes sampling in a batch way, producing static subgraphs for training. TF-GNN provides tooling to improve on this by sampling dynamically and interactively. Pictured, the process of subgraph sampling where small, tractable subgraphs are sampled from a larger graph to create input examples for GNN training. TF-GNN 1.0 debuts a flexible Python API to configure dynamic or batch subgraph sampling at all relevant scales: interactively in a Colab notebook (like this one ), for efficient sampling of a small dataset stored in the main memory of a single training host, or distributed by Apache Beam for huge datasets stored on a network filesystem (up to hundreds of millions of nodes and billions of edges). For details, please refer to our user guides for in-memory and beam-based sampling, respectively. On those same sampled subgraphs, the GNN’s task is to compute a hidden (or latent) state at the root node; the hidden state aggregates and encodes the relevant information of the root node's neighborhood. One classical approach is message-passing neural networks . In each round of message passing, nodes receive messages from their neighbors along incoming edges and update their own hidden state from them. After n rounds, the hidden state of the root node reflects the aggregate information from all nodes within n edges (pictured below for n = 2). The messages and the new hidden states are computed by hidden layers of the neural network. In a heterogeneous graph, it often makes sense to use separately trained hidden layers for the different types of nodes and edges Pictured, a simple message-passing neural network where, at each step, the node state is propagated from outer to inner nodes where it is pooled to compute new node states. Once the root node is reached, a final prediction can be made. The training setup is completed by placing an output layer on top of the GNN’s hidden state for the labeled nodes, computing the loss (to measure the prediction error), and updating model weights by backpropagation, as usual in any neural network training. Beyond supervised training (i.e., minimizing a loss defined by labels), GNNs can also be trained in an unsupervised way (i.e., without labels). This lets us compute a continuous representation (or embedding ) of the discrete graph structure of nodes and their features. These representations are then typically utilized in other ML systems. In this way, the discrete, relational in

articles.title: Chewy and other companies pull ads from 'I've Had It' podcast after hosts laugh at 'insensitive' Charlie Kirk joke
articles.summary: Hosts Jennifer Welch and Angie Sullivan apologized for laughing at a Charlie Kirk joke on their podcast in an Instagram post on Saturday.
articles._body: Jennifer Welch and Angie Sullivan apologized for their remarks about Charlie Kirk on Instagram. Theo Wargo/Getty Images The "I've Had It" podcast is losing sponsorships after the hosts laughed about Charlie Kirk. Chewy CEO Sumit Singh said the hosts' behavior didn't reflect the company's values. Hosts Jennifer Welch and Angie Sullivan apologized in an Instagram post on Saturday. A 39-second clip shared to X is turning into a massive headache for the "I've Had It" podcast. At least nine companies have pulled their sponsorships from the popular progressive-leaning culture and politics podcast after a clip of hosts Jennifer Welch and Angie "Pumps" Sullivan went viral on X last week. The clip, which has nearly 6 million views and 18,000 likes, showed the pair laughing at an X post referencing Charlie Kirk , the right-wing political activist who was assassinated last year. The clip drew criticism from some X users, who called for a boycott of the podcast. Companies began distancing themselves from the show soon after, including online retailer Chewy. We do not sponsor or support the “I’ve Had It” podcast. We unequivocally condemn violence in all forms. The comments made by the hosts do not reflect Chewy’s values or what we stand for as a company. — Chewy (@Chewy) November 7, 2026 "We do not sponsor or support the "I've Had It" podcast. We unequivocally condemn violence in all forms," the company said in an X post on Saturday. "The comments made by the hosts do not reflect Chewy's values or what we stand for as a company." Chewy CEO Sumit Singh doubled down on the company's decision in his own X post. Meanwhile, Cash App, Zenni, Casper, and Honeylove also cut ties. "Honeylove has ended our partnership with the I've Had It podcast. Violence of any kind is never acceptable, and those comments do not reflect our values," Honeylove said in an X post on Sunday. The "I've Had It" hosts posted an apology to the podcast's Instagram account on Saturday. "It was an insensitive joke, and we should not have laughed. We regret it, and we apologize," the podcast said. "Whatever our political differences, there is nothing funny about gun violence." The podcast said it donated to Everytown for Gun Safety, the largest gun-violence-prevention organization in the United States. This isn't the first time a host has landed in hot water over comments made about Kirk. ABC, owned by the Walt Disney Company, suspended and later reinstated Jimmy Kimmel's late-night talk show over his remarks about Kirk. Some employees from major companies like Office Depot and Nasdaq also disciplined employees who made negative remarks about Kirk online. The "Pivot with Kara Swisher and Scott Galloway " podcast, which discusses business, tech, and politics, has also been targeted by calls for an advertising boycott after Galloway criticized Elon Musk last week. During the first stop on the Pivot Tour 2026, Galloway, an academic who frequently writes about the tech industry, called Musk a "traitor to the West" and referenced the Rosenbergs. Julius and Ethel Rosenberg were convicted of conspiracy to commit espionage during the Cold War and were executed by the federal government. The remarks drew the ire of Jason Calacanis of the "All-In" podcast and others, including University of California San Diego professor Brian Keating. The CEO of Boom Supersonic, an American aerospace company, wrote on X that Galloway was an investor in Boom and criticized the academic's comments. "I don't mind disagreements but calling for an execution of a non-criminal (worse, an actual hero!) is a step too far," CEO Blake Scholl wrote on X on Friday. "Working to arrange a buy-out of his shares." Read the original article on Business Insider

articles.title: I bring miniature ponies into nursing homes for a living. Some residents laugh, while others cry when they see them.
articles.summary: Sarah Woodland brings miniature ponies into care homes to visit elderly residents. Their emotional reactions make her work deeply rewarding.
articles._body: Sarah Woodland brings miniature ponies to older people. Courtesy of Sarah Woodland Sarah Woodland was given two Miniature Shetland Ponies and wasn't sure what to do with them. She started bringing the ponies into care homes after testing whether they could go indoors. Four years later, she has seven ponies and runs the business full time. This as-told-to essay is based on a conversation with Sarah Woodland , founder of Dinky Ponies . It has been edited for length and clarity. Just after the pandemic, I started seeing two Miniature Shetland Ponies every single day in a field on my drive to work. I'd worked taking care of other people's horses as a groom — someone responsible for the daily care , health, management, and preparation of horses — for years, but I hadn't worked extensively with Miniature Shetland Ponies before. For some reason, though, I'd always look for those small, sturdy ponies on my morning commute. Wondering who they belonged to, I inquired about their owner and asked if I could come by to see them. Long story short, a few months later, I was given those two ponies, not entirely sure what I was going to do with them. I started a business with the ponies I didn't want them to just be field ornaments for the rest of their lives — they were horses that needed some sort of job to do. But the breed isn't capable of doing too much due to their small size. I messaged some of the mothers I knew to ask about their interest in stable management classes and sessions in handling the ponies. Hitting what felt like constant barriers , I eventually managed to start hosting parties and one-to-one sessions in locations around me — like pub car parks and random fields. Never having run a business before, I had to get to grips with organizing bookings, sending invoices , and managing a small business. It was a lot of admin to get my head around at the start. By the end of my first summer of these sessions, I knew I had to find other work for the ponies because the weather would be changing and outside sessions weren't going to work in the cold and rainy fall and winter. Very randomly, I remember seeing a photo of a horse in an elevator and wondered if my ponies could be taken into buildings and up and down elevators. To test it out, I called a friend who works at a children's  day care  up the road from me and asked if I could bring one of the ponies into the building to see how it would cope indoors and with children. There were no problems. I started bringing the ponies to elder care facilities Around the same time, I considered whether elder care homes would have budgets for me to bring the ponies in to mingle with elderly residents. I've never had experience in care homes, but imagined that being around the ponies would be a lovely treat. Sarah Woodland started taking her ponies to elder care facilities. Courtesy of Sarah Woodland I called a nursing home and asked if I could try it. I really didn't have a clue what I was doing, but reckoned I would learn by trial and error. The ponies coped, and the elderly residents absolutely loved the visit. Four years later, I'm now taking my ponies (I have seven now) to care homes and residential homes to visit elderly people and children with special needs. It's become my full-time job, and full-time passion. I've faced a lot of unexpected challenges along the way. There was no model to follow and no blueprint to copy. Everything I've built, I've built myself, learning as I've gone along. I had to learn from my mistakes Of course, I've made mistakes too, but with mistakes comes learning, and every challenge has taught me something. I've learned what works, what doesn't, what I'd do differently, and most importantly, how to keep moving forward. As the ponies' feet are quite slippery on laminate floors , I've finally found shoes for them that don't look silly. I don't like the idea of making the ponies look ridiculous, because they're working animals and should be treated with respect. Sarah Woodland trained her ponies to take elevators. Courtesy of Sarah Woodland When I take the ponies into a building, they totally trust me. They know I wouldn't put them in a position where they'd feel unsafe. It's the same when I take them into an elevator. I have given them positive reinforcement by giving them a little mint each time they go into the elevator. I must always remain calm because, in doing so, they too stay calm. They are intelligent animals that know whether I'm stressed or not and mirror my state. Having not spent time in a care home, I suppose I wasn't prepared for how much I would need to learn about what people living in care homes need. I'm now constantly learning to understand how people feel when they see the ponies. I'm learning what the right things to say are, and perhaps what things I shouldn't say. I've really enjoyed my conversations with people when I'm walking through with the ponies, and I find it hard to move on from a conversation when my hour of visiting is completed. While I limit my visits to one hour for the ponies' welfare, I revisit the care homes throughout the year so that different people have a chance to see the ponies. I would rather my visits include a limited number of people who get quality time to talk with me and interact with the ponies, rather than rushed "show-and-tell" sessions where residents only get a little time to pet the ponies before I move on. I can't figure out why the elderly love the ponies so much. They laugh, and sometimes they cry when they see them. You never know what the reaction will be. Perhaps there's something about their tiny size that makes them appear young and foal-like, not realizing that they are all actually very old. And of course, when we visit residential homes for children with special needs, or nurseries with young children, the children adore the ponies. I've taken my sons along to these visits, and have felt immensely proud watching them interact with the children

articles.title: I've spent 128 hours on Amtrak sleeper trains. Here are 6 essentials I've always packed and 4 I discovered along the way.
articles.summary: I've always packed comfortable clothes and plenty of entertainment on overnight Amtrak trips. After some experience, I started packing slippers.
articles._body: The author shares her packing essentials for overnight Amtrak trips. Joey Hadden/Business Insider I've never been without a camera on an overnight Amtrak train. I've never gone to bed without doing my whole skincare routine. I've never packed a pair of binoculars, but I will next time. Comfort, ease, and enjoyment. I pack for every overnight Amtrak trip with these three things in mind. And after 128 hours of experience, I've figured out the essentials for a fantastic experience. I've traveled through 15 states, from the East Coast to the West, in Amtrak sleeper cars. I've stayed in roomettes — roughly 20-square-foot private cabins with two seats, two beds, a table, and a sink and vanity — and bedrooms, which are double the size and also include a full bathroom. My packing list has evolved over the years. Some items have been with me since the beginning. Others come from lessons learned along the way. I've been packing a comfy outfit separately from the rest of my clothes since my first overnight train ride. Joey Hadden/Business Insider You won't catch me dressed to impress on an overnight train . I prefer to spend long days on the rails in my coziest garments. But I don't want to fish through my luggage to find them once on board. I make it easier on myself by putting a pair of sweatpants, a pair of basketball shorts, a soft T-shirt, and undergarments in a small packing cube at the top of my suitcase. I've never boarded an overnight Amtrak train without video games. Joey Hadden/Business Insider Entertainment is everything when you're stuck in place for dozens of hours. One thing that makes my cabin feel more like home is packing activities I often enjoy in my own living room. So I always pack my Nintendo Switch. The portable console is thin enough to slide easily into a tight crevice in my bag. It's loaded with all types of games to satisfy every mood, from "Animal Crossing" and various Pokémon titles to the "BioShock" series and "Red Dead Redemption," to name a few. I always have a journal on me. Joey Hadden/Business Insider I've only traveled solo on overnight trains, so I spend a lot of time thinking. I rarely make time for journaling in my daily life, but on trains I indulge in the opportunity to write out my thoughts uninterrupted. And the ever-changing view out the window is a constant source of inspiration. My camera has been my sidekick since the beginning. Joey Hadden/Business Insider On overnight trains, I spend more time with my camera in hand than my phone. You may be thinking, "Why not just use the camera on your phone ?" And I have good reasons. For one thing, I don't want to be limited by my phone's battery life and storage space. A long-haul train ride is visual overload. The view out the window is never the same as the last time you looked, and train car interiors are so distinctive compared to everyday indoor spaces that I want to photograph them from every angle possible. As a photographer, I also prefer to manually control the settings and use multiple lenses to get more variety than I could with my phone. In fact, I usually bring two cameras on these trips. I can't imagine a long-haul train ride without noise-canceling headphones. Joey Hadden/Business Insider Every overnight Amtrak train I've taken has begun with an announcement requesting that all passengers use headphones to play audio — even behind the closed doors of their sleeper cabins. I completely understand why. Sound travels far in a train car. I can often hear other people's conversations in the room next to mine. I use noise-canceling headphones to watch TV and movies, take phone calls, and listen to music and podcasts. I've always made room in my bag for skincare products. Joey Hadden/Business Insider Amtrak roomettes and bedrooms have a sink and vanity inside. Bedrooms also have a full bathroom, while roomette passengers have access to shared toilets and showers in the sleeper car. Replicating my skincare routine before bed in my tiny, moving hotel room makes me feel more at home on the rails. After a little experience, I started packing waterproof clogs. Joey Hadden/Business Insider I'll never forget my first thought when I opened the door to an Amtrak shower for the first time: "I don't have the right shoes for this." Whether the shared shower in the car or my own in a bedroom, I won't be barefoot on any train. After a couple of shower-free rides, I started bringing a pair of Crocs. I highly recommend Crocs over flip-flops, especially if you're traveling in the winter. Once dry, I find it's easier to slip on my Crocs than lace up my kicks or boots every time I leave my room. I forgot motion sickness medicine on my first two overnight rides, and I never will again. Joey Hadden/Business Insider My first two overnight train rides were 30-hour trips from NYC to Miami and back. But they felt longer. There is nothing comfortable, easy, or enjoyable about motion sickness . Take it from someone who gets woozy at the sight of lapping bath water. Without medicine, both rides felt like uphill climbs. I couldn't relax or stay present while enduring waves of dizziness. Honestly, the whole time, I just wanted to get off. But now I pack Dramamine — the less drowsy version for daytime and the original for nighttime. I sleep easier and feel better throughout my trips. I can truly enjoy the ride. And I'm never in a rush to get off anymore. I didn't think to pack a pair of slippers until my most recent overnight Amtrak ride. Joey Hadden/Business Insider In February, I took the longest train ride in America — the 53-hour California Zephyr from Chicago to Emeryville, California. It was also the longest train ride of my life so far by about 23 hours, so I thought it was worth packing a little extra comfort from home. I wear these padded Muji slippers every day around my apartment. And they were thin and squishy enough to slip into my seemingly full bag with ease. My slippers made my two-night stay feel a tad luxurious, and

articles.title: I tried Ina Garten's easy cornbread. I love the recipe so much that I now make it for every Thanksgiving.
articles.summary: Ina Garten's brown-butter skillet cornbread is really easy to make and always a hit at holiday parties. Now I make it for every Thanksgiving dinner.
articles._body: I tried Ina Garten's easy cornbread years ago. Now I make it for every Thanksgiving. Anneta Konstantinides/Business Insider I made Ina Garten's recipe for brown-butter skillet cornbread.  It was deliciously moist, with the perfect combination of sweet and savory flavors.  The cornbread was a hit at Friendsgiving years ago. Now I make the dish for every Thanksgiving. When I decided to cook a few dishes for Friendsgiving , there was no question that Ina Garten would be my source of inspiration. As a huge pasta lover, I knew I had to test Garten's recipe for overnight mac and cheese . And I'm a firm believer that no Thanksgiving table is complete without carbs, so I also made her Parmesan smashed potatoes .  That already seemed like plenty, but then I stumbled on a photo of Garten's brown-butter skillet cornbread in "The Barefoot Contessa Cookbook." In the dish's description, Garten writes that it was the "best cornbread I've ever made!" That was all I needed to hear — time to get baking! Ina Garten's brown-butter skillet cornbread needs only a few basic ingredients. Anneta Konstantinides/Business Insider To make Garten's cornbread, which serves 10 to 12 people, you'll need:  3 cups of all-purpose flour 2 cups of whole milk  1 cup of fine cornmeal (Garten says this makes moister cornbread than medium grind) 1 cup of sugar  ½ pound of unsalted butter  2 extra-large eggs, lightly beaten  2 tablespoons of baking powder  I began by melting the butter in a 10-inch cast-iron skillet over medium heat. Anneta Konstantinides/Business Insider I continued to heat the butter until it became browned but not burned, listening to Garten's advice to "watch it very carefully!"  Once the butter was ready, I poured it into a bowl and added the milk and eggs. Anneta Konstantinides/Business Insider I whisked the milk into the butter before cracking two eggs into the bowl. I have to admit, I forgot to lightly beat the eggs before adding them to the mixture — but it didn't seem to affect the cornbread at all.  I added my dry ingredients in a separate bowl. Anneta Konstantinides/Business Insider I added the flour, sugar, and cornmeal, along with the baking powder and some kosher salt.  I whisked all the dry ingredients together, then made a well in the middle. Anneta Konstantinides/Business Insider Barely five minutes had passed, and my batter was almost ready.  Then I poured the butter-and-milk mixture into the well. Anneta Konstantinides/Business Insider Per Garten's instructions, I stirred everything together with a rubber spatula until it was just combined. The "Barefoot Contessa" star said it's OK if the batter looks a little lumpy.  My batter was almost ready. But first, it needed to rest a little (relatable). Anneta Konstantinides/Business Insider Garten's recipe calls for the batter to sit for 15 minutes. She said this step is essential to getting the best cornbread possible, so be patient! After the 15 minutes were up, I poured my batter into the skillet. Anneta Konstantinides/Business Insider Make sure you don't wipe out your cast-iron skillet after melting the butter. Just throw the batter right in. I smoothed the top, sprinkled it with sea salt, and threw the cast-iron skillet into the oven. Anneta Konstantinides/Business Insider Garten's recipe says to bake the cornbread for 35 to 40 minutes at 350 degrees Fahrenheit. After 35 minutes, I stuck a knife in the middle, and it came out clean, so I knew it was ready.  One thing to note: If you're using an 11 ½-inch skillet, Garten recommends baking your cornbread for only 25 to 30 minutes.  My cornbread came out a gorgeous golden brown. Anneta Konstantinides/Business Insider Garten's brown-butter skillet cornbread makes for a beautiful centerpiece at the Thanksgiving table. (We all know no one really cares about the turkey.) But would it taste as good as it looked?  You could feel how moist the cornbread was just by cutting into it. Everyone at the table agreed it was one of the best they had ever tasted. Anneta Konstantinides/Business Insider I could write an essay on how much I love this cornbread. It was so moist and fluffy, with the sweet and savory elements working together in perfect harmony. We were all stuffed, but everyone at the table couldn't resist getting seconds of the bread.  "The salt really brought out all the flavors," my friend Oliver said. "10/10, would recommend."  "So delicious," my fellow taste tester Kayla added. "The outside had a nice salty and crunchy texture, while the inside was moist and sweet."  Garten's cornbread has earned a permanent spot on my Thanksgiving menu. Anneta Konstantinides/Business Insider There's no doubt in my mind that Garten's brown-butter skillet cornbread was the star of our meal. It was perfectly baked and still tasted just as moist when we ate leftovers a day or two later. Seeing that cornbread come out of the oven, so beautiful and golden, made me feel like I was about to get a Paul Hollywood handshake.    Now I look forward to making it every Thanksgiving . Read the original article on Business Insider

articles.title: 'Saturday Night Live' roasts Elon Musk after midterm rout: 'My car did a flip!'
articles.summary: Comedian Jeremy Culhane played Elon Musk during "Weekend Update" on "Saturday Night Live," where he fielded questions about the midterm elections.
articles._body: Jeremy Culhane as Elon Musk, and anchor Colin Jost during "Saturday Night Live" on November 7. : Will Heath/NBC via Getty Images "Saturday Night Live" roasted Elon Musk, played by Jeremy Culhane, during "Weekend Update." Culhane's Musk tried to distract the audience from his expensive US midterm election fumble. "I'm in the news because my car did a flip," the actor said. Elon Musk had a terrible, horrible, no-good, very bad week following the US midterm elections . And "Saturday Night Live" seized the opportunity. The "SNL" crew didn't hold back during the "Weekend Update" segment, when comedian Jeremy Culhane portrayed the tech billionaire discussing his US midterm election fumble. The real Musk donated at least $446 million ahead of the midterm elections to conservative political action committees, including a large chunk to supporting conservative candidates in Texas. Ultimately, it didn't matter. Texas, alongside several other traditionally red states, turned blue this election cycle. During the segment, host Colin Jost said Musk is in the news for "wasting" money on the midterm elections. "Uh, no, I'm in the news because my car did a flip. My car did a flip, remember? It was like a frickin' Hot Wheel," the impersonator said. "It was like poof! And then bah! But I was like, totally chill. I was like, 'Thug life!' Imagine." Tesla flaunted its next-generation Roadster in October by kick-flipping it in the air during a demonstration. Culhane's Musk had a similar answer when asked about his decision to halt production of Tesla's Cybertruck . Musk made the announcement two days after the midterm election. "Hey, remember when my car did a flip? It was epic. It was like poof, pah! But everyone was like, "Whoa!" But I was just like, 'Hold my beer.' Imagine,'" the comedian said. At the end of the sketch, Culhane's Musk decides to show off a new fictitious Grok feature called "vulgar roast." "Elon Musk, you're the worst thing South Africa has ever done," fake Grok said. "When you're on TV, it feels like an episode of 'Hate on the Spectrum.'" Fake Grok added: "Maybe if you have 100 more kids, one of them will talk to you." The fallout from the blue wave that swept the midterm elections was swift for Musk. His net worth fell by $33 billion in one day, while shares of Tesla and SpaceX tumbled . Read the original article on Business Insider

articles.title: I was an international flight attendant. At 36, I'm a part-time receptionist, and I'm happier than ever.
articles.summary: I traded my demanding flight attendant career for a part-time receptionist job. At 36, I've found happiness in a slower, simpler life.
articles._body: The author retired from her flight attendant career and is now happier. Courtesy of the author I spent years working as an international flight attendant, constantly traveling and chasing success. I traded my demanding career for a part-time receptionist job with a much calmer routine. At 36, I'm happier prioritizing my mental health, marriage, and the small joys of everyday life. I was born in a small town in Ukraine , raised with the quiet, persistent belief that to succeed, I had to work three times harder than anyone born in a big city. In my early adulthood, my biggest mistake was assuming that only major cities could offer real opportunities — and that I could simply squeeze my mental health into my schedule whenever I happened to have time for it. Moving to Kyiv in my early 20s felt like the ultimate dream: a chance to prove I belonged. But to survive there, I felt I had to fit a precise, demanding system. It wasn't enough to simply stay healthy; you were expected to hold a premium membership at a high-end fitness center just to prove your worth to others. You had to maintain an active, highly visible social life, eat at the right places, and project total composure. Everything was about trying to impress others. I chased corporate beauty standards, ignoring every warning sign of burnout After I graduated from college , I set my sights on becoming an international flight attendant for Ukraine's national carrier. When I landed the job, I thought I had made it. Instead, impostor syndrome hit me on day one. I felt like I was constantly falling behind my peers, so I ran as fast as I could to outrun the feeling. The author trained to be a flight attendant in her home country. Courtesy of the author I improved my English, started learning Spanish , and took on a summer schedule so punishing I was barely ever home. I spent years living out of a suitcase, navigating time zone changes, early-morning wake-up calls, and strict corporate beauty standards . I measured my worth entirely by my exhaustion, treating a packed calendar as proof that I mattered. Saying "no" to friends because of work became a badge of honor. Looking back, I knew I was burning out, but I was too overwhelmed to stop. I believed that as long as I was busy, I was safe from failure. I had my first panic attack Then, life shifted violently. After having my son, the pandemic grounded the aviation industry. Not long after, war broke out in Ukraine . We didn't choose to leave our home or plan to emigrate — war made that decision for us, uprooting our family overnight. We ended up settling in a small Ontario town — the exact kind of tranquil environment I had spent my youth trying to escape. When I first arrived, I was terrified. It was so overwhelmingly still and peaceful that, for the first time in my life, I started to hear my own thoughts. My body, conditioned by a decade of high-tension striving and constant mobility, couldn't handle the sudden stillness. Shortly after arriving, my first panic attack hit me. In the stillness, a painful truth surfaced: I had never once allowed myself to just stay with myself. My mind had always been stuffed with the next goal, the next achievement, or the next deadline. I initially believed that this small town marked the end of my ambition, but as the silence forced me to look inward, I realized I had spent nearly 10 years chasing an illusion. I leaned out and found community Unlearning that mindset wasn't immediate; slowing down turned out to be a skill I had to learn from scratch. In the fall of 2022, I found a part-time job as a receptionist in Canada, where I still work today. For the first time in my professional life, I wasn't navigating a massive corporate hierarchy or competing with thousands of employees. Working alongside just three colleagues in a calm atmosphere, I joined a community where people actually knew my name. The author says slowing down was beneficial for her. Courtesy of the author Instead of chasing the next status symbol, I made learning who I actually was my top priority. I no longer pay for an expensive gym membership to impress anyone; instead, I feel fit and strong through my home workouts. Practicing yoga in peace and serenity without a studio full of strangers makes far more sense to me now. It turns out I love early mornings. I love making my own sauerkraut and keeping a sourdough starter alive to bake rye bread. Baking fresh cinnamon rolls for our neighbors as a small thank-you for their support became one of the most grounding, relaxing rituals of my new life. I started learning French — not to climb a career ladder or get immigration points, but purely for the joy of the process. There are no deadlines now. I take my time, allow myself to feel stuck, and share my struggles openly with my tutor. Slowing down saved both my mental health and my marriage Now, at 36, I build my daily life entirely around my mental health, rather than trying to squeeze my well-being into the leftover cracks of a high-stress career. I refuse to operate in panic mode anymore. Opening my eyes to this required hard choices — letting go of old ambitions, old habits, and even certain relationships. Today, I don't maintain a big circle of friends, but I make intentional time for the special people in my life. The author says slowing down saved her marriage. Courtesy of the author Above all, this inner shift saved more than just my own peace — it transformed my marriage. In my old life, I was always home in body, but absent in spirit; my mind was constantly preoccupied with ambition. As I traded endless chasing for small, quiet moments of joy, my husband and I found a depth of connection we hadn't known was missing. Forced to flee our home because of war, we faced a crisis that could have fractured our relationship. Instead, choosing a simpler, more intentional life together bound us closer and made our family resilient in ways speed never could. I no longer want to fit in. I prefer

articles.title: Twins bought homes next door to each other to create a family compound and raise their kids together
articles.summary: Twins Sydney and Amelia Stoker are raising their kids side by side after buying Bay Area homes next door to each other in 2022.
articles._body: Amelia and Sydney Stoker made a family compound. Sydney Stoker Twins Amelia and Sydney Stoker bought homes next door to each other. They each live with their spouse and kids, but the two homes function as a compound. They eat dinner together nightly and have a shared family credit card. Amelia and Sydney Stoker always hoped they could live in the same city when they had kids . The 39-year-old twins told Business Insider they were envious of their friends who grew up with cousins around. As they pictured their adult lives, they hoped their own children could have the experience they had wanted. When the sisters were wrapping up their orthodontics residencies in the Bay Area, though, it didn't feel realistic that they could live in the same city, Sydney said. The sisters work together at Twin Smiles Orthodontics. Sydney Stoker Amelia and her husband, Adam Fagin, were looking all over the country for an oral surgeon job for Fagin, while Sydney and her husband, Paden Roder, thought they would return to Portland, Oregon, which felt familiar and more affordable than the Bay Area. Then, the perfect house changed everything. Home sweet home Fagin is from the Bay Area , and after his parents moved down the street, they kept the three-bedroom, two-bathroom house he grew up in. They saved it in case their son settled down in California, renting it out while he was completing his education. In July 2022, the house next door to Fagin's family home went on the market, giving the Stokers and their spouses an idea: Sydney and Roder could buy it and raise their kids next to Amelia and Fagin, creating a multigenerational home . The four-bedroom, two-bathroom house had everything Sydney's family would need, but she and her husband were a little hesitant. Living in the Bay Area is expensive, and they were apprehensive about how overwhelming it would be to live next door to family. "My brother-in-law was the one who convinced us," Sydney said. "He was like, 'This is just too unique to pass up. Try it, and you can always reevaluate,' which is a great attitude that he has." Sydney Stoker with her family and Amelia Stoker with her family. Sydney Stoker Plus, a building became available around the same time that the Stoker sisters could buy for their orthodontics practice . It felt like fate. Sydney and her husband bought the house in the summer of 2022, shortly after they welcomed their first child . They now have a 4-year-old, a 2-year-old, and a newborn. Amelia and her husband also have a 4-year-old and a 2-year-old. A family compound Once the Stoker sisters and their spouses were next door to each other, they decided to embrace the benefits of living so close, turning their homes into a compound that could make all their lives easier. They took down the fence between their backyards, essentially making their lots into one big property. The kids can come and go between each other's spaces whenever they want. Both houses also have an accessory dwelling unit, or ADU, in the back. The families hired two au pairs, who live in one ADU, and the Stokers' mom typically stays in the other when she visits her daughters and grandkids. Sydney's mother-in-law has been staying in the ADU in recent months while the couple turns their garage into a permanent home for her. Plus, Amelia's in-laws live down the street, so there's family everywhere. Amelia and Sydney Stoker made a family compound. Sydney Stoker The seven adults who live on the property full time work together to make the compound function. The au pairs watch all five children together, and both families eat dinner together every weeknight. Amelia's household cooks on Tuesdays, Sydney's cooks on Thursdays, and Sydney's mother-in-law, who's retired and likes to cook, makes meals on Mondays, Wednesdays, and Fridays. The families also have a shared credit card that they use for compound-related expenses, such as paper towels and dinner supplies. "My sister usually is the one who goes to Costco every week, and she'll just use that compound card," Sydney said. "We all pay on it together." The family's backyards are connected. Sydney Stoker Despite how much time they spend together, everyone still understands where their own home is, Amelia said. "Everyone knows where their place is, and everyone wants to go home at the end of the night," she added. "So by about 7:30, everyone's tucked into their own little spaces." The benefits of the compound Both Amelia and Sydney said living on a compound makes raising their kids easier, particularly since they and their spouses work full-time jobs. "I can't imagine trying to do it all by myself," Sydney said. "Everything is just seamless. I feel like we can have a third kid because of the compound." Amelia said she feels like she and her sister have more free time than their friends since there are so many people available at any given moment to help care for their kids. They eat dinner together every weeknight. Sydney Stoker The sisters added that having more family around is a stark and welcome contrast to their upbringing. "I love getting to see my nieces grow up," Sydney said. "I think about that every day, how lucky I am to see them grow up." Their husbands are on the same page, with Sydney's spouse saying he loves how close all the children are becoming because of their living situation. "I get to watch my nieces grow up alongside my own kids, and they're all developing these incredibly close relationships that I hope they'll carry with them for the rest of their lives," Roder said. "From a practical standpoint, it also makes raising young kids so much easier," he added. "There's almost always another adult nearby to lend a hand, and the kids have built-in playmates right next door. It feels like we've created our own little village, which is pretty rare these days." articles.title: I avoided club sports because of the cost and time commitment. Now I wish I'd started sooner.
articles.summary: I never prioritized club sports for my kids until my youngest joined a soccer team. Now I regret not giving my older children the same opportunity.
articles._body: The author didn't prioritize club sports for the first three of her children. Now her fourth is thriving on a soccer team, and she said she regrets not considering them more seriously in the past. Courtesy of Jamie Davis Smith. The high cost and time commitments led me to avoid club sports and travel teams with my older kids. When my youngest started surpassing his rec league teammates, I decided to look into club sports. He's learning so much more than the game, making the expense and serious time commitment worth it. Growing up, I dabbled in gymnastics and ice skating but never joined a team or had formal training. When I had children, I wasn't opposed to any of the four of them playing sports if they wanted to, but it wasn't a priority. My oldest three showed a fleeting interest in athletics, but nothing ever stuck. We tried soccer for tots, tennis in early elementary school, a rec basketball team that anyone could walk on to, and Girls on the Run , a non-competitive program for young girls. However, none of my younger kids showed much interest in playing at a higher level in a club. I briefly looked into club sports, but lost all interest once I discovered they cost thousands of dollars and require an extensive time commitment from the entire family on weeknights and weekends. That's particularly true for travel teams, which involve more serious coaching and play than rec teams. I never regretted not signing my kids up for tryouts until my youngest son developed a passion for soccer and dove headlong into the sport. Now I see what my older kids were missing, and I regret not encouraging them to try club sports, too. Do you have a parenting regret? Email Jennifer Beck Goldblatt at jgoldblatt@insider.com to share your experience with Business Insider. I reluctantly signed my son up for a club team My son started playing soccer during recess at school. Before long, he was taking a skills class and playing soccer after school, too. Then came a rec team. He had fun, but I didn't feel like the parent leading the team had enough coaching experience to help him improve. My son trained hard in our backyard and at school, and his skills soon surpassed his teammates. In fourth grade, he asked to try out for a club with an advanced travel team. He already had a passion for the sport and showed talent, but I still hesitated before saying yes. The cost and grueling schedule gave me pause, and I wasn't sure I wanted him to focus heavily on one activity while he was still so young. Nevertheless, I begrudgingly filled out the necessary paperwork and drove him to multiple rounds of tryouts. Part of me hoped he wouldn't get a spot, but I wanted to give him the chance to shine. The author said her son is learning more than just the game while playing in his new club. Courtesy of Jamie Davis Smith. When the email offering my son a place on the team arrived, I surprised myself by being thrilled. After getting over my sticker shock and confusion about how club sports actually work, I handed over my credit card and, just like that, we were all in. I bought my son multiple uniforms and worked out a complex schedule with my husband to get our son to practices and games near and far. I learned that club sports offer benefits that go far beyond better training Since joining a club team over a year ago, my son has improved tremendously in soccer, as expected. While he may never achieve his goal of playing in the World Cup , he now passes with precision and defends the ball admirably. In a short time, I've also noticed how the benefits of a club sport go far beyond better coaching. At least three times a week, I watch from the sidelines as my son takes direction and correction with grace. Being open to suggestions for improvement is a new skill I see spilling over into other parts of life, whether it's ideas about keeping his homework organized or a better approach to keeping his room clean. Additionally, although I love seeing my son's joy when his team wins, he is slowly but surely learning to handle losses better, too. Instead of getting upset immediately as he used to, he now talks through what he could have done differently. Sometimes, he accepts that his team simply had bad luck or that an unfair referee made a win more difficult than it should have been. I see these skills spilling over into other parts of his life when things don't go his way. He has also dealt with adversity, playing in the cold and rain, dealing with aches and pains, and sometimes playing with teammates he doesn't like very much. This has taught him the importance of pushing through unpleasant circumstances and finding a way to get along with everyone. I've also seen my son shift from wanting to be the team's star player to wanting to be a part of something bigger than himself through cooperation and teamwork. Plus, being part of a team has given a whole new group of friends outside of school. Club sports are a sacrifice, but it's one I wish I had made for my older kids, too More than a year into our club sports journey, my only regrets are not starting sooner and not giving my older children the same opportunities my youngest has now. I recognize what a privilege it is to offer my son this experience, something many families can't afford because of the cost and time commitment. Sometimes I lament having to plan my family's entire weekend around soccer matches and feeling rushed on so many weeknights, but I have no plans to stop and would do it again in a heartbeat. I've surprised myself by feeling disappointment when a weekend goes by and I can't watch my son play. I'm excited to see where my son's club sports journey takes him next, and what other lessons he will learn along the way. Read the original article on Business Insider

articles.title: I went from owning a home in a small town to renting in a big city. Life costs more, but it feels richer.
articles.summary: Going from owning a home in a small town in Virginia to living in a big city and renting an apartment in Washington, DC, has been good, but expensive.
articles._body: Years ago, I never would have imagined myself living in a city or happily raising a child here. Renate Flanagan I went from owning a house in a small town in Virginia to renting an apartment in Washington, DC . Living in an apartment and in a big city has been better than I expected, with some nice perks. I love having easy access to nature, a diverse mix of restaurants, and public transportation in DC. I grew up in a fairly small, somewhat rural community in central Virginia, about two hours from Washington, DC. And, in my early 20s, I got married and bought a house there. But when I got divorced at 30, I wanted to start over somewhere new. Stars seemed to align when I got a new position at my company that required me to relocate to Washington, DC . I was happy to do it and officially moved to DC in 2021. Although my hometown wasn't that far from the nation's capital, the two places felt like night and day — and a lot of my worries about living in a big city turned out to be unfounded. City living comes with perks I didn't expect My husband and I have enjoyed taking our son around DC. Renate Flanagan I love the outdoors, and was lucky to grow up living close to Shenandoah National Park . I worried that moving to a big city meant giving up access to green spaces, but I was wrong. This has not been the case in DC, which has miles of bike and pedestrian trails. Beyond that, the city is so walkable and well-connected by public transportation that some of the parks and monuments are just a few blocks' walk or a short bus ride from my home. There are lots of free museums in the area, too. I got rid of my car when I moved to the city, and I don't miss it at all. There are also lots of parks, monuments, and free museums within walking distance of my home. Renate Flanagan On top of that, I love DC's cosmopolitan energy. With all the different embassies and global organizations in the city, there's a large international community. The diversity of cultures brings a variety of restaurants with cuisines from around the world that I would never have been able to find in my small town. Living in such a major city also provides a lot of economic opportunities that can be harder to find in smaller towns. For example, many large employers have offices in the Washington, DC, area and offer higher-salary jobs that help offset the higher cost of living. Living in an apartment has been surprisingly enjoyable, too Downsizing hasn't bothered me as much as I expected. Renate Flanagan I thought going from living in a single-family house to an apartment would feel like a downgrade, but it hasn't. For one, my apartment building has some great amenities like a pool, a full-sized gym, and a 24-hour front desk. Renting has also felt more financially predictable than owning a home . When it comes to maintenance, I no longer worry about footing the bill or mapping out logistics. When something breaks, I call my apartment-management company, and they get it fixed. My rent also includes all utilities, so I don't have to worry about my bills fluctuating with seasonal heating and air conditioning costs anymore. Although I was worried that sharing walls with others would mean a lot of noise, the people in my building are generally considerate of one another. It hasn't been an issue. I also expected living in a city with over half a million people would feel cold and impersonal, but I've cultivated a small-town vibe in my neighborhood by being friendly. These days, I'm on a first-name basis with the people who work in my apartment building. I see the same groundskeepers, valets, and taxi drivers outside the hotels every day, and we wave to each other each morning when I'm on my way to take my son to day care. The city is expensive, but I just can't see myself going back to living in a small town City living has its downsides, but the good outweighs the bad for me. Renate Flanagan There's no getting around it: It costs more to live in the city. Although it's not quite apples-to-apples, for context, my mortgage on the three-bedroom single-family house I used to share with my ex was about $1,200 a month. Here, I rent a one-bedroom apartment that I share with my now-husband and son for about $2,500 a month. That's about $15,600 more a year for less space. Even though I pay more in rent than I did for my mortgage, I find the salary and career-growth opportunities here more than make up for it. I also make more now than I did before I moved. Daily living expenses for things like groceries or going out to eat are higher here than in my hometown, but to me, the convenience and accessibility of so many different things are worth it. We love having access to walking trails and museums in DC. Renate Flanagan Before I had my son, who is now 2, I thought I might want to leave DC after I started a family. Now I think the city is a great place for him to grow up. He's exposed to many different cultures every day, and his classmates have diverse backgrounds. We have free access to the zoo and all sorts of nearby history and art museums, which have lots of kid-friendly activities that are fun for parents, too. Growing up in a small town, I was intimidated whenever I visited cities and had to navigate public transportation, but it will be second nature to my son as he gets older. When the opportunity to move presented itself all those years ago, I'm glad I kept an open mind because now I don't see myself going back to a small-town lifestyle.
