articles.title: DARPA wants AI to find hidden flaws in digital markets that adversaries could exploit to wreak economic havoc
articles.summary: DARPA is studying how the rules governing online markets could be manipulated to cause disruption, rather than just how their systems could be hacked.
articles._body: US defense and security agencies, as well as federal regulators, have to combat hacks and data theft. Another challenge is bad actors who exploit gaps in the rules governing key systems, like electronic markets. DARPA hopes to close those. ANGELA WEISS / AFP via Getty Images DARPA is seeking AI tools that can uncover hidden weaknesses in digital markets. Officials warn adversaries could exploit flaws in market rules to cause economic disruption. AI and other technologies could make markets easier to exploit but also help defenders find vulnerabilities. The Pentagon's research arm is seeking new artificial intelligence tools that can uncover hidden flaws in the rules governing US financial and other digital markets and fix them before adversaries can exploit them to cause economic chaos. The Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency 's new Intrinsic Market Resilience program is aimed at protecting electronic markets tied to everything from stocks and bonds to energy and cloud-computing resources. Those critical systems have become faster and more efficient, DARPA says, but their increasingly interconnected nature has also created new avenues for disruption. "I think that the incredible advances in automated reasoning and in AI are opening new ways to defend things," Matthew Wilding, the IMR program manager at DARPA, told Business Insider. "They can be used to attack things as well, but the focus of this program is using them to defend things, to find those counterexamples and find those improvements we can make to these designs." "The program is taking these two technologies that have really advanced in the last few years and applying them to these electronic markets," Wilding said, "so that they are more resilient and more dependable going forward." The concern is less that adversaries could hack these systems or steal data, both longstanding threats, than that they could exploit weaknesses in the design of the markets themselves. The agency pointed to two historical examples of disruption. In the early 2000s, traders exploited weaknesses in California's newly deregulated energy market, contributing to a crisis that DARPA said cost $40 billion to $45 billion. That chaotic incident forced the federal government to invoke the Defense Production Act to ensure the supply of natural gas to military facilities, which DARPA said highlighted how the manipulation of market mechanisms could have serious consequences for military readiness. Disruptions have previously come for US markets. Spencer Platt/Getty Images The other example was the 2010 " flash crash ," which saw US stocks plunge within minutes amid market instability that investigators later linked in part to one individual's manipulative trading practices, among other problems. Many of those gaps have since been corrected. "The actions cost the individual nothing because the sell orders were specifically designed not to be executed by leveraging a quirk in the design of the market," DARPA said in the solicitation posting for new AI tools. The number of electronic markets and participants is on the rise, raising the risk of disruption and increasing the potential that exploitation could be deeply damaging. Adding to the problem is that the proliferation of AI and other new technologies has lowered the barrier to entry for bad actors. IMR intends to leverage some of those same systems to model markets, analyze protections, and point out potential weak points. The program isn't aimed at the kinds of rogue market manipulation regulators typically pursue, such as individuals seeking financial profit . Instead, DARPA is focused on bad actors whose goal is simply to create disruption, economic damage, or instability, aided by current inadequacies in legal and regulatory safeguards. The agency wants performers to use large language models to turn things like regulatory filings and technical specifications into computer models of how markets operate and interact. The program aims to find ways to "identify design flaws in domestic online equity markets and recommend repairs" to protect against bad actors seeking to "exploit equity market design vulnerabilities," DARPA said in the posting. If a model can't prove that a market meets a certain standard of resilience, DARPA wants it to generate a specific example of how the market could fail, allowing users to identify the weaknesses and propose a fix. "We're not just testing," Wilding said, "We're actually looking at it and analyzing it," ultimately showing "how is it resilient, how it is not resilient, and how could we make it resilient." The DARPA solicitation reflects a growing national security concern that future attacks on the US might not resemble conventional military action. Future attacks could instead exploit vulnerabilities in digital infrastructure, supply chains, or markets. Read the original article on Business Insider

articles.title: I took my kids on vacation to practice their Spanish. Our no-English rule didn't last long.
articles.summary: My kids attend Spanish immersion school in the US., A family trip to Puerto Rico gave us a different kind of language lesson.
articles._body: The author wanted her family to speak only Spanish while on vacation in Puerto Rico. Courtesy of Sandra Lee. My kids have been at a Spanish immersion school in the US since they were in preschool. On a trip to Puerto Rico, I only wanted us to speak Spanish, so they could practice their skills. The trip reminded me that language learning is ongoing and about adapting to new experiences. As my family of four began our descent to Puerto Rico , I made the announcement. There would be no more English for the duration of our trip. My kids, 9 and 11, who had been learning Spanish in immersion school since preschool, would get an opportunity to put it to good use. I thought this trip would be the perfect crash course for them before school started back up in the fall. When we landed in Puerto Rico and headed to our hotel, I realized I was going to have my work cut out. The driver spoke English, as did the workers at the front desk , restaurant waiters, and other staff. Turns out, they were just as bilingual as I was. Our no-English rule didn't last long At first, the kids were happy to skip the intense Spanish practice I had envisioned, but I still wanted us to try. Then, before I knew it, I was catching myself slipping into English, too. The author said her family didn't stick to her no-English rule for long while on their family trip to Puerto Rico. Courtesy of Sandra Lee. My husband doesn't speak Spanish, and with Duolingo as his only teacher , we often defaulted to English so he could follow the conversation. Before long, we were all speaking our own version of Spanglish, mixing languages to get our point across. My no-English rule was harder to enforce than I'd expected. Even I had a lot to learn I grew up speaking Spanish in the US, but it isn't my dominant language. Our kids being able to speak another language is important to my husband and me, so we decided to enroll them in Spanish immersion schools, starting in preschool. The Spanish language varies across countries and regions, but hearing Puerto Rican Spanish reminded me of how different the language can be. Some familiar words sounded unfamiliar, and I kept having to ask locals to describe the word they were using so I could connect it to the one I knew from Mexico, where my mother is from. The cadence and speed of conversations were different too, which made me listen more closely to what was being said. Instead of being the one helping my family navigate the language, I was the one asking questions and learning at the same time. I wanted my kids to see that Spanish isn't the same everywhere On the surface, I wanted my kids to practice their Spanish , become more confident speakers, and immerse themselves in another Latin culture, but it became more than that. As a Mexican Spanish-speaker and a parent, there was something meaningful about recognizing familiar words, trying to understand unfamiliar ones, and explaining how people could express the same idea differently. In their schools, they have Spanish teachers from different countries — including Spain, Mexico, Colombia, and Peru — all with their own different dialects, words, and intonation. The author, who grew up speaking Spanish, said the trip helped her show her kids how language can vary across regions. Courtesy of Sandra Lee. Rather than correcting my kids or testing their vocabulary, we ended up all figuring out how to communicate in a place where the Spanish we knew wasn't necessarily the Spanish we heard. I came home with a different idea of language learning When we landed in Puerto Rico, I had only one rule: to practice our Spanish before school started back up. Instead, we all slipped into English, mixed languages, and learned to navigate unfamiliar words. I realized that fluency isn't the same as knowing every word, and learning doesn't stop when the lesson ends or the school bell rings. Sometimes it means asking questions, listening, and discovering a little more about the world along the way. Read the original article on Business Insider

articles.title: I took my 80-year-old mother to Taiwan. I thought I'd be looking after her, but she proved me wrong.
articles.summary: I took my 80-year-old mom on a long international trip to Taiwan. I wasn't sure if she'd be able to keep up with the group tour, but she surprised me.
articles._body: I took my 80-year-old mom on a long international trip to Taiwan. Sue Sands I took my 80-year-old mom on an international group trip to Taiwan. I was worried the packed itinerary might be too much for her, but she proved me wrong. She was a big hit among the tour group, and I was impressed by how independent she was. Walking up the steep, winding track to the Ci'En Pagoda in Taiwan, I could already feel the mid-day sun pinking the back of my neck. Several members of our tour group were ahead of us, red-faced and out-of-breath, staring with dismay at a set of stone stairs disappearing up the hillside among the trees. Although my 80-year-old mom was the oldest in the group, younger members had been complimenting her stamina since day one. However, I still felt compelled to watch over her to ensure she didn't overdo things, and on that particular day, I was concerned about the heat and elevation. Ignoring my urging to wait in the shade, she responded by walking determinedly to the foot of the stairs and starting the ascent, buoyed by encouraging words as others passed her on the path. My mom is a good traveler, but it had been a while since she'd taken a long trip Months earlier, my husband and I had planned for our college-student daughter to meet us for a 10-day guided tour in Taiwan. When I'd idly asked my mom if she'd like to come too, she surprised us all by signing up immediately. It would be her first trip to Asia , her first group tour, and her first overseas vacation in several years. Initially impressed by her sense of adventure, I secretly grew apprehensive. My mom is a calm and cheerful travel companion on domestic trips, but I dwelt on whether she'd be comfortable navigating a long flight , new foods, and full days of sightseeing. She's fit and active, but at the end of the day, she's still 80. But during the planning process, she seemed enthusiastic and committed. She was sure she would keep up with the packed itinerary , so I decided to embrace her positive attitude. Throughout the trip, my mom kept surprising me My daughter was a huge help in the tech department. Sue Sands Once we arrived in Taipei, Taiwan , I watched in wonder as my daughter and mother bent their heads together over my mom's phone, signing her up for the tour group's WhatsApp chat. Back home, my mother would usually rather call us than text, so I figured she'd download the app and ignore it for the rest of the tour. However, with her granddaughter's regular IT support and thoughtful interactions from some of the other ladies in the group, she quickly gained confidence in her newfound skills, posting comments and exchanges in the chat. She even appeared in one of the group chat's daily photo galleries, her bright smile a contrast to the serious concentration on the faces around her. The picture was taken while we were being taught the steps of a traditional dance, and, humblingly, my mom's weekly line-dancing lessons meant she picked up the instructions more quickly than most of us. While half of us were shuffling left instead of stepping right, I had received several admiring whispers: "Your mom is having lots of fun, and she's really good." Throughout the trip, however, it turned out she had more skills of her own to share. Always curious, my husband asked about the backstory of the Chiang Kai-shek Memorial Hall as we waited outside for the changing-of-the-guard ceremony to start. Turns out, my mom knew a lot about the history of the Chiang Kai-shek Memorial Hall. Jaclyne Ortiz/Getty Images I was about to resort to Google for the answer, when my mom chimed in unexpectedly with an impressive recall from her high school history lessons. Turns out, she knew a lot more about Taiwan than I realized, and I was glad she had spoken before I could pull up a search bar. This wasn't the only time her memories saved the day. One night, I was keen to go out and join others at the night market to sample the local cuisine, but my mom was tired after a long day on the bus. Instead, we decided to experience Taiwan's convenience-store culture . Tension diffused as we headed out to the nearby 7-Eleven, loading up on local snacks to take back to the hotel room for an impromptu family picnic. Over a tuna mayo onigiri, and perhaps under the influence of canned wine , my mom shared some hilarious, new-to-me childhood stories that had all four of us laughing along. It wasn't the local food experience I was expecting, but it's one I'll remember forever. I learned to see my mom as the independent person she's always been I was proud of my mom for making it up the stairs to the Ci'en Pagoda. Sue Sands I also frequently think back to the day on the stairs. In response to my suggestion that she wait in the shade, she hiked up all those steps to reach Ci'en Pagoda above Sun Moon Lake, fittingly built by former president Chiang Kai-Shek in honor of his mother. Halfway up, I finally realized it didn't really matter to her if she saw the pagoda or not; being supported in her choice to be independent and active was the most important thing for her. I'd also realized that my mom was holding her own as part of the larger group. She was interested and engaged with our traveling companions, and was one of the first to remember names and backstories. I'd started the trip thinking I was looking after my mother by checking on her, but I ended up appreciating what the rest of the group saw — an active, engaged traveler enjoying new experiences and sharing them with her family. articles.title: I love my $115,000 home in rural Japan. I'd still warn most Americans against following my lead.
articles.summary: Keito Swan moved from the US to Japan and bought a home there. He says Americans shouldn't do the same if they're looking for an investment.
articles._body: Keito Swan moved from California to Hokkaido, in northern Japan. Courtesy of Keito Swan Keito Swan traded California for the Japanese countryside and spent $115,000 on a home. He enjoys his space and the outdoors, and is in an area where conveniences are still accessible. Swan warns that the lifestyle — and costs — of a cheap house in rural Japan are not for everyone. This as-told-to essay is based on a conversation with Keito Swan, 37, a professional gambler who moved from Modesto, California, to the countryside of Hokkaido, Japan, after buying a home. The following has been edited for length and clarity. I was actually born in Japan — there's a Navy base in Sasebo, Japan. My dad's white, my mom's Japanese. I lived there until I was 7. Then, with my father being in the Navy, we moved around a bit. I lived most of my life in Seattle and then about seven years in California. I go to Japan every winter for snowboarding , and I'd actually considered moving there before. But I thought, "It's cheap enough to just vacation. What's the point of having the liability of homeownership there when I'm not going to be living there?" It didn't really make sense to me at that time. Then I spent two years traveling — I drove the Pan-American Highway — and during that time, I came to realize I just don't think that the US is for me. Rice fields in front of Swan's home. Courtesy of Keito Swan I was considering buying a place in Argentina, but Japan seemed like an easier route for me than anywhere else because I already had citizenship, spoke the language, and knew the culture. It made the most sense. The cost of living and quality of life were definitely a huge aspect of moving there, because I can't afford that quality of life in the US — and that's as a single guy, no kids, no nothing, and making decent money. I paid a premium to live in a well-connected area of the countryside — and it's still cheaper than the US About a year and a half ago, I spent $115,000 on the property. The house is pretty old and was super moldy and falling apart, so I spent another $65,000 on a full remodel. I hired a family friend who owns a construction company to handle everything, so I didn't actually do any of it. I live at the base of Japan's biggest national park. There are probably six ski resorts within an hour of my house. I live in what's considered the countryside of Japan ; I'm surrounded by rice fields. I'm in the mountains, and there's a lot of agricultural work, but I live 15 minutes from an airport that flies directly to Tokyo. I'm 30 minutes from the second biggest city in Hokkaido. It's a very outdoorsy area — a lot of hiking and nature — but in the winters it's incredibly brutal. It's -30 Celsius, and we get meters and meters of snow. So it's not for everyone, but if you're a winter sports enthusiast like me, and an outdoors person, it's as good as it gets. I would argue that I have way more fun in Japan with my lifestyle than I do in the US in Modesto. Modesto's the almond capital of the world. It's agricultural, but I'm two hours from Yosemite, It's two hours from Lake Tahoe, and it's an hour and 40 minutes from San Francisco. So I'm more countryside in California than I am in Japan, I think. Swan's property covered in snow. Courtesy of Keito Swan When I was renting an apartment in Sausalito, just outside San Francisco, I was paying $3,200 a month, and I was renting the in-law suite of someone's house. Granted, I had an ocean view, but still. That's triple my monthly expenses for everything, not just housing, in Japan. Utilities are pretty comparable, if not cheaper, but in the wintertime, my utilities triple because I have the gas heater and I'm using more electricity. That's where my expenses go up quite a bit. But even then it's very manageable. I spend about $60 a month on electricity, $35 a month on property taxes, and $30 a month for health insurance — and that covers your dental and vision as well. I go to my local bar to eat a lot, and it's not just bar food that's deep-fried; they're actually making things from scratch. My dinners are usually 1,200 Yen, which is about $8. And it's all locally sourced food. My monthly costs in non-winter months are a little over $1,000. Moving to Japan made sense for me, but it's not for everyone My lifestyle in Japan doesn't change. I do all the same things I did in the US: I'm outdoors, I'm hiking, I'm in the national park, I'm snowboarding in the winter, and in the summer I'm doing some gardening or some yard work. I think that was one of the things I was really cognizant of, making sure my lifestyle would be good. I was intelligent enough to look into all those other factors, and I had my checklist of needs and wants, so I based where I bought on that. The reason I love my town is because I have everything; I have a hardware store, I have three convenience stores, I have restaurants, I have a bar. And if I don't have it, it's just 30 minutes away. There are a lot of places in the countryside of Japan that don't have that. Spending $180,000 on a home versus what people are seeing on social media about how cheap houses are in Japan, it seems like a lot of money. But that's why I paid a premium. I didn't pay $20,000 for a dilapidated countryside house . I paid $115,000 for a kind of dilapidated house in the countryside of Japan. In the rural parts of Japan , I don't see a situation where it makes sense to buy unless you're retired, you have some flexibility, and you're not buying a dilapidated house that's falling apart. I get a lot of accusations that I'm just trying to gatekeep by saying this, but it's a terrible financial investment. Let's say you spend $50,000 on a house and it's going to need repairs. You're probably going to spend another $50,000 on repairs. If you would have put that $100,000 into the stock market and collected your returns on that hassle-free and just rented an Airbnb for three months a year in Japan instead, you would be so much further ah

articles.title: Sailors aboard Britain's newest aircraft carrier are training to fight through darkness, rough seas, and radio silence
articles.summary: NATO is increasingly focused on reinforcing its northern flank amid a rise in Russian military activity across the Arctic and North Atlantic.
articles._body: Sailors aboard the HMS Prince of Wales in the Norwegian Sea last week. Jake Epstein/Business Insider NATO is increasingly focused on defending its northern flank as Russian military activity grows. Western naval commanders say the High North presents serious challenges for naval operations. The UK's newest aircraft carrier is training to fight through darkness, rough seas, and radio silence. ABOARD A ROYAL NAVY HELICOPTER — Fog hangs low over Norway's jagged coastline as the British helicopter flies out over the frigid waters below. The days are growing colder, bringing worsening weather and decreased daylight to the High North. The helicopter, a Merlink Mk4, lands on the flight deck of the HMS Prince of Wales , the Royal Navy's flagship. Wind whips across the deck as sailors bundled in protective gear move F-35 stealth fighter jets into position. By early afternoon, the sun is already sinking toward the horizon, complicating operations as the light fades away. Business Insider visited the Prince of Wales, the lead ship for the UK's carrier strike group, in early November while it was underway in the Norwegian Sea. The ship's deployment is part of the second phase of Operation Firecrest, a deterrence mission in the Arctic and North Atlantic. NATO is increasingly focused on reinforcing its northern flank amid growing Russian military activity in the region. But operating there, particularly during fall and into winter as the days become colder and shorter, presents formidable challenges for allied forces. The High North is a "complex environment," Capt. Ben Power, the Prince of Wales' commanding officer, said during an interview on the ship's bridge. Sailors move an F-35B on the carrier's flight deck. Jake Epstein/Business Insider Winter brings ice, persistent low-pressure systems, and thick fog. The crew has to be ready for these and trained to operate without transmitting radar signals or using radio communications, skills Power said are critical to improving its "warfighting proficiency." "All of those things are complex when you do it in the High North, far more so than other parts of the world," he said. NATO has expanded its patrols and joint operations across the Arctic and North Atlantic to monitor Russian naval activity and signal deterrence. Western officials have specifically stressed the importance of keeping tabs on Russian submarines , dozens of which are based in Murmansk on the Barents Sea. To reach the Atlantic Ocean or the Mediterranean and Baltic seas, these submarines typically sail south through the North Sea, or between Greenland, Iceland, and the UK — a strategic chokepoin t known as the GIUK gap. For NATO, a strong presence in this region is critical. "It's safe to say that we've seen an increase in Russian activity in all domains — so above, on, and particularly beneath the sea," Power said. "In terms of an assessment of their capability," he said, "I think Russia continues to pose a credible threat." Western naval officers who previously spoke with Business Insider aboard a Dutch frigate in the Arctic described how poor visibility, rough seas, and large swells, especially in the winter, can impact operations, particularly flight ops. They said climate has a direct effect on operations, making it important to regularly train in locations that will test the crew. Speaking aboard the Prince of Wales this week, Commodore Richard Hewitt, commander of the UK's carrier strike group, acknowledged the challenges of operating in the High North but commended the crew for their ability to handle the conditions. In the first phase of Operation Firecrest over the summer, the Prince of Wales supported Arctic Sentry , a NATO vigilance mission launched earlier this year to strengthen security in the High North through exercises and patrols. "This year has been focused in the High North," Hewitt said. "I can see that continuing within the North Atlantic — and quite rightly so." Read the original article on Business Insider

articles.title: Apple, please stop announcing people's emoji reactions in my AirPods
articles.summary: Siri reads out whenever someone uses an emoji reaction to a text when you're wearing AirPods. More granular controls are needed.
articles._body: I love emoji reactions. Just not on my headphones. Francesco Carta fotografo/Getty Images Your iPhone reads out whenever someone uses an emoji reaction to a text when you're wearing AirPods. I like emoji reactions — but I don't want to HEAR about them! This is, I'm pretty certain, the most urgent and pressing tech issue of the moment. Apple has been committing a grave injustice against us for years, and it's time someone speaks up and voices what the people have felt powerless to say. That brave person is me. The problem is that iMessage reactions — such as someone liking a text with the thumbs-up emoji — keep playing in my AirPods. There should be a way to turn this off. Here's the problem. If you get an iMessage while wearing your headphones, your phone will announce it: "From [name]: message here." That's really useful and helpful! I find this feature fantastic. However, when I'm wearing my AirPods, I'm typically not looking at my phone — I'm walking around, listening to a podcast while doing dishes or at the gym. These are all times I want to know if I got a new text — maybe I'm at the grocery store and my husband texts me to say we need more eggs. Great! Let those notifications rip! I love it!!! But you know what I do NOT need to know? If someone reacted with the heart emoji to a message in a group chat. The useful thumbs-up emoji is great, but I don't want to hear about it while I'm taking a walk! Business Insider Reactions in iMessage are great. They're highly efficient: sometimes you just want to give a thumbs-up to let someone know you acknowledged the message, or a heart to show you appreciate a baby photo or what have you. Apple, I salute you: this was a great feature. You really cooked with this one. However, there is no way to turn off notifications for just those reactions — you can turn off announcements of all messages in your headphones, but then it means you won't hear the "hey can you also pick up eggs" text. You can also select "time sensitive and direct messages" only (which is my current setting), but for me, those pesky emoji reactions persist. In Settings > Notifications > Messages, you can reduce the announcements. Business Insider The emoji announcement problem in AirPods is similar to another issue that long plagued iMessage: if someone isn't on an iPhone, the reactions would come in as separate messages altogether. One Android in the group and a green text bubble meant full-on chaos in the chat. I have a very active group chat with a bunch of friends who are big-time emoji reaction users, but one friend is on Android, which means it's a green bubble chat. For years, this meant that the emoji reactions were a nightmare for her — so much that she muted the group and would only rarely check in. Thankfully, in 2024, Apple mostly fixed this problem by embracing a texting protocol called Rich Communications Services. The result? Green texts could use emoji reactions normally now. See? Progress can happen! John Ternus, if you want to really make a splash as Apple CEO , I have a suggestion for you: fix this. Make a toggle switch in the Notifications settings of the Messages app so you can turn off just emoji reaction announcements. Read the original article on Business Insider

articles.title: The hottest new job perk is helping employees buy a house
articles.summary: As the housing market becomes less affordable, some employers are offering homebuying assistance benefits through companies like NestSteps and Nestment.
articles._body: Employers are helping homebuying be within reach with new benefits. panaya chittaratlert/Getty Images As competition in the housing market intensifies, many professionals say homebuying is out of reach. Some employers are offering homebuying assistance perks to entice talent in a tough market. Two CEOs say it will be the next cornerstone of employee benefits, like retirement savings. With competition in the pricey San Francisco housing market reaching new heights, Hilary Petee and her husband had given up on the dream of homeownership. "We brushed it off as something that we couldn't do," Petee, 42, told Business Insider. "We thought, 'We can't afford to do that right now. It doesn't make sense.'" But when Petee and her husband's rent increased by 8.8% in August, they began to seriously consider buying, if they could make it work. Petee, a brand manager, discovered that her employer offered Nestment, a platform that provides homeownership coaching, as an employee benefit, and she decided to try it. She and her husband have since closed on a $1.4 million home. Petee said she wouldn't have been able to do it without her homebuying coach. "It didn't feel like my husband and I were going to be able to compete in the competitive housing market in San Francisco," she said. "I was pretty excited that I would have any support at all to be able to help find a home and to understand that in San Francisco, specifically." Employee benefits, like employer-covered healthcare, retirement plans, and student loan debt relief , are a tried-and-true way to recruit and retain talented employees. As it becomes increasingly difficult to own a home in the current market, some employers are offering housing benefits as a new way to win prospective employees' hearts. The American dream is getting a little help from HR Companies like Nestment are heeding the call from employers. "Our mission at Nestment is to bring homeownership to all who want it," Nestment founder Niles Lichtenstein told Business Insider. "We know that homeownership is part of the American dream. It's part of financial wellness and also physical and mental stability." Lichtenstein founded Nestment in 2021 as a startup focused on educating first-time homebuyers, offering them services like a personal homebuying coach and AI tools that help them plan out the best way to buy a home. When customers began asking for integration into their companies, Lichtenstein obliged, launching the service as an employer benefit in early 2026. "We had a bunch of customers say, 'Can we bring this into our workplace?' We also had a couple of instances where we had organizations who said, 'Hey, we see that you're doing this learning education. Can we send this out to our employees?' Lichtenstein said. "We were like, 'there's something here.'" Your company might give you a 401k. But will they help you buy a home? Constantinis/Getty Images Larry Salazar and his wife, Cheri, came to a similar conclusion in 2025 when they launched NestSteps, an employer-sponsored benefit program that helps employees reduce the financial stress of buying a home. Salazar said his own experience attempting to break into the Southern California housing market in 2000 while working for Boeing made him realize the power of homeownership. At the time, he was overwhelmed, and ultimately bought a home once he moved to a more affordable housing market instead. "We moved for the purpose of owning our home," Salazar told Business Insider. "That was probably, for me, a moment where I started to realize something is there that we need to leverage." Employers around the country are catching on. Streaming company Twitch partnered with Denver-based company Multiply Mortgage to offer employees mortgage rate discounts. Financial services company BNY announced earlier this year that it was offering US employees who make less than $100,000 $6,500 towards a down payment — as well as education and mortgage benefits. Brooks Holtom, a professor of management at Georgetown University's McDonough School of Business, told Business Insider he could see benefits like these catching on, especially in places where it's tougher to enter the market, like in San Francisco. He cited a 2008 program at Mercy Hospital in Miami, which offered $10,000 toward a down payment to nurses who committed to five years at the hospital, as an example. As more companies begin offering benefits like these, Holtom said, others may consider it, too. "It starts with one firm in an industry offering a benefit, and when competitors see that it gets traction, helps them attract or retain employees, then there's a copycat effect — people will follow that lead," he said. "In some industries, there are arms races, especially when talent is scarce. So you see the most extravagant benefits where talent is worth the most, and where talent makes the biggest difference." Lichtenstein and Salazar both see an immediate need for their programs, which they both hope will one day become standard benefits. "You have your 401(k), I have my 401(k). Sure, we love seeing that it's growing, but how often does it impact us right now?" Lichtenstein said. "What impacts you right now is a home." Read the original article on Business Insider

articles.title: My 62-year-old mom doesn't do anything to her face, not even wear makeup. It's taught me a lot about confidence and aging.
articles.summary: My mom is 62 and doesn't wear makeup or get Botox. It's shown me about confidence, and given me an example of a different approach to aging.
articles._body: The author's mother, 62, doesn't wear any makeup. Courtesy of Jillian Pretzel My mom is 62 and has sworn off makeup, Botox, and other cosmetic enhancements. I still wear makeup, but I'm glad I grew up with her example. She's shown me another approach to aging. My mom is 62 and she's never gotten Botox or filler. She doesn't even wear makeup. These days, that's rare, especially where we live. My mom and I were both born and raised in Southern California, and here, beauty standards are high. Plastic surgery and other enhancements are common. Microneedling, chemical peels, microdermabrasion, and LED light treatment services are a "must" for many. But my mom has shown me that's not the only way to approach aging . Her decision to skip cosmetic products and procedures taught me something important about aging — something I didn't fully understand until recently. She realized in college that she wasn't interested in makeup A couple of weeks ago, after a particularly long session staring at my crows' feet in the mirror, I asked my mom why she never wears makeup . When I was growing up, she'd wear it sparingly: some eyeliner and a touch of lip gloss for a special occasion. However, for the last couple of decades, the only thing she's worn on her face is lotion. Standing at my kitchen counter, I asked if there was a certain day she decided: "Makeup isn't for me." As it turns out, there was. My mom told me it started during her freshman year of college. She'd seen her roommate put on makeup — and was horrified. The author is grateful that she grew up with her mom's example. Courtesy of Jillian Pretzel According to her, the roommate spent nearly an hour every morning applying expensive products. Then, after brushing on a few thick layers of mascara, she'd open a safety pin and use the point to separate each individual eyelash. "I already couldn't believe the time and money she spent on her face," Mom said. "But I was shocked that she was willing to put a pin next to her eye. What if there was an earthquake? What if, God forbid, she sneezed?" Mom's voice was higher than normal. Forty years had passed since she shared a dorm room with this woman, but she was still, apparently, upset about what she'd seen. So, at 18, Mom decided that makeup just wasn't for her. She's always been practical, and between the time commitment, money spent, and apparent danger to eyeballs, Mom's cost-benefit analysis said 'no' to cosmetics. "I know some people love putting on makeup," my mom said. "It can be a form of art and self-expression. But to me, it always looked like work." She had another epiphany in her 40s, when her friends started getting Botox and face lifts, and dropping a fortune on face creams. Mom decided it wasn't worth her time. In fact, she resolved that, as a rule, she wasn't going to do anything cosmetic. No more eyeliner and lip gloss even for special occasions, and definitely no plastic surgery. "As I got older, the women I knew seemed to be spending more time on their looks. I just didn't want to do that," she said with a shrug. Because they have such a strong resemblance, the author says she sees her own future in her mom's face. Courtesy of Jillian Pretzel I grew up with her example Looking back, I love that my mom ignored social pressure and beauty standards . It feels very feminist, very "rock and roll." But in the early 2000s, as Mom was swearing off cosmetics forever, I was just getting interested in them. It started when I got lip gloss in a birthday party goodie bag , and it evolved into wearing not-so-subtle purple glitter eye shadow to school. At an age when I was self-conscious about every zit (and there were many), makeup made me feel pretty and even grown-up. I liked it. Mom didn't discourage my exploration of makeup. In fact, in high school, she'd drop my friends and me off at the mall, where we'd spend too much money at the MAC counter. She, graciously, didn't make fun of my overlined lips or my overplucked eyebrows. Although I'm sure she had to bite her tongue, especially on the days I attempted "winged" eyeliner. And yet, I always secretly wondered if she disapproved. I wondered if she was disappointed that, after years of providing me with an example of how women don't have to subscribe to the whims of the beauty industry and Hollywood ideals, I was willing to drop all my Christmas money on a trendy new foundation. After talking to my mom that day in my kitchen, I realized that, for her, deciding not to invest in her looks wasn't about makeup being "good" or "bad," it wasn't even about self-confidence. It was just about choosing how to spend the precious amount of time we have in this life. She'd rather spend half an hour every morning reading a book or going for a walk than putting on makeup. She'd rather spend money on a round of drinks with people she cares about than a new eyeshadow palette. But not everyone feels the same way. At 35, I still like to wear makeup because it makes me feel pretty. And I'm not opposed to a little Botox one day. I'll admit that sometimes I look at dolled-up Hollywood stars and I think, "Man, she looks great! I want to be like her." But I wonder if, one day, I'll change my mind. Maybe one day I'll decide to spend that time, money, and energy on something else. And I think, in the end, it doesn't really matter what my mom looks like. It doesn't matter if she wants to wear makeup, or get work done, or not. But as I put on a little eyeliner and mascara this morning, I realized that I've gotten a unique advantage from my mom's no-cosmetics rule. Mom and I have always had a strong resemblance, and it's nice to know, more or less, what I'll look like at her age if I don't do anything. Her face isn't a product of fancy creams or surgery; it's just nature plus time. And even if I don't make any changes or spend another dollar trying to look pretty, maybe that's OK. I've seen my future, and I think she looks perfect. Read the original article on Business Insi

articles.title: I told my husband I wanted a sleep divorce before we got married. He thought sleeping apart meant I didn't love him.
articles.summary: I wanted separate bedrooms when I married later in life, but my husband disagreed. An unexpected health scare changed my mind.
articles._body: The author says she has found a routine to share a room with her partner. Courtesy of the author I fell in love later in life but worried that sharing a bedroom would mean losing my independence. My husband believed married couples should share a bed, and we struggled to find a compromise. After a health scare, he stayed with me, and I realized I actually enjoyed sleeping beside him. "I want separate bedrooms," I blurted out, trying to sound casual. "It's practical, not personal; I'm just such a light sleeper and…" But Michael was frowning. I knew it bothered him. I didn't know then it was a potential dealbreaker. I met Michael, an Air Force veteran and former fire chief, at our 55+ senior living community, where we bonded over themed dress-up parties. Our first was Gatsby, and we had a blast transforming into full characters while our fellow residents cheered us on. With every costume change, we grew closer and spent nights at each other's apartments. Those sleepovers cemented my resolve to sleep solo. Michael snored, and I was self-conscious about wearing my CPAP mask . I tossed and turned most of the night and woke up exhausted. I liked sleeping alone I fell for his easygoing nature and sense of humor. Michael was game for whatever elaborate getup I dreamed up. I loved being with him, but I relished getting my bed back. The author really wanted to sleep alone despite loving spending time with her partner. Courtesy of the author The truth was, it terrified me. It wasn't just about him seeing me in my sexy CPAP. After years of being single and happy as a clam sleeping alone, sharing a bedroom felt like losing my freedom. I often woke up at 2 am and scrolled my phone or turned on the TV to lull my racing mind back to sleep. I cherished my sacred sleep space, and it was worth fighting for. Apparently, falling in love complicated things. Two years later, as we planned our costumes for the western-themed party, we also discussed marriage and buying a home together. I hoped we'd reach a compromise about sleep arrangements, but Michael heard something deeper. "Sharing a bedroom is part of being married," he said. To him, sleeping apart meant rejection and a marriage lacking true intimacy . I thought evidence would strengthen my argument. Nearly one-third of US adults reported a "sleep divorce," or consistently sleeping in another bed or space, according to a 2025 survey by the American Academy of Sleep Medicine . Even Cameron Diaz once said, "We should normalize separate bedrooms," although she admitted her feelings changed after she got married. Michael smirked and shook his head. "I don't care what celebrities are doing," he said. "This is you and me." I started wondering what sharing a room would be like We married in August last year while still house shopping. I assumed we'd stay in our own apartments until we moved. But when we found our new home, with its beautiful primary suite and bathroom, I caught myself imagining us sharing a bedroom for the first time. That wasn't part of the plan. We closed on the house in September and planned to move in just before Halloween. Then, a few weeks later, I was hospitalized with SVT, a condition that spiked my heart rate , causing weakness and faintness. "I'm staying with you," Michael insisted after I was discharged with strict orders not to be left alone. I reluctantly nodded. He moved into my apartment while I recovered, and my unplanned experiment in sharing a bedroom began. The author is a nurse. Courtesy of the author As a former nurse, I joked that we make the worst patients, but this time I relented and melted under his care. I liked having him there and someone to lean on. With just one bathroom, we ended up colliding in the hallway a few times during the night. And we discovered that if Michael rolled onto his left side, his snoring stopped. He let me gently nudge him if he drifted onto his back. Michael did his own research and proudly informed me that side sleeping was healthier anyway. Mayo Clinic experts say it can help keep the airway open and reduce snoring. Apparently, he now values sleep research. Once I recovered, Michael just stayed. We never discussed making it permanent or how my whole plan quietly eroded. As more of his things appeared in my apartment, I was more relaxed at night, CPAP and all. One morning, I woke up to Michael all rolled up in the blankets from head to toe. "You look like a burrito," I laughed, and he joined in. We gradually found a nighttime routine. I introduced Michael to sleep masks so he wouldn't be disturbed if I woke up scrolling. Knowing my habit, Michael often left me love notes online to discover while I scrolled late at night. He slept soundly beside me. And it felt less like a loss of freedom and more like a gain in security. By the time we moved into our new home, I had fully embraced sharing a bedroom, the very thing I had sworn never to do. And to my surprise, it felt natural. Instead of stressful, bedtime was now tranquil; the CPAP hummed in a dark, quiet room, and Michael drifted off on his side. Somewhere along the way, I realized sharing a bedroom had less to do with sleep and more to do with fully trusting someone and letting him into the most private part of my life. I made room for Michael without losing myself. My love for him eclipsed the need for separate bedrooms. Read the original article on Business Insider

articles.title: Shaq made a backup plan in case he lost his fortune. He says it'll pay him $1 million a month starting next year.
articles.summary: NBA icon Shaquille O'Neal spoke about his guaranteed paycheck, his early Google wager, and the "stipulations" on his children's inheritance.
articles._body: Shaquille O'Neal has locked in a retirement income. Paras Griffin/Getty Images Shaquille O'Neal says a dull insurance product will pay him $1 million a month from next spring. The NBA icon said he "put a lot into annuities" to secure an income in case his investments failed. O'Neal also spoke about his early Google bet and the "stipulations" on his kids' inheritance. Shaquille O'Neal says he bought a boring financial product years ago in case he squandered his fortune, and it's poised to pay him $1 million a month starting next year. The basketball legend known as "Shaq" told the story behind his safety net during the latest episode of the "Dinner Party" podcast. He once asked a "filthy rich guy" — a "Four Seasons, Rolls-Royce" type — how to stay rich . The man pulled out a napkin, tore it in half, then half again, and said, "If you want to be wealthy, you play with 25, and you save 75 ." O'Neal — who once spent $1 million in a single day  when he was 20 — said he began saving aggressively following their conversation. Later, when he began investing his wealth, he wanted to lock in a future income in case those bets didn't pay off. "So I had so much money coming in, I put a lot into annuities," the four-time NBA champion said. "That was my fail-proof just in case the investments don't work , and this and that." An annuity is an insurance product that converts a lump sum or series of premiums into a regular stream of income payments, usually paid in retirement. O'Neal, who's touted annuities in the past, said that after he turns 55 next spring, he'll have "a lot" coming in, "almost for the rest of my life." Asked how much he expects to receive, he replied: "I don't like to brag, but I think at 55 I'll probably get a million dollars a month." O'Neal made several other memorable comments on the podcast. He recalled telling his children, " We ain't rich; I'm rich ," and informing them of the "stipulations" for receiving any inheritance from him. "Got to have a master's. Got to have a bachelor's," he said. "If you want to touch the cheese, you got to have two or three degrees." O'Neal famously promised his mother he would return to college after turning pro to finish his degree, and went on to earn a bachelor's, a master's, and a doctorate. He also revisited a famous moment in a hotel lobby where a stranger invited him to invest in Google , now Alphabet, before it went public. The legendary baller said he "put in a little bit" after running the opportunity by his "money guy," and later read in the newspaper how well early investors in Google had done. He called the Google bet a "nice big hit," but then quipped that he lost it all in his 2009 divorce , sticking his tongue out in trademark fashion. Experiences like that may help explain O'Neal's taste for annuities, an unglamorous but reliable way to secure a retirement income. Read the original article on Business Insider

articles.title: I lost my tech job and couldn't afford my mortgage. Now I live in a 100-square-foot shed in the yard and rent out my house.
articles.summary: After a tech layoff, Lauren Patton couldn't afford her mortgage. So she built a tiny home and lives there while renting the main home on Airbnb.
articles._body: Lauren Patton moved out of her home and into a tiny home in her backyard. Courtesy of Lauren Patton Lauren Patton was confident that her well-paying job provided enough security to buy a home on her own. After she was laid off from her tech job, she eventually couldn't afford her mortgage. To make ends meet, she built a tiny home in her backyard and is renting out rooms in her main home. This as-told-to essay is based on a conversation with Lauren Patton, 36, who built a tiny home in her Texas backyard. The conversation has been edited for length and clarity. After a couple of years of living in Chicago, I decided to move back to Texas and get a fresh start. This was in 2022, when the real estate market was booming, and homes in Central Texas were getting bought up quickly. I found a real estate agent on Instagram, and she helped me buy a small bungalow — two bedrooms and about 1,000 square feet — for about $400,000. I was buying alone; it was just me and my dog. I had made a very small down payment on my home and taken out a 30-year mortgage. My monthly payment was about $4,000, which was a lot at first, but I thought it was affordable given my well-paying job. At the time, I was working in tech and doing really well. I had been moving up the data science ladder, and I thought it would be a lucrative field. But I was a bit wrong about that. In early 2023, there were a bunch of tech layoffs . I found out the day after I got back from a trip to South Africa that I had been let go. I was given only two months of severance and sent on my way. I could no longer afford my mortgage For the first couple of months after I was laid off , I was OK. I took time to relax, spent time with my family, and did the things you don't get to do while you're working. Then I started looking for jobs. I wasn't super worried at first. I thought, "Hey, I was a data science manager. I'll be able to find something." But after interviewing at numerous places, nothing was happening. By then, money was tight. I had very little savings and was still paying off a lot of credit card debt. I filed for unemployment, which brought in some money, and started renting out my home on Airbnb to help cover my mortgage. To make this work, I rented a room for myself across town for about six months. But when my unemployment ran out, I had to start crashing on people's couches and driving for Lyft— basically doing whatever I could. In 2024, I reached out to a former boss and asked if I could get my previous accounting job back. I did, and while it paid much less than I was making before, it sustained me for a while. Still, I had no savings, and I had cashed out my 401(k) . I was terrified. My mortgage was just so much; I thought my home was going to go into foreclosure. I was already about 30% underwater on the home, and it had depreciated in value, so I still didn't want to sell. I was 35 and thought, "I can't keep doing this." I knew I needed to do something. That's when I came up with the idea to build a little structure in my backyard to live in. I moved out of my home and into my backyard I wasn't confident enough in my woodworking or carpentry skills, so I decided to buy a cabin-style shed kit I found out about on Instagram. I took out a loan and bought it for about $8,500. While I was building the shed , I moved back into my main house and got a roommate to help cover the mortgage. I charged about $1,200 a month for the room. It wasn't a huge portion of my mortgage payment, but it helped. Looking back, I regret buying a two-bedroom house, because there just aren't enough bedrooms to rent out. The shed is about 100 square feet, and the kit came with stackable wood slats, beams, and big windows, but it didn't include a roof or a floor. I had to build the foundation , too. I also added an outhouse with an outdoor shower and built fences and other things around the property. For the construction, I relied on YouTube and ChatGPT — though ChatGPT definitely led me astray on a few things, especially the roofing. Patton built her shed-like tiny home on her own without formal training. Courtesy of Lauren Patton I officially finished the build in March 2025, though I've been making adjustments ever since — it's never-ending. Since moving into the shed, I've been renting out my main home full-time on Airbnb and have hosted hundreds of guests. I let Airbnb handle the pricing. On a typical weekend night, I charge around $200; on a weekday during the school year, it's closer to $125. October is especially lucrative because of the Austin City Limits music festival. This October, my home had about 96% occupancy, and my gross earnings were about $6,516.70. That's not normal — occupancy and nightly rates were higher — but Airbnb deducted $619 in service fees. I also had the home cleaned seven times for about $100 each time. I put some of the money I earned toward my mortgage and bills for the shed — my total electric bill, including the shed and the house, is $550, which also includes other utilities. But overall, Airbnb doesn't cover my full mortgage, which increased by $400 a month this year because of home insurance. Living in the shed has been difficult It was tough at first, downsizing to a tiny home . Emotionally, it felt like I was regressing in life, and physically, it felt really claustrophobic. But I don't mind it as much now. I'm doing better mentally. I have most of what I need in a normal house — a TV, a desk, and a bed. But I have a tiny, itty-bitty fridge, and I don't have ice or running water, so I have to stock up on jugs of water. I've had to learn a lot about how to live in the space . When I first moved in, I had a portable air conditioner, and the humidity would reach 80%. I'd wake up soaking wet and think, "What's going on?" I'd never had to consider something like that before. Now, I run a dehumidifier 24 hours a day. The hardest part is remembering to keep everything I need on hand, because there's always one thing mis

articles.title: NCAA gameday discussion: UConn’s Jovana Popovic and  South Carolina’s Jerzy Robinson are two freshmen more than ready for college basketball
articles.summary: On Thursday, No. 2 UConn exited Ann Arbor with a rare early-season loss, felled by a strong closing kick from the No. 5 Wolverines. As both head coach Geno Auriemma and Sarah Strong emphasized after the game, the Huskies were unprepared to match the urgency or execution of the Wolverines. However, t
articles._body: Jerzy Robinson sinks a jumper for South Carolina. | Getty Images On Thursday, No. 2 UConn exited Ann Arbor with a rare early-season loss , felled by a strong closing kick from the No. 5 Wolverines. As both head coach Geno Auriemma and Sarah Strong emphasized after the game, the Huskies were unprepared to match the urgency or execution of the Wolverines. However, their lament did not apply to Jovana Popovic. With foul trouble sidelining Strong, the Serbian freshman guard emerged as the best player for the Huskies, playing with a control and confidence earned through her professional experience in her home country. Popovic’s able to get her shot off with ease, and it’s automatic. She also can accelerate off the dribble for finishes at the rim, and that same quickness allows her to be disruptive defensively. It’s only 2 games, but 36.4% of Jovana Popović’s offensive touches have resulted in self-created looks (PNR Ball Handler & Isolations). Given her 25.2% usage, this is a trend worth monitoring. May speak to UConn’s lack of a consistent secondary/tertiary shot creator… https://t.co/hb2acT4v6r — Conrado Pascual (@CP3_777) November 7, 2026 In just her second official college game, and one against a top-five team, she posted a stat line many talented players never will achieve in their careers, scoring 25 points, going 3-for-5 from 3, grabbing seven rebounds, dishing four assists and collecting three steals. The five turnovers were the only red flag. At the moment, it would be difficult to believe in UConn’s usual championship upside if not for Popovic, as she and Strong have looked like the only Huskies capable of championship-caliber play. However, UConn is UConn. Auriemma will demand that all the Huskies perform up to the program’s standards when they host No. 10 Iowa on Sunday in Storrs (2 p.m. ET, FS1). And UConn, fresh off a loss, has to be one of the most feared opponents in all of college basketball. Yet, the Hawkeyes also have a fearless freshman intent upon making an instant, ceiling-raising impact in McKenna Woliczko. Remember the name 👀 Star freshman McKenna Woliczko dropped 2️⃣2️⃣ points to help No. 10 @IowaWBB get the win over Eastern Illinois 🐤 pic.twitter.com/IeWzmrApjP — Big Ten Women's Basketball (@B1Gwbball) November 6, 2026 Woliczko profiles as a plus-version of a 3-and-D player. Standing 6-foot-2, she can drain shots from deep, while also bringing a heavy dose of effort and energy that earns her extra boards and second-chance points. Albeit against overmatched opponents, Woliczko has shown her worth, especially when she busted out for a team-best 22 points, with four 3-pointers, as Iowa routed Eastern Illinois. Elsewhere on Sunday, another top-15 matchup—an all-Carolina affair pitting No. 1 South Carolina against No. 12 North Carolina (5:30 p.m. ET, ESPN)—projects to heavily feature a pair of freshmen. Jerzy with the FINISH 💪 📺: @espn pic.twitter.com/VbiJRyzney — South Carolina Women's Basketball (@GamecockWBB) November 2, 2026 It’s been just one game, but Jerzy Robinson appears to have earned the trust of head coach Dawn Staley. As top-ranked South Carolina battled No. 20 Maryland in Paris on Monday, Robinson received 24 minutes of playing time, the second-most of any Gamecock reserve. With her strong frame and physical style, she found quick comfort on the college court, scoring 15 points. It also helped that she was 2-for-3 from 3. Six rebounds, including three offensive, will also ensure she continues to earn minutes. Although long hyped as a star prospect, Robinson possesses role-playing skills that not only will get her on the court for the Gamecocks, but also contribute to winning games. That contrasts with the freshman experience slated for UNC’s Kate Harpring. . @GamecockWBB freshman Jerzy Robinson knows UNC freshman Kate Harpring very well: "That was my roommate at USA U19 so we're pretty close. But when it comes to between those lines, she knows how it gets." pic.twitter.com/3Te2JCujm2 — Matt Dowell (@MattDowellTV) November 6, 2026 Harpring and the Heels also opened their season in Paris, except they returned stateside with a loss after falling to No. 21 Oklahoma. Harpring was fully empowered as Carolina’s first option, and it was an ugly debut for the freshman guard. Of her 26 shot attempts, only nine found the bottom of the net. Her scoring aggression also translated to just two free throw attempts. While her six rebounds, five assists and two steals were an indication of her activity, she also had seven turnovers. Kate Harpring highlights vs Oklahoma Rough game for the freshman. pic.twitter.com/YDL8dMkJGP — Kevin (@KEV1NS_LIFE) November 2, 2026 In Paris, Harpring was far from the only Heel who struggled, as the team combined to shoot 34 percent from the field, 28 percent from 3 and 59 percent from the free throw line. Sunday could be another rough one for UNC. The full-fledged Harpring Show is unlikely to succeed against South Carolina’s defense. (Although, the same would have been said about Addi Mack. ) Eventually, Harpring will be more efficient, and when all her scoring aggression comes with that efficiency, it will open up opportunities for her to use her on-ball gravity to set up scoring opportunities for her teammates. Harpring’s all-round effort also guarantees that, in those games where her shot doesn’t fall, she can still make a positive impact. A stretch of softer opponents after this Carolina showdown should also help Harpring find her rhythm. In the comments, share your early impressions of Harpring, Robinson, Woliczko and Popovic. Who has been the most impressive? Who do you expect to make the biggest difference on Sunday, and who will end up having the most impactful season? And who are the other first years that have caught your eye during the season’s opening week?

articles.title: 2026 WNBA season review: After another disappointing year, the Los Angeles Sparks are defined by uncertainty—unless one thing happens
articles.summary: When a season’s biggest highlights are the celebrations of two franchise legends, one retiring and one receiving a statute, that’s a sign it wasn’t a great season. Nneka Ogwumike, certainly, deserved all the flowers and more she received during her final WNBA season. Lisa Leslie’s statue, likewise,
articles._body: Dearica Hamby, Ariel Atkins and Cameron Brink. | NBAE via Getty Images When a season’s biggest highlights are the celebrations of two franchise legends , one retiring and one receiving a statute, that’s a sign it wasn’t a great season. Nneka Ogwumike, certainly, deserved all the flowers and more she received during her final WNBA season. Lisa Leslie’s statue, likewise, was a long overdue honor for the women’s basketball icon. Yet, that the past took priority over the present was an indictment of the state of the Los Angeles Sparks. Desperate to break a playoff drought that now has extended to six seasons, Los Angeles was aggressive ahead of the 2026 season, with Ogwumike’s return to LA exemplifying the Sparks’ pivot towards a more veteran, experienced squad suited for playoff basketball. LA, instead, was unimpressively mediocre, so much so that the organization agreed to ship out Kelsey Plum , the superstar lured to Los Angeles before the 2025 season with playoff ambitions in mind, at midseason, the most substantial step towards the franchise admitting it had erred in their attempt to accelerate their postseason return. Before Plum was sent to the Phoenix Mercury, general manager Raegan Pebley was ousted, while head coach Lynne Roberts was dismissed after the season . But, it’s still too early to proclaim that the Sparks are ready to enter a new era. New general manager Ariana Andonian has resisted to committing to a clear plan, emphasizing the desire for “sustained success” in an introductory press conference that provided little substance about her vision for the Sparks. Her hesitancy, however, is understandable. After initial reporting suggested that Sparks owner Mark Walter, under federal investigation for financial fraud, intended to retain the WNBA team within his portfolio of pro sports teams, more recent reports have emerged that indicate Walter is looking to offload the team for $700 million , with the team’s now-in-construction state-of-the-art practice facility included in the price tag. As an owner has final say over the direction of a franchise, the immediate future of the Sparks will remain uncertain until the ownership situation is settled. So after a season to forget, the Sparks await an offseason that could inaugurate a new era of LA basketball, one that, finally, restores one of the WNBA’s flagship franchises to relevance, or they could continue to muddle through mediocrity. Let’s begin to take a look at the developments that will help determine LA’s direction. In the comments, share your analysis of the state of things in Southern California, from the takeaways from the 2026 season to how they must prepare for 2027. If the Sparks improbably get the No. 1 pick, it would solve ALL their issues Did LA get good value in exchange for Kelsey Plum? We’ll find out on Nov. 15. While the process behind the trade—recognizing that, in an underachieving season, trading Plum, an impending unrestricted free agent, for any value was better that watching her walk in the offseason for nothing—was right, it is the result that really matters. While Monique Akoa Makani is a nice player, it’s the first-round draft pick, in combination with the LA’s own first rounder, that could provide needed clarity for the Sparks. Combining the Mercury’s odd with their own, the Sparks have a 36 percent chance of winning the 2027 WNBA Draft Lottery on Sunday, with a blessing from the basketball gods presumably resulting in USC superstar and LA native JuJu Watkins ending up in purple and gold in April. That outcome would solve all the Sparks’ issues, as the organization not only would be oriented around optimizing JuJu, both in terms of her on-court talent and off-court appeal, but the prospect of Watkins in LA may inspire bids to buy the franchise from Walter, in addition to encouraging more interest in the still-vacant head coaching job. But, all that is probably too good to be true, as Los Angeles’ 36 percent chance of winning the top pick is the lowest among the six lottery teams. (Rather than praying to the basketball gods, the Sparks might be better off hoping that outgoing Commissioner Cathy Engelbert, desiring to burnish her reputation as the leader who elevated the business of the WNBA, puts in a call and makes sure JuJu stays in LA.) JuJu being JuJu 🤷‍♀️ pic.twitter.com/Yy3fMnWZ0Y — USC Women's Basketball (@USCWBB) November 4, 2026 Even if, as is most likely, the Sparks end up with picks No. 6 and No. 7 in the 2027 WNBA Draft, they will at least add two young, talented players, such as LSU’s MiLaysia Fulwiley, Kentucky’s Clara Strack or South Carolina’s Tessa Johnson. In contrast to Watkins, they would be pieces in the build, not THE build. So, let’s say the Sparks do not get all the luck, leaving them with two lower lotto picks. What do you think they should do? What prospects would look good in purple and gold? Or, should they package one, or both, of the picks in a trade, again rejecting a slower rebuild by taking a chance on another star? How will LA’s new leadership evaluate the current roster? Sparks fans, unfortunately, can imagine too many alternative timelines, from one where Rickea Jackson is still a Spark to one where Dominique Malonga is dunking in crypto.com Arena to one where Angel Reese is the LA Barbie to another one where the lottery balls brought Paige Bueckers to SoCal. Instead, the Sparks are a mismatched group of players at different stages of the career. All of Dearica Hamby, Ariel Atkins and Erica Wheeler are 30 years old or older and signed for the 2027 season, with both Hamby and Atkins on contracts exceeding $1 million. Hamby’s numbers were down in 2026, primarily due to a decrease in minutes and usage. Regardless of other roster decisions, Hamby makes some sense as a keeper, as she’s a good leader who is productive and plays hard. However, if a team looking for a solid big offers value for Hamby, the Sparks should probably jump on the deal, as there has to be

articles.title: Interview: Former Georgia Tech standout and Atlanta Dream contributor Lorela Cubaj stills loves the ATL
articles.summary: Lorela Cubaj, a 6-foot-4 big, born in Italy to Balkan parents, is name familiar to women’s hoops fans. And for good reason. Over her five seasons at Georgia Tech (2017-22), she was a two-time winner of three major honors: All-ACC, ACC All-Defensive and ACC Defensive Player. Those accolades and more
articles._body: Lorela Cubaj. | NBAE via Getty Images Lorela Cubaj, a 6-foot-4 big, born in Italy to Balkan parents, is name familiar to women’s hoops fans. And for good reason. Over her five seasons at Georgia Tech (2017-22), she was a two-time winner of three major honors: All-ACC, ACC All-Defensive and ACC Defensive Player. Those accolades and more made her a second-round pick in the 2022, draft No. 18 overall by the Seattle Storm. While she would never play in Seattle, she did see WNBA action with the New York Liberty and Atlanta Dream, playing 11 games for New York in 2022 and 31 games for Atlanta across the 2023 and 2024 seasons. Since then, she’s made Europe her permanent hooping home, playing for the Italian club Umana Reyer Venezia, in addition to the Italian national team. She’s been a dominant figure on the international stage, known for her defensive play and passing ability. Swish Appeal talked to her about developing court vision, Albanian culture and why Atlanta is her home away from home. On choosing Georgia Tech over other college offers: For me, Georgia Tech was a no-brainer because I also had the luck to share my college experience with other Italians, you know, like I was with Francesca Pan for three years and then with Antonia Peresson for one year. She was my senior. I was very lucky to have them. So, it was kind of like a good transition because the school was amazing. The ACC is an amazing conference to play in, very tough. [Georgia Tech’s] location is perfect because it’s Atlanta and it’s in the city. I’m used to [living in] the city, so for me going to a college town would have been probably harder. It’s not too cold, it’s not too hot; it’s just on the east coast. Those are the factors that actually made me choose Georgia Tech, but yeah, I definitely had other options and I remember one of them was Oregon. But at the end of the day, it was too far. View this post on Instagram On returning to Atlanta and playing for the Dream: I loved it because Atlanta is my second home and I was close to the people that, after my family, I love the most. I have very strong bonds and good relationships with the people that are in Georgia Tech. I feel like that was a full-circle moment; okay, I played here as a college player and now as a pro player I’m able to come back and be in the same place. [The move] just made sense and I loved it. I love Atlanta. That’s my third home as we said before. I’m forever grateful for the opportunity and I hope that in the future I will be able to come back. View this post on Instagram A special thank you to Stefano Luigini of Luigini Development for arranging the interview.

articles.title: No. 10 Iowa opened the season with two dominant wins, and now a date with No. 2 UConn awaits
articles.summary: No. 10-ranked Iowa finished their opening week with an expected, with a lopsided 80-39 win over Eastern Illinois. On Monday, they dominated Towson 73-45 in their season opener. At first, Iowa looked lethargic. They needed time to get their feet wet, as they were still trying to get a feel for the ga
articles._body: McKenna Woliczko. | Getty Images No. 10-ranked Iowa finished their opening week with an expected, with a lopsided 80-39 win over Eastern Illinois. On Monday, they dominated Towson 73-45 in their season opener. At first, Iowa looked lethargic. They needed time to get their feet wet, as they were still trying to get a feel for the game. It turned into a low-scoring first quarter, with the Hawkeyes scratching the surface with a 17-10 lead. However, the dam burst in the 2nd quarter. They obliterated Eastern Illinois 27-8, and it was only up from there. It couldn’t have come on a better day, as Iowa’s next opponent, No. 2 UConn, was upset by No. 5 Michigan, 77-66. The Hawkeyes will face the Huskies on Sunday on the road (2 p.m. ET, FS1), and they’ll try to use this moment to their advantage, however insurmountable it may seem in theory. Hawks WIN 👏 pic.twitter.com/5yqOzl6S3W — Iowa Women's Basketball (@IowaWBB) November 6, 2026 In the end, the Hawkeyes got the best out of all their top players. McKenna Woliczko The 6-foot-2 freshman forward from California led the way with 22 points, shooting 9-for-12 from the field. While the Hawkeyes only shot 9-for-28 from the 3-point line, Woliczko was as consistent as she could be, going 4-for-6. After the game, head coach Jan Jensen celebrated Woliczko’s continued pursuit of wanting to master the game, saying: McKenna is a really good student of the game. I really love the progression. I love how she attacks it and lets that game come to her. Have a night, McKenna 😤 22 PTS, 4-6 3FG @McKennaDub x #Hawkeyes pic.twitter.com/EZnmVQnGbJ — Iowa Women's Basketball (@IowaWBB) November 6, 2026 Ava Heiden The junior center held it down in the paint with 15 points, while also leading the the way with eight rebounds. Dani Carnegie The transfer guard from Georgia came away with 12 points and grabbed seven rebounds. Chit Chat Wright Wright was a playmaker who finished with seven points and dished out four assists. Wide open Wright 👋 @ChazadiW x #Hawkeyes pic.twitter.com/04G3y6sKm6 — Iowa Women's Basketball (@IowaWBB) November 6, 2026 Jocelyn Faison The sophomore guard came away with six points and four rebounds. Taylor Stremlow The gritty junior guard was just that at both ends of the floor. Stremlow finished with five points, three assists and two rebounds. https://t.co/5q41Ym87Yx pic.twitter.com/p6n5tDBU8P — Iowa Women's Basketball (@IowaWBB) November 6, 2026 Now, Iowa can set their sights on playing the Huskies before one of the most energetic crowds in all of sports. Jensen is looking forward to the challenge, asserting: No matter the margin of victory, it’s one game. It’s all about how we use it. We’re going to go out there and make it a fun game.

articles.title: Competing in EuroLeague Women and EuroCup Women, these three players should get another look from WNBA teams in 2027
articles.summary: A little over a year ago, Sydney Taylor had just scored 55 points across two games, making nine 3-pointers, earning 16 free throws and shooting almost 45 percent from the field. Surely, such a scoring showcase was grabbing women’s hoops headlines? Nope, playing for the Polish club MB Zagłębie Sosnow
articles._body: Sydney Taylor. | NurPhoto via Getty Images A little over a year ago, Sydney Taylor had just scored 55 points across two games, making nine 3-pointers, earning 16 free throws and shooting almost 45 percent from the field. Surely, such a scoring showcase was grabbing women’s hoops headlines? Nope, playing for the Polish club MB Zagłębie Sosnowiec and competing in EuroCup Women, Taylor’s offensive earthquakes did not register among the majority of US-based fans. Neither did her 35-point showing on almost 60 percent shooting in mid-December, nor her 38-point outburst in January, where she shot almost 80 percent on 2-pointers and earned 17 free throws. Instead, it would be about six more months until Sydney Taylor’s name became widely known stateside. Signed by the Chicago Sky ahead of training camp, Taylor dropped 27 points in her fifth-career WNBA game, and as our Zachary Draves recently documented , the performance proved to be just a preview for what would become a stellar rookie season, when Taylor would emerge as a fan favorite and All-Rookie selection in an otherwise too-familiar underwhelming Sky season . From Undrafted to @chicagosky Starter Sydney Taylor has one of the best stories in the #WNBA . In this exclusive interview with @micahya_c , Sydney Taylor gives some insight into her journey and motivation. Preview below. Full Article here: https://t.co/a4EVpTZftx pic.twitter.com/z3YCTjN5Gf — MTMV Sports Network (@MTMVSN) July 20, 2026 Taylor will not be going back to Poland this offseason. Instead, she’ll be in Miami, joining Lunar Owls for Season 3 of Unrivaled. However, Taylor’s ascendance reminds that in Poland or other European locales, there are women’s basketball talents who, quietly plying their trades, could soon prove that they too belong in the WNBA. Taylor is their avatar, although she was far from the only WNBA player who, given a fair shot in the league, proved their worth in 2026. Natasha Cloud sitting there looking like a proud Vet 🤩 From Poland to the W, Sydney Taylor expressed what it meant for her to knock down the game-winner against the Aces 🙌 pic.twitter.com/f8fo2cDgEd — espnW (@espnW) August 1, 2026 There was Pauline Astier, a key player for traditional EuroLeague Women power ZVVZ USK Praha who became the starting point guard for the New York Liberty. Two experienced EuroLeaguers in Valériane Ayayi and María Conde made their long-awaited WNBA return and debut, respectively, contributing to the Phoenix Mercury and Toronto Tempo. Laura Juskaite, who also emerged as a key piece for Toronto, had suited up for a number of EuroCup or EuroLeague clubs since 2019. The same is true of Antonio Delaere, who served as bench piece for the Minnesota Lynx. Expect more WNBA teams than ever to look for hidden gems who are hooping overseas. That the Golden State Valkyries, a team that prioritized depth, and built that depth with players who had been underrated or overlooked, are champions should only further encourage other organizations to invest more intentionally in identifying players, whether in the EuroLeague, the EuroCup or European domestic leagues, who could be key contributors, or even more, in the WNBA. Through four weeks of play in both the EuroLeague and EuroCup competitions, who are some players that should be attracting a closer look? Although far from the only candidates, these three players, two of whom have gotten a sliver of a chance in the WNBA, are thus far making convincing cases. Shyanne Sellers (UMCS Lublin) A top prospect in 2025 WNBA Draft, Shyanne Sellers’ spot in the league seemed in little doubt. Yet, she fell to the No. 17 overall pick before being surprisingly cut by the Valkyries. She then could not convert a training camp opportunity with the Atlanta Dream into a roster spot. Ahead of the 2026 season, a training camp stint with the Dallas Wings also ended with a waiver.
